## Seed 36 (0x0007291B): root cause found for the sub_000371A6 crash -- fifth missing-function bug, same masking mechanism as Seed 35

Picking the `sub_000371A6` crash back up: rather than continuing to trace
which of `sub_00045C06`'s two calls faulted from the C source alone, the
`.dmp`'s own `[SCDA-ICALL-RING]` dump (crash-time ring buffer, see
`recomp_manual.c`) had the answer sitting right there as its *last*
recorded entry, one icall-failure frame before the crash:

```
[SCDA-ICALL-RING] #4 source=0x0045C0F3 target=0x0007291B ecx=0x0062CA18 esi=0x005B0910 eax=0x0045C0F3
```

`source=0x0045C0F3` lands inside `sub_00045C06` (native offset +0xED) --
an indirect call in that same function that failed to resolve, one step
*before* the `sub_000371A6` call that actually crashed. `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`'s
failure path reset `g_esp` and skipped the call outright, so whatever
`target=0x0007291B` was supposed to compute/return was left uninitialized;
`sub_00045C06` then fell through into its next statement -- a call into
`sub_000371A6` -- using that same uninitialized value as `ecx`, the base
pointer for the word-at-a-time wide-string walk. `sub_000371A6` walked off
into unmapped memory (`rax=0x10000`, i.e. 32768 words scanned with no
terminator ever found) and faulted. This resolved the open question from
the previous entry: it's not that a *string constant* was wrong, it's that
the call which was supposed to produce/validate the string pointer never
ran at all.

`functions.json`/`xrefs.json` cross-reference on `target=0x0007291B`
reproduced the exact Seed 35 pattern, but for an unresolved plain-jump
thunk (the Seed 33/34 shape) instead of a destructor body:

- **Xref**: `{'from': '0x0007292F', 'to': '0x0007291B', 'type': 'data_imm'}`
  -- an immediate operand of `mov dword ptr [0x5B6038], 0x7291B` inside
  `sub_0007292A`, storing this address into a callback/vtable slot. Never
  a jump/call edge, so the disassembler's normal function-start heuristics
  never looked at it.
- **Gap**: exactly 5 bytes, between `sub_000728D6` (ends precisely at
  `0x0007291B`) and the next detected function `sub_00072920` -- too small
  for any heuristic to have carved out its own function.
- **Real bytes** (`img.read_bytes_at_va` + capstone, confirmed directly
  against the XBE): `e9 0d f4 fd ff` = `jmp 0x00051D2D`, a plain
  unconditional tail-jump to the already-detected, widely-used routine
  `sub_00051D2D` (30 legitimate callers elsewhere per `functions.json`) --
  unambiguously a missing 5-byte thunk, not a data table entry.

Added as Seed 36 in `projects/scda/function_seeds.json`. Regenerated
disassembly (`tools/disasm/output/scda_seeded36_icallthunk`, standard
seeded command): **28,419 functions (up from 28,418)**, with
`sub_0007291B` now a clean 5-byte, 1-instruction function. Regenerated C
(`tools/recomp/output/scda_seeded36_icallthunk`, standard `--all --split
1000` command): **28,419/28,419 translated, 0 failures**. Updated
`SCDA_GEN_DIR` in `projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` and rebuilt
(`scda_recomp.exe`, RelWithDebInfo) -- build succeeded cleanly.

Note for next session: the build+configure step needed the VS-bundled
CMake explicitly (`"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual
Studio\2022\Community\Common7\IDE\CommonExtensions\Microsoft\CMake\CMake\bin\cmake.exe"`)
instead of whatever `cmake` resolves to on `PATH` -- a plain `cmake
--build build/scda ...` hit `CMake Error ... No preprocessor test for

## 2026-09-01, continued: self-correction -- Seed 36 was real but NOT the cause of the sub_000371A6 crash; the soak-test build hit the *same* crash again, now root-caused to a garbage array element in sub_00045AFE

The Seed 36 soak-test build crashed again after ~14 minutes, in the exact
same place (`sub_000371A6`, same fault instruction, same garbage value
`esi=0xB6DFFCC5` -- byte-for-byte identical to the pre-Seed-36 crash).
Re-checking the evidence that had linked Seed 36 to this crash: the
`[SCDA-ICALL-RING]`'s `source=0x0045C0F3` entry does **not** actually fall
inside `sub_00045C06` (`0x00045C06`-`0x00045CC6`, size 0xC0) -- `0x0045C0F3`
is far outside that range. That attribution was a mistake (an address
mis-read under compaction pressure); Seed 36 fixes a real, independently
byte-verified bug (`jmp sub_00051D2D` reachable only via vtable data), but
it was never related to this crash. Flagging this plainly rather than
letting a wrong causal claim stand -- Seed 36 stays in the seed list
because it is still correct and necessary, it just doesn't explain this
symptom.

Re-verified the crash properly this time using the session's own
established (and, in hindsight, skipped-too-fast) technique: disassembling
backward from the actual return address on the stack to find the
`mov ecx, GUEST_PCu; call scda_trace_pc` pattern, rather than trusting `kb`
symbol names directly. This **did** confirm the stack trace was right
after all (return address decodes to guest PC `0x00045C1C`, exactly
`sub_00045C06`'s first call site into `sub_000371A6`) -- so the call chain
`sub_00045AFE -> sub_00045C06 -> sub_000371A6` is correct, just not via
Seed 36's icall.

Traced one level further up, into `sub_00045AFE` itself (264 bytes, reads
an object at `edi` = its own `ecx` "this" parameter): it computes a
per-iteration array-element pointer `esi = MEM32(edi+0x20) + MEM32(ebp+0x10)`
(array base + index*stride), reads `ebx = MEM32(esi+4)` as a "is this slot
populated" flag, and -- only when that flag is non-zero -- dereferences
`ecx = MEM32(esi)` to get a value it eventually threads down through
`sub_000459CA`, a second `MEM32(esi)` dereference (`esi = MEM32(esi)` at
`loc_00045B76`, taken when a *different*, later-reused `ebx` test is
non-zero), and finally passes the result as `sub_00045C06`'s own `esi`
argument -- which becomes `sub_000371A6`'s corrupt string-source pointer.
Two candidate dereferences (`MEM32(esi)` at `0x00045B49`/`0x00045B76`) can
each independently be the point where a garbage array element first
becomes a garbage pointer.

Added `[SCDA-STRARG]` diagnostics (`recomp_manual.c`, new
`strcmp_arg_reports` counter) at `0x00045B49`, `0x00045B4D`, `0x00045B6D`,
`0x00045B76`, and `0x00045B7C` to log `esi`/`ecx`/`MEM32(esi)` at each
branch point in this chain, gated the same way as prior diagnostics
(capped counters, always-on). Rebuilt successfully; a fresh live run is
now capturing this chain in `scda_runtime.log` for the next crash.
**Not yet root-caused to the underlying array/element bug** -- next step
is reading the `[SCDA-STRARG]` trace lines leading up to the next crash to
see which dereference first turns up `0xB6DFFCC5` (or a value that leads
to it), then tracing that array (`edi+0x20`, `edi`'s own construction)

## 2026-09-01, continued: exact mechanism isolated -- one array slot holds leftover garbage while every sibling slot is properly zero

The diagnostic build crashed again (same spot, same value) after ~16
minutes, and this time `[SCDA-STRARG]` had the answer. The loop in
`sub_00045AFE` walks a 24-byte-stride array at `edi+0x20` (`edi` is a
stable object, guest address `0x0119B110` in every one of the three
crashes captured so far -- a persistent/long-lived object, not a
transient temporary). Seven consecutive elements immediately before the
crashing one all show the expected, healthy "empty slot" pattern:

```
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FF69 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FF81 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FF99 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FFB1 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FFC9 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B4D elem-field-zero esi=0x0000FFE1 ...
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B49 elem-field-nonzero esi=0x0000FFF9 ecx=MEM32(esi)=0x00000000 ...
```
(stride confirmed exactly 0x18 = 24 bytes between consecutive elements)
then the very next element:
```
[SCDA-STRARG] pc=0x00045B49 elem-field-nonzero esi=0x00010011 ecx=MEM32(esi)=0xB6DFFCC5 ...
```

`MEM32(esi+4)` (the "is this slot populated" flag) is non-zero -- garbage,
not a real Xbox pointer -- so the code trusts `MEM32(esi)` as valid data
too, and the resulting `0xB6DFFCC5` gets threaded down through
`sub_00045B76`'s second dereference unchanged, into `sub_00045C06`'s
`esi` argument, into `sub_000371A6`'s string-source pointer, and crashes.
This rules out a stray-write/use-after-free-elsewhere theory (the six
preceding, older-allocated slots are clean) and points at a narrower
"this one slot's memory was never zeroed when the array grew into it"
bug: either a missing/skipped zero-fill in the array's own growth code
(consistent with this session's disassembly-gap pattern, if that
zero-fill routine turns out to be another unresolved stub), or a genuine
reliance on the host allocator zero-filling memory that Windows'
`HeapAlloc`/`malloc` doesn't guarantee the way the game's own
free-list/small-block allocator (already touched this session, the
`sub_00077xxx` family) may assume.

**Next step**: `sub_00045AFE` has no static callers (`functions.json`
`called_by: []` -- reached only via vtable dispatch, matching this
session's recurring pattern), so its "this" object's class and the
function that grows the `edi+0x20` array cannot be found by static
xref alone. Needs either a live CDB session watching writes to the
specific slot address (`0x00010011`, or wherever the next crash's
offending slot lands) to catch the exact write (or non-write) that leaves
it dirty, or tracing forward from the object's construction (find what
sets up `edi+0x20` with initial capacity) to check whether the growth
path calls a zero-fill helper at all. This is a good stopping point for
the session -- three real crashes investigated, one confirmed-correct fix
(Seed 36) landed, and this fourth issue is now precisely characterized
down to the exact byte pattern and slot, ready for the next session to
pick up directly at "find what writes/should-write element index
`(0x10011-0xFF69)/0x18 = 7` slots past the loop's start."

## 2026-09-01, continued: live CDB hardware watchpoint attempt -- inconclusive, methodology issue found and flagged (not a result to trust)

Tried a live CDB write-watchpoint (`ba w1`) on the offending guest address
(`0x00010011`, host `0x00020011` given `g_xbox_mem_offset=0x10000`,
confirmed live and consistent with `xbox_memory_layout.c`'s
`g_memory_offset = g_memory_base - XBOX_MAP_START(0)`) to catch whatever
writes -- or fails to write -- that memory before the array is read. Two
separate runs (armed at `xbe_entry_point`, then armed at the very first
process breakpoint before any guest code at all) both ran to the same
crash with **zero recorded hits** on the watchpoint (`kb`/`r` after every
`g` only ever showed the same access-violation exception being re-caught,
never a genuine "Breakpoint hit" from the data breakpoint).

Before trusting that as "proof the memory is never written," ran a sanity
check: armed the identical technique on `g_esp` (written on essentially
every recompiled instruction, so a hit should be near-instant if the
technique works at all in this target). The result landed inside
`ntdll!NtWriteFile+0x14` -- not a plausible place for a write to a
recompiled-code global -- indicating either a symbol-resolution/thread
context issue at the very early point the breakpoint was armed, or a
genuine multi-threaded hardware-breakpoint propagation gap (the
recompiled guest code runs on a thread created via
`bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx`, and Windows debug registers are
per-thread; a `ba` set before that thread exists is not guaranteed to be
correctly reprogrammed onto it depending on timing/symbol state).

**Conclusion: this specific watchpoint experiment does not support any
conclusion, positive or negative, about whether the array slot is ever
written.** Do not cite the earlier "zero hits" result as evidence in
future work -- it is exactly the kind of unverified claim this project
avoids stating as fact. The reliable evidence remains the
`[SCDA-STRARG]` runtime diagnostics from the previous entry (fired from
inside the actual instrumented recompiled code, not fragile external
tooling), which conclusively show the exact slot and exact garbage value.
A trustworthy live watch, if attempted again, would need the breakpoint
armed only after `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx`'s new thread is
confirmed running (e.g. break on `bridge_run_recompiled_thread` itself,
which is on the correct thread already, then `ba` from there), or use
`~*` to apply the breakpoint across all existing and subsequently
enumerated threads.

Given the diminishing returns from further live-debugger attempts this
session, stopping here. Precise finding to hand off unchanged from the
previous entry: element index 7 (guest `0x00010011`) in the 24-byte-stride
array at `edi(0x0119B110)+0x20` holds `0xB6DFFCC5` while all six preceding
elements are cleanly zero; the owning class/constructor is still unknown
(no static callers for `sub_00045AFE`).

## 2026-09-01, continued: corrected watchpoint (armed on the actual guest-execution thread) still shows zero hits -- and this finally explains why, via a major architectural finding: 26-bit-address-bus RAM mirroring

Re-armed the write watchpoint properly this time: broke on
`scda_recomp!bridge_run_recompiled_thread` first (confirmed via `~` that
this is a distinct thread from the debugger's initial break thread), set
`ba w1 0x20011` only after landing on that thread, then ran to the crash.
**Still zero hits** -- but this time the negative result is trustworthy
(armed on the correct thread, verified), which is a real and legitimate
puzzle: if nothing writes to this exact host virtual address, how is it
non-zero?

The answer is in `src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`, which this
investigation hadn't needed to read closely before now: **the guest RAM
arena is not a single flat `VirtualAlloc` region.** It is a
`CreateFileMappingA` (page-file backed) with the *base* view mapped once
at `g_memory_base`, plus **28 additional `MapViewOfFileEx` "mirror"
views** (`XBOX_NUM_MIRRORS = 28`, `xbox_memory_layout.h:169`) at
`g_memory_base + (m+1)*64MB` intervals, all aliasing the *same physical
pages* -- explicitly modeling the real Xbox's 26-bit memory-controller
address bus, where address `0x04000448` and `0x00000448` are the same
physical byte. `templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`'s `XBOX_PTR` macro
(`(uintptr_t)(uint32_t)(addr) + g_xbox_mem_offset`) does no masking --
by design, it doesn't need to: a guest address in the `0x04000000`+ range
lands, via plain pointer addition, exactly inside the correct pre-mapped
mirror view, which is *itself* a distinct host virtual address backed by
the same physical page as the base view.

This means a write to this exact physical byte through any wrapped guest
address (e.g. `0x04010011`, `0x08010011`, ... -- anything of the form
`N*0x04000000 + 0x10011`) is *completely invisible* to a hardware
breakpoint watching only the base view's address (`0x20011`) -- x86 debug
registers watch virtual addresses, not physical pages, and this project's
own mirroring design deliberately creates 28 additional distinct virtual
addresses backing the same byte. With only 4 hardware breakpoint slots
available and 28 mirrors, exhaustively watching every alias isn't
practical.

**This substantially reframes the bug.** It is very unlikely to be
"missing zero-fill on array growth" -- the data most likely got there
through a completely legitimate write, just via a different guest address
than the one later used to read it back as this array's element. Two
live possibilities going forward:
1. The array's element/base-pointer computation in `sub_00045AFE`
   (`MEM32(edi+0x20) + MEM32(ebp+0x10)`) is itself wrong -- an indexing,
   stride, or base-pointer bug (recompiler mistranslation or an
   uninitialized/stale `edi+0x20` field) that lands on physical memory
   legitimately owned by something else entirely (consistent with the
   original observation, several entries back, that `0xB6DFFCC5` has the
   bit pattern of a small negative float -- plausibly leftover
   audio/vector data from an unrelated subsystem, not this array at all).
2. A genuine cross-mirror aliasing bug: some code writes the "same"
   logical address through a wrapped/high guest address while other code
   reads it through the low/base address, and on real hardware both
   would transparently be the same physical byte (fine), but if the
   *write* and the *read* disagree about which address range this
   particular allocation is supposed to live in, it's a real bug in the
   surrounding game/recompiler logic, not in the mirroring mechanism
   itself.

**Not yet resolved.** Next concrete step: rather than chasing the write
via more hardware breakpoints (impractical with 28 mirrors), verify
option 1 first -- check what `MEM32(edi+0x20)` (the array base pointer)
and the loop's actual intended element count/bound are, and whether the
loop is reading past a legitimate "size" into reserved-but-unrelated
memory, or whether `MEM32(edi+0x20)` itself is a corrupted/uninitialized
pointer to begin with (which would make this the same disassembly-gap or
missing-zero-fill family of bug as before, just one level further back
in the object's own construction).

## 2026-09-01, continued: root cause finally localized -- g_edi (the loop's "this" pointer) gets silently corrupted mid-loop by an unrelated allocator call, confirmed live

Option 1 from the previous entry, resolved directly: added a `pc=0x00045B27`
"array-entry" diagnostic (logs `edi`, the array base `MEM32(edi+0x20)`, and
the count `MEM32(edi+0x24)` every time `sub_00045AFE` is entered) and an
`EDI CHANGED` diagnostic at the loop's own per-iteration top
(`0x00045B3C`) that only prints when `g_edi` differs from the previous
iteration's value. Two rebuild/run cycles nailed it:

- The array-entry trace fired **exactly once** in the whole ~15 minute
  run: `edi=0x00F7FD84 base(+0x20)=0x01181E40 count(+0x24)=0x0000031B(795)
  field(+0x1C)=0x5589DB0D field(+0x28)=0x0000031B`. A single call, a
  795-element array -- entirely plausible, no red flags.
- The `EDI CHANGED` trace fired exactly twice: once expected
  (`old=0x00000000 new=0x00F7FD84`, the very first iteration), and once
  **mid-loop, with no new call to `sub_00045AFE`**:
  `EDI CHANGED old=0x00F7FD84 new=0x0119B110`.

This is conclusive: `sub_00045AFE`'s own "this" object is legitimately
`0x00F7FD84` (795-element array), but partway through the loop `g_edi`
gets silently overwritten with `0x0119B110` -- a completely different
object belonging to the small-block allocator's free path (`sub_00077xxx`
family) -- and **never restored**. Every iteration from that point on
reads `MEM32(0x0119B110 + 0x20)` (a small, unrelated pointer, coincidence
range matching the `0xFFxx`-`0x10011` addresses seen throughout this
investigation) and `MEM32(0x0119B110 + 0x24)` as if they were this loop's
own array base/count, walks that *wrong* array instead, and eventually
reads uninitialized memory past its real end -- explaining every earlier
observation (the "leftover garbage" element, why it was never written by
guest code on the watched thread, why base/count looked plausible in
isolation) in one coherent mechanism.

The log context right at the corruption moment shows the small-block
allocator's free path running in between loop iterations (via
`sub_00036116`'s destructor calls inside the loop body, which route into
`sub_00077049` -> `sub_0007708F` -> ... -> the shared multi-exit epilogue
at `0x00077171`/`0x00077172`/`0x00077173` -- several of which are seeds
from earlier this session, e.g. Seed 0x0007708F's own reasoning already
describes this as "the small-block allocator free helper"). Disassembling
the real XBE bytes for this cluster (`sub_00077049` at `0x00077049`
through the shared epilogue) shows the ORIGINAL x86 prologue pushes
`ecx, edi, esi` (in that order) and the three observed epilogue exit
points correctly match: `0x00077173` (`pop edi; pop ecx; ret`, for the
2-item early exit before `esi` was pushed), `0x00077172` (`pop esi; pop
edi; pop ecx; ret`, the normal 3-item exit), and `0x00077171` (an extra
`pop ecx` first, balancing a `push eax; call sub_00076BC8` argument
cleanup on that specific path) -- all internally consistent, not an
obvious static disassembly bug.

Live trace context (`previous_pc=0x0007711C` immediately followed by
`pc=0x00077AC6`) suggested the corruption might be near the
`0x0007711C`/`0x00077AC6` boundary, but re-reading the generated C for
`sub_0007708F`/`sub_0007714C`/`sub_00077159` shows no direct control-flow
edge from `0x0007711C` to `0x00077AC6` at all -- `previous_pc` in this
diagnostic subsystem is a coarse/sparse tracker updated only at specific
gated checkpoints, not a strict immediate-predecessor link, so this
apparent adjacency is likely misleading (the same "trust disassembly over
log adjacency" lesson from earlier this session, now applied to a
different diagnostic variable). Exactly which of the ~10 fragment
functions in this shared-epilogue cluster (`sub_00077049`,
`sub_00077088`, `sub_0007708F`, `sub_0007714C`, `sub_00077159`,
`sub_00077171/72/73`, `sub_00077AC5/AC6`, and whatever calls into this
cluster from `sub_00036116`'s destructor path) actually drops or
mis-restores `edi` has **not yet been pinned to a single instruction**.

**Not yet fixed**, but the search space is now dramatically narrower:
instead of "somewhere in a 795-iteration loop calling five different
helper functions," it is specifically "somewhere in the small-block
allocator free-path call graph reached from `sub_00036116` inside this
loop." Next step for a fresh session: add per-fragment `edi`-value
diagnostics at the entry of each function in this specific cluster
(`sub_00077049`, `sub_0007708F`, `sub_00077088`, `sub_0007714C`,
`sub_00077159`, `sub_00077171`, `sub_00077172`, `sub_00077173`,
`sub_00077AC5`, `sub_00077AC6`) to bisect exactly which fragment enters
with the correct (caller's) `edi` and exits with the wrong one -- the
same bisection technique already used successfully for the `sub_00076402`
icall investigation (Seed 35) earlier this session.

This has been an extremely long session (five real bugs investigated,
three Seeds landed and verified, one general path-mapping fix landed, and
this fourth crash's root cause narrowed from "unknown" all the way down
to a specific ~10-function call cluster). Stopping here is appropriate;
the next session has a precise, actionable starting point.

## 2026-09-01, continued: cluster bisection run -- 0x0119B110 is not garbage, it's a real, frequently-recycled object; the bug is a genuine edi-preservation leak, not a disassembly gap

Added change-only `edi` logging (`[SCDA-CLUSTER]`) at the entry of every
fragment in the suspect cluster (`sub_00036116`, `sub_00077049`,
`sub_0007708F`, `sub_00077088`, `sub_0007714C`, `sub_00077159`,
`sub_00077171/72/73`, `sub_00077AC5/AC6`). Result: **5,689 transitions
over the full run**, with `edi` cycling through a huge variety of
real-looking object addresses (`0x01181xxx` range, `0x00650128`, etc.) --
confirming `sub_00036116` is a generic, heavily-reused
destructor/free-object call, exactly as suspected, not specific to our
loop at all.

Critically: `edi=0x0119B110` (the value that ends up corrupting
`sub_00045AFE`'s loop) **first appears in this trace at log line 26204 --
long before our loop's own corruption event (~line 28979) and long before
`sub_00045AFE` is even entered (its own array-entry log was at line
28536)**. This rules out "garbage/uninitialized value" entirely:
`0x0119B110` is a real, legitimate, frequently-recycled object that
`sub_00036116` destructs/frees repeatedly throughout ordinary gameplay,
well before our loop ever runs.

This refines the bug to its true shape: `sub_00045AFE`'s loop calls
`sub_00036116` several times per iteration for its own local temporary
cleanup (`ecx = ebp + -0x1C/-0x28/-0x40/-0x10`, four separate calls in the
loop body). Somewhere inside `sub_00036116`'s own call graph -- likely
while it is *also* processing an unrelated pending free/destruct for the
`0x0119B110` object (a free-list or deferred-delete mechanism, given how
often that address recurs independently) -- `g_edi` gets set to
`0x0119B110` for that nested work and is **not restored** to the caller's
original value (`0x00F7FD84`, our loop's own object) before returning.
This is a genuine register-preservation bug in the recompiled code, not
missing translation coverage: every function in the cluster was already a
real seed/detected function with internally consistent push/pop counts
per the earlier disassembly check, so the defect is more likely a subtle
mismatch between which exit path is taken and which registers that
specific path is entitled to trash -- something only a true single-step
trace through the actual corrupting call will pin down.

**Assessment: further progress on this specific bug needs interactive,
single-instruction-level CDB stepping** (breakpoint at the loop's own
`sub_00036116` call site inside `sub_00045AFE`, then `p`/`t` stepping
through the nested call graph watching `edi` change in real time) rather
than more static log/disassembly analysis -- the log-based bisection has
now definitively localized *what* happens and roughly *where* (inside one
of `sub_00045AFE`'s four `sub_00036116` calls per iteration), but not the
exact instruction, and static disassembly of the cluster's push/pop
structure did not reveal an obvious defect. This is a natural, well-
justified stopping point for this extremely long session: the crash's
mechanism is now fully understood in principle (a real object's pointer
leaking through an unrestored register during unrelated cleanup work
overlapping with the loop's own temp-object cleanup), even though the
exact faulting instruction has not yet been isolated.

## 2026-09-01, continued: full call chain traced to the actual allocator dispatch; final pinpoint left for next session

A live, filtered hardware watchpoint on `g_edi` writes (condition: new
value `== 0x0119B110` AND `g_esp` inside the loop's known stack range)
caught the exact moment live and produced a full, reliable `kb` stack
trace (native registers directly readable since this was a live process,
not a `.dmp` -- global variables are NOT captured in this project's
minidumps, an important distinction from every earlier `.dmp`-based
session in this investigation):

```
sub_000371EA+0xbd  (return address into here)
sub_0003721B+0xeb
sub_00043DA9+0x56e
sub_000421D7+0x227
sub_00045AFE+0x1ee   <- our loop
sub_001D589D+0x100d
sub_00048B15+0x117e
...
```

with the actual break landing at `scda_recomp!sub_000360E1+0x1e1`
(`mov dword ptr [g_ecx], eax`). Reading the generated C for every function
in this chain in turn:

- `sub_000371EA` (called from `sub_0003721B`/`sub_00043DA9`/
  `sub_000421D7`, all upstream of `sub_00045AFE`'s loop): never touches
  `edi` at all; calls `sub_000360E1` as its last step before returning.
- `sub_000360E1`: a wide-string assign helper (near-identical in shape to
  `sub_000371A6`, the original crash site) -- `push ebx,esi,edi` / `pop
  edi,esi,ebx`, correctly balanced 3/3. Calls `sub_000A8D0A` (buffer
  capacity/grow helper) for its own internal allocation.
- `sub_000A8D0A`: `push esi,edi` / `pop edi,esi`, correctly balanced 2/2.
  Only calls further (`sub_001E460F`) on the "needs to grow" branch.
- **`sub_001E460F`: the actual allocator dispatch.** Pushes only `esi`
  (not `edi`), then does `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE(MEM32(eax + 4), _icall_esp)`
  -- an indirect call through the active allocator object's own vtable
  (`eax = MEM32(MEM32(0x5B57F8))`, and `0x5B57F8` is the exact "active
  allocator pointer" slot documented in the `0x0004449C` seed from
  earlier in this project's history). This function does **not** save or
  restore `edi` around the indirect call at all.

Checked `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`'s definition (`templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`):
on lookup failure it resets `g_esp` and zeroes `eax`, but touches no other
register -- and on success it just calls `_fn()` directly with no
save/restore of anything. This is correct **only if** every possible
`_fn` this can resolve to itself correctly preserves `edi` per the x86
callee-saved convention (which recompiled `sub_XXXXXXXX` functions
generally do, based on everything read this session) -- so the actual
defect, if it is in this specific call, is almost certainly inside
whatever concrete function `MEM32(eax + 4)` resolves to at this specific
site, not in `sub_001E460F`/`RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` themselves.

Attempted to resolve the concrete target address live (breaking at
`sub_001E460F`'s entry when `g_edi` still holds the loop's correct value,
then stepping forward to read `g_eax` after the vtable dereference) but
ran out of clean, unambiguous stepping room in a scripted (non-interactive)
CDB session -- `p` step counts needed to clear the generated code's
`RECOMP_TRACE_PC` call and MEM32-macro-expanded instructions weren't
precisely known, so the captured `g_eax` was still its stale pre-load
value. Also newly confirmed: **`g_xbox_mem_offset` is not a fixed
constant across runs** -- this session's various live captures read
`0x10000` in earlier runs but `0x0119AEF0` in this one, meaning the guest
RAM arena's mapped base address varies per-process-launch (consistent
with `MapViewOfFileEx`'s hint-address fallback chain in
`xbox_memory_layout.c`, not a bug, but a fact worth remembering for any
future live debugging: recompute `g_xbox_mem_offset` fresh every session,
never assume it from a prior run's notes).

**Final handoff for a fresh session**: break at `scda_recomp!sub_001E460F`
conditioned on `g_edi == 0x00F7FD84` (or re-derive the correct loop object
address fresh, since heap addresses can also vary run to run), then
single-step with `t` (step INTO calls, not `p` step-over) far enough to
observe `ecx = MEM32(0x5B57F8); eax = MEM32(ecx)` actually execute (watch
`g_ecx`/`g_eax` change via `r` after each `t`, rather than counting steps
blindly), then read the true vtable target as
`MEM32(g_eax_value + 4)` (apply `+ g_xbox_mem_offset` for the host
address, reading fresh in that same session). Once the concrete
`subXXXXXXXX` is known, read its generated C for a push/pop imbalance on
`edi` across all its exit paths -- the same method that resolved Seeds
33/34/36, just one level deeper in the call graph than any of those.

This closes out an extraordinarily long, productive session: five real
bugs investigated end to end, three Seeds (34/35/36) landed and verified,
one general `Z:\` path-mapping fix landed and verified, and this fourth
crash's mechanism fully traced through eight call-stack levels down to
a single indirect-call site -- with the exact concrete function still
one more live debugging pass away.

## 2026-09-01, continued: upstream check -- 112 commits behind, merged onto `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge`, builds clean

At the user's request, checked whether the upstream `sp00nznet/xboxrecomp`
GitHub repo (this project's own origin) had moved since the local clone,
and whether any of it addressed the mid-loop `edi` corruption
investigation. It had, substantially: `git fetch origin` showed the local
`main` 112 commits behind `origin/main` (now tagged v0.6.0, "Credit Where
Due"). Several commits are squarely in the bug class this session spent
hours on:

- `b525bc3 fix(lifter): read indirect call target before pushing` -- an
  esp-relative indirect call (`call dword ptr [esp+N]`, the shape MSVC
  gives a callback invoked through a stack argument) read its target
  *after* the return-address push had already shifted esp by four,
  dispatching through the wrong slot.
- `836c9c9`/`014eb94` -- failed indirect tail-jumps and unresolved stubs
  now consume the caller's dummy return address on failure, generically
  fixing the exact stack-imbalance mechanism behind Seeds 33/34/36 this
  session (previously only patched per-address via seeds).
- A large x87 rewrite (`3945357`, `15a7fde`, `17a5f8d`, `f55c2df`,
  `7706c66`, `83dffb6`): `fld st(i)`/`fst st(i)`/`fcomp`/binary arithmetic
  were dropping or duplicating FPU stack slots and comparing against the
  wrong operand.
- `2f0d9c6`/`ccde1f6`/`e7dd47a` -- a proper per-predecessor flag-state
  propagation pass (only inherits flags when every predecessor agrees),
  replacing a naive "copy from the previous block" approach.
- `aa812ee kernel: add xbox_ProtectMirrorsForDebug` -- Xbox RAM is mapped
  at 28 aliasing virtual addresses (26-bit address-bus mirroring); this is
  exactly why this session's hardware watchpoint on the base address never
  caught a write that had genuinely happened through a wrapped address.
- Real spawned worker threads with `RECOMP_TLS` (`__declspec(thread)`)
  per-thread register state, replacing synchronous-then-restore execution
  that deadlocked on any worker that blocks waiting for an event.
- A new `tools/abi_analysis` package and a conformance-testing harness
  that lifts real compiled code and compares it against the actual CPU --
  built to catch exactly this session's class of register-preservation
  bug automatically.

Committed the session's own uncommitted work first (Seeds 34-36, the `Z:\`
path fix, and all the live-debug diagnostics in `recomp_manual.c`) as a
checkpoint, then created `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` and merged `origin/main`.
Conflicts landed in `kernel.h`, `kernel_bridge.c`, `kernel_xbox.c`,
`xbox_memory_layout.c`/`.h`, `templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`, and
`tools/disasm/__main__.py`/`functions.py`, `tools/recomp/lifter.py`/
`translator.py`. Resolved each by hand, checking every hunk against actual
usage elsewhere in the tree rather than blindly preferring either side:

- Took upstream wholesale for anything that was purely a correctness fix
  with no SCDA-specific content (EEPROM index bug affecting Halo, the x87
  rewrite, the flag-snapshot mechanism, `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`'s target-before-
  push fix, `RECOMP_ITAIL`'s esp balance, the KDATA object-type constants).
- Preserved every confirmed SCDA-only addition: `g_xbox_fs`/`xbox_fs_*`
  (FS-segment/TIB emulation for SEH, extensively used in generated code),
  `g_icall_source` (icall-failure diagnostics), **`RECOMP_TRACE_PC`
  emission in the translator** (this session's entire live-debug
  workflow -- every `[SCDA-STRARG]`/`[SCDA-CLUSTER]`/ring-buffer

  generated code), `SEH_FRAME_HELPERS`'s per-title detection (vs.
