## 2026-09-01, continued: regenerated disasm/C with the merged tools -- builds and runs, but exits far earlier than the current working build (regression, not yet root-caused)

Regenerated disassembly (`tools/disasm/output/scda_v060`) and C
(`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060`) with the merged v0.6.0 tools, same
seeded command as always. The improved function-boundary heuristic alone
found **716 more functions with zero new seeds** (28,419 -> 29,135
detected), and unresolved stubs dropped from 1,909 to 1,297 -- direct,
measurable evidence the upstream `functions.py` fix is finding real gaps
Seeds 33-36 (and presumably many more, project-wide) were compensating
for by hand. Pointed `projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt`'s `SCDA_GEN_DIR` at
the new output and rebuilt (`build/scda_upgrade`) -- clean, `scda_recomp.exe`
produced, zero errors.

A fresh run (after copying the game/save assets the new build directory
was missing) **exits normally but far too early** -- `HalReturnToFirmware:
routine=2 - title is exiting`, reached within ~600 lines of log, right
after reading `TitleMeta.xbx`/`TitleImage.xbx`/`SaveImage.xbx` from
`UDATA`. This is well before the actor-list loop this whole session's
`edi`-corruption investigation lives in, and confirmed *not* to be the
current build's own behavior: running the untouched `main`-branch build
side by side kept going normally (log kept growing, still running when
checked) with the same save files present, ruling out a missing-asset
explanation.

Traced the exit's immediate cause via the existing `[SCDA-TLS]` diagnostic
(pre-dating this session, at guest PC `0x00052A57` -- a small CRT helper
reading `xbox_fs_read8(0x24)`/`xbox_fs_read32(0x28)` in an SEH-scope-count
pattern, then indexing a table via `MEM32(0x005EA9EC)`): that table index
comes back `0xFFFFFFFB` (-5) -- clearly uninitialized or corrupted, not a
plausible small TLS slot index. `0x005EA9EC` is a fixed guest .data
address that some earlier initializer is supposed to set to a small
positive index; whatever writes it correctly in the current working build
is not running (or not running correctly) in the freshly-regenerated one.

**Not yet root-caused.** Leading hypothesis, not yet verified: the
improved automatic gap-closing in `functions.py` merged or re-bounded a
function differently than before somewhere in the CRT TLS-initialization
path, changing behavior at a point completely unrelated to Seeds 33-36 (a
plausible, even expected, side effect of a detector heuristic changing
project-wide -- a fix in one place can shift a boundary decision
elsewhere). Confirmed the Seeds 34/35/36 are still present and applied via
`function_seeds.json` and the `Z:\` path fix survived the merge
(`kernel_path.c` unchanged, verified), so this is not a lost fix -- it's
either a new gap the improved detector's own boundary changes opened up,
or a genuine ordering/state difference from the runtime-layer merge
(RECOMP_TLS, real worker threads) affecting this specific early CRT path.

**Current status: `main` (pre-merge) remains the working, un-regressed
branch and has not been touched.** `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` builds and runs
but regresses this specific early-startup path; it must not replace `main`
until this is root-caused and fixed.

Narrowed further: `0x005EA9EC` has **no write anywhere in the disassembled
`.text` section** in either the old or new disassembly (`grep -i 5ea9ec`
on both `asm/text.asm` files gives byte-identical results, 7 reads, 0
writes) -- so whatever sets its real value either does so through a
register-indirect store (not visible as a literal operand) or the value
comes from elsewhere. Confirmed via the boot log's own section table that
`0x005EA9EC` falls inside section `.data`'s **BSS tail**
(`VA=0x005B03E0 vsize=1058680 raw=... rsize=211520 (BSS)`; offset
`0x5EA9EC - 0x5B03E0 = 0x3A60C`, past `rsize`), which
`xbox_memory_layout.c`'s `memset(XBOX_VA(sec_va), 0, sec_vsize)` zeroes
before any initializer runs -- so it should read `0` until something
writes it, not `0xFFFFFFFB`.

Two live hypotheses, neither yet confirmed:
1. `0xFFFFFFFB` is a deliberate "not yet allocated" sentinel a real
   initializer (an `RtlTlsAlloc`-shaped call, given the `[SCDA-TLS]`
   context) is supposed to overwrite with a real small index, and that
   initializer call is the thing not running/not resolving anymore --
   which would point back at the function-detection change rather than
   memory zeroing.
2. The BSS zero-fill itself is not actually happening for this address in
   the merged `xbox_memory_layout.c` (a genuine regression in that file's
   merge, separate from the disassembly regeneration) and `0xFFFFFFFB` is
   leftover host memory content -- worth testing directly by reading
   `MEM32(0x005EA9EC)` immediately after `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit()`
   returns, before any guest code runs, in a live CDB session.

Next session should start with hypothesis 2's direct live check (fastest,
most decisive test), then fall back to tracing the register-indirect
writer if the BSS zero-fill turns out to be fine.

## 2026-09-01, continued: hypothesis 2 ruled out live; found a likely race between the new real worker threads and a copy loop -- new leading hypothesis for the regression

Live check (breakpoint on `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit`, step out with `gu`, then
read `MEM32(0x5EA9EC)` immediately): reads back **`0`**, confirming the
BSS zero-fill is correct. Hypothesis 2 (broken zero-fill) is ruled out.

Armed a write watchpoint on the same address from the very start of
`xbe_entry_point` (before hypothesis-1's initializer could run) and caught
the first write. Two separate runs gave **two different final values**
(`0xFFFFFFFB` in the original smoke-test log, `0xFFFFFFDB` in this
targeted run) for what should be a deterministic recompiled program given
identical inputs -- everything else measured live this session (crash
addresses, register values, call chains) has been perfectly repeatable
run to run. Non-determinism appearing for the first time, right after
this merge introduced **real spawned worker threads** with independent
`RECOMP_TLS` register state (replacing the old synchronous-execution
model), is a strong structural clue.

Disassembling around the trap point shows the write is not a targeted
"set this one variable" store at all -- it's one iteration of a **word-at-
a-time copy loop** (`mov ecx, [r14+rbx]; mov [rdx+rax], ecx; add
[rbx+rbp], 0xFFFFFFFCu` repeating, `rax` = `g_xbox_mem_offset` each time,
so `[rdx+rax]`/`[rcx+rax]` are `MEM32(guest_dest)` stores). `0x5EA9EC` is
apparently just one word inside a larger block this loop copies, not a
deliberately-targeted "TLS index" write -- revising the `[SCDA-TLS]`
diagnostic's own naming/comment as a likely red herring from an earlier,
unrelated investigation rather than a description of what's actually
happening here.

**New leading hypothesis, not yet confirmed**: the source data (or the
destination address) for this copy loop is being computed from something
that now races between the main thread and one of the newly-real worker
threads -- e.g. a shared buffer, an allocator's bump pointer, or a loop
bound read from memory that a second thread is concurrently writing.
Real threads did not exist in the old, working build at all (everything
ran synchronously on one thread); this is exactly the kind of latent bug
a synchronous-execution model can never expose and real concurrency
immediately can. This would also explain why this exact symptom is brand
new to the merge and had never appeared across dozens of runs of the old
build this session.

**Session stopping point.** This has been an extraordinarily long
session (five real bugs investigated end to end this session alone,
three Seeds landed, one path-mapping fix landed, the edi-corruption
investigation traced to a single indirect-call site, and now a 112-commit
upstream merge landed cleanly with a precisely-characterized regression
found in the process). `main` remains the safe, working, un-regressed
branch. `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` has real, measurable value already
proven (716 more functions auto-detected, 1,909 -> 1,297 unresolved
stubs, several fixes squarely in this session's own bug classes) but
is not yet ready to replace `main` until the race-condition hypothesis
above is confirmed and fixed. Next session: identify which two threads
are live at the point of this write (the watchpoint's own thread ID,
cross-referenced against `bridge_spawn_thread` call sites logged around
the same time) and what shared state they both touch.

## 2026-09-01, continued: found a real early background thread and a NULL source pointer at the fault site; race hypothesis strengthened but not yet fully closed

Found a genuine, always-running early background thread that could plausibly
race with the main thread from very early in startup: `nv2a_ack_thread`
(`xbox_memory_layout.c`, started by `xbox_Nv2aAckStart()`), a
`CreateThread`-spawned loop that acknowledges NV2A/MCPX hardware register
bits and refreshes `KeTickCount` every iteration, yielding via `Sleep(0)`.
This thread's own writes land at `XBOX_KERNEL_DATA_BASE (0x00740000)` and
the NV2A/MCPX register blocks -- confirmed via the constant values these
areas are far from `0x005EA9EC` numerically, so this specific thread's
*own* writes are not the direct spatial collision. Its mere existence
does, however, confirm real concurrent execution starts astonishingly
early (before `xbe_entry_point` even begins), which is the necessary
precondition for any race to exist at all -- something structurally
impossible in the old, synchronous-only build.

Re-armed the write watchpoint and inspected the actual trapping
instruction precisely this time (previous pass mis-identified which
register held the loop's source pointer). The real write is
`mov edx, [rsi+rbx]` (load) then `mov [rcx+rax], edx` (store, `rax` =
`g_xbox_mem_offset`, `rcx` = `0x5EA9EC`'s host address) -- i.e. `rsi` is
the copy loop's *source* base pointer and `rbx` the shared index into
both source and destination. Checked `rsi` directly: **`!address rsi`
shows it points into the free, unmapped NULL page (base `0x0`, `MEM_FREE`,
`PAGE_NOACCESS`)**. Reading `[rsi+rbx]` only doesn't crash because `rbx`
is large enough to land the *effective* address in valid memory --  but
the base itself being exactly NULL instead of a real pointer is not a
plausible legitimate value; it looks like either an uninitialized local
in the generated code, or a guest address computation that wrapped to
exactly 0 (a large/negative guest offset added to `g_xbox_mem_offset`
overflowing 32-bit arithmetic back to zero).

This is now a stronger, more specific finding than "a race exists
somewhere": **the copy loop's source pointer is NULL at the moment it's
used**, and that pointer's value itself needs to be traced back further
(what sets `rsi` earlier in `xbe_entry_point`, and whether that
computation reads something `nv2a_ack_thread` -- or the timing of when
`g_xbox_mem_offset`/another shared global becomes valid -- can still be
mid-write when the main thread reaches it). Did not reach a fully
confirmed root cause this pass; the NULL-source-pointer finding is precise
enough that the next step is mechanical: find where `xbe_entry_point`
sets this base pointer (read the generated C source, not just native
disassembly, for the function-local `esi`-equivalent load immediately
preceding this copy loop) and determine why it can be NULL.

Given the length of this session, stopping here with a strong, precise
lead is the right call: `main` remains untouched and working;
`upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` has proven value but this regression blocks it
from replacing `main` until the NULL-source-pointer's own root cause is
found.

## 2026-09-01, continued: self-correction -- the "NULL source pointer" theory was a misread; found the real write and a more precise, testable explanation

The previous entry's native-register reading was wrong: `rsi`/`rbx`/`r14`
in that disassembly window are MSVC's own compiler-chosen host registers
for the *seven PUSH32 calls* setting up `sub_00052572`'s arguments (each
`PUSH32(esp, X)` compiles to a `[stack]=X; stack-=4` pair), not a "source
base pointer" for anything -- `rsi=0` there is just the literal guest
value `0` (`esi = 0;` in the generated C) being pushed as one of those
arguments. This was another instance of the session's own established
"don't trust an ad hoc native-register reading without confirming it
against the actual guest register" lesson, just applied to a raw
disassembly window instead of `kb` symbol offsets this time.

Reading `g_esp`, `g_ecx`, `g_esi`, `g_ebx` directly (the actual global
variables, not native host registers) at the exact same trap point gave a
clean, unambiguous answer: `g_esp=0x00F7FFD0` (a completely normal, sane
guest stack pointer -- ruling out any stack-corruption/overlap theory),
and **`g_ecx=0x005EA9EC`** -- confirming the write genuinely is
`MEM32(ecx) = eax` with `ecx` holding our watched address directly, i.e.
a real, singular register-indirect store, not a copy loop or an
argument-push side effect after all.

Reading the generated C directly around this point (`xbe_entry_point`,
guest `0x0005478D`-`0x000547CE`) shows exactly this shape:
```c
eax = MEM32(0x4F9474);
eax = eax - MEM32(0x4F9464);
ecx = MEM32(0x4F9468);
eax = eax + ecx + 0xF;
eax = eax & 0xFFFFFFF0u;              /* align up */
eax = eax + 4;
MEM32(0x6B2788) = eax;
edx = (eax < 0) ? -1 : 0;              /* cdq, sign-extend for the divide */
/* eax = eax:edx / ecx ; edx = eax:edx % ecx, using ecx = MEM32(0x4F946C) */
ecx = MEM32(0x4F946C);
...
MEM32(ecx) = eax;                       /* <-- our watched write */
```
`0x4F9474`/`0x4F9464`/`0x4F9468`/`0x4F946C` are all in the `.rdata`-ish
constant range this project has repeatedly identified as compile-time
table data (matching addresses like `0x4F5C60` etc. from earlier this
session), so `ecx` (the destination, `MEM32(0x4F946C)`) itself is very
likely a fixed compile-time constant that reliably equals `0x5EA9EC`
every run -- consistent with the destination *always* being this exact
address (matching every run's own observation), while the *value*
written (`eax`, the quotient of a division) is what plausibly differs.

The dividend is built from `MEM32(0x4F9474) - MEM32(0x4F9464) +
MEM32(0x4F9468) + 0xF`, rounded up to a 16-byte boundary, then divided by
`MEM32(0x4F946C)` -- the shape of a classic "compute an aligned
buffer/heap size from two bounds" calculation. **Revised, more precise
hypothesis, replacing the race-condition theory**: this arithmetic's
inputs may be legitimately environment-dependent in this build (e.g. if
any of those four constants is itself derived from something that shifts
with host memory layout, such as the `MapViewOfFileEx` base address
varying run to run, which this session already confirmed happens --
`g_xbox_mem_offset` measured `0x10000` in one run and `0x0119AEF0` in
another) rather than a genuine multi-thread data race on `ecx`/`0x5EA9EC`
itself. The `nv2a_ack_thread` background-thread finding from the previous
entry stands as real (confirmed real early concurrency exists) but is no
longer the leading explanation for *this specific* value's variance.

**Not yet fully closed**, but now precisely testable: next session should
read the actual values of `MEM32(0x4F9474)`, `MEM32(0x4F9464)`,
`MEM32(0x4F9468)`, and `MEM32(0x4F946C)` live at this exact point across
two runs to see which one(s) actually vary, rather than reasoning about
it further. If one of the four is not a fixed constant, that pins the
real source immediately; if all four are identical across runs and only
the division's *result* differs, that would point back toward the
division/`cdq` translation itself (an upstream lifter change, or a
genuine race after all) rather than its inputs.

Stopping here after an extremely long session: `main` remains untouched
and working; `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` is not yet ready to replace it, but
the regression is now characterized down to four specific guest addresses
and one division -- a clean, mechanical starting point for the next
session rather than an open-ended "somewhere in startup" search.

## 2026-09-01, continued: read the four candidate constants live -- they're stable, but the observed result doesn't match hand-derived arithmetic; genuinely not yet closed

Read `MEM32(0x4F9474)`, `MEM32(0x4F9464)`, `MEM32(0x4F9468)`,
`MEM32(0x4F946C)` live at the trap point in one run: `144, 0, 0,
0x005EA9EC` respectively, with `g_eax = 0xFFFFFFDB` (the value actually
stored). `MEM32(0x4F946C)` reading back exactly `0x5EA9EC` -- the
destination address itself -- confirms it as a stable pointer constant
(matches every run's destination), not a varying divisor as first framed.

Hand-deriving the expected result from the source read earlier
(`eax = 144 - 0 + 0 + 0xF = 159; eax &= 0xFFFFFFF0 = 144; eax += 4 = 148;
divide 148 by ecx=0x5EA9EC (6,203,884) -> quotient 0, remainder 148`)
does **not** match the observed stored value (`0xFFFFFFDB`). Either the
statement-to-statement mapping from the earlier read of the generated C
is subtly wrong (an intervening operation between the division and the
final `MEM32(ecx) = eax` was missed), or `eax` at store time isn't the
raw division quotient. This means the "heap-size-computation" explanation
from the previous entry, while a reasonable read of the source text, does
not actually reproduce the observed number and should not be treated as
confirmed -- it was a hypothesis that a direct numeric check has now
called into question, not a finished analysis.

**Honest status: not yet closed.** Four live debugging passes this
session narrowed the regression from "exits too early somewhere in
startup" down to one exact write instruction and its inputs, corrected
two wrong intermediate theories (NULL source pointer; race on the
destination address) along the way, and the current data raises a real,
specific, checkable discrepancy (hand arithmetic vs. observed value) for
the next session to resolve -- most directly by single-stepping from
`loc_0005478D` through to the store with `t` (not `p`), checking `g_eax`
after every guest statement, rather than computing it by hand from a
static read of the C source. `main` remains untouched and working;
`upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` still needs this resolved before it can replace
it.

## 2026-09-01, continued: a second manifestation of the same regression found in a real user run -- a legitimate retry loop that never terminates, likely the same root cause as the early exit

The user ran the `build/scda_upgrade` build directly (not one of this
session's own controlled test runs) and left it open for an extended
period; its `scda_runtime.log` showed `[SCDA-HEARTBEAT]` samples (fired
every 10,000,000 traced instructions) landing on the **exact same guest
PC, 568 times in a row**, spanning 5.68 billion instructions -- a real
hang, not a slow-but-progressing run. `g_esp` grew steadily across
samples (`0x01908A88` at the first sample to `0x044F5348` at the last,
~44 MB of net stack growth) while every other logged register stayed
constant, meaning the same short code cycle was repeating without
terminating.

Traced the hang's guest PC (`0x00371C3F`) to `sub_00371C2D`, a small
allocation wrapper: it makes an indirect call through vtable slot
`MEM32(0x4F5354)` (`RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`), and returns `0` if the call
result was negative (error path, via `sub_00052A85`) or a fixed `0x1C`
(28) otherwise. Its only caller, `sub_00076849`, uses it in a genuine
**loop**: `if (eax != 0) goto loc_00076955` branches back to *before* the
call whenever `sub_00371C2D` returns non-zero (i.e. every "successful"
28-byte allocation), and only falls through when it returns exactly `0`
(the icall-failure path). Read plainly, this is a legitimate original-game
pattern -- "keep carving fixed-size blocks out of a pool until the
underlying allocator signals it's out of room" -- that is supposed to
terminate naturally once the pool fills up on real hardware.

**This never terminates in the new build because the underlying
allocation call never reports failure.** That points straight back at
the *same* heap-availability computation this session was already
investigating for the early-exit regression (the division around
`MEM32(0x4F9464)`/`0x4F9468`/`0x4F9474`/`0x4F946C`, whose hand-derived
result didn't match the observed stored value in the previous entry): if
that computation is reporting far more available heap space than
actually exists (or never correctly signals exhaustion), it would
explain both symptoms from one root cause -- one run exits early because
some *other* code path reads the miscalculated value directly and bails,
another run instead loops forever because a *different* code path
depends on it eventually reporting "full" and it never does.

**This strengthens the case that there is one shared root cause,
not two unrelated regressions**, and gives a second, independent guest PC
(`sub_00076849`'s loop test, guest `0x0007699A`/`0x00076955`) to
instrument alongside the original write-site investigation. Next session:
watch `MEM32(0x4F5354)` (the vtable slot `sub_00371C2D` dispatches
through) and whatever backs the actual pool/arena exhaustion check on the
*real* target function, to see whether it ever reports "full" at all, or
always reports success regardless of how much has already been carved
out of the pool.

`main` remains untouched and working; the user confirmed the game assets
(`Default`, `Media`, etc.) are correctly copied into `build/scda_upgrade`
and understands crash dumps aren't expected for a hang (the process was
closed by hand, not crashed, which is consistent with everything found
here -- no crash, just an infinite loop).

## 2026-09-01, continued: live-caught the icall failure inside the hang -- the allocator vtable slot itself has been clobbered

Live-armed a breakpoint on `sub_00371C2D` first to confirm the vtable
slot's starting content: `MEM32(0x4F5354) = 0xFE0001F4` at the very first
call -- a legitimate, valid **kernel-thunk marker** (`KERNEL_VA_BASE
(0xFE000000) + slot*4`, slot `0x1F4/4 = 125`, well inside the 378-slot
table), which `recomp_lookup_kernel` resolves correctly by design. So the
loop's *first* iteration should dispatch through the real kernel bridge
successfully, matching "some allocations succeed" from the earlier
analysis.

Cleared that breakpoint and armed one on `recomp_icall_fail_log` instead,
then let the same run continue. It fired, with `sub_00371C2D` still on
the stack (confirmed via `kb`) -- but this time the failed target
(`ecx`, first arg) was **`0x1C`** (28), not `0xFE0001F4`. `0x1C` is
exactly the literal success-return value `sub_00371C2D` itself produces
on every successful allocation (`eax = 0x1C;` in its own generated C).
This strongly suggests **the vtable slot at `0x4F5354` has been
overwritten with a stale return value from a previous iteration** --
consistent with a stray write somewhere in this same hot loop clobbering
memory it shouldn't, rather than the kernel dispatch itself being at
fault.

This resolves the earlier open question of "why doesn't the loop
terminate once eax=0 on failure": `sub_00371C2D` DOES return `0` on this
failure, and the immediate caller's `if (eax != 0) goto ...` DOES fall
through correctly -- but the stack trace shows this failing call is
nested under `sub_00077194`/`sub_000774E6`/`sub_00077AC9`/`sub_00077B8E`/
`sub_0036AD60`, an outer structure that evidently keeps re-invoking
`sub_00076849`'s allocation loop regardless, which is why the hang
persists across billions of instructions even though each individual
inner-loop pass can terminate on its own. `rsi=0x044F5348` in this
register dump matches the *last* heartbeat sample's `esp` value exactly,
confirming this capture is from deep within the same long-running hang,
not an earlier, different pass.

**Updated picture, still not fully closed**: the regression looks like a
genuine memory-corruption chain -- something in this hot allocation path
writes to `0x4F5354` (or an alias of it) when it shouldn't, eventually
turning a valid kernel-thunk marker into a stale small integer, after
which every further allocation attempt through that same slot fails, and
an outer retry structure keeps calling back into the now-permanently-
broken inner loop forever. This may or may not be the same root cause as
the early-exit regression's heap-size division (previous entries) -- both
remain plausible, and are no longer assumed to be definitely the same
without more evidence. Next step: watch `0x4F5354` itself with a write
breakpoint (now that its expected value, `0xFE0001F4`, and its observed
corrupted value, `0x1C`, are both known) to catch the actual clobbering
write and its caller directly, rather than continuing to infer it from
symptoms.

## 2026-09-01, continued: self-correction -- the vtable slot is never corrupted; the earlier icall-failure capture was likely misattributed

Armed the write watchpoint on `0x4F5354` and let the run continue to
completion. It fired **exactly once**, and only once: inside
`xbox_kernel_bridge_init` (native host code, at startup, before any guest
code runs), doing the legitimate kernel-thunk-table patch this project
has always done -- writing `0xFE0001F4` (the correct marker) into the
slot. No further writes ever occur. The final read-back at the end of
this same run confirmed the slot still holds `0xFE0001F4` -- the
*correct* value, not the `0x1C` seen in the previous entry's
`recomp_icall_fail_log` capture.

This directly contradicts the previous entry's "clobbered vtable slot"
theory: if `0x4F5354` is written exactly once, at startup, to the correct
value, and never again, then every call to `sub_00371C2D` reading
`MEM32(0x4F5354)` must see `0xFE0001F4` every single time -- it cannot
observe `0x1C`. The most likely explanation is that the earlier
`recomp_icall_fail_log` capture, while genuinely landing with
`sub_00371C2D` visible in the call stack, was misattributed to *this*
icall specifically via the same "trust the `kb` return-address offset
without verifying it against the real guest PC" pitfall this session has
hit and corrected several times before -- `sub_00371C2D+0x10b` may not
be the `MEM32(0x4F5354)` call site at all if `sub_00371C2D` has more than
one internal call, or if `/O2` code layout placed adjacent code there.
That capture should be treated as unverified, not as evidence, until
re-confirmed through the backward-disassembly-to-guest-PC technique
(established earlier this session) rather than the `kb` symbol name
alone.

**Honest status after this pass**: the hang's true mechanism remains
unresolved. What is now solidly established, not just hypothesized:
- The infinite loop is real and reproducible (confirmed in an actual user
  run, not just this session's controlled tests).
- `sub_00076849`'s allocation loop and its call into `sub_00371C2D` is a
  faithful translation of a genuine original-game pattern, not obviously
  broken in isolation.
- The vtable slot it dispatches through is correctly initialized and
  never subsequently written -- ruled out as a corruption source.
- The earlier "heap-availability division produces the wrong value"
  finding (several entries back) is unconfirmed by direct arithmetic
  check and should not be relied on either.

What's needed to actually close this out is disciplined single-stepping
(`t`, not `p`) through one full iteration of `sub_00076849`'s loop while
it's actively hanging, checking `g_eax` and `g_esp` after every guest
statement against the generated C source line by line, rather than more
inference from `kb` captures or hand arithmetic -- both of which have
now individually led to wrong conclusions this session and been corrected
each time. This is a real methodology lesson for the next session:
trust direct register-level single-stepping over any form of inference,
however plausible-looking, for this class of bug.

An exceptionally long session with genuine, verifiable progress (the
v0.6.0 merge itself, 716 more auto-detected functions, several corrected
theories documented honestly rather than left standing) even though the
final regression's root cause was not reached. `main` remains untouched
and working throughout every pass of this investigation.

## 2026-09-01, continued: user-suggested experiment -- explicitly capping RAM at 64 MB (retail, not devkit) makes no difference

The user, who owns a devkit Xbox with a 128 MB RAM upgrade, asked whether
this project's runtime might be defaulting to devkit-sized RAM instead of
retail's 64 MB, and whether explicitly capping it might resolve the hang.
Checked first: `g_xbox_total_ram` already defaults to `XBOX_TOTAL_RAM`
(64 MB) unless a title calls `xbox_SetTotalRam(XBOX_DEVKIT_RAM)`
explicitly, which SCDA's code never does -- confirmed live via the boot
log ("mapped 65536 KB", i.e. exactly 64 MB) in every run this whole
investigation, including the ones that hung. So RAM size was already
correct by default, not the cause on its own.

As a cheap, low-risk experiment anyway (the idea remains sound reasoning
even though the default was already right, and something upstream could
in principle read `g_xbox_total_ram` before its default assignment ran,
a static-initialization-order question worth ruling out directly), added
an explicit `xbox_SetTotalRam(64u * 1024u * 1024u);` call in
`projects/scda/src/main.c`, right before `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit()`.
Rebuilt and ran for over 45 billion instructions (far longer than any
previous test this session, at the user's own suggestion to let it run
properly before checking) -- **hung at the exact same guest PC
(`0x00371C3F`), same frozen register values, as every previous run.**
The experiment made no observable difference. Reverting is optional (the
explicit call is harmless and arguably clearer than relying on the
default) but it does not fix anything, so it should not be mistaken for
progress toward the root cause.

This is a clean, useful negative result: RAM size/devkit-vs-retail
detection is now conclusively ruled out as a contributing factor,
narrowing the remaining search space further. The root cause is still
whatever prevents `sub_00076849`'s allocation loop from ever seeing its
exit condition, per the previous entries' still-open investigation.

## 2026-09-01, continued: found and partially fixed the real root cause -- NtQueryVirtualMemory (ordinal 217) was never routed to a bridge at all

Traced `sub_00371C2D`'s icall target through the kernel thunk table:
`g_slot_ordinals[125] = 0xD9 = 217`, i.e. **`NtQueryVirtualMemory`** --
exactly the "is my memory pool still free" check the earlier entries'
loop analysis predicted must exist. Checked `bridge_for_ordinal(217)` in
`kernel_bridge.c`: **there was no `case 217` at all** -- it fell through
to `default: return NULL;`. `kernel_thunk_dispatch`'s own "no bridge"
path then unconditionally sets `g_eax = 0` (`STATUS_SUCCESS`) without
ever calling the real `xbox_NtQueryVirtualMemory` implementation (which
does exist, correctly, in `kernel_memory.c`, and is even wired into the
project's *other*, older kernel-thunk table in `kernel_thunks.c` -- just
never ported into the newer `bridge_for_ordinal` dispatch that
`kernel_thunk_dispatch` actually uses). This is the confirmed root cause
of every hang investigated this session: the "is the pool full yet"
check always answered "no, plenty of room" by construction, regardless
of real memory state, so `sub_00076849`'s allocation-retry loop could
never see its exit condition.

Added `bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory` (translating `BaseAddress` via
`XBOX_TO_NATIVE` before it reaches the real, host-address-only
`VirtualQuery()` call inside `xbox_NtQueryVirtualMemory` -- confirmed via
the crash below that this translation is necessary, not optional) and
registered `case 217: return bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory;`. First attempt
used the textbook 4-argument NT signature
(`BaseAddress, MemoryInformation, MemoryInformationLength, ReturnLength`)
and crashed immediately -- `kb` showed the fault inside
`xbox_NtQueryVirtualMemory`'s own `memcpy`, writing through a garbage
`MemoryInformationLength` read off stack slots the caller never
populated. Reading `sub_00371C2D`'s own generated C source confirmed why:
it pushes only **two** stack dwords before this icall, not four --
matching this project's own earlier (pre-merge) comment,
`"NtQueryVirtualMemory(2), Xbox-specific signature"`, which the v0.6.0
merge's arg-count table had silently widened to the generic 4-argument
NT shape (`case 217: return 16;`) without anyone noticing it didn't match
how SCDA actually calls it. Fixed the bridge to the real 2-argument
shape (`BaseAddress, MemoryInformation`, with a conservative fixed
length and no return-length output) and reverted the arg-count table
entry back to 8 bytes.

**Rebuilt and reran: the crash is gone, but the hang is not.** The loop
still spins forever at the same guest PC, now confirmed live to be
genuinely calling through to the real `xbox_NtQueryVirtualMemory`
implementation every iteration (`[KERNEL] summary: ... latest ordinal
217 (slot 125)` recurring in the log) rather than the old unconditional
stub success. This narrows the remaining gap precisely: routing is now
correct, but `VirtualQuery()`'s *result* itself doesn't signal "pool
full" the way the game expects -- `VirtualQuery` reports whatever state
a given address genuinely has (free/reserved/committed), it does not
fail just because overall memory is scarce, and the real Xbox kernel's
`MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` layout is smaller/different from Win32's, so
whatever fields SCDA's own loop logic actually inspects in the returned
struct are very likely misaligned or wrong given this bridge currently
writes Win32's raw layout into the guest buffer.

**Genuine, confirmed progress, not yet a complete fix.** Two real
project-level defects were found and one is now fixed (the missing
routing); the second (the Xbox `MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` struct layout
mismatch, and/or the loop's actual base-address progression logic) is
now the sole remaining blocker and is precisely characterized rather
than an open-ended "somewhere in memory management" search. Next
session: find the real, documented (or bisected) Xbox kernel
`MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` field layout, and check what
`sub_00371C2D`'s two stack arguments actually mean (is `STACK_ARG(1)`
really the output buffer, or could the second argument be something
else entirely given the Xbox-specific shape) -- ideally by disassembling
the real, un-emulated Xbox kernel's own `NtQueryVirtualMemory` export if
a reference kernel image is available, rather than guessing the struct
shape.

`main` remains untouched and working throughout. This was a very long
session that ended with real, verifiable forward movement on the actual
root cause, even though the fix isn't complete yet.

## 2026-09-01, continued: the hang is GONE -- fixed the real Xbox MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION field order using Cxbx-Reloaded's own reverse-engineered signature; a new, later issue found

At the user's suggestion, looked for an external reference for the real
Xbox kernel's `NtQueryVirtualMemory` rather than guessing further.
Cxbx-Reloaded (a separate, long-running Xbox emulation project that had
to reverse-engineer the exact same kernel export) has it documented:

```c
XBSYSAPI EXPORTNUM(217) xbox::ntstatus_xt NTAPI xbox::NtQueryVirtualMemory(
    IN PVOID BaseAddress,
    OUT PMEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION Buffer
)
```

confirming the 2-argument shape already fixed. Critically, their
reversed struct layout is:

```c
typedef struct _MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION {
    PVOID AllocationBase;
    DWORD AllocationProtect;
    PVOID BaseAddress;
    SIZE_T RegionSize;
    DWORD State;
    DWORD Protect;
    DWORD Type;
} MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION;
```

**`AllocationBase` comes first, `BaseAddress` third** -- Win32's own
`MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` puts `BaseAddress` *first* and
`AllocationBase` second. This is exactly the layout mismatch the
previous entry suspected: the bridge was raw-copying the host
`VirtualQuery()` result (Win32 field order) into the guest buffer, so
every field SCDA's own loop logic inspected was one slot off from what
it actually held.

Rewrote `bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory` to build the Xbox-ordered struct by
hand (`BRIDGE_MEM32` writes at the correct offsets: `AllocationBase` at
+0x00, `AllocationProtect` at +0x04, `BaseAddress` at +0x08, `RegionSize`
at +0x0C, `State` at +0x10, `Protect` at +0x14, `Type` at +0x18),
translating the two pointer fields back to guest VAs
(`host_ptr - g_xbox_mem_offset`) rather than delegating to
`xbox_NtQueryVirtualMemory`'s generic Win32-shaped implementation.

**Result: the hang at `pc=0x00371C3F` is completely gone.** Rebuilt and
ran -- zero `[SCDA-HEARTBEAT]` entries at all (the process didn't even
survive to the first 10-million-instruction sample before moving on),
confirming the allocation-retry loop now terminates essentially
immediately rather than never. The process proceeded past everything
this whole multi-day merge investigation had been stuck on, into CRT
static-initializer table iteration (`source=0x00058133`, the
project's own pre-existing `[SCDA-CRT-ITERATOR-CLOBBER]`-adjacent code
path), and exited cleanly via `HalReturnToFirmware` rather than hanging
or crashing.

**A new, later, separate issue surfaced immediately behind it**: the
constructor-table iteration's first entry (`target=0x004ED998`) is a
valid, plausible function pointer, but after roughly 20 entries the
iterated `target` values become obviously random garbage
(`0xE3045812`, `0xF29CCB2C`, `0x22250225`, ...), and the exit reason
itself is nonsensical (`HalReturnToFirmware: routine=5966092` -- a
plausible `HalReturnToFirmware` routine code is a small integer like 1
or 2, not six million). This strongly suggests the memory pool this
session's whole investigation was chasing gets built *successfully* now,
but is built **too small** -- the exhaustion signal this fix provides is
real and no longer always-false, but its exact trigger point (how much
"available" `VirtualQuery` needs to report before SCDA's loop decides
it's done) does not yet match what the real Xbox hardware's own,
simpler memory manager would have reported, so the pool ends up
undersized and the constructor-table walk runs off the end of real data
into uninitialized memory.

**This is genuine, substantial, verified progress -- the specific hang
this entire v0.6.0-merge investigation focused on is resolved.** The
newly-surfaced issue is a distinct, separate, and much further-along
problem (CRT initialization, not memory-pool bootstrapping), and a
reasonable place to continue in a fresh session rather than an
open-ended continuation of the same chase. `main` remains untouched and
working; `upgrade/v0.6.0-merge` is closer than it has been all session to
being viable, though this newly-found issue still blocks it from
replacing `main`.

Next session: instrument the CRT constructor-table walk
(`source=0x00058133`) to find where real entries stop and garbage
begins, and compare against how many constructors the game actually
ships (should be discoverable via the XBE's own static-initializer
section) to determine whether the pool's size needs to more closely
track a specific value the game itself expects, rather than whatever a
raw host `VirtualQuery()` happens to report for an arbitrary queried
address.

## 2026-09-01, continued: ground truth from real hardware -- got the actual retail SCDA disc running under xemu (real Xbox CPU/kernel emulation) and traced the real algorithm

At the user's suggestion, rather than continuing to infer the correct
`sub_00371C2D`/`NtQueryVirtualMemory` usage pattern from source reading
alone, found this machine already has a fully-configured **xemu**
install (`AppData/Roaming/xemu/xemu/xemu.toml`) with a real MCPX
bootrom, an `evox.bin` BIOS, an Xbox HDD image, and -- critically -- the
`dvd_path` already pointing at `scda.iso`, the actual retail Splinter
Cell: Double Agent disc image. Extracted the portable `xemu.exe` build
from an existing download and confirmed it's genuinely QEMU-based (prints
`QEMU emulator version 9.2.1`), which means the full QEMU instrumentation
toolkit is available: `-d exec,cpu -dfilter <start>+<length> -D <logfile>`
logs every executed instruction and full register state within a chosen
guest address range, without needing an interactive debugger at all.

Launched xemu with `-d exec,cpu -dfilter 0x00371c00+0x400` (note: QEMU's
`-dfilter` wants `start+length`, not `start-end` -- the first attempt
errored with "Invalid range" until corrected) and let it boot the real
game. This produced **real hardware-emulation execution traces at guest
address `0x00371c2d`** -- the exact same address this whole session's
`sub_00371C2D` investigation has been centered on, now observed running
the *actual*, unmodified retail disc rather than our own recompiled
translation.

The captured trace (163 loop iterations before the emulator was closed)
shows the real algorithm clearly: `EAX` (the `BaseAddress` argument to
each `NtQueryVirtualMemory` call) **increases monotonically** --
`0x00000000 -> 0x007f0000 -> 0x00820000 -> 0x00830000 -> ... ->
0x00f80000 -> 0x00fa0000 -> 0x00fd0000 -> 0x01000000` -- with `EBX`
(the returned `RegionSize`) varying per region as real, distinct memory
regions are walked. This is a straightforward **forward walk enumerating
every distinct memory region from guest VA 0 upward**, each call
advancing to `BaseAddress + RegionSize` for the next query -- not the
binary-search pattern an earlier, too-small two-sample read of this same
data briefly suggested. By the last captured entries the walk had
reached `0x01000000` (16 MB), roughly a quarter of the way through 64 MB
total RAM, confirming this loop is expected to run for a substantial
number of iterations on real hardware too (not a tight, few-iteration
check) -- consistent with `sub_00076849`'s loop being a genuine,
lengthy pool-construction pass by design, not something that should
terminate after a handful of calls.

This directly validates the fix's fundamental approach from the previous
entry: doing a real, translated `VirtualQuery()` per call and reporting
genuine region boundaries is the right shape of behavior; the walk is
supposed to advance address-by-address through real memory state, not
receive a single verdict. The remaining open question (from the previous
entry: pool built too small, garbage in the later constructor-table
entries) is now something that can be checked directly against this
real trace rather than guessed at -- capturing more of the real
algorithm's iterations (and, if possible, the address where it
naturally terminates) is now the most concrete next step, alongside
re-checking our own build's behavior against the same address-progression
shape (does `sub_00076849`'s loop advance `EAX`/`BaseAddress` the same
way call to call, or does it stall on repeating the same address).

**This is a valuable, reusable capability going forward, not just a
one-off for this bug**: whenever a similar "is our kernel bridge's
behavior actually right" question comes up, the same
`xemu -d exec,cpu -dfilter <addr>+<len> -D <logfile>` technique can
capture real hardware/kernel ground truth for direct comparison, without
needing to trust reverse-engineered documentation from other emulator
projects (useful as it was this session) or guess from the game's own
disassembly alone.

## 2026-09-01 (cont'd) -- longer xemu capture + "pool too small" root-cause progress

Standing methodology confirmed and saved permanently to memory (per user
request): for hard-to-root-cause XboxRecomp bugs, open xemu and check real
Xbox hardware behavior at the address in question, as a matter of course --
not just a one-off for this bug.

**Longer xemu capture** (`-dfilter 0x00371c00+0x1000`, this time run through
the user's own gameplay up to the main menu): captured 163 full iterations
of `sub_00371C2D` (up from 163 -> same count, but this time to the loop's
actual end -- the earlier capture was cut short mid-loop). The real loop
terminates with the last queried BaseAddress at **EAX=0x00FD0000 (~15.8MB)**,
immediately followed (next instruction, loc_00371C3B) by ECX=0 and ZF set --
the real hardware's exit condition. EAX (the NTSTATUS-looking result read at
loc_00371C3B, post-call) is **0x00000000 (STATUS_SUCCESS) on every single one
of the 163 real-hardware iterations**, including the very last one -- i.e.
the loop is not driven by NtQueryVirtualMemory ever returning an error/
negative status; some other condition (region size, State field, or the
seed/target address arithmetic) ends it.

**Our build's current behavior** (post-fix, CDB on scda_v060/`RelWithDebInfo`):
`sub_00371C2D` is called **exactly once**, then the whole allocation-pool
loop exits and the process proceeds (this matches the earlier-observed
"pool built too small" symptom -- CRT constructor table garbage after ~20
entries, nonsensical `HalReturnToFirmware` routine code). Traced the caller
(`sub_00076849`'s loop body, recomp_0003.c around loc_00076930-loc_000769A7):
sub_00371C2D's own internal branch (jl on the NtQueryVirtualMemory result)
returns eax=0x1C (28 = sizeof Xbox MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION) on success,
0 on an internal-error path; the *caller* only keeps looping while that
return value is non-zero, i.e. **the caller loop is designed to continue as
long as NtQueryVirtualMemory keeps succeeding** -- consistent with the real
trace (EAX=0 i.e. success on every one of the 163 iterations, loop
continues) and consistent with our build's single successful call *also*
being non-zero-returning, so a single success alone does not explain why our
loop stops after one pass.

Deeper trace of the caller's own loop-continuation arithmetic (recomp_0003.c
~75920-75940) shows it advances the probed address by the returned
`RegionSize` field and exits once accumulated size, rounded to an allocation
granularity, reaches a target derived from a requested-size parameter --
*provided* the region's `State` field equals `0x10000` (MEM_FREE) with a
zero remainder. Confirmed via CDB: our build's first (only) call already
returns `eax=0x1C` (success path taken, matching real hardware), but the
**seed/start address is wrong**: `MEM32(0x64D28C)` (the global the loop reads
as its first probed address) evaluates to **0x00F80690** in our build --
some address deep in guest stack space -- instead of starting near the low
end like real hardware's captured first sample. `0x64D28C` turns out to be
used elsewhere as a small pointer/struct (offsets +0/+4 accessed, initialized
via a call to `sub_00076818`), not a bare literal -- so this may be an
allocator-arena bookkeeping cursor (e.g. "current heap end") rather than a
literal VA-enumeration seed, which would also explain why it isn't 0; if so,
the actual mismatch against real hardware may be in what feeds *that*
cursor (an earlier heap-end/highest-used-address computation), not in
`sub_00371C2D`/`NtQueryVirtualMemory` itself. **Not yet conclusively
resolved** -- next step is to trace `sub_00076818` and whatever computes the
initial value written to `0x64D28C` before this loop ever runs, and to get a
clean read of the real hardware's post-call MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION fields
(State/RegionSize) from the xemu trace's raw registers to compare directly
against our own, rather than only the BaseAddress progression.

`main` branch remains completely untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 -- NtQueryVirtualMemory hang genuinely fixed (self-corrected mid-session mistake)

Continuing from the "pool too small" investigation: traced the actual x86
bytes of sub_00371C2D via a standalone XBE parser + capstone (not just the
recompiled C, and not the wrong references/xboxversion/default.xbe, which
turned out to be a different XBE entirely -- had to switch to the actual
build/scda_upgrade default.xbe to get correct addresses).

**A mistake made earlier in this thread, caught and corrected**: initially
concluded NtQueryVirtualMemory's BaseAddress parameter is passed BY
REFERENCE, based on misreading sub_00371C2D's "push [esp+8]" x2 as pushing
the same value twice. It doesn't -- esp moves by -4 between the two PUSH32s,
so they read two *different* source stack slots. Redid the push-order
arithmetic by hand against the caller's actual disassembly (sub_00076849)
and confirmed: STACK_ARG(0) is the plain BaseAddress *value*, STACK_ARG(1)
is the Buffer *pointer* -- exactly what the very first pass of this fix
(2026-09-01) already had. The by-reference "fix" was reverted.

That mistake, while it stood, caused a real regression that's worth
recording: dereferencing STACK_ARG(0) as a pointer read the wrong guest
memory, which combined with `XBOX_TO_NATIVE(0)` returning NULL for a
legitimate guest-VA-0 query (also fixed this session -- guest 0 is a real
address the pool loop probes, not a null-pointer sentinel here) and with
querying past the end of our flat 64MB mapping (also fixed, now capped and,
better, synthesized) produced in turn: an underflowed AllocationBase
(0xFFFF0000), a 300k+ iteration oscillation at the mapping's edge, and
finally (after fixing those two) a clean-looking but still-wrong infinite
loop where the probe address froze at 0 forever with identical state on
every one of 300M+ calls (SCDA-HEARTBEAT confirmed the hang was real, not
just sampling noise).

**Root cause, now confirmed fixed**: with the calling convention corrected
back to by-value BaseAddress / by-reference Buffer, and with a synthesized
two-region MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION model (below `xbox_GetHeapEnd()` ==
MEM_COMMIT, from there to `g_xbox_total_ram` == one MEM_FREE region --
replacing a raw host `VirtualQuery()` of our flat mapping, which could never
produce the FREE state the game's loop is looking for), the pool-population
loop now completes in two allocations (1MB + 64KB, matching
`XBOX_HEAP_BASE` == 0x00F80000 ≈ 15.5MB, encouragingly close to real
hardware's observed ~15.8MB loop-termination point from the xemu trace) and
the process runs to a clean `HalReturnToFirmware` exit with **zero**
SCDA-HEARTBEAT samples, confirmed across a clean rebuild + run. The original
hang, in all its forms investigated this session, is gone.

**Still open, separate, pre-existing issue**: the process now reaches the
exact same "pool too small" symptom already documented in the 2026-09-01
entries -- `[SCDA-CRT-ITERATOR-CLOBBER]` fires almost immediately and the
CRT static-initializer table walk (source=0x00058133) produces garbage
ICALL targets from report #4 onward, ending in `HalReturnToFirmware` with
routine=5966092 (not a small sane exit code). This is NOT something today's
changes introduced -- it's the next layer down, previously reached only
briefly before the hang masked it. Next investigation target.

`main` branch untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- CRT-ITERATOR-CLOBBER root-caused and fixed: a split loop, not the pool

The "pool too small" symptom (CRT static-constructor table walk producing
garbage after the first few entries) turned out to be unrelated to pool
sizing at all -- traced it to a completely different bug, found by walking
backward from the exact constructor call (target=0x0045C0E9) that immediately
preceded the corruption:

`sub_0045C0E9` tail-jumps into `sub_00071217`, a **CRC-32 table generator**
(standard reflected-input, MSB-first, polynomial 0x04C11DB7, 256 entries at
guest VA 0x0062A5D8). The disassembler's function-boundary detection cut
`sub_00071217`'s recognized range off right after the ONE-TIME setup plus
the very first table entry (index 0) -- the per-entry reload for every
*remaining* index lives at 0x00071223, reached only via an explicit `call`
from the entry-0 completion code (`sub_0007123E`), not a fallthrough/jump
the boundary heuristic could follow. That address was never disassembled as
part of any function and fell through to the generic unresolved-stub
fallback, which returns immediately -- without finishing the table *and*
without restoring `ebx`/`esi`/`edi` the way the real "table finished" path
would have. The corrupted `edi` (left pointing mid-table, ~0x0062A5DC)
leaked back into the CRT static-constructor iterator that had called all
this indirectly, overwriting its fixed end-pointer (expected 0x005B1D58) --
exactly the mechanism `[SCDA-CRT-ITERATOR-CLOBBER]` was built to detect.

**Fix**: added a manual override (`scda_crc32_table_finish_00071223` in
`projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c`, registered in `recomp_lookup_manual`)
that finishes the CRC table in native C -- the algorithm is a well-known,
unambiguous standard, more reliable here than trying to recover exactly
which raw bytes the disassembler skipped -- then performs the same epilogue
(`pop edi, esi, ebx`; consume the return address) the "table complete" path
would have.

Confirmed via rebuild + run: `[SCDA-CRT-ITERATOR-CLOBBER]` fires once (down
from firing on effectively every constructor call before) and the CRT
constructor walk proceeds far past where it used to fail -- the run reaches
genuine gameplay-adjacent code (actor/vector allocation and free cycles,
`[SCDA-VECTOR-FREE]`, 14,000+ traced PCs) that this whole multi-day
investigation had never reached before.

**New finding, not yet fixed**: a longer run (40s) hits a *different*,
later hang: `SCDA-HEARTBEAT` stuck at pc=0x00046D15 (a hash-bucket chain
walk -- `ecx = edx + (eax*9)*4`, following `MEM32(ecx)` as a "next" link
until either a key match or a `0xFFFFFFFF` end-of-chain sentinel) for
580,000,000+ calls with completely static register state
(ecx==edx==0x4FE85150, esi==0xCBF36687 -- likely the CRC32-hashed lookup
key). The chain-walk loop itself is straightforward and looks correctly
translated; the likely cause is that the hash table it's walking was built
with bad data (e.g. a self-referencing "next" link, entry 0 pointing to
itself, forming a cycle instead of terminating at -1) rather than a
translation bug in this specific loop. Not yet investigated further --
next session's target.

`main` branch untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- second split-loop fix (hash-table rehash), and a deeper/separate hang found

Found and fixed a second instance of the same bug class as the CRC-32
table generator: `sub_00046EC8` rehashes an open-addressed, index-linked
hash set into a newly allocated backing array via `sub_00046F00`'s
per-record copy body, looping while `ebx < [edi+4]`. The loop's back-edge
(`loc_00046F21`) jumps into the *middle* of `sub_00046EC8`
(0x00046EEF -- the per-iteration index-allocation setup, not anything
inside `sub_00046F00` itself) -- an edge the disassembler's per-function
analysis can't see, since it originates from a different function's
generated code. 0x00046EF2 was therefore never disassembled as reachable
and fell to the unresolved-stub fallback, silently truncating every
rehash partway through and leaving the rest of the new bucket array at 0
(the as-allocated value) instead of properly linked/marked-empty.

**Fix**: `scda_hash_rehash_continue_00046EF2` in
`projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c` -- rather than reimplementing the
copy body natively (real dynamic data, unlike the CRC table's fixed
algorithm), it replicates only the missing setup fragment and calls back
into the already-correctly-translated `sub_00046F00` to run the next
iteration, exactly matching what the real instruction at 0x00046EF2 does.
Registered in `recomp_lookup_manual`; `recomp_funcs.h` now included in
`recomp_manual.c` so generated functions (`sub_000A8D0A`, `sub_00046F00`)
can be called directly.

**Confirmed NOT sufficient to fix the observed hang**, however: a rebuild
+ 40s run hits the *exact same* `SCDA-HEARTBEAT` freeze at pc=0x00046D15
as before this fix, byte-for-byte identical register state
(ecx=edx=0x4FE85150, esi=0xCBF36687, edi=0x00045974). That the fix made
zero observable difference here means this specific hash table's
corruption doesn't go through the rehash path at all -- or the real root
cause is upstream of it entirely. Worth noting: `edi` (the hash-table
`this` pointer for the stuck lookup) is 0x00045974, which falls in the
.text code-address range, not any plausible heap/data address -- strongly
suggesting the corruption is a bad `this` pointer arriving at the lookup
call already wrong (a stack/register corruption further up the call
chain), not something local to the hash-table code itself. Three call
sites for `sub_00046CE5` (the lookup) exist in the generated code
(0x000463E7, 0x00047488, 0x000474DE return addresses) -- next session
should identify which one is live here and trace backward from there
live (CDB or another xemu comparison) rather than guessing further from
static analysis alone.

Keeping the sub_00046EF2 fix regardless -- it fixes a real, confirmed bug
(the same class as the CRC-32 one) that will matter for any OTHER hash
table that does hit its rehash path, even though it isn't what's blocking
this particular run.

`main` branch untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- hash-chain hang narrowed down to sub_0024A50B, root cause not yet found

Live-traced the EDI corruption feeding the hash-bucket-chain hang (edi
expected 0x005A570C throughout sub_0004721E, per its own prologue) using a
new watch in scda_trace_pc (`[SCDA-EDI57570C-CLOBBER]`, gated by extending
the file's existing per-address trace whitelist -- discovered along the way
that RECOMP_TRACE_PC is a complete no-op outside six CMake-configured
address ranges *and* scda_trace_pc has its own internal whitelist gate on
top of that; both had to be extended to observe this call chain at all).

Traced the call chain precisely: `sub_0004721E` (edi=0x5A570C, correct) →
`sub_0004640F` (a hash lookup on a *different* table, correctly saves/
restores edi via matching PUSH32/POP32, confirmed structurally sound) →
vtable dispatch at 0x0004744A (`MEM32(eax+0x10)`) → `sub_000360A3` (doesn't
touch edi at all) → calls `sub_001C445D` (confirmed balanced: one
PUSH32(edi)/POP32(edi) pair, all paths converge on the same epilogue) →
tail-jumps to `sub_0024A50B`. Watching immediately before/after this last
hop (pc=0x000360B2) shows **edi is still a valid heap pointer
(0x0109B4C0) going in**, and **is 0x00045974 (the same constant value
every single time, across all sessions this bug has been observed) by the
time control returns to the outer caller (pc=0x00047456)**. So the
corruption happens inside `sub_0024A50B` specifically.

`sub_0024A50B`'s own code looks structurally balanced too (one
PUSH32(esi)/PUSH32(edi) pair at entry, one matching POP32(edi)/POP32(esi)
pair at its single exit label 0x0024A525, reached either directly when
`eax==0` at entry or after an indirect vtable call at 0x0024A517
otherwise) -- by itself this shouldn't corrupt anything regardless of
which branch is taken. Added `[SCDA-0024A517-ICALL]` logging (icall
target resolution) to check whether that indirect call is even reached,
but haven't yet confirmed which of the two paths actually executes on the
run that hangs -- `eax` observed downstream (after the function has
already returned) can't be trusted to reflect the branch decision made
inside the function, since other code may have reset it in between.

**Not yet resolved.** Next step: get eax's value *at entry* to
`sub_0024A50B` (not downstream) to know which path is taken, and if it's
the direct (no-icall) path, look further upstream still -- the constant,
reproducible 0x00045974 value (not attributable to anything read/written
by any of the three functions inspected so far) suggests the real culprit
may be even earlier in the chain, or a stack-corruption effect (a stale
value sitting in a stack slot that gets read instead of the genuinely
pushed edi, from an imbalance elsewhere) rather than a straightforward
missing-preserve bug like the two split-loop fixes found earlier today.

Kept the new watch infrastructure (`[SCDA-EDI57570C-CLOBBER]`,
`[SCDA-0024A517-ICALL]`) in place, extended for reuse -- it already
proved its worth once by immediately revealing the false-positive at the
function's own entry point and by cleanly narrowing the search from "some
call site" to "specifically inside sub_0024A50B" in a handful of
rebuild+run cycles.

`main` branch untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- found the actual root cause: a dangling stack pointer in a global singleton slot

Traced the EDI corruption all the way back to its true source, confirming
it against the real x86 bytes (not just the generated C) at every step to
rule out another translation misreading like earlier today's.

`sub_0024A50B`'s "this" (`g_ecx`) is consistently a **guest stack address**
(0x00F7Bxxx range) rather than a heap object, and that stack address comes,
unmodified, from a chain of pure pass-throughs (`sub_000360A3` → the vtable
dispatch at 0x0004744A → `MEM32(0x005B5800)`). `0x005B5800` is a global
"current resource/error object" slot. Confirmed against the real
disassembly (standalone XBE parser + capstone, same technique used for the
NtQueryVirtualMemory ABI fix) exactly what writes it:

```
0x00048CB9: lea ecx, [ebp - 0xfc]      ; ecx = address of a LOCAL, stack object
0x00048CBF: mov [ebp+0x68], 1
0x00048CC6: call sub_00045647          ; constructor: writes vtable=0x4F7108
                                        ; to [ecx], fields at +4/+8/+2C/+30/+34,
                                        ; returns `this` (== ecx) in eax
0x00048CCB: mov [0x5b5800], eax        ; global := address of that STACK object
```

This is genuine, correctly-translated original game code (verified against
real bytes, not a lifter mistake) -- `sub_00045647` is a normal C++
constructor for a lightweight stack-allocated object (an error/result
object, given the vtable and the surrounding `[0x5ED140]`/`[0x5ED144]`
status-code checks right before it) that legitimately returns `this`. The
bug is that **the global `0x005B5800` is left pointing at that object long
after its enclosing function has returned and its stack frame has been
reused for something else** -- by the time `sub_0004721E` reads
`MEM32(0x5B5800)` much later (a separate call, a separate stack region
entirely), it's reading whatever unrelated data now occupies that stack
slot, which happens to no longer look like a valid object -- producing the
"this" pointer that eventually reaches `sub_0024A50B` as raw stack noise
and, through it, the corrupted EDI that hangs the hash-bucket-chain walk.

This is very likely either (a) something that's supposed to clear/reset
`0x005B5800` back to 0 once the transient object goes out of scope and

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- A/B/C comparison confirms: EDI corruption IS a real bug, pinned to the vtable dispatch itself

Implemented the three-point comparison suggested by the user's advisor
(A: immediately before MEM32(0x5B5800) is written; B: immediately after;
C: immediately before sub_0004721E reads it back), logging identical
fields (guest PC, EAX-EDX, ESI/EDI, ESP/EBP, the slot value, and the first
28 bytes of the object it points to) from both our recomp build and xemu
against the real disc.

**Points A/B**: our build and real hardware match closely --
esi=0x005E3E30, edi=0x005E6E20 identical in both at the write point; both
store a genuine stack address into the global (confirmed: this part of
the "dangling pointer" picture is completely normal, matching behavior).

**Point C, our build**: the object at `0x5B5800` is still mostly intact
(vtable + first 3 fields unchanged from point B) -- the earlier "dangling
pointer got silently clobbered" theory was too simple; the object itself
isn't obviously corrupted by the time it's read back.

**Point C, real hardware -- the decisive result**: traced the SAME call
chain (loc_00047440 -> loc_0004744A -> vtable icall -> loc_00047456) on
real hardware. EDI is **0x0081BE84 both immediately before and immediately
after the vtable call** -- completely unchanged. Our recomp build, at the
exact same two points, shows EDI going from a valid value into

call chain (sub_000360A3 / sub_001C445D / sub_0024A50B or the underlying
icall dispatch) -- not expected divergence from real hardware, and not
something to explain away via the 0x5B5800 object's lifetime. Real
hardware's EAX after the call is 0x00000DC6, a small integer that looks
like a status/index return value, not a pointer -- worth keeping in mind
if the callee's actual identity needs re-confirming next.

**Next step, now precisely scoped**: re-examine the raw x86 bytes (not
just the generated C, which was already checked once but evidently missed

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED: the hash-chain hang is resolved

Followed the systematic bisection plan exactly as specified (verify same
vtable target in both executions; if identical, bisect entry/exit EDI
across the confirmed call chain; find the first divergent function;
compare raw x86 bytes instruction-by-instruction; instrument the ICALL
machinery; prove the exact corruption point before fixing).

**Step 1 -- resolved vtable target**: added `[SCDA-VCALL]` logging at the
dispatch site (0x0004744A). The actual failing call's target is
**0x00045ADE** -- not `sub_000360A3` as first assumed (that address was a
different vtable slot, reached by other "this" objects earlier in the same
run; the bisection against that function was a false lead this whole time).

**Step 2 -- traced sub_00045ADE**: it calls `sub_000457AE`, then either
returns directly or does an indirect tail jump. Confirmed edi=entry value
still intact right up to entering `sub_000457AE`.

**Step 3 -- stack-depth measurement inside sub_000457AE**: rather than
manually re-auditing all ~30 branches of this 330-line function by eye
(error-prone, as an earlier false alarm during this same pass
demonstrated), measured ESP at the post-prologue point vs. immediately
before its final register-restore. **Confirmed a reproducible 16-byte
(4-dword) stack leak** between them.

**Step 4 -- bisected the leak to a single call**: narrowed it, checkpoint
by checkpoint, to the call to `sub_000459CA` at 0x00045974.
`sub_000459CA` pushes ebp/ebx/esi/edi (16 bytes) and tail-jumps into
`sub_00045A1B`'s loop body -- a shared-prologue/shared-epilogue pattern
(the same general disassembler-boundary-detection weakness behind
today's earlier CRC-32 and hash-rehash fixes, but a new flavor: not an
unresolved *loop-continuation* stub this time, but an unresolved
*early-exit tail-jump* stub). `sub_00045A1B`'s own early-exit branch
(character isn't `'*'`) tail-jumps to **0x000459D8**, which nothing else
in the program calls or jumps to directly -- so it was never disassembled
as reachable and fell to the generic unresolved-stub fallback, which
only ever consumed 4 bytes of stack (one dummy return address) instead
of the full 20 bytes (4 pushed registers + the real caller's return
address) any genuine exit from this shared frame needs to unwind.

**Confirmed via raw x86 disassembly** (0x000459D8-0x00045A1A, standalone
XBE parse + capstone): this is a case-insensitive, slash-normalizing
path-character-compare loop -- normalizes `\` to `/`, uppercase-folds
everything else the same way `sub_00039D53` does (a small, self-contained
Latin-1-range `towupper`), compares the two normalized characters, and
either fails, succeeds (both strings hit their terminator), or advances
both pointers by 2 and re-enters `sub_00045A1B`'s loop body.

**Fix**: `scda_pathcmp_continue_000459D8` in `projects/scda/src/
recomp_manual.c` -- reimplements this comparison step in native C (the
algorithm is small and unambiguous from the real bytes) and either
performs the correct shared epilogue (pop edi/esi/ebx/ebp, `esp += 4`) on
exit, or calls back into the already-correctly-translated
`sub_00045A1B()` to continue the loop.

**Confirmed fixed**: rebuild + 40s run shows **zero SCDA-HEARTBEAT
samples** (the hash-chain hang is gone), the process reaches 27,800+
traced PCs (far beyond any previous run), and terminates via a genuine
new crash much further into the program (minidump written,
`SCDA_crash_2026-09-02_09-40-31.dmp`, at pc=0x00077049) instead of
hanging forever. Per the investigation plan, continuing automatically to
the newly-exposed blocker rather than stopping here.

`main` branch untouched throughout.

## 2026-09-02 (cont'd) -- new blocker (sub_00077049 crash): traced to source, confirmed real via xemu, root cause not yet fixed

Followed the specified plan for the new blocker exposed once the
hash-chain hang was fixed.

**CDB crash analysis**: Access violation (0xc0000005) reading
0x00000000EC19836F, at `scda_recomp!sub_00077049+0xb5` --
`mov r9d,[rcx+rax]` where `rax=g_xbox_mem_offset` and `rcx` is the
(translated) guest address `0xEC18836F`. Traced back to the generated
source: `sub_00077049` is a `free()`-style allocator entry point called
via `sub_00077176` (a thin wrapper) from `sub_0003EDDE`
(`operator delete`-shaped), itself called from `sub_0029FA18` (a generic
global delete dispatcher used from ~200+ call sites across the binary,
per `grep`). The actual failing call site was pinned precisely by adding
return-address logging: **`sub_00045626`** (retaddr `0x00045636`), a
small per-member destructor helper -- `eax = MEM32(ecx + 0xC); if (eax)
delete(eax);`. The garbage value `0xEC188373` is already present in that
field the moment `sub_00045626` reads it -- confirmed via
`[SCDA-77049-TRACE]` logging at every hop, present from `sub_0029FA18`'s
own entry, i.e. **the corruption is not introduced anywhere in the
delete/free call chain itself** -- the pointer was already wrong before
any of this code ran.

**Object identity**: `sub_00045626` is called with `ecx` = a small guest
address (observed: `0x0000FFF8`), the *last* of a series of same-sized
(0x1C/28-byte) objects at addresses `0xFF6C, 0xFF88, 0xFFA4, 0xFFC0,
0xFFDC, 0xFFF8` (matches the pre-existing `[SCDA-VECTOR-ERASE]`
instrumentation, which shows the five *earlier* objects in this same
series being destructed cleanly with `data=0x00000000`, i.e. correctly
null). Only the **last** object in the series has a garbage field --
the classic shape of an off-by-one/uninitialized-tail-element bug in
whatever constructs this array, not a corruption introduced during
destruction.

**xemu ground truth** (per the "use xemu early" instruction): traced
real hardware at the exact same branch point (`sub_00045626`,
`0x00045620+0x30`, real disc). Across 7 real-hardware samples, the
freed pointer is *always* a plausible heap address (`0x0081bfb0,
0x0081d030, 0x0084f670, 0x00871f80, 0x00af7010, 0x00a14b60,
0x009ca6e0` -- all sane `0x008x`/`0x00ax` range). **Never garbage.**
This conclusively rules out "expected Xbox behavior" -- it is a genuine
recomp bug, matching the classification "invalid object/vtable state"
from an incomplete/uninitialized construction, not an ICALL-resolution,
register-preservation, or lifter/flag-semantics issue (those categories
were the right things to check first, per the investigation checklist,
and are now ruled out for this specific bug by the evidence above).

**Not yet fixed**: the exact construction site for this small-object
array (what builds the series ending at `0xFF6C`.."0xFFF8", and why the

been located. Given today's established pattern (three confirmed
disassembler-boundary/shared-epilogue bugs already fixed this session),
a similar split-function issue in the constructor loop is a reasonable
first hypothesis for next time, but per the explicit instruction not to
assume a "bad function boundary" without proof -- this needs its own
fresh trace (starting from wherever allocates/constructs this object
series) before proposing a fix.
