## 2026-09-04 (continued 30): `sub_000412FE` wild-vtable-pointer crash
root-caused and FIXED -- `_fixup_icall_esp_save`'s prologue-clamp
scanner didn't skip the frame-publish lines every standard-prologue
function emits, so a failed indirect call rewound `g_esp` back over
the function's own callee-saved-register frame; per the user's
staged plan (guest-PC first, xemu only where the local evidence still
leaves an open question), the bug proved fully provable from the
generated C alone and never needed a live xemu comparison

**Traced the host crash to guest semantics first** (per the user's
explicit "don't fixate on host addresses" instruction). The minidump's
`mov edx, dword ptr [rcx+rax]` at `sub_000412FE+0x23f` sits inside the
runtime's inlined `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` bookkeeping (`g_icall_source =
0x00041327u; ...`), which pins the guest PC precisely: the original
XBE at `0x00041327` is

```
0004130F: mov edi, ecx              ; edi = this
0004131A: mov eax, dword ptr [edi]  ; eax = this->vtbl
00041325: mov ecx, edi
00041327: call dword ptr [eax+0x48] ; virtual call, vtbl slot 18
```

an ordinary virtual dispatch through `this`'s own vtable pointer. The
crash is the read of that vtable pointer's slot 18 itself -- meaning
`eax` (`this->vtbl`, read one instruction earlier) was already
garbage. `func_id` places `sub_000412FE` in `game_vtable`/`cls_120`
(vtable `0x004F6420`, slot 6), so this is a method calling another
virtual method on its own `this` -- the object's own vtable pointer,
not some unrelated pointer, was corrupted.

**Traced the object identity, not just the load, per the user's "don't
stop at the crash load" instruction**: the caller, `sub_00043455`,
passes `this` as a *global, hardcoded constant* -- `mov esi,
0x005E6E20` -- reused across three separate virtual-call sites in the
same loop body (`0x434f5`, `0x43540`, `0x43561`, each `mov ecx, esi;
call ...`). The call immediately before the one that crashes,
`sub_00041F56`, was already visible in the very first crash log this
session captured (before this investigation even started) as an
`[ABI]` violation: `esi 005E6E20->00041F00 edi 005E6E20->00042055` --
esi/edi coming back from that call holding values that look like guest
code addresses, not the global object's address. Since `sub_00043455`
reuses `esi` unchanged across all three call sites, a callee that
fails to preserve it corrupts every subsequent virtual call in the
loop, and `sub_000412FE` is simply the next one down that dies on it.

**Root cause, in `tools/recomp/translator.py`'s
`_fixup_icall_esp_save`**: this pass inserts `{ uint32_t _icall_esp =
g_esp; ... RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE(...); }` around each indirect-call site so
a failed lookup (`RECOMP_ICALL_IS_CODE` rejecting the target -- exactly
the `[ICALL] target 0x00000000 is not code` warnings already visible
in every crash log this session) can roll `g_esp` back to its
pre-argument value instead of leaking pushed arguments. Two mechanisms
decide where that save point lands:

1. A push/pop *count* comparison classifies a register as "the
   function's own callee-saved frame" (stop the backward scan here) vs
   "an argument" (absorb it and keep scanning) -- `push count <= pop
   count` means saved. `sub_00041F56` pushes `esi` **14** times (the
   original x86 idiom `xor esi,esi` then reuses the zero repeatedly as
   an argument value across all three of its own virtual calls) but
   pops it only **once** (the epilogue's real restore) -- `14 <= 1` is
   false, so the count heuristic never recognises the prologue push as
   a save at all.
2. A **positional** fallback exists specifically for this case: walk
   forward from the function's own entry label through its literal
   `push ebp; mov ebp, esp; sub esp, N; push ebx; push esi; push edi`
   prologue, and clamp the save point to never land above the end of
   that walk -- regardless of what the count heuristic decided. This
   is the mechanism that was supposed to catch `sub_00041F56`.

The positional walk breaks on `sub_00041F56` (and on **every**
standard-prologue function in the codebase) because `_lift_mov()`
unconditionally emits two more lines right after `ebp = esp;` --
`g_ebp = ebp; /* publish frame for frameless callees */` and
`g_seh_ebp = ebp;` (`lifter.py:1320,1329`, added so a frameless callee
reached through a tail jump inherits the right frame) -- and the
walk's sequential check expects `esp = esp - N;` to appear
*immediately* after `ebp = esp;`. It does not: those two publish lines
sit in between, the check fails to match, and the walk stops two lines
early, landing on `g_ebp = ebp;` -- **before** the `push ebx/esi/edi`
run it exists to protect. With both mechanisms defeated, the save
point for `sub_00041F56`'s first indirect call landed at the very top
of the function, before its own prologue pushes. Since the icall's
target does fail validation on some runs (the null-icall warnings
right before this crash in every log), `g_esp = saved_esp` on that
failure path rewinds `g_esp` back over `push ebx; push esi; push
edi` -- and the function's own epilogue, still trusting its normal
stack offsets, later pops `edi`/`esi`/`ebx` from three slots that were
never the real saves, handing the caller back whatever three unrelated
stack words happened to sit there (here, guest code-address-shaped
values -- likely leftover `PUSH32(esp, <return-address literal>)`
bookkeeping from a nearby call). This is a generic bug: it affects
every function with the standard `push ebp; mov ebp,esp` prologue
*and* an indirect call in its first basic block *and* a callee-saved
register that is also reused as a repeated argument value elsewhere in
the same function (the specific combination the count heuristic
misses) -- not specific to SCDA or to this one function.

**Fix** (`tools/recomp/translator.py`, `_fixup_icall_esp_save`'s
prologue-detection walk): after matching `ebp = esp;`, skip the two
frame-publish lines (`g_ebp = ebp; ...` then `g_seh_ebp = ebp;`, each
optional/independent) before checking for `esp = esp - N;`. ~20 lines,
comments cite the exact failure shape found here.

**Regression test added**: `test_icall_save_clamp_skips_the_frame_publish_lines`
in `tools/recomp/test_call_retaddr.py`, reproducing `sub_00041F56`'s
generated-code shape (including the two publish lines) and asserting
the save point still lands after the `PUSH32(esp, ebx)` prologue push.
Ran the full `tools/recomp/test_*.py` suite: all pass except the same
3 pre-existing NEG/carry-flag failures already documented as unrelated
from the v0.7.x merge (`test_lifter_carry`), confirmed unaffected by
this change.

**Regenerated and rebuilt**: disasm unchanged (this is a `tools/recomp`
codegen fix, not a disassembly one); recomp translated 26,679/26,679,
0 failed. Verified directly in the regenerated
`recomp_0001.c`: `sub_00041F56`'s `_icall_esp` save now sits
*after* `PUSH32(esp, ebx); PUSH32(esp, esi); PUSH32(esp, edi);`,
exactly where it belongs. Canonical rebuild clean.

## 2026-09-04 (continued 31): `sub_003675D7` wcscpy-into-garbage-pointer
crash -- `0x0005EECE` disassembly gap found, statically proven, and
FIXED via a seed (a generic engine-level fix was tried and reverted
after it reopened the 2,482x duplicate-alias cluster); the fix is
correct but does not resolve the crash, because the true cause turned
out to be one layer deeper -- a CRT constructor that never runs, so
the game's real heap allocator never replaces its null-object
placeholder. That is the next boot blocker, not yet investigated.

**Guest-PC and semantics determined first, exactly as before**: the
crash instruction `sub_003675D7+0x88: mov word ptr [rcx+rax], dx`
maps to guest `0x003675DF`, inside a two-instruction wide-char copy
loop (`MEM16(ecx) = LO16(eax); ecx+=2; edx+=2; if (...) goto`) --
`sub_003675D7` is a plain `wcscpy(dst=ecx, src=edx)` (params at
`[esp+4]`/`[esp+8]`), confirmed against the generated C and the
original XBE disassembly. The crash is the very first write: `ecx`
(the destination) is already `0x74000000`-shaped garbage before the
copy starts.

**Traced the pointer backward, call by call, not just the crash
load**: `sub_003675D7` is reached only through a 5-byte tail-jump
thunk (`sub_00067886`) from `sub_000370F1`, a `CStringW`-style
"append" method. Its shape: call a length-of(source) helper, call
`sub_000A8D0A` (grow `this`'s length/capacity fields by that much),
re-read `this`'s buffer pointer (`MEM32(esi)`, freshly, since growth
can reallocate), compute the append position (`buffer + old_len*2 -
2`), then `wcscpy` the new text there. `sub_000A8D0A` itself grows
`this+4`/`this+8` (length/capacity) unconditionally, and when growth
is needed calls `sub_001E460F` -- the actual allocator dispatch --
storing whatever it returns directly into `this+0` (the buffer
pointer), no null check.

**`sub_001E460F` disassembled**: `ecx = MEM32(0x005B57F8)` (the
global "current allocator" object), `eax = MEM32(ecx)` (its vtable),
then an indirect call through `MEM32(eax+4)` (vtable slot 1),
`g_icall_source = 0x001E462Eu`. This exact `g_icall_source` value has
appeared in every `[SCDA-ICALL-RING]`/ABI dump captured all session,
always with `target=0x0005EECE` -- always failing
`RECOMP_ICALL_IS_CODE`. `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`'s failure path sets
`eax = 0` on a rejected target, which `sub_001E460F` then stores
straight into the buffer pointer -- so the buffer was null from the
very first allocation, growing further with each append (the length
field keeps climbing correctly) while the buffer stays 0, and the
final `wcscpy` writes to `0 + huge_offset`, landing at
`0x74000000`-ish.

**Statically proved `0x0005EECE` is a genuine, distinct entry point
the disassembler dropped**, not data or an artifact: the global
allocator singleton lives at `0x005B5ADC` (its initial value, read
directly from the XBE's `.data` section -- this object is
compile-time-constant, not runtime-allocated). Its vtable is at
`0x004FD944` in `.rdata`, a real static vtable, read directly:

```
slot 0 (+0x0):  0x0005EEC9   (detected -- called_by 0x00072CBD)
slot 1 (+0x4):  0x0005EECE   (NOT detected)
slot 2 (+0x8):  0x0003E60B
slot 3 (+0xC):  0x0003E60E
slot 4-6:       0x004528E7 (shared)
slot 7 (+0x1C): 0x0003E60E
```

`0x0005EECE` sits 5 bytes after `0x0005EEC9` and disassembles to a
complete, independent 2-instruction stub (`xor eax, eax; ret 0x14`),
its own distinct stack-cleanup immediate (`0x14`, vs. slot 0's
`0x10`) proving it is a *separate* method, not a continuation of slot
0's body -- MSVC packs runs of trivial COM-style null-object stub
methods like this back-to-back with nothing marking a boundary
between them (this block also holds three more undetected/unreferenced
stub instances at `0x0005ED3`/`0x5ED8`/`0x5EDD`).

**Root cause in `_pass_data_ptr_targets`**
(`tools/disasm/functions.py`): the data-table scan does find
`0x0005EECE` (it is a genuine pointer into executable bytes in
`.rdata`), but rejects it because it falls inside the range an
*earlier* alias (`0x0005EEC9`, itself alias-detected via
`_pass_tail_jump_targets`) already claims -- the exact range check
this session added earlier to fix the 2,482x duplicate-alias bug
(`ffe089d`). That check is correct for the bug it was built for (many
unrelated pointers landing inside one large undetected function,
which really is one function, not many) but wrong for this shape (two
genuinely distinct, individually vtable-referenced short stubs that
merely sit close together with no internal boundary to tell them
apart).

**A generic fix was attempted and reverted.** Tried teaching
`_pass_data_ptr_targets` to distinguish the two shapes with a tightly
capped (`max_insns=8`) probe from the *new* candidate's own address,
accepting it as a separate alias only when it resolves to a `ret`
well before the already-claimed alias's inherited end (added
`DisasmEngine._probe_returning_end`/refactored
`probes_as_returning_body` to share it). This correctly accepted
`0x0005EECE` -- but also let through **867** duplicate aliases for
the *exact* `0x004620B0` cluster the 2,482x fix collapsed to 1,
because a large real function apparently has enough internal points
that reach *some* `ret` within 8 instructions that instruction count
alone does not separate "a short independent stub" from "a
rediscovery of the same big body". Not safe to ship a fix that
reopens an already-fixed 2GB-image-size regression for one address;
reverted the bypass in `functions.py` (kept the harmless
`_probe_returning_end` refactor, dropped the now-unused
`probe_short_returning_end` wrapper it briefly grew).

**Fixed narrowly instead, the way Seeds 33-36 and `0x00036603` were
this session**: added `0x0005EECE` to
`projects/scda/function_seeds.json` with the full static/runtime
evidence above. `_pass_seed_aliases` (already hardened against the
same range-check gap earlier this session) picks it up cleanly.

*failed lookup*; it is null because the game is, correctly, calling a
real "do nothing" allocator. The actual bug is one layer further
back: something is supposed to replace that null allocator with a
real one, and never does.

**Confirmed via a second, targeted trace** (temporarily reusing the
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` slot, cleaned up afterward):
`function_seeds.json` already documents `0x0004449C` as "the CRT
constructor thunk 0x0045A6B0 target... calls sub_0003EB58 to replace
the null allocator at 0x005B57F8 with the real allocator object
0x005B1EF0" (an existing seed from earlier this project's work, added
for a different reason -- a disassembly-boundary gap -- but it names
exactly this mechanism). Traced both: `0x0004449C` **never fires, not
once**, in the whole run; every `sub_000360E1` (temp-CStringW
constructor) entry, all the way to the crash, sees
`MEM32(0x005B57F8) == 0x005B5ADC` -- the null allocator, unchanged
from its static initial value, never replaced.

**Conclusion**: the `0x0005EECE` disassembly gap is closed, correctly
and generically (a real, distinct entry point the disassembler now
recognises, via the established seed mechanism, with no regression
risk to the already-fixed 2,482x cluster). It was not, however, this
session's actual boot blocker -- that is why `0x0004449C` never runs,
which stays open for the next session. Candidates not yet
distinguished: the constructor call chain leading to `0x0004449C`
itself never being reached (a different, upstream code-path issue);
the call existing but its own indirect-call target failing
(`RECOMP_ICALL_IS_CODE` rejecting it, matching this session's
recurring failure-masking pattern); or a disassembly-coverage gap in
the constructor-dispatch table itself, the same class as

## 2026-09-04 (continued 33): NtQueryVirtualMemory spin loop root-caused and FIXED -- a MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION field-order bug in bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory. Massive boot progress: past UMD/disc reads into worker-thread allocator activity. New blocker: 256MB heap allocation request exhausts the 48MB Xbox heap.

Continuation of continued 32's new blocker (indefinite NtQueryVirtualMemory
spin, ordinal 217, constant guest ESP, hundreds of millions of calls).
Followed the requested static-reconstruction-first methodology.

**Loop reconstructed statically.** The only call site is 0x00371C35
inside sub_00371C2D (a thin 2-argument NtQueryVirtualMemory wrapper,
called from sub_00076849, the memory-pool-claiming loop already named
in bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory's own 2026-09-01 comment). sub_00076849
keeps a 0x1c-byte (28-byte) MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION buffer at
[ebp-0x2c] and repeatedly calls sub_00371C2D(address=[ebp-0x2c],
buffer=&[ebp-0x2c]) -- i.e. the buffer's own BaseAddress field doubles
as both the query's input address and, after the call, the walk's
accumulator. Per iteration: State (buffer+0x10, [ebp-0x1c]) is
compared against 0x10000 (MEM_FREE); if not free, RegionSize
(buffer+0x0C, [ebp-0x20]) is added onto the BaseAddress slot
([ebp-0x2c]) to advance to the next region, and the query repeats.
Exit requires State == MEM_FREE, BaseAddress aligned to a divisor at
0x64d62c, and RegionSize large enough. In compact form:

    query(address) -> {BaseAddress, AllocationBase, AllocationProtect,
                        RegionSize, State, Protect, Type}
    address = address_returned_BaseAddress + RegionSize   (loop's own advance)
    loop again while State != MEM_FREE (or size/alignment insufficient)

**xemu ground truth not needed.** The bug was provable directly by
comparing the exact stack offsets the disassembled game code reads
([ebp-0x2c]=+0x00 BaseAddress, [ebp-0x28]=+0x04 AllocationBase,
[ebp-0x24]=+0x08 AllocationProtect, [ebp-0x20]=+0x0C RegionSize,
[ebp-0x1c]=+0x10 State, [ebp-0x18]=+0x14 Protect, [ebp-0x14]=+0x18
Type -- the standard, well-documented Win32/XDK MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION
layout) against bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory's actual write order.

**Root cause found:** `bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory` (kernel_bridge.c)
wrote the first three fields in the WRONG order: AllocationBase (a
constant 0 in both branches) at +0x00, AllocationProtect at +0x04,
BaseAddress at +0x08 -- instead of BaseAddress at +0x00,
AllocationBase at +0x04, AllocationProtect at +0x08. (+0x0C onward --
RegionSize/State/Protect/Type -- were already correct.) Since the game
reuses +0x00 as its walk accumulator, every call clobbered it with the
constant 0 instead of the real queried address; the following
`address += RegionSize` step then always computed a value depending
only on RegionSize, never on where the walk actually was. With
heap_end/total_ram from xbox_GetHeapEnd()/g_xbox_total_ram this
produces a stable 2-value oscillation (addr -> heap_end-addr -> addr
-> ...) that never lands in the MEM_FREE region above heap_end --
exactly the observed symptom (indefinite spin, constant ESP, zero
forward progress).

**Fix:** reordered the three fields to the correct, standard
BaseAddress/AllocationBase/AllocationProtect layout. Single call site
in the whole game (confirmed via xrefs), so this is a narrowly-scoped,
generic bridge-semantics fix, not an SCDA-specific hardcode -- no
return value was hardcoded, no loop was skipped or forced to succeed.

**Verification.** No disasm/recomp regeneration needed (pure C kernel
fix). Rebuilt via the canonical build\scda_upgrade tree (2026-09-04
18:38, SHA-256
4C93766554918176353271FE3493EA11B0628539F539E44ADB59C408A47DC718).

that never invokes the device emulation) is not yet established; that
is the next concrete question for whoever picks this up, per the
requested threading/plumbing check rather than assuming NV2A register
semantics are at fault.

nothing in the statically-visible code explains how this field
acquires the near-zero value observed live, or what it *should* hold

## 2026-09-04 (continued 35): NV2A PFB-wait spin -- full static+xemu reconstruction, corrected twice, narrowed to a precise, well-evidenced root cause: the D3D device struct is still un-created when the push-buffer flush code runs

Continuation of continued 34's `sub_004A12B0` spin, following the
full static-reconstruction-then-xemu-ground-truth methodology
requested. Two of this entry's own intermediate conclusions turned
out to be wrong and are corrected in place below -- kept visible
rather than silently rewritten, since each correction is itself load-
bearing evidence for what follows.

### Step 1: loop reconstructed statically

`sub_004A12B0` (D3D.asm, called from `sub_004A1600` -> `sub_004A1740`
-> `sub_0049CE00` -> `sub_00077194` -> `sub_000774E6` ->
`sub_000778BC` -> `sub_00077B61`, confirmed live via CDB stacks taken
twice, several seconds apart, both landing at the identical
instruction):

    eax = MEM32(0x4AB668)              ; the global D3D device struct pointer
    eax = MEM32(eax + 0x1C28)          ; a field inside it
    MEM32(eax + 0x100410) |= 0x10000   ; set the "kick" bit
    while (MEM32(eax + 0x100410) & 0x10000) ;   ; wait for hardware to clear it

Compact form:

    query = MEM32(MEM32(0x4AB668) + 0x1C28)
    MEM32(query + 0x100410) |= 0x10000
    loop while MEM32(query + 0x100410) & 0x10000

### Step 2: first hypothesis (NV2A hardware register) -- CORRECTED

Initially matched offset 0x410 (low 16 bits of 0x100410) against
`NV_PFB_WBC` in `nv2a_regs.h` and its `NV_PFB_WBC_FLUSH` bit -- an
exact numeric match, but the wrong explanation. Live CDB memory
inspection of the *actual* address involved showed the polled guest
VA sits near 0x100410-0x1007C0, nowhere close to the real 0xFD000000
NV2A aperture, and traced `struct+0x1C28`'s role in `sub_0049A3D0` to
an embedded shader-constant-cache table, not obviously a pointer slot.
Retracted the hardware-register reading (see the previous, now-
superseded corrections in continued 34 above).

### Step 3: xemu ground truth resolves the ambiguity

Traced `sub_0049A3D0`/`sub_0049D210`/`sub_004A12B0` on real hardware
via `xemu.exe -d exec,cpu -dfilter 0x49a3d0+0x100,0x49ce00+0x4980 -D
<log>` against the retail disc. At the equivalent guest PC
(`0x004A12CE`, right after `mov eax, [eax+0x1C28]`), **EAX = 0xFD000000
exactly** -- QEMU even flags it with `cpu_io_recompile: rewound
execution` (its own I/O-aperture-access detection). This *reinstates*
the original reading: `struct+0x1C28` genuinely is meant to hold the
NV2A aperture base pointer; the earlier "it's just a shader-cache
table" doubt was about the field's *other* use elsewhere
(`sub_0049A3D0`), not this one -- MSVC evidently reuses the same
struct offset for two different purposes depending on code path,
which is why grepping for a plain scalar write to it found nothing.

### Step 4: the real writer, found statically from the xemu-confirmed constant

`grep -in "0xfd000000"` across `D3D.asm` found exactly one hit:
`sub_004A3911` (`mov dword ptr [ecx], 0xfd000000`, then pokes several
more absolute NV2A registers: `0xFD001804`, `0xFD600140`,
`0xFD009140` -- the first of these matches an already-known comment in
`xbox_memory_layout.c`, "Halo faults reading 0xFD001804... a few
instructions after Direct3DCreate8 returns", independently confirming
this is genuine device/NV2A-engine bring-up code). Traced the call
chain: `sub_0049D210` (device creation -- zero-inits a 0x2520-byte
struct at `0x4AB670`, then `mov [0x4AB668], edi` publishes the pointer)
calls `sub_004A2220`, which -- **conditionally** on `sub_004A0F90`
returning non-negative -- passes `ecx = &struct+0x1C28` into
`sub_004A3E04` -> `sub_004A3911`, writing the real base pointer.
`sub_004A0F90` requests a large allocation via `sub_00055936` ->
`sub_0005468B`/`sub_000546CE`; on failure it returns `0x8007000E`
(E_OUTOFMEMORY), and `sub_004A2220` skips the whole base-pointer setup
block on a negative return.

This looked like a complete, tidy chain, especially since this same
run's log already showed `xbox_HeapAlloc: out of memory (requested
268439552, ...)` right before reaching `sub_004A12B0` -- and since
`[0x4ADE04]` (the size fed into this exact allocation) traces back
through `sub_0049D1F0` to `sub_002E6904`, which reads the *same*
`0x6513A4`/`0x6513A8`/`0x6513C8` "launch data" array already
documented (2026-09-03, "continued 11/12") as sometimes empty and
whose corruption was traced to an EDI-preservation bug in
`sub_001D5208`, supposedly fixed and CLOSED as of "continued 21".

### Step 5: instrumented and measured directly -- the OOM chain is a red herring

Added a temporary, narrowly-scoped diagnostic (`[SCDA-NV2ABASE-CHAIN]`,
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` bracketing `sub_004A0F90`-
`sub_004A1300`) to check the hypothesis directly instead of trusting
the coincidence. Result: **`sub_004A0F90` and `sub_004A2220`'s
post-call checkpoint never fire at all.** The only thing that fires is
`sub_004A12B0` itself, exactly once, with **`struct_base
(MEM32(0x4AB668)) = 0x00000000`** -- the device object has not been
created yet by the time this code runs. The 268MB heap-OOM messages
and this call are just adjacent in the log, not causally linked; the
`sub_004A0F90` chain traced in Step 4 is real code that exists and
would explain a *skipped* base-pointer write, but it is not what is
happening here -- `sub_0049D210` (device creation) itself has not run
yet, so there is no struct to skip a field in.

### Step 6: threading hypothesis raised, then CORRECTED

An earlier, less careful CDB stack sample (10-12 frames via plain `k`)
bottomed out at `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx` / `kernel_thunk_dispatch`
/ `sub_00052572`, suggesting this ran on a worker thread racing ahead
of device creation. Verified properly this time with `~*k n 8` (every
thread's stack, not just the current one): **the spin runs on thread 0
(the main/only game thread)**. The process has 5 threads total: thread
0 (main, in the spin), threads 1-3 (generic Windows thread-pool
workers, `NtWaitForWorkViaWorkerFactory` -- OS infrastructure, nothing
to do with the game), and thread 4 running **`nv2a_ack_thread`**, our
own runtime's NV2A hardware-acknowledgement simulator, idle in
`SleepEx`. The earlier worker-thread reading was a frame-walk artifact
from over-trusting a deep, unverified `k` dump through several
frameless functions -- exactly the pitfall this session already knew
about and had specifically taken care to re-verify with paired samples
for the *shallow* frames each previous time. Retracted; this is
ordinary single-threaded main-path code, further up the same call
chain identified in Step 1/CDB.

### Step 7: the existing NV2A_ACK mechanism already handles this exact register -- and is not the problem

`xbox_memory_layout.c`'s `nv2a_ack_thread` (a real, already-shipped
mechanism, not something to build) walks a table `NV2A_ACK[]` clearing
hardware "busy" bits against the *real* NV2A aperture (`g_nv2a_memory`,
based at Xbox VA `0xFD000000`) once per loop iteration, specifically
because "against plain RAM the bit is set and nothing ever clears it,
so the title spins forever" -- and its very first table entry is
**`{ 0x100410, 0x00010000u }, /* PFB flush kick, Halo 0x001EF930 */`**,
labelled with the *identical* handshake shape (`mov [eax+0x100410],
edx; L: test [eax+0x100410], 0x10000; jne L`) already fixed for Halo.
This mechanism is correct and already covers our exact register/bit --
it just cannot help here, because the guest is polling `struct+0x1C28
+ 0x100410` where `struct+0x1C28` is near-zero (guest VA
~0x100410-0x1007C0, ordinary low RAM), not the real
`0xFD000000 + 0x100410` aperture address `nv2a_ack_thread` actually
services. Confirms this is purely a **base-pointer/initialization-
ordering** problem, not a missing-hardware-emulation problem.

### Where this leaves it

Root cause, precisely stated: **by the time the main thread's D3D
push-buffer flush code (`sub_0049CE00` -> ... -> `sub_004A12B0`) runs,
the global D3D device object at `0x4AB670` (published via
`MEM32(0x4AB668)`) has not been created** -- `sub_0049D210` (device
creation) either has not executed yet in program order, or executed
and was subsequently reset (a second write site, `sub_0049D2A0`-area,
does `mov dword ptr [0x4AB668], 0`, matching a device-destroy/reset
path -- not yet checked which). Given `struct_base=0` is dereferenced
completely unguarded here (`test byte ptr [esi+8], 4` with no
esi-null check), a real Xbox executing this exact instruction sequence
with `esi=0` would fault outright -- since Halo/SCDA both ship and
this is stock game code, real hardware provably never reaches this
call with the device un-created, meaning **something upstream that
gates or orders this call differently on real hardware is missing or
reordered in scda_recomp**. That is the concrete next step: find what
calls `sub_0049CE00`'s ancestor chain, and why it runs (or is allowed
to run) before `sub_0049D210`, rather than continuing to chase the
NV2A/heap-allocation angle further -- both are now confirmed
unrelated to the actual failure.

Removed the temporary `[SCDA-NV2ABASE-CHAIN]` hooks and reset
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` to idle. No src/tools changes survive
from this entry (investigation/documentation only) -- confirmed via
`git status`.

`2408fc40c920c8ff07ed880ee5d4a0d8e06205abb90e2729242fc32dcfba7474`
(identical behaviour to the continued-33 build; no code changes this

## 2026-09-04 (continued 36): traced the "why does device creation not run yet" question -- found and fixed a real constructor disasm gap along the way, but it does not resolve the sub_004A12B0 spin; root cause narrowed to a missing null-check whose correct behaviour depends on real-vs-zeroed low guest memory

Continuation of continued 35's open question ("why does
sub_0049CE00 -> ... -> sub_004A12B0 run before sub_0049D210?").
Traced upward through the static call graph and found, then fixed, a
real bug -- but it turned out to be a red herring for this specific
symptom. Documented in full since the fix itself is correct and
worth keeping, and the negative result narrows the remaining
question meaningfully.

### The constructor gap (real bug, fixed, kept)

`sub_0049D210`'s three callers are `sub_0003FCA5`, `sub_0003FCDD`, and
`sub_002E2BB1`. Traced `sub_002E2BB1` up one level
(`sub_002E75CE`, called_by: [] -- i.e. reachable only via a vtable,
never via a direct call/jump our xref scanner tracks). Found its
owning vtable by searching the XBE's raw bytes for the literal
pointer `0x002E75CE`: exactly one hit, at file offset `0x5655e0` (VA
`0x005696D8`+offset), inside a clean 78-entry vtable (`0x5696D8`-
`0x569810`) alongside other already-known functions
(`sub_002E6904`, the launch-data-array reader from continued 33/35).
Found the vtable's own installer by searching for xrefs to
`0x5696D8`: two hits, `0x002E738B` (a constructor) and `0x002E7AC9`
(a destructor). `0x002E738B` sits inside an **undetected disasm
gap** immediately after `sub_002E7367` (`0x002E7367`-`0x002E7381`) --
confirmed by reading the raw bytes there directly: a genuine,
substantial (528-byte) constructor (`push ebx/esi/edi; mov esi,ecx;
call sub_002E68E0; mov dword ptr [esi], 0x5696D8; ...`), reached only
via a `jump` xref (tail jump from `0x002E7A9B`, no call edge), and
confirmed to be an **unresolved stub** in the current build
(`recomp_stubs_unresolved.c`: `/* 0x002E7381: not detected */`) --
the exact same "shared-tail/constructor swallowed by a preceding
function's boundary" shape as Seeds 33-36 and `0x0005EECE`/the 1,419-
entry CRT table this session.

Seeded `0x002E7381` (mechanical, well-cited evidence: the exact
vtable-pointer immediate it writes matches the vtable containing our
target method exactly). Regenerated: 28,111 -> 28,113 functions,
`sub_002E7381` now a proper 528-byte function ending exactly at the
next already-known boundary (`0x002E7591`), duplicate-end-address
count unchanged (still max 4, no regression). recomp translated
28,113/28,113, 0 failed.

### The fix does not resolve the sub_004A12B0 spin -- verified directly

Rebuilt and re-instrumented (temporary `[SCDA-DEVCREATE]` hooks,
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` reused across several rounds -- one
round's whitelist edit briefly dropped two of the four hooked
addresses by accident, caught by their lines simply never firing
despite CDB confirming the code did execute, and fixed before drawing
conclusions from it). With the constructor fix in place:
**`sub_0049D210` still never fires. `sub_0049CE00` still fires with
`struct_base = 0x00000000`.** A CDB stack sample confirms the process
is stuck at the exact same `sub_004A12B0` spin as before, same call
chain. The constructor fix is real and shipped, but it was not the
mechanism gating device creation for *this* code path -- `sub_002E75CE`
and its whole ancestor chain were a hypothesis about what *should*
trigger device creation, not something confirmed to be part of the
actual failing call sequence (which never includes it -- the real
call stack is `sub_00077B61` -> `sub_000778BC` -> `sub_000774E6` ->
`sub_00077194` -> `sub_0049CE00` -> `sub_004A1740` -> `sub_004A1600`
-> `sub_004A12B0`, entirely within the memory-allocator's debug-
marker-emission path, never touching `sub_0003FCA5`/`sub_002E75CE`
at all).

### Refined next hypothesis

`sub_0049CE00` dereferences `MEM32(0x4AB668)` (the device struct
pointer) completely unguarded -- `mov ebp, [0x4AB668]` immediately
followed by `mov ebx, [ebp+0x1A08]`, no null check anywhere. Two
explanations remain open, and this session did not have time to
distinguish them:

1. **Something upstream should gate this call and doesn't in
   scda_recomp** -- i.e. real hardware genuinely never reaches
   `sub_0049CE00` (via this allocator path) before device creation,
   for a reason not yet found (a different ICALL-failure-masking gap,
   a missing check elsewhere, or a boot-order divergence upstream of
   everything traced so far).
2. **Reaching this code with a null device pointer is itself normal on
   both platforms**, and the actual divergence is in what `[ebp+0x1A08]`
   and friends read when `ebp=0`: on real Xbox hardware, low guest
   memory near address 0 holds real, meaningful kernel structures
   (the console's own low-memory kernel data), while scda_recomp's
   equivalent low addresses are just zeroed RAM -- so the *same*
   `ebp=0` state could take a completely different branch on real
   hardware (skipping the flush) versus scda_recomp (triggering it),
   without device-creation timing being different at all.

Explanation 2 would be a much deeper, more general finding (bearing on
any future "reads through a low/null pointer behave differently"
case, not just this one), and is the leading theory given how many of
this session's other bugs have been silent-failure/wrong-defaults
patterns rather than pure ordering bugs. Not yet distinguished --
next session should check, via xemu, exactly what real hardware's
`[ebp+0x1A08]`/`[ebp+0x1C28]` etc. actually contain when `ebp` is
observed to be near-zero at this call site (if that state occurs on
real hardware at all), rather than continuing to chase the call graph
further upward.

Verified clean: final build with diagnostics fully removed
(`scda_recomp.exe`, 2026-09-04 21:25, SHA-256
`c03c424f9272e6ad608820e9dfdb141d0024adb8601c52b0667c1978f46ec8ec`)
reproduces the identical, crash-free spin with no regression.

`0x002E7381`), `projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` (comment/idle reset
only). `recomp_manual.c` has zero net changes (temporary hooks added
and fully removed across several rounds this entry).


## 2026-09-04 (continued 37): xemu ground truth via QEMU gdbstub -- "explanation 2" (real-vs-zeroed low memory) from continued 36 is DISPROVEN; "explanation 1" (something upstream must gate device creation) confirmed as the right track

Followed up on continued 36's open question directly against real
hardware, per the standing methodology, since local static evidence
had stopped being conclusive.

### Method

`xemu.exe` is QEMU-based and exposes a standard GDB remote-serial
stub (`-s` = `-gdb tcp::1234`). Wrote a small ad-hoc Python client
(no `gdb` binary available in this environment) implementing just
enough of the protocol to set a software breakpoint (`Z0,<addr>,1`),
continue (`c`), and read registers/memory (`g`, `m<addr>,<len>`) once
stopped.

### Result: MEM32(0x4AB668) is already valid the very first time sub_0049CE00 runs

Set a breakpoint at `0x0049CE05` (the instruction right after
`sub_0049CE00`'s entry, `mov ebp, dword ptr [0x4AB668]`) on a fresh
boot and continued once. First hit, direct memory read (not a
register capture, so unaffected by the reconnect issues below):

    MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x004AB670

-- the real, valid device-struct pointer, matching `sub_0049D210`'s
own published value exactly. This is the *first* time this guest
address executes during the whole boot, and the device is already
created. This directly disproves continued 36's "explanation 2"
(that reaching this code with a null device is normal on both
platforms and the divergence is in what garbage low memory contains):
real hardware simply never reaches this code with a null device at
all, not even once. "Explanation 1" -- something on real hardware
gates or orders this call so it never happens before device creation,
and that gate is missing or broken in scda_recomp -- is the
confirmed direction.

### What didn't work: pinning down the exact caller

Attempted to catch `sub_0049D210` (device creation) itself with a
second breakpoint to read its return address and identify the real
trigger. This was not reliable: the first attempt's client crashed on
a read timeout while a stop reply was apparently still in flight, and
subsequent reconnects to the same gdbstub produced visibly corrupted/
misordered packets (a `qSupported` query once came back as a stale
`T02thread:01` stop packet) -- an artifact of this ad-hoc client, not
of the hardware. A clean, fresh boot with a single long-lived
connection then waited a full 10 minutes without the breakpoint firing
at all, suggesting `sub_0049D210` either runs much later than
`sub_0049CE00` (i.e. the two are not directly related the way
continued 36 assumed -- something else populates or already holds a
valid `0x4AB668` before device "creation" proper runs) or requires
interaction this unattended run never produces. Not resolved; the
`sub_0049D210` ancestor chain traced statically in continued 36 may
not even be the right thing to keep following -- what actually matters
is finding what, on real hardware, guarantees `0x4AB668` is valid by
the time the memory allocator's debug-marker path can run, which may
not be `sub_0049D210` at all.

### Where this leaves it

Confirmed direction for the next session: something in scda_recomp's
early boot sequence is missing or failing silently, such that
`MEM32(0x4AB668)` is still 0 when `sub_0049CE00` first runs -- this is
now established as abnormal (real hardware never observes it), not an
artifact of low-memory content differences. The concrete next step is
to find whatever sets `0x4AB668` to a valid pointer *before* first
reaching `sub_0049CE00` on real hardware (not necessarily
`sub_0049D210` -- that assumption is now unconfirmed), most likely via
a cleaner, single-session xemu watchpoint on the `0x4AB668` write
(the same successful technique already used for `0x6513A4`/`0x6513A8`
in "continued 12") rather than chasing call-graph ancestors by
static reasoning alone.

No code changes this entry (xemu ground-truth investigation only).


## 2026-09-04 (continued 38): xemu QEMU-gdbstub ground truth pins the real device-creation call chain; scda_recomp's divergence narrowed to a ~0x300-byte, no-`ret` span inside sub_00048B15 with no ordinary exit

Direct follow-up to continued 37's plan (a live write-watchpoint on
`0x4AB668` instead of further static call-graph guessing). Wrote two
reusable scripts under `tools/debug/` (`xemu_4ab668_watchpoint.py`,
modeled directly on the existing `xemu_6513a8_watchpoint.py`; and
`xemu_2e75ce_caller.py`/`xemu_4ab668_caller.py` for stack-window
follow-ups) implementing just enough of the GDB remote-serial protocol
to arm software breakpoints/write-watchpoints and read registers/
memory over `xemu.exe -s` (QEMU's gdbstub) -- no `gdb` binary is
available in this environment.

### Confirmed: real hardware's device pointer is set at t=1.48s by sub_0049D210

Booted with `-s -S` (CPU frozen at reset) so the watchpoint arms before
any code runs, avoiding continued 37's "missed the write, value already
non-null" problem. `Z2,4ab668,4` (write watchpoint) fires exactly
twice: once at `t=0.20s`, `eip=0x8002EAAA` (kernel .bss zero-fill,
`rep stosd`/`rep stosb`, `0x4AB668` just happens to fall inside a bulk
zeroed range -- not a meaningful write), then at **`t=1.48s`,
`eip=0x0049D259`, value `0x00000000 -> 0x004AB670`** -- and the raw
bytes at that EIP (`c705a8bf4a0001000000893578b64a00`) decode to
exactly `mov dword ptr [0x4ABFA8],1; mov dword ptr [0x4AB678],esi`,
matching `sub_0049D210`'s own disassembly at `0x0049D259`/`0x0049D263`
byte-for-byte. This is unambiguous, direct confirmation (not a register
capture, immune to the reconnect corruption below) that `sub_0049D210`
runs and publishes the real device pointer very early in boot, well
before any UMD/disc activity.

### Confirmed: the real caller is sub_002E75CE -> sub_002E2BB1 -> sub_0049D210

Broke directly at `sub_002E75CE`'s own entry (`0x002E75CE`, which has a
normal prologue per `functions.json`, so `[esp+0]` at entry is reliably
the true return address -- no stack-depth guessing needed). Result:
return address `0x00049819`, i.e. the caller is the call site at
`0x00049816` (`call dword ptr [eax+0x68]`, exactly 6 bytes earlier, an
`ff5068` vtable-slot-26 call). `ecx` (this) `= 0x008DDB30`. Resolved
`0x00049816` statically: it lives inside `sub_0004934E`, a 5,202-byte,
`called_by: []` (vtable-dispatch-only) mega-function whose OWN seed
predates this session (`function_seeds.json`: "Initializer continuation
reached by the direct jmp at 0x00048F18; previously emitted as an
unresolved tail-call stub"). `0x00048F18` (`jmp 0x4934e`) sits at the
very end of `sub_00048B15` -- **the same "main game initializer"
function this whole project's history (from 2026-08-19 through today)
already identifies as `sub_00048B15`, called once, directly, from
`sub_00054722`** (itself adjacent to the XBE entry point).

An earlier attempt to catch `sub_0049D210` directly with a fresh
breakpoint (not frozen-boot) was unreliable -- the client crashed on a
read timeout mid-wait, and a reconnect to the same gdbstub produced
visibly corrupted/misordered packets (a `qSupported` query once came
back as a stale `T02thread:01` stop packet). Not trusted; superseded
by the frozen-boot watchpoint approach above, which is clean.

### A necessary self-correction: status140=1 is normal on both platforms, not a fault condition

Before accepting `sub_00048B15`'s own tail (`0x48EE1` fallthrough,
gated by `cmp [0x5ED140],0; jne sub_00048F1D`) as "the" path real
hardware uses, checked this project's own much older history
(`docs/SCDA_WORKLOG.md`, 2026-09-02/09-03 entries around
`MEM32(0x5ED140)`): **every single trace this whole project has ever
taken shows `status140` (`MEM32(0x005ED140)`) as non-zero, confirmed
via xemu at a nearby checkpoint (`0x00048C9A`) to be non-zero on real
hardware too.** That means the `jne 0x48f1d` branch at `0x48ED1` is
what real hardware actually takes here as well -- **not** the `0x48EE1`
fallthrough tail this session initially assumed was the device-creation
path. Re-checked `sub_00048F1D`'s own `calls_to`: it calls
`sub_00071B49` directly too -- the exact same function
`sub_00048B15`'s own fallthrough tail calls right before its `jmp
sub_0004934E`. **Both branches converge on `sub_00071B49`**, which is
therefore the real shared gateway toward the `sub_0004934E` ->
`sub_002E75CE` -> `sub_002E2BB1` -> `sub_0049D210` chain confirmed
above -- not the `0x48EE1` fallthrough exclusively as first assumed.
This correction does not affect the core finding below, which sits
entirely upstream of this branch.

### The core, still-open finding: scda_recomp diverges before either branch is even reached

Instrumented `sub_00048B15` directly (temporary hooks, since removed):
confirmed live that execution reaches `0x00048BBE` (`status140 <- 1`,
matching the existing `[SCDA-STARTUP-STATUS]` watcher exactly) but
**never reaches `0x00048EC9` or `0x00048ED1`, ~0x300 bytes later in the
same function**, despite `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` labels genuinely existing at
both addresses in the generated C (confirmed by reading
`recomp_0002.c` directly -- this is not a missing-label artifact like
earlier sessions' `0x004A12CE` mistake). Checked the raw disassembly
for every instruction between `0x48BBE` and `0x48EC9`: **no `ret`
exists anywhere in that span** -- control can only leave via one of its
~20 nested calls
(`sub_00048856`, `sub_00070BDA`, `sub_000715C7`, `sub_00042082`,
`sub_00067886`, `sub_0003E9D9`, `sub_00045647` x2, `sub_00045584`,
`sub_00043455`, two vtable calls (`[eax]`, `[edx+4]`/`[eax+0x14]`),
`sub_00044C15`, `sub_001CAD08`, `sub_001CB603`, `sub_001D589D`,
`sub_00070B06`, `sub_000371A6`, `sub_000370F1`, `sub_00067886` again,
`sub_001D47CF`, `sub_00070854`) never returning normally -- an SEH-
based early exit (unwinding out of `sub_00048B15` entirely on an
exception, rather than a plain `ret`) is the leading hypothesis, not
yet confirmed. Boot visibly continues past this point regardless (UMD
reads, the allocator debug-marker path, etc. all still run later), so
whatever exits `sub_00048B15` here does so in a way its caller
(`sub_00054722`) tolerates and continues from -- consistent with SEH
unwind-and-continue rather than a fatal fault.

One historical lead worth reopening rather than re-deriving from
scratch: a 2026-08-25-dated entry (line ~430 in this file) traces this
*exact* neighbourhood on an older pre-merge build --
`sub_00048B15 -> sub_00042082 at call site 0x00048C0F -> sub_0005355F`
(which "initializes an ANSI path and calls Xbox ordinal 190
(`NtCreateFile`) as an existence/open check") -- and a later entry
explicitly states "The old `sub_00048B15` early-return ... issues are
resolved and must not be treated as current blockers." Given the
substantial `v0.7.x` merge and extensive disasm/seed changes since
then, either this exact fix regressed, or a *different* early-exit in
the same function has appeared -- worth checking first before
re-deriving the divergence point from nothing.

### Next steps (concrete, in order)

1. Bisect the `0x48BBE`-`0x48EC9` span directly (hooks at each call
   site listed above, narrowing which one never returns) rather than
   re-tracing the whole function's history.
2. If a call there fails via SEH, find the fault and its Xbox-side
   handler expectations -- likely another instance of this session's
   recurring "silent ICALL/exception-masking" pattern.
3. Re-check whether the pre-merge `sub_00042082`/`sub_0005355F`/
   `NtCreateFile` lead from 2026-08-25 is still relevant post-merge.

## 2026-09-04 (continued 39): the sub_00048B15 "no-`ret` span" mystery is solved -- it isn't a translation bug, it's the legitimate call chain descending into the already-known sub_004A12B0 spin

Direct bisection of continued 38's open finding (`sub_00048B15` reaches
`0x48BBE` but never `0x48EC9`/`0x48ED1`, no `ret` anywhere in that span).

### Method

Traced every basic-block boundary in `0x48BBE`-`0x48EC9` via a temporary
`[SCDA-48B15-BISECT]` hook (`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` set to that
range, matching whitelist entry added to `scda_trace_pc`'s gate). Since
this span has no internal loop and every conditional jump stays inside
the same window, the address of the *last* hit before the trace goes
silent pins the divergence directly -- no need to guess which of the
~20 nested calls is the culprit one at a time.

**Result: the last hit is `loc_00048CF8`**, which reads a "current
resource/error object" pointer out of the SAME global (`0x005B5800`)
already implicated in the 2026-09-02 EDI-corruption investigation
(`sub_0004721E`'s vtable dispatch through this object) --
`ecx = MEM32(0x5B5800); eax = MEM32(ecx); call [eax]` (vtable slot 0,
arg=1). `loc_00048D04` (the very next block, right after the call)
never fires.

Extended `RECOMP_SCDA_ICALL_PROBE`'s whitelist (`templates/runtime/
recomp_types.h`) with this call's source (`0x00048D02`) to capture the
resolved target, and read the object/vtable/slot-0 values directly
inside the bisection hook (safe: the block doesn't mutate them before
the call). **`obj=0x00F7FDD4 vtbl=0x004F7108 slot0_target=0x00045D0B`**
-- `vtbl=0x4F7108` matches continued 2026-09-02's own confirmed
constructor trace for this exact object exactly, and `0x45D0B` is a
legitimate, in-range code address, not a null or wild pointer.

### The trap: assuming silence meant a hang, when it meant "still running, just deeper"

First read of this result looked exactly like the earlier "silent
ICALL-failure" bug class this whole project has repeatedly found: no
crash, no `[ICALL]` unresolved-target log line, no crash dump, but also
no further progress after 90+ seconds of wall-clock waiting with the
trace window still covering the call target. That combination is what
every previous silent-ICALL bug in this project looked like, so it was
treated as one until directly disproven.

**Attached `cdb` (x64, since `scda_recomp.exe` is a 64-bit host binary
despite emulating a 32-bit Xbox target) to the still-running process**
and got a full stack trace instead of guessing further:

    scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x1d0
    scda_recomp!sub_004A1600+0x7b2
    scda_recomp!sub_004A1740+0xb6
    scda_recomp!sub_0049CE00+0x2a0
    scda_recomp!sub_00077194+0x165b
    scda_recomp!sub_000774E6+0x12cf
    scda_recomp!sub_000778BC+0xea8
    scda_recomp!sub_00077B61+0x14e
    scda_recomp!sub_0003EDCC+0xba
    scda_recomp!sub_001E460F+0x297
    scda_recomp!sub_0007166C+0xc0f
    scda_recomp!sub_00045F02+0x110
    scda_recomp!sub_00045E42+0xa88
    scda_recomp!sub_00045D0B+0x1585
    scda_recomp!sub_00048B15+0x10b9
    scda_recomp!sub_00054722+0x321
    scda_recomp!sub_00054701+0x169
    scda_recomp!sub_000524DA+0x608
    scda_recomp!bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx+0x181
    scda_recomp!kernel_thunk_dispatch+0x212
    scda_recomp!sub_00052572+0x374
    scda_recomp!xbe_entry_point+0x261

**This is decisive: the icall at `0x48CF8` DID resolve, DID call
`sub_00045D0B`, and execution genuinely descended 13 more real stack
frames** (`sub_00045E42` -> `sub_00045F02` -> `sub_0007166C` ->
`sub_001E460F` -> `sub_0003EDCC`) straight into **the exact,
already-known call chain from continued 34-36**
(`sub_00077B61` -> `sub_000778BC` -> `sub_000774E6` -> `sub_00077194` ->
`sub_0049CE00` -> `sub_004A1740` -> `sub_004A1600` -> `sub_004A12B0`,
spinning at the same offset as every prior session's capture). It never
returns to `loc_00048D04` in `sub_00048B15` for the mundane reason that
the callee never returns *at all* -- not because of a masked exception,
a mistranslated icall, or a missing `ret`.

### This unifies two previously-separate investigation threads

Continued 34-36 characterized the `sub_004A12B0` spin and its immediate
callers (`sub_00077194` and below) in detail, but never had the
*upper* half of the call chain -- how boot reaches `sub_00077B61` in
the first place. That upper half is now known precisely: it is
`sub_00048B15`'s own tail region, through the `0x5B5800` transient
"error object" 's vtable slot 0. The `sub_002E75CE`/`sub_002E2BB1`/
`sub_0049D210` chain traced in continued 38 (device-pointer write path)
is real and confirmed, but is a *different, unrelated* branch of
`sub_0004934E` -- not on the path that leads to the spin.

### Root cause: still open, now precisely inherited from continued 36

The spin itself was never fixed; this session only proves *how it's
reached* from `sub_00048B15`, closing the "no-`ret`" mystery without
resolving the underlying blocker. Continued 36's two competing
explanations (both still open) apply unchanged:

1. Something upstream should gate this call and doesn't in
   `scda_recomp` (real hardware never reaches `sub_0049CE00` via this
   path before device creation, for a reason not yet found).
2. Reaching this code with a null device pointer (`sub_0049CE00`'s
   unguarded `mov ebp, [0x4AB668]`) is itself normal on both platforms,
   and the real divergence is what `[ebp+0x1A08]` etc. read when
   `ebp=0` -- real low guest memory holds meaningful kernel structures
   near address 0, scda_recomp's equivalent is just zeroed RAM.

Next session should follow continued 36's own next step: check via
xemu what real hardware's `[ebp+0x1A08]`/`[ebp+0x1C28]` actually
contain when `ebp` is observed near-zero at this exact call site (if
that state occurs on real hardware at all), rather than continuing to
widen the call graph upward -- the upward direction is now fully
mapped from `xbe_entry_point` to the spin.

All temporary hooks removed: `[SCDA-48B15-BISECT]` and the

`templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`. Both files are byte-identical to
their continued-38 state (confirmed via `git diff --stat`, zero
changes). Only `projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` carries a lasting change
(idle trace window reset, comment updated to record the resolution).

-- no crash, identical `sub_004A12B0` spin (same call chain, re-confirmed

## 2026-09-05 (continued 40): xemu ground truth on continued 36's open question -- the vtable dispatch matches real hardware exactly; the divergence is a missing skip/gate somewhere in the sub_00045D0B..sub_0049CE00 chain, not the icall itself or thread ordering

Direct follow-up to continued 39, re-checking continued 36's original
"explanation 1 vs 2" question against real hardware now that the full
upper call chain (`xbe_entry_point` through the spin) is known.

### Check 1: does real hardware resolve the same icall target at 0x48D02?

New script `tools/debug/xemu_48d02_and_49ce00.py` (modeled on the
existing `xemu_scda_5b5800_trace.py` breakpoint-with-step-over
pattern) breaks at `0x00048D02` (the icall in `sub_00048B15` found in
continued 39) and at `sub_0049CE00`'s entry, reading the resolved
vtable target and the device pointer at each hit.

**Result: identical.** Real hardware resolves the `0x48D02` icall to
`target=0x00045D0B` -- the exact same function scda_recomp calls. The
vtable dispatch itself is correct; this specific divergence class
(wrong ICALL target) is ruled out here.

`sub_0049CE00` was hit 26 times in a ~4-minute capture window, **always
with `device_ptr=0x004AB670`** (valid) -- reconfirming continued 37's
finding that real hardware never observes a null device there, with a
much larger sample than continued 37's single check.

### Check 2: is this a thread-scheduling/ordering artifact?

`scda_recomp`'s `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx` runs the thread start
routine **synchronously, inline** (confirmed by reading
`kernel_bridge.c`) rather than as a real concurrent OS thread -- a
plausible source of boot-order divergence if real hardware's device
creation happened concurrently on a separate thread. Checked
`scda_runtime.log`: only **one** `PsCreateSystemThreadEx` call ever
happens before the spin swallows the process, so this specific path
isn't racing against a second thread scda_recomp forgot to run.

To settle it definitively anyway, wrote `tools/debug/
xemu_48b15_entry_vs_device.py`: arms `sub_00048B15`'s own entry
breakpoint (`0x00048B15`) and a write watchpoint on `0x4AB668`
*simultaneously* in the same fresh boot, and reports which fires
first.

**Result: `sub_00048B15` is entered at t=1.266s with `device_ptr` still
`0x00000000` -- the SAME state scda_recomp is in at this point. The
real device write happens later, at t=1.485s** (matching continued
38's earlier, separately-confirmed timing). **`ENTRY first` --
confirmed, not a threading/ordering artifact.** Real hardware
genuinely runs `sub_00048B15`'s early body, including the `0x48D02`
icall, before its own device gets created (via its own later
tail-jump to `sub_0004934E`, per continued 38).

### What this leaves: a missing skip/gate between sub_00045D0B and sub_0049CE00

Given both checks above rule out a wrong icall target and a
thread-ordering artifact, and real hardware enters this exact code path
with the exact same null device state scda_recomp does, the only
remaining explanation is continued 36's "explanation 1" precisely
localized one level deeper than before: **somewhere in the nested call
chain `sub_00045D0B -> sub_00045E42 -> sub_00045F02 -> sub_0007166C ->
sub_001E460F -> sub_0003EDCC -> sub_00077B61 -> sub_000778BC ->
sub_000774E6 -> sub_00077194 -> sub_0049CE00`, real hardware's
translated code must contain a check (most likely on the device
pointer's validity, or a flag gating whether the allocator
debug-marker path should run yet) that makes it skip or defer the
`sub_0049CE00` call when the device isn't ready -- and scda_recomp's
translation of that exact check is missing, mistranslated, or takes
the wrong branch**, letting scda_recomp fall through into
`sub_0049CE00`'s unguarded `mov ebp, [0x4AB668]` / `mov ebx,
[ebp+0x1A08]` with a null pointer, landing in the `sub_004A12B0` spin
that real hardware never reaches this way.

This also finally answers continued 36's "explanation 2" (real-vs-
zeroed low guest memory near address 0): moot. Real hardware never
executes `sub_0049CE00` with `ebp=0` at all in this window, so what
`[ebp+0x1A08]` would contain in that state is irrelevant -- the
divergence is entirely about *whether* this call happens, not what it
reads once it does.

### Concrete next step

Bisect the 10-function chain above on **scda_recomp** directly (not
more xemu tracing -- the real-hardware side of this question is now
fully answered): find which of the ~10 functions' translated branches
disagree with their own disassembly, focusing on any comparison against
`0x4AB668`/the device pointer or a related "device ready" flag that
might be inverted, skipped, or reading the wrong operand. This is a
local, static bisection (compare generated C against raw disassembly
per function, in call order starting from `sub_00045D0B`), the same
technique used successfully throughout this project for prior
"silent gate" bugs.

### Boot-stage summary (for tracking against the Ubisoft-logo goal)

Still entirely within kernel/engine initialization -- no window,
graphics device, or asset loading has been reached yet.  Confirmed
boot order so far: `xbe_entry_point` -> `sub_00052572` ->
`kernel_thunk_dispatch`/`PsCreateSystemThreadEx` (single, synchronous
"thread", not a real fork) -> `sub_000524DA` -> `sub_00054701` ->
`sub_00054722` -> `sub_00048B15` (the long-established main
initializer) -> [the missing-gate divergence, this entry] -> (on real
hardware only, so far) `sub_0004934E` -> `sub_002E75CE` ->
`sub_002E2BB1` -> `sub_0049D210` (actual D3D device creation, confirmed
happens at t=1.485s on real hardware). scda_recomp has not yet been
observed to reach `sub_0004934E` at all -- it never gets that far
before the spin. Once the missing gate is found and fixed, the
concrete next milestone is confirming `sub_0004934E`'s device-creation
tail actually runs in scda_recomp too (not yet directly observed, only
inferred it should from the real-hardware trace) -- that is very
likely most of what stands between here and a window/device existing
at all, which is itself a prerequisite for any asset loading
(including the Ubisoft logo) to begin.

No code changes this entry (xemu ground-truth investigation only, plus
two new read-only debug scripts under `tools/debug/`).

## 2026-09-05 (continued 41): the sub_004A12B0 "spin" is very likely a huge-but-finite loop, not an infinite one -- traced the wrong trip count to a LEB128 decode reading a probably-aliased/uninitialized stack field

Direct follow-up to continued 40's next step: static bisection of the
10-function chain `sub_00045D0B -> ... -> sub_0049CE00`, comparing
scda_recomp's branch decisions against real hardware's at each internal
conditional in the first two functions of that chain.

### Method

Read `sub_00045D0B`'s and `sub_00045E42`'s generated C against their own
disassembly and identified 5 conditional branches whose outcome could
plausibly matter: two status/return-value checks in `sub_00045D0B`
(`0x45D36`, `0x45D6F`, `0x45D86`) and two loop-gating checks in
`sub_00045E42` (`0x45E6B`, `0x45E87`). Wrote `tools/debug/
xemu_45d0b_branch_bisect.py` to read the exact register/memory value each
branch's `cmp`/`test` consumes on real hardware, and mirrored the same
5 checkpoints in `scda_recomp` via a temporary `[SCDA-45D0B-BRANCH]`
hook (`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` = `0x45D0B`-`0x45ECA`).

### Result: identical control flow, wildly different loop trip count

Real hardware runs this exact call chain **three times** within one
capture window (a generic per-resource-type routine, not a one-shot
call), each time taking the identical branch pattern scda_recomp takes:
`status144==0` (fallthrough), `sub_0003ED6E` return varies 0/1 (both
matched at least once), `[ebx+0x18]==1` (always takes the loop). No
branch disagreement anywhere in these 5 checkpoints -- **the control
flow itself is correct.**

The one number that diverges enormously is the loop trip count read at
`sub_00045E42`'s `0x45E87` (`[ebp+8]`, cast as `int32_t`, gates `for` vs
skip): real hardware's three calls show **363, 795, and 8610** --
scda_recomp's first (and, per continued 39's stack trace, only reached)
call shows **169648**. Two+ orders of magnitude off. Since each loop
iteration recurses through `sub_00045F02` -> `sub_0007166C` -> ... down
to the `sub_004A12B0`-adjacent code from continued 38-40, a trip count
this large would run for an enormous but **finite** amount of wall-clock
time -- this looks less like a genuine infinite spin and more like
scda_recomp having wandered into a "wrong but not unbounded" loop that
was never actually going to terminate within any observation window
this project has used so far (max ~90s of dedicated waiting).

### Traced the count to a LEB128-style stream decode, then to a probably-aliased stack field

`[ebp+8]` isn't a plain input -- it's an **out-parameter written by
`sub_0005FBDA`**, called just before the check (`0x45E71`). Read
`sub_0005FBDA`'s full body: it's a byte-by-byte variable-length integer
decoder (7-bit groups, continuation-bit and sign-bit handling matching
a signed LEB128/VLQ scheme), reading bytes via icalls through a stream
object (`edi`, this function's first argument) and accumulating the
result into `*esi` (the out-pointer, i.e. `sub_00045E42`'s own
`[ebp+8]` slot). This function is a generic "decode one VLQ from a
stream" utility, not something specific to devices or rendering.

Traced `edi` (the stream/descriptor argument) back to its origin:
`sub_00045E42` receives it as `MEM32(ebp+0xC)`, which `sub_00045D0B`
passes as the literal address `esi+0x20` (`esi` = the "0x5B5800"
transient object from continued 38/39 -- confirmed by re-checking
`sub_00048B15`'s icall site at `0x48CF8`: `ecx = MEM32(0x5B5800)` feeds
the vtable lookup *and* is the `ecx`/"this" the callee receives
unchanged, so `sub_00045D0B`'s `esi` genuinely is that same transient
object). That is: the "stream" being decoded is a raw 12-byte region
(`+0x20`/`+0x24`/`+0x28`) of the SAME small stack object continued
38/39 already track.

Read `sub_00045647` (the transient object's constructor) and its own
callee `sub_00045601` against the raw x86 bytes (via `capstone`, not
just the generated C, to rule out a disasm-boundary artifact like
continued 36's swallowed-constructor bug): confirmed byte-for-byte --
the constructor genuinely only ever touches `+0x0/+0x4/+0x8/+0x2C/
+0x30/+0x34` (directly) and `+0xC..+0x1C` (via `sub_00045601`, a
nested sub-object constructor). **`+0x20/+0x24/+0x28` are never written
by anything in the construction chain.**

### A suspicious exact address match, not yet confirmed live

Separately, `sub_00048B15` calls `sub_00045584` with `ecx = ebp + -220`
(`this`) a few instructions after constructing the transient object at
`ebp + -252` (per continued 38's already-documented constructor call).
**`-220` and `-252 + 0x20` are the same number** (`-0xDC` either way) --
i.e. `sub_00045584`'s "this" is, numerically, the exact same address as
the transient object's `+0x20` field. This is either (a) intentional
stack-slot reuse by the original MSVC compiler between two
non-overlapping-lifetime locals (in which case whatever
`sub_00045584`/its callees `sub_00044AEE`/`sub_0024A50B` do there is
the *real*, intended initialization of this region, and a bug in
scda_recomp's translation of one of those three functions would fully
explain the wrong count), or (b) a coincidental alias this session
mis-attributed while reading arithmetic across three separate
functions by hand. **Not yet confirmed either way** -- reading
`sub_00045584` shows it only *reads* `[esi+4]` (expecting a value
already there) and forwards it onward; it doesn't visibly *write*
`[esi]`/`[esi+4]` itself, which cuts against explanation (a) somewhat,
but its callees might.

### Next step

A live xemu check reading the literal computed address
(`sub_00048B15`'s own `ebp - 0xDC`) immediately before and immediately
after the `sub_00045584` call, to see what real hardware actually has
there at each point -- this settles whether explanation (a) or (b)
above is correct, and if (a), narrows the actual bug to whichever of
`sub_00045584`/`sub_00044AEE`/`sub_0024A50B`'s translations differs
from the original bytes. No further static reading is likely to
resolve this faster than one more targeted watchpoint.

### Bearing on the Ubisoft-logo goal

This likely fully explains the `sub_004A12B0` "spin" tracked since
continued 34: not a deadlock, but a loop with a trip count roughly
20-450x too large, driven by one corrupted/misread field a few function
calls upstream. If confirmed and fixed, `sub_00048B15` should finish
its early body in a normal amount of time, reach its `jmp
sub_0004934E` tail (continued 38's confirmed real device-creation path),
and create the D3D device -- likely the single largest remaining step
before any window or asset loading (including the Ubisoft logo) can
begin. Still entirely within kernel/engine initialization.

Temporary hooks (`[SCDA-45D0B-BRANCH]`, the 5-address whitelist entry,
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2`) fully removed; `recomp_manual.c` is
byte-identical to its continued-40 state (confirmed via `git diff
--stat`). Only `CMakeLists.txt`'s idle-window comment changed.

Final clean build verified: `scda_recomp.exe`, 2026-09-05 00:32,
SHA-256 `f3e61943900aa4240d2f119eec564ca7dbe15839361449f55de20c01e484eaae`
-- no crash, identical `sub_004A12B0` call stack (re-confirmed live via
`cdb`), no regression.

New debug script: `tools/debug/xemu_45d0b_branch_bisect.py` (read-only,
same GDB-remote pattern as prior scripts).

## 2026-09-05 (continued 42): the ebp-220/transient_obj+0x20 alias is real but irrelevant -- self-correction, and the actual byte source for the wrong loop count is a renderer object's own "read byte" vtable method

Direct follow-up to continued 41's open question (real vs. coincidental
stack-slot alias). Wrote `tools/debug/xemu_45584_alias_check.py`:
breaks at `sub_00045584`'s entry, captures `ecx` ("this"), dumps three
words there; breaks again at the return site in `sub_00048B15`
(`0x00048CE1`) and at the icall site (`0x00048CF8`) to see whether
anything changed, and to directly confirm the numeric alias against
`MEM32(0x5B5800)+0x20`.

**Confirmed: `ecx` at `sub_00045584`'s entry IS numerically identical to
`MEM32(0x5B5800)+0x20`** (`0xD00B1BB0` in this capture) -- continued
41's suspicion of an exact address match was correct, not a hand-tracing
error. **However, all three words there are `0x00000000` at every one
of the three checkpoints, on real hardware, throughout.** `sub_00045584`'s
call chain (`-> sub_00044AEE -> tail-jmp sub_0024A50B`) does not write
anything visible there in this run.

### Self-correction: this alias does not feed the loop count

Re-reading `sub_00045E42`'s and `sub_0005FBDA`'s generated C more
carefully (the calling convention was easy to mis-trace by hand across
three nested functions, and continued 41 got it wrong): the call at
`sub_00045E42`'s `0x45E71` passes `sub_0005FBDA` **`ebx` (the renderer
object, `MEM32(transient_obj+0x2C)`) as its first parameter** (becomes
`edi` inside `sub_0005FBDA`) and **the ADDRESS of `sub_00045E42`'s own
`[ebp+8]` stack slot** (not `transient_obj+0x20` -- that address, held
in local `edi`, was already consumed by the earlier, unrelated
"reserve capacity" icall at `0x45E68` and plays no further part) as the
out-parameter. `sub_0005FBDA` decodes its LEB128-style value by calling
**the renderer object's own vtable slot 1** (`MEM32(MEM32(edi)+4)`,
`edi` = the renderer, not the transient object) repeatedly, one byte at
a time, and writes the result into `sub_00045E42`'s `[ebp+8]` slot --
which is what `0x45E87` then checks as the loop count.

So: the `transient_obj+0x20`/`ebp-220` alias found in continued 41 is
real, but it feeds the earlier "reserve capacity" call's size arguments
(currently `0/0` on real hardware, presumably benign), **not** the
value that diverges. The actual byte source for the wrong count is
**the renderer object's own "read one byte" vtable method** -- an
entirely different, not-yet-identified function.

### Refined next step

Identify what `MEM32(renderer_vtable + 4)` resolves to (both platforms)
and what buffer/cursor/file it reads from -- this is the renderer
object obtained via `sub_00045D0B`'s `MEM32(0x5B57FC)+0x54` call
(itself not yet identified either). Given the value scda_recomp
produces (169648) is a "real" but wrong number rather than an
all-zero/garbage pattern, the most likely explanations, in order of
suspicion: (1) the renderer's internal read cursor/position differs
between platforms (reading from the wrong offset in an otherwise
correct buffer), (2) the underlying buffer/resource content itself
differs (wrong file, wrong resource selected, or a corrupted read
upstream), (3) a wrong icall resolution at one of `sub_0005FBDA`'s five
per-byte call sites. A live comparison of the icall target address and
the raw bytes returned across the ~2-3 read calls (one per LEB128 byte)
between scda_recomp and real hardware would distinguish these directly
-- no further static reading is likely to be faster.

No code changes this entry; one new read-only debug script.

Files: `tools/debug/xemu_45584_alias_check.py` (new).

## 2026-09-05 (continued 43): identified the renderer's "read byte" method and pinned the divergence to the read cursor/buffer content, not the dispatch

Direct follow-up to continued 42's refined next step: identify
`MEM32(renderer_vtable + 4)` and what it reads from, on both platforms.

### Method

Wrote `tools/debug/xemu_renderer_readbyte_id.py` (first pass -- caught
mostly unrelated `sub_0005FBDA` calls from a different caller,
`0x00044A50`, whose small ASCII-range single-byte values don't match
continued 41's confirmed counts) then `tools/debug/
xemu_45e71_decode_trace.py`, which isolates only the call made from
`sub_00045E42` (`0x45E71`) by checking the return address on the stack
at `sub_0005FBDA`'s own entry. Hit and fixed the same "plain continue
re-hits a software breakpoint forever" pitfall this project has hit
before (already documented in `xemu_scda_5b5800_trace.py`'s own
comment) for three separate breakpoints in the new script before it
worked correctly.

### Real hardware, isolated: two calls fully traced, matching continued 41 exactly

    call 1: this=0x007E2060 vtbl=0x004F69C0 target=0x00040BB0
            bytes: 0x5B, 0x0C -> decoded count = 0x31B (795)
    call 2: this=0x00868CC0 vtbl=0x004F6F08 target=0x0004438C
            bytes: 0x6B, 0x05 -> decoded count = 0x16B (363)

Confirms continued 41's counts came from real, meaningful stream reads
(not garbage), and that **different renderer objects use different
vtables/reader implementations** -- `0x00040BB0` (a buffered-stream
reader shape: fields at `+0x48/+0x4C/+0x50/+0x54` bookkeeping a
position/size/capacity, with a "refill" icall via `[this]+0x70` when
the buffer runs low) for call 1, a different function
(`sub_0004435A`+0x32, `tail_jump_alias`) for call 2.

### scda_recomp, same isolated call: same dispatch, different bytes

Mirrored the exact same checkpoints in scda_recomp via temporary
`[SCDA-DECODE-COMPARE]` hooks. Had to correct one attempt mid-session:
`g_ebp` is only republished immediately before SEH-sensitive calls
(per this file's own `g_seh_ebp` convention) -- it does **not** survive
a plain nested call unmodified, so reading it after `sub_0005FBDA`'s
own per-byte icalls returns a stale, unrelated frame. Fixed by computing
each function's own `ebp` from `g_esp` at that function's entry instead
(`RECOMP_TRACE_PC` fires before `push ebp; mov ebp,esp` runs, so
`ebp == (g_esp at entry) - 4`, and that value stays valid for the rest
of the call since `ebp` is never reassigned afterward), filtered by the
return address on the stack -- the same isolation technique as the
xemu script. Also had to correct a second mistake: the renderer object
isn't actually read at `0x45D86` (a *different*, conditional icall that
never fires on this exact platform run) but at the unconditional
`MEM32(esi+0x2C) = eax` assignment at `0x45D36`, fed by an *earlier*
icall (`0x45D24`).

**Result:**

    scda_recomp: renderer=0x01082060 vtbl=0x004F69C0 target=0x00040BB0
                 bytes: 0x5C, 0x6E -> decoded count = 0x1B9C (7068)

### Analysis: the dispatch is correct, the stream content/position is not

**Vtable and target function are IDENTICAL to real hardware's call 1**
(`0x004F69C0`, `0x00040BB0`) -- the icall resolution, vtable layout, and
which reader implementation gets used are all correctly translated.
The renderer object's own address differs (`0x01082060` vs
`0x007E2060`), which is expected and irrelevant (a heap pointer, not
data content).

**The bytes read are wrong**: `0x5C,0x6E` vs real hardware's `0x5B,0x0C`.
Notably, the *first* byte is off by exactly one (`0x5C` = `0x5B + 1`)
while the second byte is completely different (`0x6E` vs `0x0C`) --
this pattern (near-miss on the first byte, wildly different
immediately after) is the signature of a **read cursor/position
one-or-few bytes off in an otherwise-correct buffer**, rather than a
wrong file, a wrong resource, or a broken decoder: a shifted cursor
reads real neighbouring data (explaining the close-but-wrong first
byte) and then drifts arbitrarily as the two platforms' encodings
resynchronize completely differently from that point on.

### Next step

Trace what sets the buffered reader's position/cursor fields
(`this+0x48/+0x4C/+0x50` in `sub_00040BB0`'s own layout) for this
specific renderer object, on both platforms, at the moment
`sub_00045D0B` obtains it (the icall at `0x45D24`) -- almost certainly
an off-by-a-few-bytes bug in whatever populated or advanced this
reader earlier in boot (a header size miscalculation, an extra/missing
field read, or a length-prefix mistranslation upstream of this exact
object). This is now a narrow, concrete target rather than an open
"which of ~10 functions" question.

All temporary hooks removed (`[SCDA-DECODE-COMPARE]`, the
`RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` window, the whitelist entries);
`recomp_manual.c` confirmed byte-identical to its continued-42 state.
Final clean build verified: `scda_recomp.exe`, 2026-09-05 01:43,
SHA-256 `70001a88764ffeced4f2e1f8eee6f274a2138dfe639a88bfe02ce16544f4b845`
-- no crash, identical `sub_004A12B0` spin (re-confirmed live via

## 2026-09-05 (continued 44): the read cursor divergence is pinned to DynamicXbox.umd's own footer/directory offset -- real hardware's reader object matches the file's actual bytes exactly

Direct follow-up to continued 43's "shifted read cursor" finding.

### The string that broke the case open

`sub_00045D0B`'s constructor call chain (`sub_00048B15` -> `sub_00045647`,
already characterized in continued 38/39) passes a literal pointer,
`0x4F6D90`, as one of the constructor's three arguments. Reading it
from the XBE directly: a UTF-16 string, **`z:\Default\DynamicXbox.umd`**
-- a real, already-extensively-investigated archive file from this
project's 2026-09-02 sessions (`docs/SCDA_WORKLOG.md` lines ~2233-5822:
the UMOD/Unreal-package format, its footer layout, and a byte-identical
extraction of `System/SplinterCell4Xbox.ini` from it were already
verified correct back then -- but for a *different, later* read, not
this one).

Also independently confirmed `sub_00045601`'s nested constructor
(inside the transient `0x5B5800` object, already tracked since
continued 38) initializes a struct with `MEM32(this)=0x9FE3C5A3` -- the
exact UMOD magic number the 2026-09-02 sessions already documented from
the format's own footer (`unreal_umod.bms`: magic + INFO_OFF +
INFO_LIMIT + VER + CRC, 20 bytes at EOF-20).

### Ground truth, computed directly from the file (independent of both platforms)

Parsed `build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/Default/dynamicxbox.umd`
(confirmed same SHA-256 as continued 3's already-verified copy,
`d7ae7df5fcf09e65bce2cfda24299b55644fd9dbacbe2176ed99ac53055c186`)
directly in Python per the already-documented footer format:

    size=0x7279B5 magic=0x9FE3C5A3 info_off=0x712FF0
    info_limit=0x71E7FF ver=1 crc=0x5589DB0D
    bytes at info_off: 5B 0C 27 44 61 74 61 58 62 5C 53 79 73 74 65 6D
    compact-index(FILES) at info_off = 795, consuming exactly 2 bytes (0x5B, 0x0C)

This is the actual, on-disk truth: the UMOD's own "FILES" directory
count is 795, encoded as `0x5B, 0x0C` starting exactly at `info_off`.

### Real hardware: the reader object matches this ground truth in every field

`tools/debug/xemu_reader_struct_dump.py` dumps the reader object's own
memory (isolated to the exact call already confirmed in continued 43)
at the moment `sub_0005FBDA` is entered:

    +0x00: 004F69C0 00000064 00000258 0000007F
    +0x40: 005B5AF0 007279B5 00712FF0 00712FF0
    +0x50: 00000000 00000800 007E20C0 00000000
    +0x60: 9FE3C5A3 00712FF0 0071E7FF 00000001
    +0x70: 5589DB0D 00620058 0078006F 0075002E   (UTF-16 "box.u...")

**Every footer field matches the independently-computed ground truth
exactly**: file size (`+0x44` = `0x7279B5`), current read position AND
info_off (`+0x48`/`+0x4C` = `0x712FF0` -- it has just sought there),
magic (`+0x60` = `0x9FE3C5A3`), info_off again (`+0x64`), info_limit
(`+0x68` = `0x71E7FF`), ver (`+0x6C` = `1`), crc (`+0x70` =
`0x5589DB0D`), followed by fragments of the UTF-16 path. `+0x54=0x800`
(2048) matches the already-documented "hundreds of sequential
2048-byte reads" block size from continued 3. **Real hardware's reader
is provably, exactly correct** -- it parsed the real footer and seeked
to the real `info_off`, which is why it reads `0x5B,0x0C` -> 795,
exactly matching the file.
