## 2026-09-05 (continued 44, conclusion): scda_recomp's UMOD reader is positioned at the wrong offset (0x14 instead of info_off) at the exact point sub_00045D0B's call needs it

Continuation of this entry's in-progress note above -- the scda_recomp
side of the reader-object dump landed.

    scda_recomp: reader object = 0x01082060
      +0x40: 005B5AF0 007279B5 00000014 00000000
      +0x50: 00000800 00000800 010820C0 00000000
      +0x60: 6572435B 5D746964 5F540A0D 64657243   ("[Cre" "dit]" "\r\nT_" "Cred" reversed-LE)
      +0x70: 3D307469 6E5C6E5C 6E5C6E5C 6E5C6E5C   ("it0=" "\n\n" x4 as literal backslash-n text)

### Correcting the framing from the in-progress note

The `+0x60` region is not a distinct "parsed footer struct" separate
from the read buffer -- `+0x58` (`007E20C0` real / `010820C0` ours)
is a pointer to exactly `object_base + 0x60` on *both* platforms, i.e.
`+0x60` onward *is* the reader's own embedded read buffer. Real
hardware's dump showing clean footer fields there (magic, `info_off`
twice, `info_limit`, `ver`, `crc`, then the path string's tail) means
its buffer had just been filled by seeking to and reading the file's
trailing footer block. scda_recomp's buffer instead holds `"[Credit]
\r\nT_Credit0=\n\n\n..."` -- confirmed (independently, via a direct
file search) to be the literal first bytes of `dynamicxbox.umd` at
file offset `0x0`, the start of a packed, uncompressed credits-text
member.

**The load-bearing evidence is the position bookkeeping, not the buffer
bytes themselves**: `+0x48`/`+0x4C` (current position / window end) are
`0x712FF0`/`0x712FF0` (both equal to the file's real `info_off`) on
real hardware, but `0x14`/`0x00000000` on scda_recomp. Since this
breakpoint fires at `sub_0005FBDA`'s *entry* -- before that call's own
per-byte reads run -- these fields reflect whatever an *earlier* step
left the reader positioned at. Real hardware's earlier step correctly
seeks this reader to the archive's footer/`info_off` before this call
needs it; scda_recomp's does not -- the reader is still (or again)
positioned near the very start of the file, mid-way through the
unrelated credits-text member, when this call runs.

### Next step (concrete, unchanged in substance from the in-progress note)

Find and trace the code that positions this reader before
`sub_00045D0B`'s call runs -- almost certainly a "read the footer /
seek to `info_off`" routine that should execute earlier in the boot
sequence. Compare, on both platforms, either (a) whether that routine
runs at all and with what computed target offset, or (b) whether a
boot-ordering divergence causes some *other*, credits-related read to
run on this shared reader *after* it *should* have been correctly
positioned but *before* `sub_00045D0B` consumes it, clobbering the
position. Either way, the fault lies upstream of `sub_00045D0B` itself
-- its own code and `sub_0005FBDA`'s decode are provably correct
(continued 43).

## 2026-09-05 (continued 45): REAL FIX -- sub_00040A88 hand-translated; the sub_004A12B0 spin is resolved, boot progresses much further

Direct continuation of continued 44's "find what should seek this reader
to info_off" next step. This entry both finds the root cause and fixes
it -- the first non-diagnostic, behavior-changing fix since the
sub_002E7381 constructor gap in continued 36.

### Root cause found: sub_00040A88 is a badly fragmented disassembly, not a translation bug

Traced edi's value back through scda_runtime.log's pre-existing
RECOMP_ABI_CHECK diagnostic (already built into this project, compiled
into every non-AB_TRACE build, and apparently never connected to this
investigation before): a warning already sitting in the log read
"[ABI] sub_00040A88: edi esp(epilogue never ran)" with
edi 005E6E20->007279A1 -- and 0x007279A1 is exactly dynamicxbox.umd's
real file size (0x7279B5) minus 0x14 (20), i.e. filesize - 20, the
classic "seek to the trailing footer" target offset for the UMOD
format continued 44 already reconstructed.

Checked sub_00040A88 in functions.json: detection_method
"imm_ref_target", only 4 instructions, has_prologue: false. Read the
real bytes directly via capstone against default.xbe (not the broken
generated output) and found a complete, 90-byte, 41-instruction
function running 0x00040A88-0x00040AE2 and ending in a genuine ret 4 --
the auto-generated body stopped after only the first 4 instructions.
The cause: six addresses inside this one real function (0x40A8C,
0x40A90, 0x40A94, 0x40A98, 0x40A9C, 0x40AA0, each exactly 4 bytes
apart) got individually registered as spurious "function starts" by
tools/disasm/functions.py's _pass_imm_ref_targets pass (each one
decodes to something that looks like a valid function body ending in a
ret, satisfying that pass's own gap-and-probe heuristic, even though
they're really just mid-body addresses of the one real function).
_build_functions then treats every entry in the candidate set as an
independent boundary regardless of confidence score, so the first of
these false starts (0x40A8C) truncated the real function at 4
instructions -- textbook match for the class of bug documented in
_pass_imm_ref_targets's own docstring (Half-Life 2's CUtlRBTree
comparator hole), just via a different false-positive source (multiple
imm-ref hits inside one body, not zero). Confirmed independently:
sub_00072655 and sub_00070854 (both called from the real function's
error-handling path) list 0x00040A9C and 0x00040AA0 among their own
called_by entries -- i.e. the disassembler's own call-target analysis
already knew these "functions" call out from inside what should be a
single body.

Read the real instructions in full (calling convention cross-checked
against sub_000518FE's -- ret 16 -- and sub_00072655/sub_00070854's --
both plain ret, caller-cleans -- own correctly-generated bodies, all
already-existing generated functions, not guessed): this is the UMOD
reader's own Seek(this=ecx, targetPos=[esp+4]) method. It calls the
underlying host seek (sub_000518FE), does best-effort error reporting
if that fails, and -- unconditionally, regardless of the seek's
success -- writes [esi+0x48] = edi and [esi+0x4c] = edi (edi being the
target position argument) and clears [esi+0x50] (invalidating any
buffered data). Since the auto-generated stub never reached this code,
those position fields never got updated to info_off -- exactly the
missing step continued 44 was looking for.

### Fix: hand-translated override in recomp_manual.c

Added a complete, faithful void sub_00040A88(void) definition to
recomp_manual.c, wired in via the existing --exclude-manual mechanism
(tools/recomp/manual_scan.py) -- no changes to the disasm tool itself;
a smaller, more contained fix that doesn't touch the
_pass_imm_ref_targets heuristic other callers may still legitimately
need. One real subtlety: recomp_manual.c is hand-written, not a
RECOMP_GENERATED_CODE translation unit, so the bare eax/ecx/esp/esi/edi
register-alias macros aren't active there by default (deliberately,
per recomp_types.h's own comment, "to avoid polluting hand-written
code") -- and RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE's own macro expansion uses the bare
names internally, so a hand-written body that calls it needs those
aliases active at the call site, not just at reads/writes the author
controls directly. Fixed by scoping #define eax g_eax (and
ecx/esp/esi/edi) locally around just this one function, #undef-ing
them immediately after, matching the exact scheme RECOMP_GENERATED_CODE
uses without touching the rest of the hand-written file.

Regenerated via the canonical recomp-only command (same scda_v060
disassembly, no re-disassembly needed since this is purely a
generation-time exclusion):

py -3 -m tools.recomp build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/default.xbe --all --split 1000 --gen-dir tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen --output-dir tools/recomp/output/scda_v060 --disasm-dir tools/disasm/output/scda_v060 --func-id-dir tools/func_id/output/scda_seeded_corrected --exclude-manual projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c --skip-binary-check --verbose

"Excluding 1 functions defined in projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c";
28112/28113 functions generated (0 failed) -- the one exclusion is
sub_00040A88, now declare-only in recomp_funcs.h.

## 2026-09-05 (continued 46): sub_004A1490's stall is a genuine NV2A push-buffer GET-pointer wait, not a translation bug -- this is GPU command-processor emulation work, not a disasm fix

Direct follow-up: investigated the new stall point continued 45's fix
uncovered.

### Method

Read sub_004A1490 (0x4A1490-0x4A15FA) via capstone against default.xbe
and its own generated C: a push-buffer space-reservation routine
operating on the D3D device object (MEM32(0x4AB668), the same device
pointer tracked since continued 38). Two candidate wait-loops at the
tail: 0x4A15C7 (`cmp eax,edi; jb 0x4a15c7`, re-reading a "get pointer"
value from memory each pass) and 0x4A15E4 (an icall loop). Added
temporary rate-limited `[SCDA-4A1490-SPIN-*]` hooks (print first 5 hits
then every 200,000th, to avoid flooding on a genuine tight spin) plus
unconditional hooks on the rarer surrounding checkpoints.

### Result: confirmed genuine hardware-wait spin, not a bug

`[SCDA-4A1490-SPIN-A]` (the 0x4A15C7 loop) fires continuously --
6.4 million+ hits observed in a ~20s window, every single one reporting
the *exact same* values: `edx(getptr_addr)=0x80009000
*edx(getptr)=0x00000003 esi(writeptr)=0x00000009`. The "get pointer"
value never changes across millions of iterations -- this is not a
translation bug, it is code correctly waiting for a condition our
emulation never satisfies.

### What 0x80009000 actually is

Not an NV2A MMIO register (those live at guest VA 0xFD000000+, per
xbox_memory_layout.c's own `XBOX_NV2A_BASE`) -- 0x80000000+ is Xbox's
"contiguous memory" window, where physical page P is visible at guest
VA `0x80000000 + P` (documented in this file's own
`xbox_ContiguousAlloc`, which places framebuffers and push buffers
there for exactly this reason). Per that function's own comment: "Xbox
D3D writes its pushbuffer position to the NV2A as `VA & 0x0FFFFFFF` and
reads the GPU's position back as `GET | 0x80000000`" -- i.e. the real
NV2A hardware's command-FIFO puller writes its progress (the GET
pointer) directly back into a location inside the push buffer's own
contiguous-memory allocation, and the driver polls that location
(ordinary `MEM32`, not an MMIO read) to know how much space it can
reuse. `0x80009000` is that feedback location for this specific
device's push buffer (allocated at contiguous offset `0x9000`).

Confirmed via `src/nv2a/nv2a_core.c`'s own comments: `NV_PFIFO_CACHE`
(the per-channel pusher/puller state) and `NV_USER` (the per-channel
MMIO submission area) are both explicitly `STUB_ENTRY`s, with the code
comment "PFIFO - command FIFO (stub for Phase 1). Full PFIFO with push
buffer processing comes in Phase 2-3." **Nothing in this project's NV2A
emulation currently decodes or executes push-buffer commands, so
nothing ever advances the GET-pointer feedback value -- any code
waiting for the GPU to "catch up" on buffer space spins forever.**

### This is not a quick fix -- flagging for a scoping decision

Every prior fix this project has made in the CPU-recompilation layer
(seeded functions, hand-translated fragments, ABI corrections) is a
faithful-translation problem with a mechanically verifiable right
answer. This is different in kind: it requires the NV2A emulation to
actually *do* something -- at minimum, write an advancing GET value
back to the polled contiguous-memory location as push-buffer commands
are (even nominally) consumed, and at most, real command decoding
sufficient to eventually produce a picture. This is squarely GPU
command-processor emulation work, already flagged as incomplete in the
code's own comments, not a disassembly or translation bug. Left
un-implemented this entry pending a scoping conversation: even a
minimal "pretend the GPU instantly drains the buffer" stopgap (write
PUT back as GET, unconditionally) is a different class of change from
everything fixed so far and deserves an explicit decision before
committing to it.

### Cleanup and verification

All temporary hooks removed; `recomp_manual.c` confirmed byte-identical
to its continued-45 state (`projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` carries only
the idle-window comment). Final clean build verified: `scda_recomp.exe`,
2026-09-05 10:44, SHA-256
`33079b8c784a773c6eaae50201f6f6fba0023598e823c84bf8741f02b690b823`
-- no crash, identical push-buffer wait (same behavior as during the
bisection, just without the diagnostic hooks). No code changes to
`src/nv2a/` this entry; investigation only.

### Bearing on the Ubisoft-logo goal

`sub_004A1490`'s wait is very likely the direct blocker between here
and any visible output: it is a push-buffer space check gating further
D3D command submission, and real NV2A command processing (or a
deliberate stopgap standing in for it) is what real hardware has and
scda_recomp does not. This is the first blocker so far that sits in
the GPU emulation layer rather than the CPU recompilation layer -- a
different subsystem, and likely a meaningfully larger scope of work
than any fix so far.

## 2026-09-05 (continued 47): minimal PFIFO consume-only bring-up unblocks sub_004A1490 -- boot reaches AvSetDisplayMode for the first time ever

Direct follow-up, user-directed: implement the smallest possible PFIFO
bring-up (not a command processor) per explicit instructions -- derive
the wait condition from the title's own channel structures rather than
hardcoding the observed address, no `sub_004A1490`-specific patch, no
SCDA special-casing inside the shared emulator.

### Where PUT/GET actually live

Disassembled `sub_004A1490` (0x4A1490-0x4A15FA) against
`build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/default.xbe` with the project's
own `tools.disasm.loader`/capstone (not `references/xboxversion/`,
which is a different XBE revision -- see the 2026-09-02 note above).
The tail wait loop is:

```
0x4a15bd  mov edx, [esi+0x30]   ; edx = device+0x30  (pointer TO the get value)
0x4a15c0  mov esi, [esi+0x2c]   ; esi = device+0x2c  (the put counter itself)
0x4a15c3  mov eax, esi
0x4a15c5  sub eax, edi
0x4a15c7  mov ecx, [edx]        ; ecx = *edx = the get value
0x4a15c9  mov edi, esi
0x4a15cb  sub edi, ecx
0x4a15cd  cmp eax, edi
0x4a15cf  jb  0x4a15c7          ; spin until enough of [device+0x2c] has been
                                ;   "consumed" per *[device+0x30]
```

and the same fields appear at the function's own entry (`mov eax,
[esi+0x30]; mov ecx, [eax]` at 0x4a1497/0x4a149a). So `device+0x2C` is
a raw put counter this driver tracks itself, and `device+0x30` is a
pointer to a separate location holding the get counter -- previously
identified (continued 46) as guest VA `0x80009000`, a fixed spot in
the contiguous-memory window that nothing ever writes to. `device`
itself is `MEM32(0x004AB668)`, the same D3D device pointer tracked
since continued 38.

This confirmed continued 46's read: the wait is not against an NV2A
MMIO register at all (those live at `XBOX_NV2A_BASE` = 0xFD000000+),
it is the driver's own private "put counter / pointer-to-get-counter"
bookkeeping, most likely originally seeded once from a real GET MMIO
read OR'd with `0x80000000`, then cached for fast polling. Nothing in
this project ever advances the target of that pointer.

### The fix: reuse the existing generic bring-up mechanism, don't build a new one

`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c` already has exactly the mechanism
this shape needs, built and documented in an earlier session but never
called from anywhere: `xbox_Nv2aMirrorFence(device_ptr_va, put_off,
get_ptr_off)`. Every tick of the existing `nv2a_ack_thread`, it
re-reads `device = *device_ptr_va`, then `put = *(device+put_off)` and
`get_ptr = *(device+get_ptr_off)`, and copies `put` into `*get_ptr` --
"treat everything submitted so far as consumed", derived live from the
title's own fields every poll, not a one-shot hardcoded address. This
*is* the generic, minimal, consume-only PFIFO semantics asked for; it
already existed, it just had no caller.

Registered it from `projects/scda/src/main.c` (the per-title
bootstrap, where `xbox_Nv2aFrameCounter`-style per-title wiring
belongs -- not inside the shared `src/kernel/` or `src/nv2a/` code,
which stays title-agnostic):

```c
xbox_Nv2aMirrorFence(0x004AB668u, 0x2Cu, 0x30u);
```

placed right after `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit()` succeeds (which is where
the ack thread that polls the registered mirrors is already started).
The three constants are this compiled binary's own D3D global/field
layout, read straight off its disassembly -- not a value invented for
the emulator, and not a hardcoded copy of `0x80009000` (the mirror
tick re-derives the get-pointer address fresh every poll, so it would
keep working even if that pointer's target moved).

No changes to `src/nv2a/` or `src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`: the
generic mechanism was already correct, it only needed a caller. No
`NV2A_PFIFO_IMMEDIATE_CONSUME`-style new compile-time switch was added
-- `xbox_Nv2aMirrorFence` is already exactly that shim, already named
and commented as bring-up-only where it's defined (see its own comment
block, continued from the earlier fence-mirror work).

### Verification

Rebuilt `scda_recomp.exe` (canonical `cmake --build build/scda_upgrade
--config RelWithDebInfo --target scda_recomp`), ran it undisturbed,
killed cleanly via `taskkill` (not cdb) after confirming continued
activity, and read the resulting `scda_runtime.log`:

- `NV2A fence mirror: device at 0x004AB668, PUT +0x2C -> *(GET +0x30)`
  printed at startup -- registration took.
- `sub_004A1490` no longer appears anywhere as a stall point.
- Boot proceeds through the same config/menu-path lookups as continued
  45, then reaches, for the first time in this project's entire
  history: `[AV] SetDisplayMode mode=0x0801010D format=0x00000012
  pitch=2560 fb=0x0008C000` -- a real `AvSetDisplayMode` call with a
  concrete mode, pixel format, pitch and framebuffer address.
- No `[SCDA-CRASH]` entries; no new crash dump (`SCDA_crash_*.dmp`)
  from this run's timestamp (2026-09-05 11:0x); process ran stably for
  5+ minutes undisturbed before being killed for this check.

## 2026-09-05 (continued 48): route the already-written AvGetSavedDataAddress bridge (ordinal 1) -- warning silenced, no behaviour change, next stall is genuinely silent

Direct follow-up to continued 47's new stall point (unbridged ordinal
1, slot 137, right after the first-ever `AvSetDisplayMode`).

### Finding: the bridge already existed, fully correct, just never routed

`docs/formats/kernel-exports.md` names ordinal 1 as `ULONG
AvGetSavedDataAddress(void)`. `kernel_bridge.c` already has a complete,
correct wrapper for it:

```c
static void bridge_AvGetSavedDataAddress(void)
{
    g_eax = (uint32_t)xbox_AvGetSavedDataAddress();
}
```

backed by `xbox_AvGetSavedDataAddress()` in `kernel_hal.c`, which just
returns a plain `ULONG` global (`g_av_saved_data_address`, set by the
`AvSetSavedDataAddress` counterpart) -- no pointer, no allocation. It
was sitting, commented out, inside the dispatch switch's "NOT ROUTED,
deliberately" block, a group that exists specifically for wrappers with
a host/guest memory-model hazard (allocate-on-host, free-on-host,
write-a-host-pointer-into-a-guest-dword -- see that block's own Halo
postmortem). `AvGetSavedDataAddress` has none of that: it neither
touches guest memory nor returns a pointer, so it never belonged on
this list -- it looks to have been swept in with the rest of the
`stdcall_args_for_ordinal()`-audit sweep and never individually
reviewed.

### The fix

One line, moved from the "NOT ROUTED" block into the routed "Display"
group next to `case 3: bridge_AvSetDisplayMode`:

```c
case   1: return bridge_AvGetSavedDataAddress;
```

plus a comment at the "NOT ROUTED" block explaining why this one entry
was pulled out of it, so a future reader auditing that list doesn't
wonder why it's gone.

Rebuilt, ran undisturbed, killed cleanly via `taskkill` (not cdb),
diffed the resulting `scda_runtime.log` against continued 47's:

## 2026-09-05 (continued 49): the silent stall is the game's own disc-error screen -- a local game-data completeness question, not a code bug

Direct follow-up to continued 48's "genuinely silent" stall (no log
output at all past `AvSetDisplayMode`). Found the answer with a cdb
stack snapshot, not a translation fix.

### The stall is `sub_0003FCA5`'s own tail, a real `jmp $`

Attached cdb non-invasively (`-pv`, so quitting does not kill the
target) and ran `~*k`. The live thread's PC sat at
`scda_recomp!sub_0003FCA5+0x1780`, disassembling to a self-referencing
`jmp` (`ebfe`). Checked the real x86 bytes at the corresponding guest
address (0x3FE6E) against `default.xbe` with the project's own
`tools.disasm.loader` + capstone: **the retail binary has the exact
same `jmp 0x3fe6e` there.** This is not a mistranslation -- the
original Xbox binary contains a genuine infinite loop at that address.

The instructions immediately before it select one of five localized
string pairs (by an `eax` value 0-4) and pass them to
`sub_000587B0` (twice, with format IDs `0x30`/`0x50`) before calling
`sub_0049CC50` and falling into the loop. Reading those string
addresses out of the XBE as UTF-16LE:

```
"There's a problem with the disc you're using."
"It may be dirty or damaged."
```

(plus IT/ES/FR/DE translations at neighbouring addresses.) **This is
the classic Xbox "disc read error" dialog code path.** On real
hardware it prints this message and halts -- exactly the `jmp $`
translates to. The recompiled binary is behaving exactly as
translated; the question is why this path is taken at all.

### Why: a failed file lookup, visible in the log all along

The runtime log's `[PATH]`/`[FILE]` lines (present in every run since
continued 45, never connected to this stall before) show the game
repeatedly failing to open
`\Device\CdRom0\Default\DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin` under every
device/path mapping this project tries (`0xC0000034`/`0xC000003A`,
STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND / STATUS_OBJECT_PATH_NOT_FOUND). The
locally staged game data (`build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/`)
has:

- `Default/DataXb/LMaps/common.lin` (1,924,977 bytes) -- one level
  too high, no `menu` subfolder.
- `Default/DataXb/LMaps/Menu/Menu.lin` (1,388,955 bytes) -- a
  differently-named, differently-sized file that already sits in the
  right folder.

Neither is `DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin`.

### A probe, and why it was reverted

To test the path-matching hypothesis, copied
`LMaps/common.lin` into `LMaps/Menu/common.lin` (non-destructively --
the original was left in place). This did let the lookup succeed and
boot progressed dramatically further, past `sub_0003FCA5` entirely and
deep into a new call chain (`sub_004A1740` -> `sub_004A1600` ->
`sub_004A12B0`, confirmed via a fresh cdb stack snapshot) -- further
than any prior session.

**But this was a false lead.** `LMaps/common.lin` is 1,924,977 bytes,
a completely different size from the legitimate `Menu/Menu.lin`
(1,388,955 bytes) already sitting in that folder -- clearly a
different asset, not a duplicate that just needs moving. Feeding it in
under the wrong name produced a new, clearly-bogus failure a few steps
later: `xbox_HeapAlloc: out of memory (requested 423845888, used
2408448/50855936)` -- a ~404 MB allocation request, impossible even on
real 64 MB retail Xbox hardware. That is the signature of a size field
being read from the wrong place in the wrong file, not genuine further
progress. The probe copy was reverted (renamed to
`common.lin.wrongcopy_disabled` in the local build output folder, not
deleted -- this is game data, not a repository file, so there is
nothing to commit here either way).

A speculative bisection hook was added to `recomp_manual.c` /
`CMakeLists.txt` anticipating the probe would hold up (targeting
`0x4A12B0`-`0x4A1800`, where the deeper stack landed: a live cdb
snapshot pinned it at `sub_004A12B0+0x1e4`, disassembling nearby to a
`bt ecx, 0x10` bit-test -- plausibly another GET/PUT-style wait, not
yet confirmed). Since the probe it depended on was reverted, the hook
was never exercised under real conditions and has been removed again
rather than left half-verified; both addresses are preserved here for
whoever resumes this once the data question below is settled.

### This is the user's call, not a code fix

Whether `DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin` is:

1. a real asset missing from the currently staged game-data copy
   (would need a correct copy from a verified clean disc/ISO extraction
   at exactly that path), or
2. never meant to exist there on retail media, with the repeated
   failed lookups being normal probing before the game falls back to
   something else this project has not reached yet,

is a question about the completeness/correctness of locally staged
game data, not something resolvable by further guessing inside this
codebase. Flagged for the user rather than acted on unilaterally.

### Cleanup and verification

Reverted the bisection hook (`recomp_manual.c`) and its trace window
(`CMakeLists.txt`, back to idle `0x0u`/`0x0u`). Rebuilt; ran
undisturbed with the probe copy reverted, confirming the clean
baseline (the disc-error trap) is unchanged and no new regression was
introduced by any of this entry's exploration.

### Bearing on the Ubisoft-logo goal

The path from here to a window is now completely mapped up to this
exact blocker: fix (or confirm irrelevant) the `menu\common.lin`
lookup, and boot demonstrably continues into new push-buffer-adjacent
territory (`sub_004A1740`/`sub_004A1600`/`sub_004A12B0`) that has never
been reached before. This is very likely the last blocker standing
between here and a real window -- but it needs a real, correctly-sized
asset, not another guess.

`projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` (bisection hook added and fully

## 2026-09-05 (continued 50): traced "menu" all the way to its source -- and found the whole `common.lin` thread is very likely a red herring, not the disc-error trap's cause

Direct follow-up, at the user's explicit direction: **do not** add a
kernel-path fallback (stripping `menu\` and retrying) -- that would
paper over a real translation bug, if one exists, with a silent guess.
Instead, trace the exact construction of the finished
`"...LMaps\menu\common.lin"` string back to its source, one call frame
at a time, and only fix the first place scda_recomp and real hardware
actually diverge.

### Method: walk the call chain one verified hop at a time

Corrected the previous entry's `caller_return` guesses, which had been
read from the wrong stack offset (that value turned out to be a
legitimate PHANDLE argument, not a return address). This entry's
approach instead:

1. Added a kernel-bridge hook (`bridge_NtCreateFile`/`bridge_NtOpenFile`)
   reading `g_icall_source` (the guest PC of the indirect-call
   instruction that reached the bridge -- already tracked for the
   `[KERNEL]` log line) and the exact guest VA of the `ANSI_STRING`
   buffer (via the same two-pointer-hop `bridge_get_xbox_path()` already
   uses), filtered to paths ending in `common.lin`.
2. Confirmed every one of the 7 observed open attempts funnels through
   `sub_000511E7` (a generic "open by path" helper -- also used for INI
   files, per an existing hook from an earlier session) via the *same*
   `icall_source=0x00051309`, a call site *inside* that generic helper --
   too generic to say who built the string.
3. Added a hook at `sub_000511E7`'s own entry (`arg0 = MEM32(g_esp+4)`
   is the path, `MEM32(g_esp)` is the true caller return address,
   readable before the prologue runs -- same technique the file's
   pre-existing `SCDA-OPTIONAL-INI-OPEN` hook already used). Found two
   distinct immediate callers: `sub_00040260` and `sub_00040FAC`.
4. Disassembled `sub_00040FAC` (0x40FAC-0x412FD) in full: it is a
   generic "fetch N config properties from a this-object via
   `vtable+0x48`, concatenate with baked-in drive-letter defaults
   (literal ANSI strings `"D"` at 0x4F64A0, `"T"` at 0x4F6920), then
   open" helper, reused for many different files. Its own `arg0` is a
   lookup *key*, not a path -- explains why an earlier filter on it
   never matched.
5. A wide stack-window dump at the `sub_000511E7` hit showed the full
   wide (UTF-16) string `"D:\Default\DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin"`
   already sitting in the immediate caller's own locals, with the
   caller's return address (`0x00048FF4`) landing inside `sub_00048B15`
   -- the main boot dispatcher this whole project has tracked since the
   very first sessions.
6. Disassembled the surrounding region of `sub_00048B15` in full
   (0x48B15-0x49026). Found a flag at `[ebp+0x6c]` gating whether an
   extra segment gets appended before `"common.lin"`, set only when
   `MEM32(0x005ED144) != 0` **and** a lookup of the string
   `"ForceOwnCommonLin"` succeeds against the object at `0x5E6E20` (the
   long-known "placeholder/default" object, not a real manager --
   already characterized in the 2026-09-03 `MEM32(0x5B57FC)` sessions).
   `MEM32(0x005ED144)` itself is set by `sub_0003EAE3`, which checks a
   *different* config object (`0x5E3E30`) for a `"LINEARSAVE"` property
   -- both read as command-line/launch-parameter-style switches (three
   sibling strings found: `LINEARSAVE`, `LINEARLOAD`, `LINEARLOAD=`).

### Live verification overturned the leading hypothesis

Armed hooks at the three decision points (`0x48BBE`, `0x48BDC`,
`0x48BE2`) and ran scda_recomp. Result: **`status144=0`, so the entire
`ForceOwnCommonLin`/`LINEARSAVE`-gated block never executes.** The
`[ebp+0x6c]` flag never gets set through this path at all -- yet the
finished string still contains `"menu"`. This rules out the
command-line-switch hypothesis entirely: whatever inserts `"menu"`
does so *unconditionally*, in the segment built *before* this gated
block.

Reading the disassembly again with that correction: the unconditional
segment is built via `sub_001D4A5A` called on `esi`, where
`esi = MEM32(0x6513A4)[MEM32(0x6513C8)]` -- **the exact same
"launch/map array" bounds-checked read this project already
root-caused and fixed once**, 2026-09-03 "continued 11/12", for an
unrelated symptom (`HalReturnToFirmware(2)` firing early). That
earlier fix left `MEM32(0x6513A8)` (the count) at a real `32` instead
of `0`, meaning `esi` should be a real array element, not `NULL`, by
this point in boot -- but rather than assume the old fix still holds
here, this entry added one more live checkpoint (`0x48F1D`) to confirm
it directly.

**Confirmed: `index=0 count=32 base=0x010DA398` -- in range, `esi` is a
real element, not NULL.** The old fix holds; this is not a repeat of
that bug. Index 0's array element's relevant property is `"menu"`,
straightforwardly and correctly read from a live, valid object. There
is no evidence of a translation bug in *this* read.

### The actual finding: the common.lin failure is treated as non-fatal

With both leading hypotheses (a launch-parameter switch, and an
empty/out-of-bounds map array) ruled out by direct measurement, read
what `sub_00048B15` does with `sub_00040FAC`'s result immediately after
the call (`0x48FF4`-`0x49013`):

```
cmp eax, -1                  ; did every device-root attempt fail?
mov eax, [ebp+0x54]
je  loc_00049013             ; yes -> skip the success-path cleanup call...
...
loc_00049013:                ; ...and land HERE regardless either way
cmp [ebp+0x58], ebx
...
call sub_0003F280            ; execution continues completely normally
```

**A failed `common.lin` open is not treated as an error here at all**
-- no message, no branch to any error handler, no early return. Boot
continues into `sub_0003F280` and beyond exactly as if the open had
succeeded, just without whatever the (skipped) success-path call
(`sub_00044C86`) would have set up. This strongly suggests
`DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin` is a legitimate **optional per-entry
override** (index 0 of the map array happens to be named/tagged
`"menu"`, i.e. the frontend's own array slot, and an override
`common.lin` for it is simply absent -- exactly consistent with what
the user described: the real, base `common.lin` lives directly under
`LMaps\`, not under a per-map subfolder, and this lookup for a
per-map-specific override is *expected* to miss for most or all map
entries).

**This means the entire `common.lin` thread investigated across
continued 47-50 was very likely a red herring with respect to the
disc-error trap.** The actual trap (`sub_0003FCA5`, reached via
`sub_0004934E` and its descendants, confirmed by every cdb stack
snapshot this whole arc) is triggered by something else further into
that call chain -- not examined at all in this entry, since this
finding only became clear at the very end of it.

Removed all temporary hooks added this entry (`kernel_bridge.c`'s

## 2026-09-05/06 (continued 51): the disc-error trap's real root cause found and fixed -- xbox_NtCreateFile never returned STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY

Direct follow-up to continued 50's pivot: the disc-error trap
(`sub_0003FCA5`) is reached via a completely different chain than
`common.lin`'s own failure handling, so this entry went straight at
that trap's real caller instead.

### Method: find who actually calls the trap

`sub_0003FCA5`'s own body was already known (continued 49) to
unconditionally converge on the error-message-and-halt code no matter
which internal branch it takes, so the real decision has to be made by
whoever calls it. Added a hook at the trap's own entry (`0x0003FCA5`,
before its prologue runs, so `MEM32(g_esp)` is still the genuine
return address) and ran a lean build.

**Result: `return=0x000403A8`**, a caller inside `sub_00040260` -- a
function briefly touched in continued 50 and set aside as "just
another generic multi-device-root prober." Disassembling the exact
surrounding bytes (`0x4037C`-`0x403A8`) showed the real logic:

```
cmp ebx, -1
jne loc_406fc                ; open succeeded -> skip all of this
call sub_00052A2F            ; read back a stashed "last error" code
cmp eax, edi(0)
jbe loc_403a8                ; <=0 -> benign, continue
cmp eax, 3
je  loc_403a8                ; 3   -> benign, continue
cmp eax, 2
je  loc_403a8                ; 2   -> benign, continue
cmp eax, 0x7b(123)
je  loc_403a8                ; 123 -> benign, continue
mov eax, [0x5E6E0C]          ; the installed error-handler pointer
                              ;   (== sub_0003FCA5, set once at
                              ;   sub_00048B15's own entry)
test eax, eax
je  loc_403a8
call eax                      ; <-- calls sub_0003FCA5, THE TRAP
```

`sub_00052A2F` reads back a Win32-style error code that a companion
setter (`sub_00052A57`, called from `sub_00052A85`, which itself calls
a kernel thunk at `[0x4F5180]` -- `RtlNtStatusToDosError`) stashed into
thread-local storage right after the failing open. Added two more live
checkpoints (`0x0004038A` for the error-code value, and confirmed
`0x000403A8`'s caller again) and ran again:

```
[SCDA-ERRORCODE-CHECK] sub_00052A2F() returned eax=2  -- benign
[SCDA-ERRORCODE-CHECK] sub_00052A2F() returned eax=5  -- NOT benign -- fires
[SCDA-DISCERROR-CALLER] return=0x000403A8 ... ebx=0xFFFFFFFF esi=0x005E6E20
```

**5 is `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`.** The first open attempt correctly gets
`ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` (2, benign); the second gets
`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` -- not a "file missing" answer at all, and not
one of the four codes this title's own error handling recognises as
non-fatal.

### Root cause: opening a directory as a plain file

Reading `bridge_RtlNtStatusToDosError`'s table confirmed `5` only ever
comes from mapping `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` (`0xC0000022`). Added a
temporary unconditional log in `xbox_NtCreateFile` (`kernel_file.c`,
the Win32 branch) for every `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` failure, printing the
resolved host path and its actual filesystem attributes:

```
[SCDA-ACCESSDENIED-DETAIL] win_path=...\Default          attrs=0x10 (IS A DIRECTORY) ...
[SCDA-ACCESSDENIED-DETAIL] win_path=...\TDATA\5553005e   attrs=0x10 (IS A DIRECTORY) ...
```

**The title is probing whether `Default` (the disc root) and
`TDATA\<title-id>` (its save-data folder) exist, by trying to open them
as plain files** -- a completely ordinary directory-existence check.
On real Xbox hardware, `NtCreateFile` checks the target's actual type
against the caller's `FILE_DIRECTORY_FILE`/`FILE_NON_DIRECTORY_FILE`
request *before* opening anything, and answers
`STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY` (`0xC00000BA`) when a non-directory open
lands on a directory -- a status this title's own open-wrapper (inside
the `sub_000511E7` chain, confirmed by disassembly to explicitly test
`cmp esi, 0xC00000BA`) is written to handle.

`xbox_NtCreateFile`'s Win32 branch never performed that check: it just
called `CreateFileW` on the directory path without
`FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS`, which Win32 always refuses with the
generic `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` -- a status the title was never written
to expect from a directory-existence probe, so it fell through to
"something is seriously wrong" and called the installed disc-error
handler.

### The fix

Added `STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY` (`0xC00000BAL`) to `kernel.h`
alongside the other `STATUS_*` definitions, and in
`xbox_NtCreateFile`'s non-directory-open branch, check
`GetFileAttributesW` before ever calling `CreateFileW`: if the target
exists and is a directory, return `STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY`
directly (matching real NT kernel behaviour exactly), instead of
attempting a Win32 open that can only fail with the wrong status. All
temporary diagnostic hooks (`recomp_manual.c`'s
`SCDA-DISCERROR-CALLER`/`SCDA-ERRORCODE-CHECK`, `kernel_file.c`'s
`SCDA-ACCESSDENIED-DETAIL`) removed again; `recomp_manual.c` and
`CMakeLists.txt`'s trace window confirmed net-zero/idle.

### Verification: the disc-error trap is gone

Ran the fixed build undisturbed. The `[FILE] -> 0xC00000BA FAILED`
lines confirm the new status is really being returned for the
`Default`/`TDATA\<title-id>` probes, and -- for the first time in this
entire project's history -- **the disc-error trap does not fire.**
Boot proceeds measurably further and reaches a new, different blocker:

```
[PATH] \Device\Harddisk0\Partition5\ -> partition image
[FILE] -> 0x00000000
xbox_HeapAlloc: out of memory (requested 786436096, used 2408448/50855936)
```

A ~750 MB allocation request against a 50 MB heap -- a new, unrelated
issue, not investigated this entry. No crash, no new dump.

Build verified: `scda_recomp.exe`, 2026-09-06 02:11:03, SHA-256
`bcdf249b6fff4f4dcf81e382968dcbadf285aea69ed5abe37c853ca279d303a3`.

### Bearing on the Ubisoft-logo goal

This is the single biggest confirmed step this whole multi-day arc has
made: the disc-error trap that has anchored every session since
continued 45 is gone, fixed at its real, verified root cause (a
missing, well-documented NT status code this project's Win32
`NtCreateFile` bridge never implemented), not papered over with a
guess. The new heap-size blocker is the next milestone to clear.

Files: `src/kernel/kernel.h` (one new `STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY`
definition), `src/kernel/kernel_file.c` (the real fix -- a
directory-type check before the non-directory `CreateFileW` call).
`projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c` and
`projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` confirmed net-zero/idle after removing
this entry's diagnostic hooks.


## 2026-09-06 (continued 52): next blocker after the disc-error-trap fix -- the 750MB heap-alloc failure is a correct, expected NT status; the real hang is sub_004A12B0 spinning again, on a second call path this time, confirmed against xemu to be a device-creation-ordering bug, not a hardware-emulation gap

Direct continuation of continued 51, following its own noted next
blocker.

### The 750MB `xbox_HeapAlloc` failure is not a bug

Added a temporary diagnostic in `xbox_HeapAlloc()` (size > 10 MB logs
`g_icall_source`) and a second one in `bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory`
(logs `alloc_type` at its fallback checkpoint), both removed after use
(`git diff --stat` confirms net-zero on `xbox_memory_layout.c` and
`kernel_bridge.c`). Traced the call to guest PC `0x00371BD6`, inside
`sub_00371BC3` (`xbox_NtAllocateVirtualMemory` kernel-export wrapper,
confirmed via `labels.json`), called from four sites in the CRT's own
heap-growth machinery (`0x00076880`-`0x00076bc7`). The failing request's
`alloc_type` is `0x103000` = `MEM_COMMIT(0x1000) | MEM_RESERVE(0x2000)
| MEM_TOP_DOWN(0x100000)` -- a combined reserve-and-commit of the exact
size of the Z: cache partition (`0x2EE01000` = 750 MiB + one page,
matching `part_sectors[5]*512` from `kernel_path.c` exactly). Because
`MEM_COMMIT` is set, neither of `bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory`'s two
existing pure-`MEM_RESERVE` fallbacks (`xbox_ReserveAlloc`, then the
halving loop) apply -- both explicitly guard on
`!(alloc_type & 0x1000)`, correctly, since a genuine *commit* of 750 MB
cannot be honoured out of a 64 MB console any more honestly by
pretending to reserve free address space for it. `STATUS_NO_MEMORY` is
the right answer here, and it is what we already return. Confirmed live
(two identical failures, each an independent call, not a retry loop)
that the game's own code handles this failure gracefully -- no crash,
no corruption, execution continues normally afterward.

### The actual hang: sub_004A12B0 again, via a new call path

Running longer (90+ s) showed `scda_runtime.log` stops growing right
after the second heap failure, while `Get-Process` CPU time climbs far
faster than wall-clock time (91 s CPU in ~15 s wall across two samples)
-- a genuine busy spin on at least one thread, not a blocked wait. A
non-invasive CDB stack snapshot (`-pv`, both threads) pinned it at
`sub_004A12B0+0x1d0` -- **the exact same function already root-caused
and fixed in continued 45** -- but reached this time via a different
chain: `xbe_entry_point -> main -> sub_00052572 ->
kernel_thunk_dispatch -> bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx ->` (running
inline, as call #1/"the main game thread" per that bridge's own
first-call convention) `sub_000524DA -> sub_00054701 -> sub_00054722
-> sub_00048B15 -> sub_00048F1D -> ... -> sub_0007188A ->
sub_0010D5C1 -> sub_001E460F -> sub_0003EDCC -> sub_00077B61 ->
sub_000778BC -> sub_000774E6 -> sub_00077194 -> sub_0049CE00 ->
sub_004A1740 -> sub_004A1600 -> sub_004A12B0`. This diverges from
continued 45's fixed chain right after `sub_0007188A` -- a different
internal branch, newly reachable now that the disc-error-trap fix lets
boot proceed differently through file-open results upstream. The
loop's guard is unchanged from continued 34/45's reconstruction:

    eax = MEM32(MEM32(0x4AB668) + 0x1C28)
    test [eax + 0x100410], 0x10000

### xemu ground truth (per explicit user instruction this session: xemu comparison before any fix)

Killed the stale, long-idle `xemu.exe` from an earlier session and
relaunched fresh (`-s -S`, GDB stub) using its own persisted
`xemu.toml` config -- the explicit CLI relaunch with all drive/bios
args duplicated them (xemu's own launcher re-adds its stored config on
top of new CLI args) and failed with "drive ... exists"; the bare
`-s -S` relaunch using the persisted config worked. New script
`tools/debug/xemu_004a12b0_devptr_check.py` (kept, reusable) breaks at
`sub_004A12B0` entry and logs `MEM32(0x4AB668)` and its `+0x1C28`
field on every hit. Result, first hit at t=1.5s and every one of ~500
subsequent hits identically: **`MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x004AB670`
(the real device struct) and `struct+0x1C28 = 0xFD000000` (the real
NV2A aperture base) already, every single time** -- on real hardware
the device is always already created by the time any call path reaches
`sub_004A12B0`, and the poll genuinely hits the real NV2A PFB write-
back-cache register, which the project's existing `nv2a_ack_thread` /
`NV2A_ACK[]` table (`{0x100410, 0x00010000u}`, added for Halo) already
answers correctly.

Cross-checked scda_recomp's own live state at the same point via CDB
(`dd` at guest VA `0x4AB668` directly -- confirmed the runtime maps
Xbox VA 1:1 onto host address, `g_memory_base == XBOX_BASE_ADDRESS`,
no offset, so no translation arithmetic was needed): `MEM32(0x4AB668)
= 0x0C47C708`. This is *not* zero this time (unlike continued 34's
first analysis of the original occurrence) but also not a valid device
struct -- the bytes at that address disassemble as ordinary x86 code
(`63 e8 d8 8a 6a ff ba ...`), i.e. it is a stray value that happens to
alias into `.text`, not a real heap allocation. Not yet traced to its
writer.

### Conclusion and next step

This is confirmed to be an **initialization-ordering bug**, not a
missing-hardware-emulation gap -- exactly the same class of bug
continued 45 already fixed once for the *first* call path into this
same function. The existing NV2A acknowledgement machinery is correct
and sufficient once the device pointer chain is valid; nothing GPU-
side needs to change. Per this session's explicit instruction (xemu
comparison before any fix, PFIFO-style minimal fix only if actually
warranted), no fix was applied this entry: the register-wait itself is
not the kind of gap the PFIFO bring-up work addressed, and forcing the
device-pointer chain to a fake value here would be exactly the kind of
workaround this project rules out. Next concrete step for whoever picks
this up: trace what writes `0x0C47C708` into `0x4AB668` on this second
call path (via `sub_0049CE00`'s ancestor chain, starting from
`sub_00077B61`/`sub_0003EDCC`, mirroring continued 38/45's approach for
the first path) and why real hardware's equivalent call path either
does not run this early or already has the device created by then.

No src/tools changes survive this entry except the new, reusable xemu
debug script (`tools/debug/xemu_004a12b0_devptr_check.py`) and this
documentation; `git diff --stat` confirms `xbox_memory_layout.c` and
`kernel_bridge.c` are net-zero. `xemu.exe` and `scda_recomp.exe` both
terminated at the end of this entry.


## 2026-09-06 (continued 53): the 0x4AB668 corrupting write is not visible to guest-instruction tracing at all -- narrowed to a host-side write or a legitimate large pointer hitting this project's known virtual/physical aliasing gap

Direct continuation of continued 52's noted next step (find what writes
`0x0C47C708` into `0x4AB668`), per explicit user approval to continue.

### Static write sites ruled out

Grepped every generated translation unit for literal `0x4AB668` (or
`0x004AB668`) as a write target: exactly three exist. `sub_0049A5B0`
writes `0`. `sub_0049D210` (device creation, already known from
continued 34/45) writes `edi`, but `edi` is always the compile-time
constant `0x4AB670` at that point (`edi = 0x4AB670;` is a literal, not
computed) -- it can never produce `0x0C47C708`. `sub_0049D210`'s own
failure path writes `0` again. None of the three static writers can
produce the observed value, confirming continued 52's suspicion that
the real write is indirect (a computed-address store landing on
`0x4AB668` by coincidence or by corrupted arithmetic), which static
grep cannot find.

### cdb hardware write-breakpoint attempts -- environment friction, no false negative established

Tried a genuine (non `-pv`) CDB attach with `ba w4 <addr>` to catch the
write live. Three attempts, each defeated by tooling/environment
issues rather than a clean negative result: (1) attaching to an
already-running process and hardcoding the host address `0x4AB668`
(reusing continued 52's identity-mapping finding from a *different*,
already-initialized process) got zero hits in 3+ minutes while the
debuggee's CPU time climbed far faster than wall clock -- the fixed
"identity mapping" address is evidently not reliable across separate
process launches (ASLR/heap-layout dependent), so the watchpoint was
very likely armed on the wrong linear address the whole time; (2)
launching fresh under CDB (`cdb.exe scda_recomp.exe`) with the same
hardcoded address reproduced the same zero-hit result, supporting that
reading; (3) breaking at `xbe_entry_point` first, then computing the
watch address from the live `g_memory_base` symbol
(`poi(scda_recomp!g_memory_base)+0x49b668`) before arming -- this run
collided with a leftover process from attempt (2) that had not been
cleaned up (two `cdb.exe` + two `scda_recomp.exe` running
concurrently, sharing the same working directory/log file), invalidating
its result too. Not pursued further given the tooling cost already
spent; a clean repeat of approach (3) alone, without a concurrent stale
process, is the natural next attempt if this angle is picked up again.

### Guest-instruction tracing: a clean, wide-window run found ZERO changes

Ruled out one whole class of explanation cleanly. Added a temporary,
address-independent watcher to `scda_trace_pc()`
(`[SCDA-4AB668-WATCH]`, same technique as the existing 0x6513A8
launch-array watcher: unconditionally compare `MEM32(0x4AB668)`
against its previous value on every traced PC, log on change) and
widened `RECOMP_TRACE_START_2`/`END_2` to `0x0-0x500000`, i.e.
effectively the entire `.text` range (matching the `SCDA_AB_TRACE`
full-trace pattern). Rebuilt (full rebuild -- the trace-window macros
are used throughout every generated translation unit) and ran to
completion, past the heap-alloc failure and deep into the
`sub_004A12B0` spin (confirmed via the `[SCDA-HEARTBEAT]` diagnostic
already built into the spin loop, `pc=0x004A12F0`, ~19.9 billion loop
iterations logged before the process was stopped). **Zero
`[SCDA-4AB668-WATCH]` lines the entire run.** Since this window covers
essentially every instruction the title's own recompiled code
executes, this rules out the write happening through *any* directly
translated guest instruction, anywhere, before the hang. Removed the
watcher and reset the trace window; `git diff --stat` confirms
`recomp_manual.c` is net-zero (`CMakeLists.txt` keeps only the
explanatory comment, values idle again, matching this project's
established convention for closed-out trace hooks).

### What this leaves: two candidate explanations, neither confirmed

1. **A host-side (C, not translated-guest) write.** Kernel bridge
   functions and the XBE/section loader write guest memory directly in
   C (`BRIDGE_MEM32`, `memcpy` into `XBOX_VA(...)`) and are invisible
   to `scda_trace_pc` entirely. A large buffer copy (a partition-image
   read, a `NtWriteFile`, `MmAllocateContiguousMemory`, etc.) landing
   on `0x4AB668` by a wrong base/size computation would look exactly
   like this. Confirmed the loader itself is not at fault: the XBE's
   own section table places `0x4AB668` at offset `0x11468` into the
   `D3D` section, whose `raw_size` (0x10310) is smaller than its
   `virtual_size` (0x13C94) -- i.e. `0x4AB668` is in that section's
   BSS tail -- and the loader's `memset(XBOX_VA(sec_va), 0, sec_vsize)`
   correctly zeroes the *entire* virtual size, including this tail,
   before copying the initialized portion. So the address starts at 0
   after loading; the value must change afterward, at runtime.

2. **`0x0C47C708` may not be "garbage" at all.** It is **not** producible
   by wraparound of a within-RAM address (`XBOX_TOTAL_RAM` is 64 MiB =
   `0x04000000`, and `0x0C47C708 mod 0x04000000 = 0x0047C708`, a real,
   plausible `.text` code address -- consistent with the earlier finding
   that the bytes there disassemble as ordinary code). This is *exactly*
   the shape of this project's own long-documented, deliberately-deferred
   gap (`kernel_bridge.c`'s `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` comment: "real
   hardware wraps *physical* addresses while translating virtual ones
   ... modelling every guest address as physical is the gap"). If some
   allocator handed back an address at or above `0x0C000000` (e.g. a
   large `NtAllocateVirtualMemory`/reserve request satisfied from
   `xbox_ReserveAlloc`'s above-RAM window, or any address a title
   validly computes but that only makes sense wrapped through real
   hardware's physical bus), and a *different*, legitimate code path
   (not the known `sub_0049D210` static device) stores that address as
   a per-thread or secondary device object into `0x4AB668`, this would
   not be corruption of the value at all -- it would be a real pointer
   whose *mirroring/wraparound behaviour* is what is missing, matching
   category 2 exactly. Not confirmed: which code writes it, or whether
   `0x0C47C708` was ever a valid allocation return value in this run.

### Where this stands

Both explanations point away from a simple "find the wrong instruction
and fix it" style bug and toward either kernel-bridge code (harder to
isolate without a working live write-breakpoint) or the pre-existing,
consciously-deferred virtual/physical aliasing gap (a bigger, already
known architectural item, not a quick fix). Given the tooling friction
encountered this entry and the size of the remaining candidate causes,
this is a natural pause point to check in on scope/priority rather
than continuing to spend rebuild/run cycles narrowing it further.

No src/tools changes survive this entry (temporary watcher and
widened trace window both fully reverted, confirmed via `git diff
--stat`); the explanatory comment in `CMakeLists.txt` is kept per this
project's convention for closed investigative threads. `scda_recomp.exe`
rebuilt clean at the end (matches committed source, no leftover
diagnostics) but not otherwise re-verified this entry (no fix was
made). All `scda_recomp.exe`/`cdb.exe` processes terminated.


## 2026-09-06 (continued 54): one clean, working hardware write-breakpoint run -- confirmed NOT a tooling failure this time, still zero hits; the "legitimate aliased pointer" reading is now also weakened by a static check

Direct continuation of continued 53, per explicit user instruction for
one final, strictly-controlled CDB attempt (no rebuild, single-process
discipline, address computed live from the running process, stop on
any further tooling failure rather than retrying indefinitely).

### Root-caused why the first two CDB attempts got zero hits: not the aliasing gap, a symbol-resolution race

`bp scda_recomp!xbe_entry_point` issued as the very first command after
attach/launch silently failed to resolve (no error, just never fires)
-- confirmed by a follow-up `-pv` snapshot of the "stuck" run showing
`sub_004A12B0+0x1d0` (i.e. the process had run to completion past the
supposed breakpoint without ever stopping), even though the symbol
resolves fine once queried separately (`x scda_recomp!xbe_entry_point`
-> valid address). Fixed by issuing `.reload /f` before `bp`. With that,
the breakpoint fired correctly this time: confirmed live by watching
`Get-Process` -- the process sat at 0 CPU / ~4 MB working set (i.e.
genuinely suspended, pre-init) for several seconds, then resumed and
grew normally once `g` was issued after arming the watchpoint. This is
a real, reproducible fix for a real tooling gap (CDB batch mode not
guaranteeing symbols are loaded before the first `-c` command runs on
a freshly-attached/launched target), worth remembering for any future
CDB batch-mode session against this binary.

### The watchpoint itself: confirmed correctly armed, still zero hits

`ba w4 poi(scda_recomp!g_memory_base)+0x49b668` set immediately after
the (now-working) `xbe_entry_point` stop, guaranteeing `g_memory_base`
was already valid (it's initialized well before guest code starts) and
computed fresh for this specific process launch (no stale
cross-process address reuse, continued 53's suspected cause of the
first failed attempt). Let it run: `Get-Process` CPU climbed
continuously and linearly for 100+ seconds of wall time (47 -> 259s
cumulative CPU) with **no pause** -- if the watchpoint had fired, the
process would have frozen at 0 CPU growth the moment it hit, exactly
as observed for the `xbe_entry_point` breakpoint. It did not. This
run had none of continued 53's confounds (verified single
`scda_recomp.exe` + single `cdb.exe` pair throughout, breakpoint
resolution independently confirmed) -- a clean negative result, not a
tooling failure, per the user's own stated criterion for when to stop
retrying and treat the result as real.

### Reconciling with the full-guest-trace's own zero-hit result (continued 53)

A hardware write-breakpoint at the correct host linear address catches
*any* write that lands on that physical byte range, regardless of
whether it comes from translated guest code or host-side (kernel
bridge) C code -- so this result subsumes and strengthens continued
53's guest-instruction-only trace finding rather than just duplicating
it. Considered whether this project's own documented RAM-mirroring
(`xbox_memory_layout.c`: `CreateFileMappingA` + multiple
`MapViewOfFileEx` calls aliasing the same physical pages at 64 MB
intervals, real OS-level page sharing) could explain a false negative
here -- it cannot: mirrored views share the *same physical pages*, so
a write through any mirror's distinct linear address is visible
immediately through a read at the primary region's address too (which
is exactly what both the CDB watchpoint, watching the primary address,
and the software watcher in `scda_trace_pc` -- which re-reads the
primary address fresh every call -- would observe). A watchpoint tied
to one linear address only fails to see writes through a *different*
linear address when the two do not share physical backing, which is
not the case for this project's mirrors. So the mirroring mechanism
does not account for the null result either.

### The "legitimate aliased pointer" reading is now also weaker

Per the user's own suggested check: `0x0C47C708 & 0x03FFFFFF (64 MiB
mask) = 0x0047C708`, a real, in-range `.text` address. Disassembled
`0x0047C6E0`-`0x0047C73A` to see what actually sits there: `0x0047C708`
falls on the **second byte of a 2-byte `jge` instruction**
(`0x0047C707: jge 0x47c55e`, encoding bytes at 0x47c707-0x47c708) --
not a function entry, not even an instruction boundary. A genuine
pointer value (to a function, a vtable slot, a return address) would
essentially never land mid-instruction like this. This weakens, though
does not fully disprove, the reading that `0x0C47C708` is a legitimate
address a title validly computed and that our address-space model
simply fails to re-alias correctly -- it looks more like arbitrary
numeric noise that happens to decode as *some* instruction sequence
when disassembled (any sufficiently long x86 byte string will), which
is weak evidence on its own, as noted (but not fully acted on) in
continued 52.

### Where this leaves it

Neither of continued 52/53's two candidate explanations survives this
entry cleanly: hypothesis 1 (a host-side/kernel-bridge write) is now
hard to reconcile with a correctly-armed hardware watchpoint seeing
nothing at all, and hypothesis 2 (a legitimate large pointer hitting
the known virtual/physical aliasing gap) is weakened by the
mid-instruction landing spot. Per the user's explicit instruction, no
behaviour change was made and none should be until one cause is
actually proven -- this is reported as an open, harder-than-expected
question rather than resolved in either direction. Considered whether
`xbox_HeapAlloc`'s "reuse a freed block first" logic could hand back a
region carrying an unrelated previous tenant's leftover bytes without
any write instruction targeting `0x4AB668` -- but that path
`memset()`s the block to 0 on every reuse before returning it
(`xbox_memory_layout.c`), and `0x4AB668` is a fixed static address in
the `D3D` section (well below `XBOX_HEAP_BASE`) rather than inside any
heap-managed block regardless, so this lead does not hold up either.
No further CDB/tooling attempts are recommended without a genuinely
new angle.

No src/tools changes this entry (investigation and documentation
only); no rebuild was needed or performed. All `scda_recomp.exe` and
`cdb.exe` processes terminated at the end.


## 2026-09-06 (continued 55): MAJOR CORRECTION -- the entire "0x0C47C708 corruption" thread (continued 51-54) was reading the wrong host memory address; the real value at 0x4AB668 is 0, and the actual root cause is the same "device struct not yet created" class already found in continued 34-36, now on a second call path

Direct continuation of continued 54, following the user's own
read-side-provenance methodology (verify the watched value at
watchpoint-arm time; break at the actual consuming read; compare the
value the CPU loads against a dump of the "canonical" address) rather
than another writer search.

### Step 1 (per the requested methodology) immediately falsified this whole thread's premise

Armed a fresh breakpoint at `xbe_entry_point`, computed the "canonical"
host address the same way every earlier entry did
(`poi(g_memory_base)+0x49b668`), and dumped it immediately -- **it
already read `0x0C47C708`, before a single instruction of guest code
had executed.** Per the user's own decision tree, result (A): "the
value was already wrong before arming" -- meaning the change happened
even earlier than assumed, so the premise needed to be checked before
going further, not silently trusted.

### Root cause of the false reading: my own address-translation formula was wrong, not the runtime

Broke instead at the actual consuming instruction --
`scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x17e`, found by disassembling the *compiled*
function directly (`uf scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0`) and locating
`mov eax, dword ptr [rax+4AB668h]`, with `rax` loaded from
`g_xbox_mem_offset` a few instructions earlier -- i.e. the ground-truth
host address the game itself actually uses is
`g_xbox_mem_offset + <guest VA, unmodified, including the 0x10000
base>`. On this hit: `rax = 0x10000`, and `dd rax+4AB668h L1` (the
address the CPU actually read) gave **`0x004BB668: 00000000`** -- host
address `0x4BB668`, value **0**. The "canonical" address I had been
computing and watching this entire investigation
(`poi(g_memory_base)+0x49b668`, deliberately *subtracting*
`XBOX_BASE_ADDRESS` (0x10000) from the guest VA before adding
`g_memory_base`) evaluates to `0x4AB668` when `g_memory_base=0x10000`
-- one full `XBOX_BASE_ADDRESS` (`0x10000`) *below* the real address
the runtime uses. Checked why: `g_xbox_mem_offset` is set from
`g_memory_offset = (uintptr_t)g_memory_base - XBOX_MAP_START`
(`xbox_memory_layout.c`), and `XBOX_MAP_START` is `0x00000000`, **not**
`XBOX_BASE_ADDRESS` (confirmed in `xbox_memory_layout.h`: `#define
XBOX_BASE_ADDRESS 0x00010000` / `#define XBOX_MAP_START
0x00000000`) -- so the correct formula is `host = guest_va +
g_memory_base`, full stop, no subtraction. My mental model going back
to continued 51's very first `-pv` snapshot ("host == guest, identity
mapping, because `poi(g_memory_base)+0x49b668` happened to equal
`0x4AB668`") was built on this same wrong subtraction and never
re-derived from the actual generated code until this entry.

### What this means for continued 51-54

**Every dump, watch, and hardware breakpoint in continued 51 through 54
was reading/watching guest VA `0x49B668` (an unrelated location 0x10000
bytes into the `D3D` section, near its start), not guest VA `0x4AB668`
(the real D3D device pointer slot).** `0x49B668` legitimately holds
`0x0C47C708` as ordinary static data there (not corruption of
anything -- nothing was ever supposed to be tracking that address).
Concretely:

- Continued 51's original "MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x0C47C708" `-pv` finding:
  wrong address, coincidental data.
- Continued 52's static write-site analysis (`sub_0049A5B0`,
  `sub_0049D210`) was for the *right* literal address (`0x4AB668`
  appears correctly as a compile-time constant in the generated
  `MEM32(0x4AB668)` calls -- that part was never in question) but
  the live values compared against it were from the wrong host
  location, so the "none of the 3 static writers can produce
  0x0C47C708" reasoning, while true, was answering an irrelevant
  question.
- Continued 52's full-.text guest-trace watcher and continued 53/54's
  CDB hardware watchpoint were both watching the *wrong host address*
  the entire time -- their "zero hits" results are explained trivially
  (nothing ever needed to write there for this investigation's
  purposes) and prove nothing about the real `0x4AB668`.
- Continued 54's "0x0047C708 lands mid-instruction, weakening the
  legitimate-pointer reading" observation is retracted along with
  everything built on the wrong address; it was never evidence about
  the real slot either way.

### The real value, and the real root cause

`MEM32(0x4AB668)` (verified via the actual consuming instruction,
`sub_004A12B0+0x17e`) is **`0`** at the point the second call path

sub_004A1740 -> sub_004A1600 -> sub_004A12B0`, confirmed live via `kb`

`sub_0049D210` (device creation) has not run yet by the time this

mistake derailed the investigation into chasing a phantom "corrupting

### Disassembling the guard reframes the entire investigation

Read the actual guest bytes around `0x00077487`-`0x000774DF` (the
generated C at this address, `recomp_0003.c:50139`-`50213`, is a
faithful, unremarkable translation of the retail bytes -- confirmed,
not the bug). The guarded call is not part of D3D/push-buffer code at
all:

    ecx = MEM32(esi + 0x30)          ; pool remaining-size field
    eax = MEM32(ecx + 4) & ~3
    edx = [ebp+8] + 0x10             ; requested size + header
    if (eax < edx) goto OOM_report;  ; not enough room
    ... (normal path: carve the block, return it)

    OOM_report:
        push 0; fldz; push ecx; fstp [esp]; push 0xFF0000; push 0xF0;
        push 0; push 0;
        call sub_0049CE00             ; <-- the function this whole
                                       ;     thread has been calling
                                       ;     "the D3D push-buffer flush"
        push 0; call sub_0049CC50
        push 0x7D0 (2000); call sub_00052D5A   ; Sleep(2000)?
        return 0 (allocation failed)

This is the classic Xbox/MSVC-CRT-derived "out of memory: show a
warning, wait, fail" idiom, not GPU/push-buffer code -- `sub_004A12B0`
(reached from inside `sub_0049CE00`'s own call tree, per the original
stack trace) is apparently a **debug-overlay/warning-display routine**
called *as a side effect* of this failure path, not the thing that was
hanging in the earlier "spin" characterization at all. This retroactively
reframes continued 34 through 57's shared premise (that `sub_004A12B0`
is D3D push-buffer submission code, e.g. "NV2A PFB write-back-cache")
as likely wrong for *this* call path specifically -- worth keeping in
mind that the *first* path's fix (continued 45) may be addressing a
genuinely different function role than this second one, even though
both reach the same address.

### The guard's own entry function IDs the caller precisely

`sub_00077194`'s prologue (`push ebp; mov ebp,esp; sub esp,0x24; push
esi; mov esi, eax; ...`) shows the calling convention is **not**
thiscall-via-ecx -- `EAX` is `this`, matching the caller
(`0x0007784d`: `push esi` (a size) `; mov eax, 0x64d2a0` (this) `;
call 0x77194`). `0x64D2A0` is a **fixed global address, not a
per-object pointer** -- and it is the exact same global this session's
much earlier "750MB heap-alloc failure" investigation
(this-session's own log excerpt) already found inside the CRT's own
low-level heap-growth code (`mov ebx, dword ptr [0x64d2a0]` at guest
`0x00076825`-ish, part of `sub_00076849`'s heap-grow machinery). This
is the **same CRT small-block-heap manager singleton**, and the
calling code (`0x777cc`-`0x77859`, a coalescing free-block merge/
insert routine -- `0x64d2e0`/`0x64d2e4`/`0x64d2d4`/`0x64d5d8` are all
consistent with MSVC's small-block-heap internal free-list-by-size-
bucket bookkeeping) is **freeing/returning a block to the heap's own
internal small-object arena**, not allocating a title resource.

### The live values are the real smoking gun

`[SCDA-77487-POOLCHECK]` (temporary, added, used, fully removed --
`git diff --stat` net-zero on `recomp_manual.c`, `CMakeLists.txt` back
to idle) logged 12 hits in a real `scda_recomp.exe` run. The last one
succeeds normally (`pool_ptr=0x010CC000, requested=0x70, needed=0x80,
ok`) -- an ordinary small allocation. The **11 that fail all share the
same `esi=0x0064D2A0`** (the CRT heap singleton) and show a striking
pattern:

    pool_ptr=0x01080008 requested=0x01081000 (~16.5 MB)
    pool_ptr=0x01081FE8 requested=0x01082000
    pool_ptr=0x010828C8 requested=0x01083000
    pool_ptr=0x01087FC8 requested=0x01088000
    ... (each pool_ptr and each requested size climbing by roughly
        0x1000-0x5000 per call, `requested` always landing just past
        the *previous* call's `pool_ptr`)

`requested` (`[ebp+8]`, the size of the block being returned/coalesced,
per the caller trace above) is not a plausible small-object size at
all -- it looks exactly like consecutive memory *addresses*
(`0x0108xxxx`, all 4 KB-aligned), not byte counts, and it grows in
lockstep with `pool_ptr` itself. Combined with `pool_ptr`'s own tiny,
inconsistent `pool_avail` values (`0x1FF8`, `0x1018`, `0x5738`, ...,
nothing resembling a stable arena size), this looks like the CRT
allocator is being asked to coalesce/return a series of **absurdly
large, monotonically growing "freed block" sizes** that plausibly
originate from the very allocation failure already documented earlier
this session: the guest's own `0x00371BC3`
(`xbox_NtAllocateVirtualMemory` wrapper) retry/cleanup logic around
the 750 MB Z:-cache-partition `VirtualAlloc` failure. Not yet proven
-- the two investigations have not been directly linked by a traced
call chain, only by the shared `0x64D2A0` singleton and the
suggestively address-shaped "sizes" -- but this is now a concrete,
falsifiable hypothesis rather than a vague "device not created" one.

### Traced the malloc() call upward through three thin wrapper functions to identify its exact shape

`sub_000774E6` (malloc) <- `sub_000778BC` (realloc: `cmp eax,esi;
jne...; cmp ebx,esi; jne...` is the classic `realloc(NULL,0)==nothing`
/ `realloc(p,0)==free(p)` / `realloc(NULL,n)==malloc(n)` dispatch,
`eax`=size, `ebx`=ptr) <- `sub_00077B61` (a bare two-argument

by disassembly, `mov eax,[esp+8]; push ebx; mov ebx,[esp+8]; call

caller `0x0003EDD4` inside `sub_0003EDCC` itself), which forwards its
own first two of five stack arguments (`ret 0x14` = 20 bytes = 5
DWORDs) straight through -- the shape of a debug/placement
`operator new(size_t size, void* ptr, ...)`-style CRT entry point, not
a plain `malloc`. `sub_0003EDCC`'s only caller in this session's own
records is `sub_001E460F`, already characterized in an earlier session
as "the CStringW allocator dispatch" -- i.e. **a CStringW (or
equivalent wide-string class) is trying to reserve a buffer sized from
the raw partition byte count.**

`786432002 = (786432000/2 + 1) * 2` -- exactly the shape of a CStringW
buffer-allocation formula (`(nChars + 1) * sizeof(WCHAR)`) with
`nChars = 393,216,000`, i.e. **half the partition's byte size, used
directly as a wide-character count with no unit conversion**. This is
now a fully concrete, arithmetically-verified mechanism, not a
plausible-sounding guess.

size=0x2EE00002`. Both values are independently unambiguous: `0x001E4631`

`grep` across all `recomp_*.c`), immediately after `sub_001E460F`'s own
`g_icall_source = 0x001E462Eu` assignment -- the two facts corroborate

### A genuine puzzle, resolved: sub_001E460F's own entry hook never showed a matching call

Hooking `sub_001E460F`'s own entry (`RECOMP_TRACE_PC(0x001E460Fu)`,
confirmed present in the generated code) and logging its stack argument
("count") never produced a hit above 64K, even though the function
provably executed enough to reach its own internal `g_icall_source =
0x001E462Eu; ...icall...` line 3735 times over the run (confirmed by
removing the size filter and counting every hit). Ruled out, in order:
a stale build (forced a `touch` + full recompile, unchanged result), a
worker-thread/TLS split (`GetCurrentThreadId()` logged identical on
both sides of the puzzle), and a stack-corruption false positive on the
return-address reading (the deeper `esp` value at the actual failing
call, `0x00F7A478` vs. the shallow `~0x00F7FE10` of the first five
calls, proved it really was a separate, much later, much deeper
invocation, not a coincidence). The actual resolution: **I had the
multiplication backwards.** `sub_001E460F`'s own body computes `edx =
MEM32(this+8) * count` -- I had assumed the *count* argument was the
huge number; the 3735-call trace's very last entry, immediately
preceding the failing `sub_0003EDCC` call, showed the opposite:
`elem_size=0x2EE00002 count=0x00000001`. The object's own `[this+8]`
field -- not any caller-supplied count -- already held 786432002 before
this call even began, which is why filtering on "count" found nothing:
count was always small (1 or 2) every single time, including the one
that mattered.

### Layer 2: sub_0010D5C1 is a two-line RAII wrapper that stores its single argument into both this+4 and this+8 unchanged

    sub_0010D5C1(this=ecx, value=[esp+4]):
        this->field0 = 0
        this->field4 = value
        this->field8 = value      ; == "elem_size" as read by sub_001E460F
        sub_001E460F(this, 1)     ; count is hardcoded to 1 here

No multiplication, no unit conversion, no misuse of a length as a
character count (continued 58's CStringW hypothesis is retracted) --
this is a plain "allocate a buffer of `value` raw bytes" wrapper
(`count=1` because it's a single buffer of `value` total bytes, not `N`
elements of some fixed size). A hook here (`caller=0x000718C7,
value=0x2EE00002`) pinned the real origin one level further up.

### Layer 3: sub_0007188A -- a UTF-16 stream reader that sizes its buffer directly from the stream's reported length, +2 bytes for a BOM/terminator

Disassembled the caller site directly (no further hooks needed --
static reading was conclusive at this depth):

    ecx = [ebp+0x10]                      ; a stream/reader object
    ... call [vtable+8]  -> esi           ; open/attach, esi = new object (non-null on success)
    eax = MEM32(esi)
    ... call [eax+0x50]  -> edi           ; length-of-stream query
    push 1
    push edi + 2                          ; <-- becomes sub_0010D5C1's "value": length + 2
    call sub_0010D5C1                     ; allocate a (length+2)-byte buffer
    ... mov byte ptr [ebx],0 / [ebx+1],0  ; zero the first two bytes (BOM slot)
    ... cmp byte ptr [ebx],0xFF / [ebx+1],0xFE  ; classic UTF-16 BOM (FF FE) detection

This is a generic "read an entire text stream into a buffer sized to
its length, then sniff for a UTF-16 BOM" routine -- exactly the shape
of a config/INI/text-resource loader, not anything partition- or
device-specific in itself. `edi` (the "length") is `786432000` exactly
(`+2` = `786432002`, matching every earlier layer).

### Layer 4/5: the "stream length" is Win32's own, honest GetFileSize() on the sparse Partition5.img host file

`edi`'s `[eax+0x50]` virtual call is this reader object's "get length"
method, which -- through the kernel bridge -- ultimately resolves to
`xbox_NtQueryInformationFile`'s `XboxFileStandardInformation`-style
case (`kernel_file.c`), which calls Win32 `GetFileSize`/`GetFileSizeEx`
directly on the resolved host `HANDLE`. The Partition5 handle is backed
by `Partition5.img`, a real host file `kernel_path.c` creates and
`SetEndOfFile`s to exactly `part_sectors[5]*512 = 786432000` bytes
(continued 51/52). **This answer is not wrong, not corrupted, and not
a bug in the bridge's arithmetic** -- it is the literal, correct size
of the host file backing the device. The runtime log's own ordering
confirms the whole chain fires immediately after `[PATH]
\Device\Harddisk0\Partition5\ -> partition image` / `[FILE] ->
0x00000000` (the successful open), exactly matching this call graph.

### The actual bug, now precisely located

Something calls this generic UTF-16 text-stream reader
(`sub_0007188A`'s ancestor chain) **on the just-opened raw Partition5
device handle**, treating a raw block device as if it were a small
text file. Real hardware almost certainly never reaches this with a
device handle at all -- either its NT layer answers a
`FileStandardInformation`-style query on a *device* object (as opposed
to a *file* object) differently from a regular file (a distinct object
type, likely erroring or returning something not usable as a buffer
length), or the higher-level code that decides to invoke this reader
on Partition5 in scda_recomp is itself following a path real hardware
does not take at this point. `kernel_path.c`'s own comments already
note the device-vs-file distinction exists on real Xbox but is not
modelled here (`xbox_NtCreateFile`'s directory-vs-file check, fixed in
continued 51, is the sibling of this same class of gap). Confirmed via
the disassembly that `xbox_NtQueryInformationFile`/`kernel_file.c`
makes no distinction at all between a device-backed handle and an
ordinary file handle when answering this query -- it always calls
`GetFileSize` on whatever host `HANDLE` it has.

### Why the earlier "device creation" and "0x0C47C708" threads were both real dead ends, now fully explained

`sub_004A12B0` is invoked from deep inside this failure's own
CRT-level "allocation failed, warn and sleep" handling (continued 57) --
nothing about D3D, NV2A, or device creation is involved in triggering
it on this path; it happens to be reachable from generic CRT
diagnostic code for unrelated historical reasons. Both retracted
threads (continued 34-38's device-ordering theory and continued
51-54's corrupted-pointer theory) were investigating real, correctly-
observed symptoms of this one root cause without yet having the
context to see it.

### Recommended next step (not implemented this entry, per standing methodology: confirm real-hardware semantics before changing kernel-bridge behaviour)

Check via xemu what a `FileStandardInformation`-style query (or
whatever the guest's reader actually issues) returns for a device
object opened the same way real hardware's equivalent code would open
Partition5 at this point in boot -- and separately, find what
guest-side condition decides to run this UTF-16 reader against
Partition5 in scda_recomp in the first place (a bisection of
`sub_0007188A`'s own caller chain, xemu-compared, is the natural next
step, matching this project's own established practice of checking
real hardware before writing a kernel-bridge fix). The two candidate
fix shapes are: (a) `xbox_NtQueryInformationFile` should reject or
answer this query differently for a device/partition-image-backed
handle than for an ordinary file, mirroring continued 51's directory-
vs-file fix; or (b) the true bug is further upstream (why is a text
reader being pointed at the raw partition device at all), in which
case the query answer is a correct red herring and the fix belongs in
whatever guest-visible state feeds that decision.

All five temporary hooks (`SCDA-3EDCC-CALLER`, `SCDA-1E460F-CALLER` in
