## 2026-09-06 (continued 60): xemu ground truth answers continued 59's open question decisively -- it's hypothesis (2), not (1): real hardware never feeds sub_0007188A anything but small text files, from the exact same call site scda_recomp also uses

Direct continuation of continued 59, per explicit user request to
settle which of the two candidate fix shapes is right before writing
any code.

### The check

New script `tools/debug/xemu_7188a_reader_check.py` (kept, reusable;
uses the `continue_pending`/interrupt-before-cleanup discipline from
continued 56/57) breaks at `sub_0007188A`'s own entry and at the
length-query result site (`0x000718B7`, `mov edi, eax` right after
`call [eax+0x50]`, so `eax` already holds the queried length). Ran
against a fresh, clean xemu session (killed the previous stale one
first) for 900 seconds against the retail disc.

### Result

89 hits total (44 function-entries, 45 paired length reads) between
t=1.3s and t=17.8s, then **zero further hits for the remaining ~880
seconds of the window**. Every single one of the 89 calls: (a) comes
from the **exact same return address, `0x00046558`** -- one call site,
almost certainly a loop over a fixed list of small text/config
resources read early in boot; (b) reads a length between **170 and
33,038 bytes** -- ordinary small text-file sizes, several orders of
magnitude below even 1 MB, let alone the ~750 MB Partition5 figure.
Real hardware **never** calls this reader again after that initial
burst, and never with anything resembling a device-sized length.

### What this settles

This is direct, decisive evidence for **hypothesis (2)**: the
`xbox_NtQueryInformationFile`/`GetFileSize` answer itself is not the
bug -- it is honestly answering whatever handle it is asked about,
exactly as continued 59 already argued. Real hardware's own guest code
simply **never asks this question about Partition5, or about anything
partition-sized, at all**. scda_recomp's own trace (continued 59)
showed the failing call arriving from the **same caller address,
`0x00046558`** -- i.e. scda_recomp reaches the exact same loop real
hardware uses for its normal small-resource reads, and at some
iteration inside that loop, resolves a handle to the raw Partition5
device instead of whatever small file real hardware's equivalent
iteration opens there. The bug is in scda_recomp's own path/handle
resolution feeding that loop, not in the kernel bridge's query
answer -- changing `xbox_NtQueryInformationFile` to special-case
device-backed handles would be exactly the kind of workaround this
project's standing methodology rules out (masking a wrong handle with
a special-cased answer, rather than fixing why the handle is wrong).

### Concrete next step

Find the resource loop at guest `0x00046558`'s call site and the list
it iterates (very likely file paths or resource IDs, given the small,
varied lengths and the fixed caller). Bisect which iteration/index
scda_recomp resolves differently from real hardware -- the earlier
`common.lin`/`menu` path-construction investigation (continued 50) is
a plausible sibling of this same list, worth checking first for
overlap before assuming a new, unrelated resource. A live hook at
`0x00046558`'s own call site logging the resolved file/handle identity
per iteration, compared against the same 89-call sequence from this
xemu run (same lengths, same order, if the list is deterministic), is
the natural way to pinpoint exactly where the divergence happens.

### Process hygiene

`xemu.exe` launched fresh, killed cleanly at the end. No src/tools
changes besides the new, reusable debug script. No behaviour change.


## 2026-09-06 (continued 61): the failing config load's path is a genuine empty string, fed by a property/section object whose "get name" vtable call succeeds but writes nothing -- the fallback-across-device-roots pattern from continued 50 is confirmed as the same mechanism, now identified precisely

Direct continuation of continued 60, per the identified next step
(bisect which resource-loop iteration diverges from real hardware).

### The path is empty, not merely wrong

A temporary hook at `sub_000464EC`'s entry (the single-file config
loader, per an earlier session's own characterization; its call to
`sub_0007188A` is the resource loop `0x00046558` continued 60 already
ground-truthed) logged every call's path argument. Two calls stood
out immediately before the runtime log's `[PATH]
\Device\Harddisk0\Partition5\ -> partition image` line: one with
`path="S"` (a single byte, itself suspicious -- likely a UTF-16
string misread as bytes by this diagnostic's own ANSI-style reader,
not necessarily meaningful on its own) and, immediately preceding the
fallback sequence, **`path=""` -- a genuinely, fully empty string**.
The runtime log's own `[PATH]` lines confirm this directly: the empty
path is tried against `\Device\CdRom0\Default\`,
`\Device\Harddisk0\partition1\TDATA\5553005e\`,
`\Device\CdRom0\Default\` again, and finally
`\Device\Harddisk0\Partition5\` -- four device roots, one empty
filename appended to each, exactly matching `kernel_path.c`'s own
long-standing description of this pattern ("different device roots
are the game's own fallback attempts"). The first three correctly
return `STATUS_FILE_IS_A_DIRECTORY` (continued 51's fix, working as
intended -- a bare device-root path with nothing appended really is
being opened as a non-directory file, and the directory check catches
it). **The fourth does not**, because `kernel_path.c`'s
`xbox_partition_device_path()` special-cases a bare
`\Device\Harddisk0\PartitionN\` path *before* any directory-type check
ever runs, redirecting straight to opening `Partition5.img` as a
plain file -- which succeeds, because that host file is a real,
ordinary file (not a host directory), so `GetFileAttributesW`'s
`FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY` check (continued 51) never has a chance to
apply.

### Traced the empty path to its source: a "get name" vtable call that succeeds while writing nothing

The caller (`sub_0004721E`, guest `0x000474FC`, matching the
already-known "FConfigCacheIni property-parsing" characterization)
disassembles cleanly:

    eax = MEM32(ecx)                    ; "this" object's vtable
    push &local_buffer                  ; [ebp-0x220]
    call [eax+0x10]                     ; a "get name/path" style method
    test eax, eax
    jl <early-return, never calls sub_000464EC>
    ... (several more calls building on the same buffer) ...
    push [0x5B57FC]                     ; a fixed global (extension/flag?)
    push &local_buffer                  ; the SAME buffer -- now used as the path
    call sub_000464EC

The failure path (`jl`, i.e. a negative/error return) is not taken --
this call **succeeds** (`eax >= 0`) but the buffer it was supposed to
fill with a name ends up empty. This points at a specific
property/section entry (whatever `ecx`/`esi` is at this call, part of
a list `sub_0004721E` iterates) whose own "name" field is empty,
rather than a translation bug in this glue code itself, which
faithfully forwards whatever the vtable call produced.

### Where this leaves it

The mechanism is now fully understood, from the D3D-adjacent-looking
hang all the way down to a single empty string: **some config/property
list entry that scda_recomp processes has an empty name**, that empty
name flows unmodified through a legitimate, correctly-implemented
device-root fallback loop, and only succeeds unexpectedly because the
Partition5 special-case in `kernel_path.c` does not perform the same
directory-type check `xbox_NtCreateFile` already performs for
ordinary paths. Two independent things could each be considered "the
bug", and both may be worth fixing:

1. **The empty name itself** -- find which property/section object in
   scda_recomp's list has this empty entry, and why (a genuinely
   missing/corrupted list entry the earlier launch-array and
   constructor-list bugs in this project's history would make a good
   first place to check for a sibling; or a legitimate "no name here,
   skip this one" sentinel that the guest's own code is supposed to
   check for before ever reaching the file-open fallback, and does
   check on real hardware -- xemu never reaches this loop with
   Partition5 at all, continued 60).
2. **The Partition5 special-case bypassing the directory check** -- a
   defense-in-depth fix regardless of (1): `xbox_partition_device_path`
   -backed opens should presumably answer the same directory-vs-file
   question `xbox_NtCreateFile` already asks for ordinary paths, so
   that *any* stray non-directory open against a bare partition root
   (empty filename or otherwise) fails the same honest way instead of
   silently succeeding against the raw image file.

Neither implemented this entry, per standing methodology -- reporting
back to the user with both candidate fixes before writing any code,
since (2) in particular changes behavior for every title using
`kernel_path.c`'s partition-image mechanism, not just this one path.

Temporary `[SCDA-464EC-INIPATH]` hook (two revisions) fully removed;
`git diff --stat` confirms `recomp_manual.c` net-zero. Trace window
reset to idle. `scda_recomp.exe` rebuilt clean at the end. No

## 2026-09-06 (continued 62): xemu ground truth on the get-name fallback -- real hardware's SAME call returns -1 (correctly skipping this config entry) far more often than scda_recomp even reaches the branch at all; the divergence is upstream, not in this call's own logic

Direct continuation of continued 61, per the user's explicit
instruction: identify the object/vtable slot, compare return value and
buffer content between xemu and scda_recomp, and if xemu shows the same
success+empty result, look at what should have kept this entry out of

### Identified the exact call precisely

`sub_0004721E` tries `MEM32(0x5B5800)`'s own "get name" vtable method
first; only if that object is null/its call fails does it fall back to
`MEM32(0x5B57FC)`'s own "get name" method (guest `0x0004749A` ->
`0x000474A9`, target `sub_00045ADE`) -- the exact call continued 61
found returning success with an empty buffer in scda_recomp. Live in
scda_recomp: `obj1=0x00F7FDD4` (a **stack address**, not the heap/global
pointer one might expect for a persistent registry -- itself worth
keeping in mind, though not yet explained), `obj2=0x00F7FE98`,
`target2=0x00045ADE`, `retval=0`, buffer entirely zero.

### xemu comparison

New script `tools/debug/xemu_4749a_getname_check.py` (kept, reusable;
uses the established interrupt-before-cleanup discipline) broke at the
same call site and its result point, logging every hit unfiltered (no
size/emptiness threshold -- the question here is the call's *shape*,
not rarity). Result, all 60 hits captured within a ~1-second window
(t=14.2s-15.2s):

- `obj1`/`obj2` are consistently non-null, real (heap-shaped, `0xD00Bxxxx`)
  pointers -- real hardware also takes this exact fallback branch, and
  does so **constantly**, not rarely.
- **`retval = 0xFFFFFFFF (-1)` on every single one of the 60 hits, with
  no exception.** Per the disassembly already read in continued 61
  (`test eax,eax; jl 0x474FC`), a negative return here makes
  `sub_0004721E` skip this config entry entirely -- it never reaches
  `sub_000464EC`/the file-open fallback loop at all for these calls.
  Real hardware's buffer still shows readable partial content
  ("C", ".") despite the -1, consistent with the callee writing
  something before/regardless of its own failure signal, but the
  caller doesn't use it either way once it sees the negative return.

### The real divergence is frequency, not this call's own correctness

scda_recomp's own capture (continued 61/this entry) shows this
fallback branch fires **exactly once** in an entire run through to the
heap-alloc failure -- not dozens of times like real hardware's
observed 60-in-one-second burst. This reframes the question again:
it is not "does `sub_00045ADE` compute the wrong thing" (its target
address, object identities, and general shape match between xemu and
scda_recomp) -- it is **why does scda_recomp barely ever reach this
fallback branch at all, when real hardware reaches it constantly, and
why does the one time it does reach it return the opposite polarity
result (0/success instead of -1/failure) than every one of real
hardware's 60 observed instances**. Both facts point to something
upstream of `sub_0004721E`'s own object-1/object-2 dispatch --
plausibly the same class of bug this project has repeatedly found
before (a loop-count, array-bounds, or register-preservation issue
feeding a batch/loop that should call into this config-lookup path
many times per boot, matching real hardware, but in scda_recomp
calls into it far less and, on its one call, gets the calculation
inside `sub_00045ADE`/`sub_0000457AE`'s lookup chain wrong for this
specific key).

### Concrete next step

Trace `sub_0004721E`'s own caller and count how many times it (and, in
turn, `sub_0004721E`/this fallback branch) actually run in scda_recomp
vs. the same ~60-in-1s burst on real hardware -- a frequency mismatch
this large should be easy to confirm or rule out with a simple hit
counter on `sub_0004721E`'s own entry on both sides, without needing
to chase `sub_00045ADE`'s internal lookup logic yet. If the counts
already diverge before reaching `sub_0004721E`, the bug is further up
the chain (the same "why does the caller only iterate once" question
already asked of similar loops earlier in this project's history); if
the counts match but the outcome still differs only on this one call,
then `sub_00045ADE`/`sub_0000457AE`'s own lookup (keyed on something
this project has not yet identified) is where to look next.

threads) continuously execute code inside that same huge address range
regardless of boot progress, so wall-clock cost scales with total
runtime, not with progress toward hit #745.

Abandoned both attempts (no lasting code changes -- confirmed via
`git diff --stat` before moving on).

### Static analysis narrowed it to one real candidate, which turned out to be a red herring

Grepped every generated `MEM32(0x5B57FC) = ...` assignment across
`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/*.c` and resolved each to its guest
label. Found exactly 4 write sites: the already-proven-dormant
`0x0004A2D6` placeholder initializer (2026-09-03), and three inside
`sub_00048AED` (a save/temporarily-clobber-with-placeholder/restore
idiom around a call to `sub_00047AC4`). Built a narrow slot-2 window
(0x47000-0x48C00) bracketing both `sub_0004721E` and `sub_00048AED` to
test the hypothesis that `sub_00047AC4` fails to preserve ESI across
the call, corrupting the restore. Result: `sub_00048AED` **never fires
at all** in this run -- the hypothesis was wrong, but the same
unconditional watch (armed from process start this time, not gated to
hit #744) still caught the real transition within that same window:
value changes from `0x005B5AE0` (0x48B15) to the legitimate placeholder
`0x005E6E20` (0x48B85), and *then*, much later (`previous_pc=0x001D560E`,
a hit from the unrelated `sub_001D5208` slot-7 window, confirming the
actual write happens somewhere with no active trace coverage), directly
to the bad value `0x00F7FE98` at guest PC `0x00047A53` -- except
`0x47A53` doesn't write that slot either (it only reads
`MEM32(0x5B57F8)`, a different, adjacent global, then makes a vtable
call). The write itself happened in un-instrumented code between the
two windows.

### Hardware watchpoint (cdb) pinpointed the actual writer in seconds

Rather than keep guessing trace windows, attached `cdb.exe` (x64,
matching `scda_recomp.exe`'s PE machine type -- it is a 64-bit host
process even though it recompiles 32-bit guest code) to the process,
broke after `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit` returns, read the live
`g_memory_base` pointer via its PDB symbol, computed the host address
of guest `0x5B57FC` (`g_memory_base + 0x5B57FC`, confirming the
existing `host = guest_va + g_memory_base` formula), and set a 4-byte
hardware write breakpoint on it with a command list that dumps
registers and a full native call stack on every hit, then resumes.
Native speed, no software-tracing overhead at all -- hit twice within
the first second of execution:

1. `new=0x005E6E20` (the legitimate placeholder) at
   `sub_00048B15+0x321`, called from `sub_00054722` /
   `sub_00054701` / `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx` /
   `xbe_entry_point` -- ordinary early boot.
2. `new=0x00F7FE98` (the "bad" value) at **`sub_00071B49+0xd3`**,
   called from `sub_00048F1D+0x19c6`, in turn from `sub_00048B15+0x23f6`.

### The "bad" write is not corruption -- it is the original game legitimately repurposing this global slot

Read `sub_00071B49`'s generated code at the write site
(`recomp_0003.c:30662`): it is the function's **own prologue**, before
any nested call:
```
eax = MEM32(ebp + 0x20);   /* 7th stack argument */
...
MEM32(0x5B57FC) = eax;
```
`ebp+0x20` is a genuine cdecl stack argument, not a corrupted register.
Traced both static call sites in `sub_00048F1D`
(`recomp_0002.c:15382-15393` and `:15408-15419`): the 7th pushed
argument in both is `eax = ebp + -56` -- **the address of a local stack
buffer in the caller's own frame**, pushed deliberately. So
`MEM32(0x5B57FC)` is not a single-purpose "file manager object"
pointer at all: it is a shared global slot the original Xbox binary
reuses for whatever the current call context needs, and `sub_00071B49`
legitimately points it at a caller-local scratch buffer for its own
duration. `0x00F7FE98` is a real, valid stack address for that purpose
on this run -- not garbage, not a corrupted register, not a
translation bug. This overturns the entire "stack corruption" framing
from continued 63 and the 2026-09-02/03 thread it referenced.

### What this actually means, and where it reconnects

The real bug is not the write -- it is that `sub_0004721E`'s hit #745
(the fallback get-name read of this same slot, from the unrelated bulk
config-enumeration loop) executes **while** `sub_00071B49` still has
the slot pointed at its own scratch buffer, instead of after whatever
should restore it. `sub_00071B49` is reached through
`sub_00048B15 -> sub_00048F1D`, i.e. through the **same
device/graphics-init call chain** already identified as running at the
wrong point in boot order in the continued-34-to-41 investigation
(`sub_00048B15 -> sub_0004934E -> sub_002E75CE -> sub_002E2BB1 ->
sub_0049D210` device creation) -- a thread that was left open with
"root cause of *that* remains open: `sub_0049CE00` itself has no
null-check on the device pointer, and it is not yet established
whether reaching it with a null device is itself abnormal". This new
finding is independent evidence for the same underlying hypothesis:
graphics/device init is interleaving with the config-load loop at a
point in the boot sequence where real hardware's ordering keeps them
apart.

Separately (not yet causally linked, flagged only for completeness): a
pre-existing `[ABI]`-check line fired for `sub_00071B49` in the same
run (`ebx 007279A1->005E6E20 esi 005E6E20->00000001 edi
00000001->00F7B374`, recent icall targets including `0003EDCC`), i.e. a
real register-preservation mismatch somewhere inside this same
function, on this same call. Not yet established whether this is the
mechanism that causes the interleaving (e.g. a wrong branch taken
because of a clobbered register) or an unrelated, independent bug in
the same neighbourhood.

### Where this leaves it

Root cause of the *specific* `MEM32(0x5B57FC)` divergence is now fully
proven at the instruction level (not guessed): it is a call-ordering
overlap between two independent subsystems, not a translation/ABI bug
at the write site itself. Fixing it properly means resuming the
continued-34-to-41 device-creation-order investigation (why does this
graphics-init chain run interleaved with the config loop on
scda_recomp but not on real hardware) and/or explaining the `[ABI]`
mismatch inside `sub_00071B49` -- both larger threads than a local
write-site fix. Not pursued further this entry without checking in
first, since the fix location has moved to a different, larger,
already-partially-mapped investigation than the one the user's
instructions were scoped to.

## 2026-09-06 (continued 65): the [ABI] violation in sub_00071B49 is REAL and isolated to one exact pop -- but xemu reaches the identical vtable target cleanly, proving the stack imbalance is a downstream SYMPTOM of a branch/data divergence inside sub_000457AE, not a generic ABI/translation bug

Per the user's precise instructions: determine whether the ebx/esi/edi
violation reported for `sub_00071B49` is (1) a genuine ABI/translation
bug, (2) a legitimate special convention/false positive, or (3) merely
a consequence of the already-known device-init-ordering divergence --
using entry/return register comparison against xemu, restricted to
just the causing call/return path. `MEM32(0x5B57FC)` itself left
unpatched throughout, as instructed.

### Static read: sub_00071B49 restores ebx/esi/edi correctly on paper

Read `sub_00071B49`'s full 189-instruction body
(`recomp_0003.c:30644-31035`). It pushes ebx/esi/edi once at entry,
uses them as scratch (loop counter, a constant, and later a local
buffer pointer), then explicitly **pops all three back to their entry
values in the middle of the function**, at guest `0x71CE2` (right after
a `sub_00070B06` call) -- and never touches them again afterward. This
is a normal, valid x86 idiom (free callee-saved registers early once
done needing them as scratch); if every intervening call preserves
them correctly, the real epilogue at `0x71DA8` needs no further
save/restore, and the function should pass the ABI check by
construction.

### Full-function bisection pinpointed the exact pop that goes wrong

Added `[SCDA-71B49-FULLBISECT]`, tagging every checkpoint across the
whole function body with ebx/esi/edi and an invocation counter (only
one invocation of `sub_00071B49` occurs in a run). Result, read
directly:
- `0x71CE2` (immediately before the pop-triple): `ebx=0x100 esi=0x62A9F0
  edi=0x00F7B774` -- exactly the expected mid-function scratch state.
- `0x71CEC` (immediately after): `ebx=0x005E6E20 esi=0x00000001
  edi=0x00F7B374` -- **not** the entry values
  (`ebx=0x007279A1 esi=0x005E6E20 edi=0x00000001`).

The shift is precise: the restored `esi` equals entry `edi`, the
restored `ebx` equals entry `esi`, and `edi` picks up an extra,
unrelated stack value -- the exact signature of the pop-triple reading
from a stack position **one dword too shallow**. Reconstructing esp
arithmetic checkpoint-by-checkpoint from the same log (every push/call/
cleanup pair balances exactly, confirmed line by line) isolates the
source precisely: the icall at guest `0x71C65` (`ecx=MEM32(0x5B57FC);
eax=MEM32(ecx); push edx; call [eax+0x10]`, a thiscall-style virtual
method taking one stack argument) never gets that one pushed argument
(`edx`) cleaned up -- neither by the callee (self-cleaning "ret 4") nor
by the caller afterward -- leaving a permanent 4-byte debt that the
`0x71CE2` pop-triple later reads through.

### Tracing the icall: a real function, reached via a real but divergent branch

Logged the resolution at `0x71C56` (right before the icall):
`obj(0x5B57FC)=0x00F7FE98` (the caller-local scratch/context object from
continued 64), `vtable=0x004F7108`, `target(+0x10)=0x00045ADE` -- a
real, already-known function (the same "get-name" helper
`sub_0004721E` uses for its own fallback branch). Read
`sub_00045ADE`'s and its callee `sub_000457AE`'s full bodies: **the
success path is provably balanced** (`sub_000457AE` does a correct
"ret 4"; `sub_00045ADE`'s success branch at `0x45AEE` does likewise) --
but the **failure path** (`0x45AF5`, taken when `sub_000457AE` returns
0) does `RECOMP_ITAIL` into a *second* vtable slot on a *nested*
object, without any stack adjustment of its own (a tail dispatch, by
design -- correct for that idiom). Instrumenting `0x45AEA`/`0x45AF5`
directly showed: **for this exact object (`this=0x00F7FE98`), the
failure branch is the one taken**, tail-dispatching through
`sub_0003EA10+0x17` (guest `0x3EA27`) -- one of a run of 8 classic
MSVC multiple-inheritance "this-adjusting" thunks
(`ecx=[ecx+4]; eax=[ecx]; jmp [eax+offset]`) laid out consecutively,
which by construction never touch the stack themselves and simply
forward cleanup responsibility further down the chain.

### xemu ground truth: the identical target resolves and returns cleanly on real hardware

Wrote `tools/debug/xemu_71b49_full_abi_check.py`, breaking at
`sub_00071B49`'s entry, the `0x71C56` icall site, both sides of the
`0x71CE2` pop, and the `0x71DA8` return. Real hardware:
- Resolves the **identical** `vtable=0x004F7108`,
  `target(+0x10)=0x00045ADE` at the icall site (same function, same
  vtable -- this part of the dispatch is not itself divergent).
- Shows `ebx/esi/edi` **exactly restored** at `0x71CEC` and `0x71DA8`
  (`MATCH=True`), matching entry values (`ebx=0 esi=0x0081FE60
  edi=1`) precisely -- **no stack imbalance at all** for this same call.

This settles the three-way question: it is **not** a legitimate
special convention that both platforms share (ruled out -- real
hardware shows no imbalance), and it is **not** a generic ABI/
translation bug in the recompiler's call/icall mechanics themselves
(ruled out -- the exact same resolved target, `sub_00045ADE` via the
exact same vtable, completes cleanly on real hardware). The only
remaining explanation is that **real hardware and scda_recomp take
different branches inside `sub_000457AE`** for this call (real
hardware's succeeds, cleanly "ret 4"-ing; scda_recomp's fails, falling
through the tail-dispatch chain to a target whose own convention does
not match what the `0x71C65` caller assumes) -- i.e. **category 3**:
this is a downstream consequence of an earlier data/branch divergence,
not a bug in this call chain's own translation.

### Where this leaves it

The `[ABI]` violation is real, fully explained mechanically, and
correctly attributed -- but its cause sits one layer further upstream,
in whatever makes `sub_000457AE`'s lookup succeed on real hardware and
fail on scda_recomp for this specific scratch object (a "does this
name/config entry resolve" question, structurally similar to every
other lookup-divergence this session has chased). Per the user's own
decision rule, this is not a case for a local ABI/translation fix --
the next step is resuming the continued-34-to-41 device-creation-order
investigation with this as new supporting evidence, not patching
`sub_00045ADE`/`sub_0003EA10`'s thunk chain (which behaves correctly by
construction and is exercised safely elsewhere in the game).
`MEM32(0x5B57FC)` was not modified, per instruction.

same function, at `0x48B90`, unconditionally) is non-zero -- which it
always is by this point -- control goes to `loc_00048CB2` and calls

and the literal string `0x4F6D90` ("`z:\Default\DynamicXbox.umd`",
already identified in continued 44) as an argument. **This second
call's return value, not the first object, is what `MEM32(0x5B5800) =
eax` publishes.** Continued 67's claim that `ebp-56` and the object
behind `MEM32(0x5B5800)` are the same construction was wrong -- it
read the code too coarsely and missed this second, always-taken branch.

filename-aware UMD/archive reader, published to the global

to a success path (`loc_000406FC`) on the first handle `!= -1`; only
if all four fail (or the post-open allocation at `0x40715`/`0x4073E`
via the global allocator `MEM32(0x5B57F8)` returns null) does it fall
through to `loc_0004075A` (`eax = 0`).

### Ruled out: not an unresolved-icall artifact

Before trusting continued 72's `POST-ICALL eax=0` as "the function ran
and internally failed", checked whether `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` even
dispatched to `sub_0004023A` at all -- an unresolved icall target
silently sets `eax=0` **without calling the target**, a known failure
mode in this codebase (Seeds 33/34/35/36 in
`projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt`). `recomp_icall_fail_log` logs every
such failure unconditionally (`[ICALL] source=... target=...`,
uncoupled from any trace window). Grepped continued 72's own capture
(`scda_443d0_run3.log`) for `target=0x0004023A`: **no match**, while
53 *other* unresolved-icall failures for unrelated targets are present
in the same log. This confirms `0x0004023A` **is** being resolved and
actually called -- continued 72's `NULL` return is real, not a
dispatch artifact.

To see which of the four directory attempts fails, narrowed

-> `sub_0049CE00` -> `sub_004A1740` -> `sub_004A1600` ->

No source, `CMakeLists.txt`, or generated-code change happened between

## 2026-09-08 (continued 74): reproducibility question answered -- NOT persistent backing-store state (a measurement bug produced a false positive there); the real, still-unexplained factor is a GPU (NV2A) fence-wait spin the main thread now reaches almost immediately, bypassing the entire sub_00048B15 chain

Per the user's explicit request: parked `sub_0004023A` root-causing and
investigated reproducibility first, aiming for a binary decision
between (A) persistent backing-store state changing the boot path, or
(B) a genuine thread/timing race.

### Step 1: actual backing stores

From `src/kernel/kernel_path.c` (`xbox_translate_path`/`xbox_path_init`,
read-only, not modified): `game_dir` = the exe's own directory
(`build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo`, since `default.xbe` lives
there -- `main.c`'s `adjacent_xbe` check); `save_dir` =
`<exe_dir>/recomp_saves`. Within `recomp_saves`:

| Xbox path | Host backing | State found |
|---|---|---|
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition1` (raw, E:) | `Partition1.img` (2.2GB) | sparse, 0 bytes actually written |
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition2` (raw, C:) | `Partition2.img` (500MB) | sparse, 0 bytes written |
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition3`/`4` (raw, X:/Y:) | `Partition3.img`/`4.img` (750MB each) | sparse, 0 bytes written |
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition5` (raw, Z:) | `Partition5.img` (750MB) | sparse, **128KB written** (see below) |
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition2\<path>` | `SystemData/` | empty |
| `\Device\Harddisk0\Partition3/4/5\<path>` | `Cache/` | `Cache/Default/DynamicXbox.umd` (7.5MB, stable since Sep 3) |
| `T:\<path>` | `TitleData/` | empty |
| `U:\<path>` | `UserData/` | empty |
| `Z:\<path>` (drive letter, not raw device) | **`game_dir` directly**, not `save_dir` -- a deliberate override (see the rule's own comment in `kernel_path.c`) so the missing disc-to-cache copy step doesn't matter | n/a, read-only |
| `D:\`/`Y:\` | `game_dir` directly | read-only |

Also found (not part of the guest-visible backing store, but
host-side persistent artifacts in the exe directory): a pre-existing
`scda_umd_dump_3526.bin` (a diagnostic dump, unrelated, stable since
Sep 4) and rotating `scda_runtime.log`/`scda_stdout.log` files.

### Step 2/false start: an `alloc=` measurement bug produced a false "state changed" signal

Wrote `tools/debug` scratch script `inventory_saves.py` (not committed
-- superseded by the correction below) to snapshot every backing file's
size/mtime/SHA-256, using `du -b <path>` for the multi-GB partition
images (too big to hash) as a stand-in for "how much is actually
written". Its very first capture showed all five `PartitionN.img`
files at **full allocation** (matching their logical size exactly),
which read as "something fully formatted/wrote to every partition
image" -- a dramatic, surprising result that looked like a strong
Option-A signal.

**Self-caught before acting on it further**: cross-checked with plain
`du -h` (sparse-aware by default) on the same file and got `0` for
`Partition1.img` -- flatly contradicting the script's `du -b` reading
of 2359820288. Isolated the cause directly:
`du -b Partition1.img` == `du --apparent-size -b Partition1.img` ==
2359820288, while `du -h` (no `-b`) == `0`. **This `du` build treats
`-b` as forcing apparent-size, not actual block allocation** -- the
inventory script's entire `alloc=` column was measuring logical file
size, not real disk usage, for every capture made with it. There was
no partition-formatting event; every `PartitionN.img` was sparse and
empty (except `Partition5.img`'s 128KB) at every point checked today,
including right now. Recorded here so this exact `du -b` pitfall isn't
repeated.

### Step 3: controlled A/B, corrected

Made a real backup first, per instruction:
`recomp_saves_baseline_backup_2026-09-08/` (robocopy, `/E /COPY:DAT`,
sibling of `recomp_saves/`) before touching anything. `rm -rf` on
`recomp_saves` itself was refused by the sandbox; used `mv` (rename
aside) instead throughout, which is equally non-destructive and kept
every intermediate state recoverable (`recomp_saves_setaside_2`,
`recomp_saves_setaside_3_lastfresh` are the leftover fresh-state
captures from this entry, safe to delete manually).

**Series A (fresh reset, `recomp_saves` absent so `xbox_path_init`
recreates it from scratch)**: 3+ separate launches, `[SCDA-74-REPRO]`
armed at `sub_000443D0` entry and its `0x44419` icall-return (same
window proven live in continued 72). **Zero hits in every run**,
verified with generous wait times (12s, 25s, 30s+) and confirmed via
non-invasive `cdb -p <pid> ~*kb` that the main thread was already deep
in an unrelated call chain within about a second of launch in every
case -- not "still booting", genuinely already past whatever point
`sub_000443D0` would fire from.

**Cross-check**: restored the original (pre-continued-74) `recomp_saves`
via the setaside rename and reproduced the exact same `du -h`-verified
sparse layout (`Partition1-4.img` = 0 bytes, `Partition5.img` = 128KB)
as every fresh run -- i.e. the "old" and "new" states are, correctly
measured, **identical**. Since identical persistent state produces the
identical (now-unreachable) outcome on every launch, **Option A
(persistent state determines the path) is ruled out.**

### The actual thing the main thread is stuck in

`cdb`'s stack for the main thread, in every recent launch, bottoms out
in a tight spin inside `sub_004A12B0`
(`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_0026.c:125226-125230`):

```
loc_004A12F0: ;
    if (TEST_NZ(MEM32(eax + 0x100410), 0x10000)) goto loc_004A12F0;
```

`eax` there resolves through `MEM32(0x4AB668)` -- the exact address
`main.c` passes to `xbox_Nv2aMirrorFence(0x004AB668u, 0x2Cu, 0x30u)` at
startup -- i.e. this is a **GPU (NV2A) command-fence acknowledgement
wait**, and thread 4 in the same process is `nv2a_ack_thread`, sitting
in `SleepEx` rather than servicing it at the moment of capture. The
call chain reaching this spin
(`sub_0004721E`/`sub_00047505`/`sub_00062237`/`sub_000464EC`/
`sub_0007188A`/`sub_0010D5C1`/`sub_001E460F`/`sub_0003EDCC`/
`sub_00077B61`/.../`sub_004A12B0`) runs entirely through functions
already established elsewhere in this session as ordinary, frequent,
per-frame machinery (`sub_0004721E` alone: 745 calls/boot on real
hardware per continued 63) -- consistent with the game having already
rendered normally for a while before landing in this particular fence
wait, not with an early-boot short-circuit.

This does **not** yet explain why `sub_000443D0` itself is skipped --
if the game reached real per-frame rendering, it must have passed
through (or around) that whole config-search chain already, one way or
another, and our probe should have caught it if it ran during the
window it was armed for. That gap is unresolved. What is established:
the boot no longer reliably parks anywhere near `sub_000443D0` long
enough (or at all) to observe it with the current setup, and it does
reliably, reproducibly park in this GPU-fence spin instead, regardless
of backing-store freshness.

### Interim conclusion on the A vs. B question

**Option A is ruled out** (see above). **Option B (thread/timing race)
is the standing explanation**, but the specific mechanism identified
this entry -- a possible NV2A fence-acknowledgement race between the
main thread and `nv2a_ack_thread`, plausibly load-sensitive given how
much concurrent tooling (multiple `cdb` attaches, Python/xemu
processes, background builds) has been running during today's whole
investigation -- has not been proven as *the* cause of the
`sub_000443D0` non-reproducibility specifically, only observed
consistently alongside it. Per instruction, no fix attempted; this is
report-and-decide.

### Where this leaves it

Needs direction: (a) investigate the NV2A fence-wait spin/race directly
(a new, likely more fundamental thread as it may explain other
instability beyond this one chain), (b) try reproducing
`sub_000443D0` again under deliberately low concurrent system load
(no parallel `cdb`/`xemu`/build activity) to see whether that alone
restores the old behavior, or (c) something else. `sub_0004023A`
root-causing remains parked either way until a reliable repro exists.

## 2026-09-08 (continued 75): low-system-load reproducibility test -- timing/system-load hypothesis REJECTED; 5/5 fresh, low-load runs still land in the sub_004A12B0 NV2A fence spin, never reaching sub_000443D0

Per the user's explicit request: a short, deliberately low-load
reproducibility test (no parallel builds, no xemu, no `cdb` attach
during the actual run) before deciding between Option A/B.

### A detour that caught a real, previously-invisible build-config bug

First attempt used a new mechanism to avoid needing 3 separate
`RECOMP_TRACE_PC` windows (only one scratch slot, slots 3-7 permanently
claimed by other live checks): an opt-in `SCDA_REPRO_MARKERS` hook
inside `RECOMP_ABI_CALL` itself (`templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`),
firing a one-shot marker for `sub_000443D0`/`sub_0004023A`/
`sub_004A12B0` on every direct call, independent of trace windows.

It silently never fired for any of the three, despite `cdb` proving
`sub_004A12B0` was genuinely on the stack. Root cause, found before
trusting the "never reached" reading: **`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/`
has its own `recomp_types.h`, and `target_include_directories` lists
that generated-output directory *before* `templates/runtime/` -- every
generated `.c` file's `#include "recomp_types.h"` silently resolves to
the gitignored shadow copy, not the template.** My edit to the real
template had zero effect on the compiled binary; the shadow copy (kept
in sync with the template, but only up to whenever it was last
generated) was still the pre-edit version. Confirmed by diffing the two
files with line endings normalized: byte-identical except for my
un-propagated edit. This is a standing pitfall for *any* future edit to
`templates/runtime/*.h` for this project -- worth its own follow-up,
not fixed here (out of scope for this entry; noted for the user).

Patched the shadow copy directly to test the fix, confirmed the
mechanism works in principle, then abandoned this approach anyway (see
below) and reverted both copies -- `git checkout` for the tracked
template, a manual reconstruction for the gitignored shadow copy (its
diff was captured above, so the revert is exact).

### The method actually used

Switched to the already-proven `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` mechanism from
continued 72/74: a single narrow window (`0x000443D0`-`0x000443D1`,
one instruction), printing `[SCDA-75-REPRO] REACHED sub_000443D0`
exactly once if hit. Cheapest possible probe, already known not to
perturb timing meaningfully (continued 72 used the same style of
window successfully).

Five fresh-reset runs (`recomp_saves` renamed aside before each, so
`xbox_path_init` recreates it from scratch every time), each launched
alone with **no other tool running concurrently** -- no `cdb`, no
xemu, no parallel build -- and left alone for 15-20 seconds before
being killed via `taskkill`. A single post-hoc `cdb -p <pid> ~0 kb`
snapshot was taken **after** each run had already settled (never
during the actual boot/start window), solely to identify where the
process ended up, per the user's constraint.

### Result

**0 out of 5 runs printed the marker.** Every run's post-settle `cdb`
snapshot showed the identical stack from continued 74:
`sub_004A1600` -> `sub_004A1740` -> `sub_0049CE00` -> `sub_00077194`
-> ... -> `sub_004A12B0` (the NV2A fence-wait spin). CPU time
consistently far exceeded wall-clock time for the ~15-20s window in
every run (e.g. 1-4 minutes of CPU time), consistent with a tight
busy-wait, not a hang/block.

### Decision, per the user's own branching instructions

All five low-load runs reproducibly land in the `sub_004A12B0` fence
wait and never reach `sub_000443D0`. Per instruction: **the
timing-/system-load hypothesis is rejected. Proceeding directly to the
NV2A fence mechanism itself is the next step**, not a
443D0-run-vs-fence-spin-run comparison (that branch was for the
opposite outcome). `sub_0004023A` root-causing remains parked.

## 2026-09-08 (continued 76): NV2A fence-spin identification attempt inconclusive -- contradictory ground truth between `cdb` stack walks and `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` instrumentation; stopping to report rather than keep guessing

Per the user's instruction (having rejected the timing hypothesis in
continued 75): attempted to pin down the NV2A fence mechanism itself
-- which register, expected vs. actual value, why `nv2a_ack_thread`
doesn't service it. Ran into a genuine contradiction between two
"ground truth" sources that could not be resolved within this entry.

### The infrastructure already exists and looks sound on paper

`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c` already has a purpose-built,
title-agnostic NV2A busy-bit acknowledgement system (`NV2A_ACK` table,
`nv2a_ack_thread`), built and proven for exactly this pattern on Halo
(`0x100410`/`0x10000`, "PFB flush kick" -- the same register/bit
`sub_004A12B0`'s spin checks). `nv2a_ack_thread` runs continuously,
clearing that bit (and others) every iteration, and the aperture is
mapped at `XBOX_NV2A_BASE + g_memory_offset` so `MEM32` reads through
the same offset the guest uses. On paper, nothing about this looks
SCDA-specific or broken.

### Attempt 1: read the actual dereferenced pointer chain -- never fired

Added a probe at `sub_004A12B0`'s own spin-check PC (`0x004A12F0`) to
print `MEM32(0x4AB668)`, its `+0x1C28` dereference, and the busy
register's value -- to check whether the guest's computed "aperture
pointer" really equals the mapped `0xFD000000` base. **Zero hits**,
despite `cdb` (across many independent captures, several different
builds) consistently attributing the parked thread to exactly this
function.

### Attempt 2: whole-function and wide-range windows -- also never fired

Suspecting a probe placement error, widened `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` to cover
the *entire* `sub_004A12B0` body (`0x004A12B0`-`0x004A1360`, its full
176 bytes) with a "log every unique PC once" tracer. **Zero hits.**
Then widened further to the whole `0x4A0000`-`0x4B0000` 64KB
neighbourhood. **Still zero hits**, even though `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` is
the literal first statement of every generated block and cannot be
skipped if that guest code executes at all -- this is not a timing or
sampling issue, it is definitive: none of these guest addresses
executed during the probe window.

### A disassembly-level check muddied things further

A direct, symbol-independent check (`cdb`: read `eip`, disassemble at
it) on the *wide-window* build caught the main thread with EIP
literally inside `scda_recomp!scda_trace_pc+0x3ae2` -- i.e. genuinely
executing inside our own accumulated instrumentation function, not
guest code, at that instant. `scda_trace_pc()` has grown very large
over 75 "continued" entries' worth of accumulated diagnostic branches;
this raised a real alternative hypothesis (boot is merely very slow
under that accumulated weight, not stuck) that needed testing.

### Attempt 3: a much longer wait plus a heartbeat -- also silent

Reverted to the single proven `sub_000443D0` marker (from continued
75) plus a heartbeat that prints on `scda_trace_pc`'s very first call
and every 500,000 calls after. Ran **2 full minutes** (vs. the usual
15-20s) with no other tool running. Result: **the heartbeat never
printed even once** -- `scda_trace_pc()` was not entered a single time
in 2 minutes, even though `tasklist` showed 4:22 of CPU time
accumulated in that span. This rules out the "just slow inside
scda_trace_pc" hypothesis for *this* build/window combination: the
CPU time is being spent somewhere that never touches any
`RECOMP_TRACE_PC`-instrumented address at all -- consistent with real,
sustained execution of un-instrumented native (compiled guest or host)
code, but inconsistent with the earlier disassembly capture that
placed EIP inside `scda_trace_pc` under the wide-window build.

### Where this leaves it

Two solid, ground-truth facts stand from this session's work and are
not in question: (1) `sub_000443D0` is not reached, reproducibly,
under both low and (implicitly, given 2 minutes of silence)
higher-latency conditions; (2) the process burns real CPU the whole
time regardless. Everything about *where exactly* that CPU time goes
is now contradictory between `cdb`'s stack walks (consistently name
`sub_004A12B0` et al., across many builds) and direct
`RECOMP_TRACE_PC` instrumentation of those exact same guest addresses
(consistently zero hits, including a whole-function and a 64KB-wide
window). Rather than keep guessing with more probes, stopping here to
report the contradiction plainly -- continuing to add ad hoc
instrumentation without a hypothesis that actually fits both
observations risks spending more effort chasing an artifact than
finding the real mechanism. Candidate explanations not yet
distinguished: `cdb`'s stack walker is unreliable for these
frame-pointer-omitted (`fpo_leaf`) functions and has been misattributing
frames all along (in which case the real location is unknown and
needs a different identification method entirely, e.g. single-stepping
via a real breakpoint rather than a snapshot attach); or the hang is
genuinely inside compiled guest code that happens to fall entirely
between our probe points every time by some structural reason not yet
understood; or something else not yet considered. `sub_0004023A`
root-causing remains parked.

### SC4 XBE Bloom diagnostics, 2026-09-08

The separate `SC4_xbe_hack` work remained read-only in this milestone: the
retail XBE and all ISO files were untouched. A segmented GDB scan found 24
live `COMBINER_CONTROL=0x00011104` state records. Their local dumps isolate
`0x006FA470` as the exact normal-Bloom record because it additionally has
`ShaderProg=0x00008421` and `Alpha0=0xD830D930`, both observed on the Bloom
draw. A one-shot read watchpoint is prepared for this one record to identify
its CPU consumer and static producer before an XBE patch is attempted.

The boot-time write watch proved the static source at XBE raw offset
`0x005D78F4` / VA `0x005DACD4`. A direct four-byte change
`04 11 01 00 -> 00 00 00 00` in that one normal-Bloom template was packaged
as `scda_bloom_exact_combiner_zero.iso`. The user confirmed it works in-game;
Night Vision remains correct. This validates the effect-specific data patch,
not a change to a shared renderer path.

The combined artifact `default_scda_graphics_fixes.xbe` was then produced
from the original XBE with only the three independently validated edits:
smoke composite skip (`0x002EC475`), pixel state null (`0x005D239C`), and the
exact Bloom combiner null (`0x005D78F4`). Its companion ISO is
`scda_graphics_fixes.iso`; original game XBE restoration and all three byte
ranges were verified after the build. The combined runtime visual test remains
separate from the individual validations.

### SC4 XBE Bloom diagnostic, 2026-09-08

The separate `SC4_xbe_hack` investigation did not modify the retail XBE or
an ISO in this step. A segmented live-memory GDB scan in a normal Bloom scene
found 24 copies of the verified NV2A `COMBINER_CONTROL=0x00011104`, all in

gap, so this is the first usable dynamic candidate set. The active render
objects and known parent range contain no direct copy. A read-only local dump
of the 24 candidate records is prepared to identify the record selected by

executes" fact, bypassed `RECOMP_TRACE_PC`/`scda_trace_pc` entirely:

exact address would have tripped the breakpoint within microseconds

## 2026-09-08 (continued 78): the NV2A fence-spin at `sub_004A12B0+0x1d0` is CONFIRMED real after all -- continued 77's "disproof" was an address-drift artifact of a different build, not a genuine negative; full 18-frame real call stack captured from an actual breakpoint stop, and a frozen zero field at the loop's base pointer is the new lead

### EXE/PDB match sanity check

`cdb -z scda_recomp.exe -c "lmvm scda_recomp; q"` (static, no running

and reports it as "private pdb symbols" with no mismatch warning --
the embedded signature and the loaded PDB agree; EXE and PDB are from
the same build. The recurring `*** WARNING: Unable to verify checksum`
is unrelated: it flags the PE optional-header `CheckSum` field being
`00000000` (unset by the linker, normal for local/unsigned builds),
not a symbol/PDB mismatch. This concern from continued 77 is closed;
it was never the mechanism behind any prior misattribution.

### Round 1: entry breakpoints on the three innermost outer-frame candidates

Launched under `cdb -o -g -G ./scda_recomp.exe -c "bp
scda_recomp!sub_004A1600; bp scda_recomp!sub_004A1740; bp
scda_recomp!sub_0049CE00; g"`. Over 120s, `Get-Process` CPU climbed
150 -> 375 (225 CPU-seconds of wall 120s, i.e. roughly two threads

Seven candidate entry points now cleanly miss under real breakpoints,

### Method change: raw RIP sampling instead of stack-walk-based guesses

Launched `scda_recomp.exe` with no debugger at all (a plain run), then
did six quick, independent, **non-invasive** attach/detach snapshots
(`cdb -p <pid> -c "~* r rip; .detach; q"`), reading only the raw
instruction pointer of every thread -- no symbol resolution, no stack
unwinding, nothing that continued 74-77 had reason to distrust. Result
across all six snapshots: five of six threads sat at fixed addresses
in `ntdll`/`KERNELBASE` (blocked in a syscall, as expected for idle
worker threads), and **one thread's RIP** landed, every single time,
within a 24-byte window (`...cb570` .. `...cb588`) inside the
process's own module. Ten more snapshots (16 total) confirmed the same
tight window, never leaving it.

Translating that window through the module's actual runtime base
(read via `lm m scda_recomp` on the same live process) and the
`scda_recomp.map` ground truth gave an exact hit: **`sub_004A12B0`,
offsets +0x1d0 through +0x1e8** -- the very function and the very
neighbourhood of the offset that continued 74-76 originally suspected
and continued 77 believed it had disproven.

### Reconciling with continued 77's "disproof"

Static disassembly of the *current* (idle-instrumentation, freshly
rebuilt) binary at that address:

```
scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x1d0:
  mov     ecx,dword ptr [r14+r13]
  mov     rax,qword ptr [scda_recomp!g_xbox_mem_offset]
  add     ecx,100410h
  mov     ecx,dword ptr [rcx+rax]
scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x1e4:
  bt      ecx,10h
  jb      scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x1d0
```

This is exactly the NV2A busy-bit poll (register offset `0x100410`,
bit 16 / mask `0x10000`) from continued 74's original hypothesis.
Continued 77's breakpoint had been set on a *different* build -- one
with `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` actively instrumented at this exact call site,
which inserts extra bytes (`mov ecx, 4A12F0h; call scda_trace_pc`)
ahead of the loop and shifts everything after it by a few bytes. The
symbolic offset `+0x1d0` computed against that instrumented layout did
not land on the same byte in the now-current, idle-instrumentation
layout used throughout this entry. In short: continued 77 disproved
one exact byte address in one specific build; it did not disprove the
underlying loop, and the two are not the same claim. This is a
correction to continued 77's conclusion, not an extension of it.

### Confirming a real, live internal loop (not just a hot re-entry)

A first real-breakpoint attach at the address derived from the raw-RIP
scan (`bp <live-address>; g`) fired within about a second of resuming
-- immediate confirmation this exact byte executes. A follow-on,
auto-continuing capture (`bp <addr> ".printf ...; g"`) produced an
enormous, useful-but-dangerous amount of output very quickly (log grew
to ~125 MB within roughly 20 seconds before being caught and killed;
noted below under process hygiene) -- but every single one of the
many thousands of captured hits showed **identical** register state:
same `rip`, same `r14` (a heap pointer), same `r13` (`0x3b0`, a fixed
struct offset), same dereferenced value (`[r14+r13] == 0`) every time.
Frozen registers across thousands of hits could mean either "the loop
truly spins with unchanging state" or "this call site is instead being
re-entered fresh, extremely often, with coincidentally identical
inputs" -- these are different claims and the frequency data alone
does not distinguish them.

A second, deliberately minimal test resolved this: attach, hit the
breakpoint exactly once, capture the real stack (`k 12`), then single
step (`p`) eight times with no auto-continue. **The same breakpoint
fired again after exactly six single steps** -- six being exactly the
instruction count of the loop body above (`mov`, `mov`, `add`, `mov`,
`bt`, `jb`). Stepping through byte-for-byte and landing back on the
same address is conclusive: this is a genuine, internal, unconditional
re-execution of the loop body within one call, not an external
re-invocation. The bit tested at `MEM32(g_xbox_mem_offset + 0x100410)`
never clears.

### The real call stack, captured live (not inferred from an async attach)

From the same single controlled stop, `k 12` gave a full, real x64
unwind (frame 0 is exact by construction -- it's the live breakpoint
stop, not a guessed innermost frame from an asynchronous attach):

```

sub_004A1600+0x7b2
sub_004A1740+0xb6
sub_0049CE00+0x2a0
sub_00077194+0x165b
sub_000774E6+0x12cf
sub_000778BC+0xea8
sub_00077B61+0x14e
sub_0003EDCC+0xba
sub_001E460F+0x297
sub_0010D5C1+0x118
sub_0007188A+0x65e
sub_000464EC+0x59b
sub_0004721E+0x23c2
sub_00047505+0x15c
sub_00062237+0x1bd8
sub_00065F31+0x1030
sub_001D79F6+0x45e
```

This is the same set of frames (`sub_004A1600`, `sub_004A1740`,
`sub_0049CE00`, `sub_00077194`, `sub_000774E6`, `sub_000778BC`,
`sub_00077B61`) that rounds 1-2 of this entry set *entry* breakpoints
on without a single hit in 240s combined. That is now explained: each
of those functions was called exactly once, on the way into the spin;
their prologues never execute again while the callee spins forever
underneath them, no matter how long a breakpoint sits on the entry
instruction. Testing entry points cannot detect a call chain that is
already inside its terminal frame. This also means the historical
`~*kb`-based captures from continued 74-76 identifying this exact

untrustworthy in general (async stack-walk of a frame that might not

instruction ("danach nur noch diese konkrete Schleife untersuchen")

## 2026-09-08 (continued 79): root cause of the `sub_004A12B0` spin found -- it polls a fixed low guest address instead of a real NV2A register because the D3D device pointer at guest `0x4AB668` is 0; `CreateDevice`'s only caller (`sub_0003FCA5`) is absent from the full, real call stack from `xbe_entry_point` down to the spin

Per instruction ("bitte in Schritt 4 einsteigen" -- step 4 of the
prior instruction: "danach nur noch diese konkrete Schleife
untersuchen").

### Reading the guest source of the loop

The generated C for `sub_004A12B0` (guest `ecx`=`esi`="this") makes
the mechanism explicit in a way the x64 disassembly alone did not:

```c
eax = MEM32(0x4AB668);         /* the D3D device pointer (a fixed guest global) */
eax = MEM32(eax + 0x1C28);     /* a field inside that device struct */
ecx = MEM32(eax + 0x100410);
ecx = ecx | 0x10000;           /* kick: set the busy bit */
MEM32(eax + 0x100410) = ecx;
loc_004A12F0:
    if (TEST_NZ(MEM32(eax + 0x100410), 0x10000)) goto loc_004A12F0;  /* wait for hardware to clear it */
```

`eax` here is exactly the register the x64 build spills to
`[this_ctx + 0x3b0]`, which continued 78 found frozen at `0` across
every sampled iteration.

### Where `0x4AB668` comes from

`grep` for writes to `MEM32(0x4AB668)` across the generated code finds
exactly three, all inside `sub_0049D210` (a `CreateDevice`-shaped
function: it touches `MEM32(0x4ADE04)`/`MEM32(0x4ADE00)` init flags,
zeroes a large struct with `rep stosd`, and calls `sub_004A2220` for
the real init work):

- success path: `MEM32(0x4AB668) = edi` where `edi = 0x4AB670` -- a
  **fixed** guest struct address, not a heap allocation.
- two failure/reset paths (`sub_004A2220` returning negative, or an
  unconditional reset elsewhere) set it back to `0`.

`sub_0049D210` is called from exactly one place in the entire
generated codebase: a callsite inside `sub_0003FCA5`, guest return
address `0x0003FD2F`.

### Live memory readout at the exact moment of the spin

Non-invasive attach, reading through `g_xbox_mem_offset` (confirmed
`0x10000` -- guest RAM is mapped at a fixed low host base, so
`host = guest_va + 0x10000` for ordinary `MEM32` accesses):

```
MEM32(0x4AB668)          = 0x00000000   <- device pointer: never set (or reset)
MEM32(0x4AB670 + 0x1C28) = 0x00000000   <- the fixed device struct's own field, also 0
MEM32(0x100410)          = 0x758DC8FE   <- bit 16 (mask 0x10000) is 1 in this value
```

This closes the loop completely: because the device pointer is `0`,
the guest code's own address arithmetic degenerates to `eax = MEM32(0
+ 0x1C28)`, which itself reads as `0`, so the "hardware register"
being polled is not a register at all -- it's `MEM32(0x100410)`, an
ordinary, un-emulated guest RAM location holding whatever was last
written there for unrelated reasons. Its bit 16 happens to be `1`.
Nothing in the emulator has any reason to ever clear that bit, because
nothing treats `0x100410` as a real NV2A register when it is reached
through a null device pointer -- so the loop cannot terminate by
construction, independent of scheduling, timing, or the NV2A_ACK
table's own correctness for the *real* register case.

### The full call stack, entry point to spin, in one real breakpoint stop

`bp scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0+0x1d0; g; k 40` on a fresh, undebugged
launch gave the complete, real x64 unwind for the whole thread, not
just the segment continued 78 had already captured:

```
xbe_entry_point+0x261
main+0x214
sub_00052572+0x374
kernel_thunk_dispatch+0x212
bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx+0x181
sub_000524DA+0x608
sub_00054701+0x169
sub_00054722+0x321
sub_00048B15+0x23c6            <- the historical milestone address; confirmed reached
sub_00048F1D+0x1a19
sub_0004934E+0x12281
sub_0003B78F+0x137
sub_001D79F6+0x45e
sub_00065F31+0x1030
sub_00062237+0x1bd8
sub_00047505+0x15c
sub_0004721E+0x23c2
sub_000464EC+0x59b
sub_0007188A+0x65e
sub_0010D5C1+0x118
sub_001E460F+0x297
sub_0003EDCC+0xba
sub_00077B61+0x14e
sub_000778BC+0xea8
sub_000774E6+0x12cf
sub_00077194+0x165b
sub_0049CE00+0x2a0
sub_004A1740+0xb6
sub_004A1600+0x7b2
sub_004A12B0+0x1d0             <- the spin
```

`sub_0003FCA5` (`CreateDevice`'s only caller) is absent from this
entire chain, on the whole thread, from the process entry point down.
This is confirmed for the currently-stuck thread only; it does not by
itself prove `sub_0003FCA5` never ran at all (a different thread, or
an earlier and since-unwound call on this same thread, could have run
it already -- succeeding and later being reset, or failing outright).
It only proves this exact call chain does not require having called
it as an ancestor, and that whatever should have created the D3D
device has not left a live pointer at `0x4AB668` by the time this
chain reaches its terminal, unrecoverable frame.

### Where this leaves it

Two concrete hypotheses remain open and are distinguishable with a
single well-placed check:

1. `sub_0003FCA5`/`sub_0049D210` (`CreateDevice`) has never executed
   at all by this point -- an ordering bug: something calls this NV2A
   kick/wait logic before device creation has had a chance to run.
2. `CreateDevice` *did* run (on this thread, earlier, before the
   segment of the call chain captured above, or conceivably on
   another thread) and failed -- `sub_004A2220`'s internal init
   returned negative, triggering the rollback path that resets
   `MEM32(0x4AB668)` back to `0`.

Telling these apart needs either a one-shot breakpoint on
`sub_0003FCA5`'s entry, armed from process start and left running past
the point where the thread gets stuck (if it never fires before the
thread parks in the spin, hypothesis 1 is confirmed; if it fires and
`sub_004A2220`'s return value is negative, hypothesis 2 is confirmed),
or a narrow, single-address `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` window on
`sub_0003FCA5`/`sub_0049D210`/`sub_004A2220` if a breakpoint proves
inconclusive for some reason. Not yet attempted -- reported for an
explicit go/no-go before continuing, per the user's established
step-by-step pattern this whole investigation.

artefact -- killing the process to force a flush produced no hit
lines in either log).

### Isolating the variable: does the *known-good* breakpoint alone still work?

Suspecting the three new breakpoints had somehow interfered, the test
was stripped back to exactly the single breakpoint
(`sub_004A12B0+0x1d0`) that fired within about a second in continued
78 and 79, repeated multiple times there without exception. Run three
more times, each in isolation, each with a genuinely quiet wall-clock
window (30s, then 20s, undisturbed by any polling in between so as
not to reintroduce the load this entry was trying to rule out as a
confound) before killing to force-flush the log and check for
`Breakpoint 0 hit`. **All three isolated re-runs failed to reach it.**
Four for four failures total this entry, on the exact same
`scda_recomp.exe` (`LastWriteTime` re-verified unchanged at
2026-09-08 18:24:39 -- not rebuilt since continued 78) that produced
sixteen consistent raw-RIP hits and multiple real-breakpoint
confirmations earlier in this same session.

### A plausible, unconfirmed suspect: persistent state written during today's own testing

`recomp_saves/Partition{1,2,3,4,5}.img` under
`build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/` all show a `LastWriteTime` of
today, several hours after this session's testing began, i.e. written
by one or more of today's own runs. This session ran a large number
of `scda_recomp.exe` launches this entry and the previous two, many
terminated with `Stop-Process -Force` (immediate process kill, no
graceful shutdown) rather than a clean exit. If the title (or the
kernel layer) persists any state to those partition images on an
unclean kill -- or if a partially-written file from an interrupted
save is read back on the next launch -- that is a concrete, plausible
mechanism for the boot path to have silently changed between continued
79 and this entry, without any code or configuration change. This is
flagged as a suspect, not confirmed: no diff of the partition images
before/after was taken, and no alternative explanation (a timing
change, a different kind of race, something unrelated to persisted
state entirely) has been ruled out either.

### Why this stops the investigation here rather than continuing into hypothesis 1 vs 2

Testing whether `sub_0003FCA5` fires before the spin is meaningless if
the spin itself cannot currently be reproduced at all -- there is
nothing to compare "before" against. Continuing to add breakpoints or
reasoning on top of a boot path that has just demonstrably stopped
reproducing would repeat the exact mistake the user's original
reproducibility methodology (from early in this investigation arc) was
designed to prevent. This is reported rather than chased further
alone.

### Where this leaves it

The continued 78-79 findings (the loop's mechanism, its dependency on
`MEM32(0x4AB668)`, the full real call stack, `sub_0003FCA5` being
`CreateDevice`'s only caller) are unaffected by this entry -- they were
established with solid, repeated, real-breakpoint evidence while the
path was still reproducing. What is now in question is only whether
that exact path is *still* the one this build takes on a fresh launch,
given today's accumulated `Stop-Process -Force` history. Before any
further work on the `sub_0003FCA5` question, the open item is to
re-establish reproducibility -- most directly, by restoring a known
`recomp_saves/` snapshot from before today's testing (if one exists)
or accepting a fresh/clean save state, then re-confirming with a
single quiet, undisturbed run whether the `sub_004A12B0+0x1d0`
breakpoint fires again as it did in continued 78-79. Not yet attempted
-- reported for direction before continuing.

**Static/mechanical checklist, first pass.** `XBOX_FS_BASE` is no
longer a single process-wide constant (`RECOMP_TLS uint32_t g_fs_base`,
confirmed in both `xbox_memory_layout.h` and `templates/runtime/
recomp_types.h`). The main thread gets a TIB for free -- the TLS
default initializer (`= XBOX_TIB_MAIN`) gives every thread that never
reassigns it the loader-built value automatically, no special-case code
needed. A spawned worker calls `xbox_AllocThreadTib()` in
`bridge_thread_main`, which copies the `tib_size`=0x40 template, sets
its own SEH-chain end (`0xFFFFFFFF`) and its own TLS block/slot-0
pointer. One gap confirmed real: **no corresponding free.**
`PsTerminateSystemThread` returns the worker's *stack*
(`xbox_FreeThreadStack`) but never the TIB block `xbox_AllocThreadTib`
allocated from the guest heap via `xbox_HeapAlloc` -- a per-spawn leak,
present in upstream unchanged (not introduced by this merge), bounded
in practice by however many times a title actually spawns workers (see
below: currently exactly once for SCDA's observed boot, so a handful of
KB, not a growth risk today).

**A second, more consequential architecture finding, found while
tracing where `XBOX_FS_BASE` is actually read.** SCDA carries its own,
independent, already-thread-local fs: storage -- `g_xbox_fs` (`static
RECOMP_TLS uint8_t g_xbox_fs[0x10000]`), added 2026-09-01 (`bda6c15`),
accessed via `xbox_fs_read8/16/32`/`xbox_fs_write8/16/32`, with an
explicit comment: "rather than upstream's flat-guest-memory-at-
XBOX_FS_BASE approach: this keeps per-thread TIB/stack-bounds/TLS state
correct, which a single shared guest-memory TIB cannot provide for a
multi-threaded title." Confirmed in `lifter.py` (`_fmt_mem_read`/
`_fmt_mem_write`, lines ~156-169): every `fs:[N]` access in *generated
game code* dispatches to `xbox_fs_read*/xbox_fs_write*`, never to
`MEM32(XBOX_FS_BASE + N)`. So `XBOX_FS_BASE`/`g_fs_base` is invisible
to recompiled game code entirely; the only consumers are three lines in
hand-written kernel C: `bridge_RtlUnwind` (`BRIDGE_MEM32(XBOX_FS_BASE)`,
3 call sites), the host-only `fence_readable()` null-guard (runs
exclusively on `nv2a_ack_thread`, a `CreateThread`-spawned host thread
that never calls `xbox_AllocThreadTib()`, so unaffected), and the
one-time self-pointer init at boot. Net effect for SCDA: `e35c8be`
fixes cross-thread interference in `bridge_RtlUnwind` specifically (all
threads previously shared guest address `0x1000` as the unwind chain
head there), *not* the CRT-`_lock()`-deadlock class the upstream commit
message describes for Half-Life 2 -- that class was already closed by
SCDA's independent, pre-existing `g_xbox_fs` design.

**The load-bearing correction.** Built a temporary diagnostic
(`[FS-DIAG] host=<tid> guest=<main|worker> fs_base=... fs:[0]=...
fs:[4]=...`, one print at the end of `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit`'s TIB
setup and one right after `xbox_AllocThreadTib()` in
`bridge_thread_main`) to empirically confirm main-vs-worker separation
before removing the hooks. Main thread printed correctly: `fs_base=
0x00001000 fs:[0]=0xFFFFFFFF fs:[4]=0x00770094`. **The worker-thread
print never fired.** `scda_runtime.log` shows exactly one
`PsCreateSystemThreadEx` call for the entire boot:

    [KERNEL] PsCreateSystemThreadEx #1: routine=0x000524DA ctx1=0x00054701 ctx2=0x00000000

-- and `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx`'s own logic
(`kernel_bridge.c`, `is_first_call = (g_thread_mode ==
XBOX_THREAD_MODE_INLINE) && (g_thread_call_count == 0)`) treats the
*first* call, in the default `XBOX_THREAD_MODE_INLINE` SCDA has never
opted out of, as the game's own entry point: it runs `fn()` directly on
the calling thread's register state, never through
`bridge_spawn_thread`/`CreateThread`/`bridge_thread_main`. SCDA never
calls `xbox_SetThreadMode`, so it stays INLINE, and this run's single
`PsCreateSystemThreadEx` call -- `routine=0x000524DA`, the exact
function continued 32/33 identified as the entry point of what was
described there as "a background worker thread" -- **runs on the same
single host thread as everything else.** No second host thread exists
at any point in this boot.

This overturns continued 32/33's own conclusion (and this session's
repetition of it in the stage 4 and stage 5-approval writeups): a CDB
stack sample showing `bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx` as a frame proves

execute on the boot's one and only host thread. `e35c8be`'s TIB-per-
thread mechanism is therefore not merely "dormant" for the current spin

  entry) -- it is a *nested* object obtained by two further lookups
  performed in the caller (`sub_0004721E`'s own name-lookup result,
  then `sub_0004693B` on that found entry). Deterministic across two
  fresh boots on the corrected disc: outer object `0x0081BE80`, nested
  object `0x0082C784`, match at real-boot t=1.33s, fields populated
  (`base=0x0082E290 buckets=0x00838E10 mask=0x00000008`) by t=1.45s.

  hardware write-watchpoint on the nested object's three fields**
  (`tools/debug/xemu_47505_first_write.py`, new): after ~20 write hits

  unconnected allocations at the same recycled address (confirmed by

  (`0x0082E290`/`0x00838E10`/`0x00000008`) all land at guest eip

  (`functions.json`: `called_by: ['0x00077B61']`).
- **`sub_000778BC` is a generic `realloc()`-style heap-growth routine**
  (confirmed by reading its full generated C, `recomp_0003.c:50859`):
  it either completes a normal boundary-tag-based grow-and-copy (the
  path taken here, ending in the `0x00077A2C` memcpy) or, if the
  requested size `eax` is `>= 0xFFFFFFE0` (i.e. effectively negative
  when treated as signed -- an overflowed/oversized request), takes an
  **OOM branch**: `call sub_0049CE00` (warn), `call sub_0049CC50`,
  `call sub_00052D5A` (`Sleep(0x7D0)` = 2000ms), then falls through to
  the same return point. `sub_000778BC`'s own `calls_to` list
  (`0x000774E6`, `0x0049CE00`, `0x0049CC50`, `0x00052D5A`) matches this
  exactly.

  to the tail of scda_recomp's own already-documented, previously
  captured (continued 86, real `k 100`) live spin call stack**:
  `sub_0004721E -> sub_000464EC -> sub_0007188A -> sub_0010D5C1 ->
  sub_001E460F -> sub_0003EDCC -> sub_00077B61 -> sub_000778BC ->
  sub_000774E6 -> sub_00077194 -> sub_0049CE00 -> sub_004A1740 ->
  sub_004A1600 -> sub_004A12B0 (spin)`. A one-hop frame walk from the

  before trusting `[ebp]`/`[ebp+4]`; `sub_00077B61` itself is
  `fpo_leaf`, so its own `[ebp+4]`/`[ebp]` are inherited from ITS

### CONCLUSION -- not a new divergence

This closes the continued 86 "OPEN" question by identifying it as the
**same bug already root-caused in continued 58-61**, not a new one:
`sub_0004721E`'s first call lazily populates its nested container by
reading a resource via the identical `sub_0007188A`-rooted chain that
continued 58-59 already proved misreads Partition5.img's raw device
`GetFileSize()` (a legitimate ~750MB) as a small text file's
char-count, producing a wildly oversized `realloc()` request. On xemu
this chain reads a genuinely small file, the size is reasonable,
`sub_000778BC` completes its normal grow-and-copy, and the container
ends up populated. On scda_recomp the identical call chain is
reached (matching, edge for edge, the historical `k 100` capture), but
per `sub_000778BC`'s own branch condition an oversized request routes
into the OOM branch instead: the container is left empty (no memcpy
ever runs) AND, as a side effect of that same OOM branch's warn+sleep
handler, `sub_004A12B0` gets invoked and spins on its own separate,
already-understood `MEM32(0x4AB668)==0` condition. Both observed
symptoms (empty container, the spin) are downstream consequences of
one upstream cause, not two problems.

resolution has an empty name**, causing `kernel_path.c`'s existing

### A real, previously-undocumented cdb tooling limitation, discovered and confirmed this entry

Guest register state (`g_eax`, `g_ecx`, `g_esp`, etc.) is
`RECOMP_TLS`-qualified (`__declspec(thread)`) storage inside
scda_recomp's own host process -- **not** reflected in the host CPU's
actual registers at any cdb breakpoint. A conditional breakpoint like
`.if (@rcx == 0x48caa)` or a bare `r eax` at a `RECOMP_ABI_CALL`-based
function's entry reads whatever the *host x64 calling convention*
happens to have left in that register (irrelevant, since every
recompiled `sub_XXXXX` takes no real parameters and communicates
purely through these TLS globals plus real guest memory) -- not guest
state. Confirmed by testing `?? g_eax` (fails, "Couldn't resolve
error"), `x scda_recomp!g_eax` (fails, "Memory access error"), and
`!tls -1` (returns an all-zero TLS slot array for the live thread,
unexplained but consistent with `x`/`??` both failing). **Two
techniques remain fully reliable for scda_recomp under cdb**: (a)
breakpoint hit/miss at a function's entry (valid signal regardless of
register content, and real host stack walks (`k`) remain valid too,
since every `RECOMP_ABI_CALL` is a genuine host `call`/`ret`), and (b)
direct guest **memory** reads via `dd <g_memory_base + guest_va>`
(guest memory is a real mapped region, not TLS -- `g_memory_base`
itself resolves fine via `x scda_recomp!g_memory_base`). Any future
session needing guest *register* values at a specific PC should not
attempt this via cdb at all -- either add a temporary permanent
`[SCDA-*]`-style `fprintf` hook (accepting the multi-file, 1+ hour
full-rebuild cost documented below) or find a still-unexplored TLS
resolution path (`!teb`, manually computing `TEB->
ThreadLocalStoragePointer[_tls_index] + field_offset`) before spending
further time on `bp <symbol>`/`r $tN = <symbol>`, both of which were
also independently reconfirmed to hang in every fresh `-o -g -G`
launch tried this entry (consistent with continued 87's own finding,
now additionally confirmed to hang identically for `r $tN = <symbol>`,
not just `bp <symbol>`).
