### SC4 XBE graphics: ShadowToggler C-pass correlation (2026-09-09)

The ReShade and NV2A capture were run in the same process.  The C-confirmed
host pair (`VS=1DAD10B2`, `PS=89F55E8C`) maps to a four-vertex NV2A draw with
`SHADERPROG=1`, `COMBINER_CONTROL=11104`, final inputs `0E/1C80`, and texture
formats `11288/7710C88/661068C/7710C8C`.  Its live CPU chain is
`0030114C -> 0022961B -> 002C655E -> 001CB929`.  Static inspection shows the
first address is a shared renderer VTable entry (table VA `00568D6C`), not a
safe patchpoint.  A new xemu-only capture dumps argument words for precisely
this signature; no XBE or ISO was altered.

The first C-frames capture re-observed the target exactly once (OpenGL program
209 / pixel CRC `291F1CBF`) but emitted no compact register line.  The cause is
now identified: PFIFO/PGRAPH consumes the draw asynchronously, where
`current_cpu` is intentionally null.  The fix is not an XBE change: DMA_PUT
submit-history now saves the producer's eight GPRs and bounded `ESI`/`EDI`
object words synchronously, and the exact state retrieves the matching history
entry by its pushbuffer range.  Build completed 2026-09-09 14:08:01:
`qemu-system-i386w.exe`, 86,207,339 bytes, SHA-256
`1E04DF14746222D4F565C122093DCA45986D56803D42638F216966CDCF450779`.
The existing ReShade-state launcher remains observational and self-cleans its
own output log before launch.

The corrected asynchronous capture produced twelve `sc4_shadow_c_submit`
records.  The exact target was matched to pushbuffer ranges and yielded caller
families `0030114C`, `002F381A`, `002F49AD`, `002EAB7F`, `002F40C5`,
`002F6611`, and `002293E1`.  This is decisive negative evidence against a
single static patch at the shared renderer or combiner value: those locations
serve several material/quad paths.  No XBE bytes were changed; the captured
register/object words are retained for the next resource-specific comparison.

## 2026-09-09/10, continued 89: `sub_0004023A`'s function boundary was
truncated at 91 of its real 1324 bytes -- root-caused, fixed via a full
Disasm→func_id→Recomp→Build regeneration (not a code patch), VERIFIED FIXED.
A new, deeper blocker (the same `\LMaps\menu\common.lin` / Partition5 / OOM
chain, now reached through the *real* dispatch) immediately follows.

### The path-construction chase that led here

Continuing directly from continued 88's open question (why does the
container end up empty), this entry followed the `\LMaps\common.lin` open
end to end. xemu's real hardware opens exactly `D:\Default\DataXb\LMaps\
common.lin` (no `\menu\`) immediately before `SplinterCell4xbox.ini`.
scda_recomp instead tried 18 variants of `...\LMaps\menu\common.lin` (never
the correct string) and then made no further `NtCreateFile` calls at all for
the rest of the observed window.

Traced the guest call chain for the *correct* xemu open via a manual EBP-walk
at the real kernel `NtCreateFile` (resolved dynamically through the ordinal-
190 kernel-import thunk, not guessed): `0x0004909F` (an already-instrumented
trace point) → `sub_00071B49` (the vtable-0x4F7108 icall dispatch, matching
the historical `[SCDA-71BE6-ICALL]` hooks) → `sub_00045D0B` → `sub_000443D0`
→ an address (`0x00040350`, immediately after a `call 0x511e7`) that
`functions.json` had **no function at all** for -- landing 91 bytes into
`sub_0004023A`'s *detected* body, past its recorded end.

### Root cause: not a heuristic bug, a truncated-function detection bug --
and not the cache either

Disassembling from `0x0004023A` (the function's real, correctly-detected
start) straight through the "end" at `0x00040295` shows the code continuing
completely normally, with no prologue of its own, all the way to a genuine
`ret 0xC` at `0x00040766`. Real size: 1324 bytes; detected size: 91. The 6-
instruction gap this leaves (`0x40295`-`0x40766`) contains the entire path-
join-and-open logic that would have produced the correct string.

Instrumented `FunctionDetector._build_functions`/`_find_function_end`
directly (no output files touched) and confirmed the **current** checked-out
`tools/disasm/functions.py` already computes `sub_0004023A`'s correct
`0x0004023A`-`0x00040766` span immediately, unprompted. The fix was already
in three local commits from four-five days earlier: `ffe089d` ("fix missing
range-check causing 2482x duplicate-alias bloat"), `3381db5`, `c4a7ebf`,
`aeb406b` (2026-09-04/05). `tools/disasm/output/scda_v060/functions.json`
had genuinely already been refreshed on the morning of 2026-09-09 (rerun by
an earlier part of this same session) and already showed the corrected span
-- but `tools/func_id/output/scda_seeded_corrected/identified_functions.json`
(a *separate*, required intermediate stage the recomp translator also reads
via `--func-id-dir`) was still dated 2026-08-24, and `tools/recomp/output/
scda_v060`'s generated C still showed the old, truncated body. The disasm
fix alone was not enough; the pipeline has three stages that all consume
each other's output, and only the first had been re-run.

Checked `AnalysisCache._opts_key()` in `tools/disasm/cache.py` before
assuming a broken cache key: it already hashes the source of every `.py`
file in the package, so it was never blind to the `functions.py` fix. The
actual reason `tools/disasm/output/scda_v060` sat stale for eleven days was
operational -- nobody re-ran the disassembler for that directory in that
window -- not a cache defect. `CACHE_VERSION` was bumped 1→2 anyway as a
cheap, explicit backstop next to the source-hash check (commit `3dc9149`),
with a comment recording this finding so a future detection fix doesn't get
misdiagnosed as a cache bug again. Added `tools/disasm/test_cache_version.py`
(3 cases: old version rejected, current version with identical inputs
accepted, changed input still invalidates regardless of version).

**After any change under `tools/disasm/`, the full `Disasm → func_id →

Answered the "why is the name empty" question fully via chained,
narrowly-gated diagnostic hooks (each removed and rebuilt clean before
the next round; process gated by matching the known value so no hot
loop was ever touched):

  `0x4F5BE0`). Confirmed identical on xemu via one passive vtable scan
  (vtable `0x004FE948`, same `+0x9C` raw value `0xF4A2AD76`, same
  shared `+0x98`/`+0x24` cross-references) -- Fall C, not a data
  divergence. `sub_0004721E`'s own blanking of it at `0x47404` (no
  match among 4 hardcoded category strings) is therefore original,
  identical-on-both-platforms behavior, not a bug.
- The real divergence is one level further down: `sub_0004721E`'s
  *fallback* manager (`MEM32(0x5B57FC)`) is, on xemu, the exact same
  populated 795-entry object as the primary manager
  (`MEM32(0x5B5800)`) -- confirmed aliased as early as `t=3s` after
  boot and unchanged through `t=60s` (10 checkpoints, single passive
  interrupt each, gdbstub `?`-query drain bug found and fixed along
  the way: this xemu build's gdbstub does not push an unsolicited stop
  reply after a raw `0x03` break-in, an explicit `?` query is
  required, and a second, delayed async notification can still arrive
  after that and must be drained before trusting the next read).
  On scda_recomp, the same global is written exactly once, by
  `sub_00071B49` (dynamically confirmed call site, retaddr
  `0x00049058`), to a **freshly constructed, permanently empty**
  scratch object (`table_count=0`) -- and never touched again. No
  code path that would alias it to the primary manager (the pattern
  exists elsewhere in `sub_0004934E` at guest PC `0x4A2E6`/`0x4A2F2`,
  duplicated twice in the generated output for two inlined contexts;
  both instrumented, neither ever fires in this run) is reached before
  the icon lookup.
- Traced why the scratch object stays empty: `sub_00071B49`'s own
  caller, `sub_00048F1D`, builds the path
  `"D:\Default\DataXb\LMaps\menu\common.lin"` (confirmed byte-exact via
  hook, both the pre-copy source and the copied destination buffer)
  and opens it via `sub_00040FAC`, which returns `0xFFFFFFFF` on

  scratch table is never populated.
- Chased the resulting "empty search still returns success" behavior
  one more level: `sub_00045ADE`'s fallback tail-chain (`ecx =
  MEM32(esi+4)`, recurse into that object's own slot 4) bottoms out,

  (`0x00F7B7BC`, vtable `0x004F61E0`), whose own slot 4
  (`sub_0003EA27`) is itself another one-level indirection

  fallback, not obviously a bug in itself; the return value that
  ultimately reaches `sub_0004721E` as "0, not -1" was not traced past

## Entry: the actual root cause -- not a data problem, a disassembly gap; fixed, boot progresses well past the old blocker

Following the `\menu\common.lin` thread to its actual conclusion
(explicit user go-ahead, since it touches a previously-closed
investigation) resolved the whole session's -- and several previous
sessions' -- main blocker. Full chain, traced with narrowly-gated hooks
each removed immediately after use:

1. `common.lin` and `SplinterCell4Xbox`/`SplinterCell4User.ini` genuinely
   don't exist -- confirmed against the real disc ISO via
   `extract-xiso -l`, not just the local copy. Not a data-completeness
   bug. Both are evidently optional (a per-map override, a per-user
   settings file that doesn't exist yet on first boot).
2. The resulting empty scratch resource-manager object
   (`MEM32(0x5B57FC)`, from earlier entries) gets searched for an empty
   name during icon lookup. `sub_000457AE` correctly returns 0
   ("not found") for the empty table -- that part was never broken.
3. `sub_00045ADE`'s caller-facing convention is `eax==0` from
   `sub_000457AE` means *not found, fall through to the parent-catalogue
   tail-chain* (`ecx = MEM32(esi+4); tail-jmp to that object's own
   vtable slot 4`) -- also correct, an ordinary chain-of-responsibility
   pattern.
4. That tail-chain's target, for this specific object, is guest VA
   `0x0003EA27`. Live-confirmed (`g_icall_source`/`icall_target` read
   right before the `RECOMP_ITAIL`): the target really is `0x0003EA27`.
   But a matching hook placed directly at that label's own
   `RECOMP_TRACE_PC` never fired -- not once, in a run where the
   fallback branch itself fired three times. Contradiction resolved by
   checking `recomp_dispatch.c`: `0x0003EA27` isn't in it. It's real,
   disassembled code (part of `sub_0003EA10`'s own byte range -- the
   disassembler correctly recognized the region as reachable), but only
   a function's own entry address becomes a dispatch-table slot; this
   is a label mid-function, and the original game reaches it exclusively
   via indirect (vtable) dispatch, never fallthrough or a direct call --
   so it could never surface as a "missing function" the ordinary way.
5. `RECOMP_ITAIL`'s generic fallback for an unresolved target is
   `g_eax = 0; g_esp += 4;` -- silent, by design, for the overwhelmingly
   common case where a failed icall is genuinely inert. For this one
   caller it isn't: `eax == 0` from *this* API means "found, at index
   0", not "not found". The empty table's search spuriously "succeeds",
   `sub_0004721E` treats the empty name as resolved, and that's what
   ultimately drives `sub_000464EC -> sub_0007188A -> sub_000778BC` into
   requesting a Partition5.img-sized allocation -- the exact OOM this
   whole investigation (across several prior sessions too) chased.
6. xemu comparison for this specific mechanism wasn't even necessary at
   fix time -- it was already established two entries ago that
   `MEM32(0x5B57FC)` is aliased to the real, populated primary manager
   on xemu from `t=3-4s` onward, so it never reaches this fallback path
   with an empty table there at all.

**Fix** (`projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c`, the project's existing
`recomp_lookup_manual()` override table -- same mechanism already used
for several other "address never disassembled as its own function"
fixes in this file, e.g. `scda_460f0_earlyexit_0004612B`): re-derived
the *entire* thunk family byte-for-byte from `compare/orig/default.xbe`
(`0x0003EA10`-`0x0003EA9F`, 19 entries total, each
`mov ecx,[ecx+4]; mov eax,[ecx]; jmp [eax+N]`, 7 or 8 bytes depending on
whether N is zero) rather than patching only the one observed address,
since all 18 internal labels after `0x0003EA10` share the identical
failure mode. Registered all 18 (`0x0003EA10` itself already resolves
normally, it's a real generated function entry).

Rebuilding and running with just that fix landed on the *next*
unresolved target the same way exposed it: `0x00074792`, a 4-byte
`mov eax,[ecx+0x2C]; ret` getter, same failure class. Fixing that
uncovered `0x00039E08`, a 9-byte `xor eax,eax; cmp [ecx+0x34],eax;
setz al; ret` boolean getter, also fixed the same way. Each of the
three fixes was verified by rerunning and confirming the just-fixed
address had dropped out of the crash handler's `[SCDA-ICALL-RING]`
dump and the boot had visibly progressed further before the next crash.

End state after all three: the original OOM is gone. The boot now
reads real UMD data off the disc image, opens `menu_loading0-5.tga`,
`menu_intro.bik`, `menu_loading.bik`, and `lipsyncxbox.umd` (from both
the HDD cache and the CD-ROM) -- assets nothing in this project's
history had reached before. It then crashes on two *different*,
genuinely more complex unresolved targets, `0x00045738` and
`0x00045775` -- both have real internal `call`/conditional-branch
instructions, not simple leaf getters, so hand-writing them the same
way would be guesswork rather than a disassembly-completeness fix.
Left for the next round: add them as `function_seeds.json` entries and
regenerate properly through `tools.disasm`/`tools.recomp` instead.

No changes to `sub_0004721E`, the resource managers, Partition5, the
lookup table, or `kernel_path.c` -- this fixes the actual translation
gap, not a symptom of it. All exploratory diagnostic hooks (the
`sub_00045ADE` precise-gate trace, the `sub_00040FAC` empty-path
entry/result hooks, the `sub_00071B49` flag dump) removed and verified
absent (`grep -rl "DIAG-\|_diag_"` empty across

## 2026-09-10/11: chasing the new heap-budget OOM past the fixed thunk-family bug -- caller chain traced two levels deep, root cause not yet settled

Direct continuation of the session above, per an explicit user-provided
five-step plan: pin down the exact failing allocation (size, caller,
heap state, growth pattern), rule out a leak-like repeat pattern,
compare passively against xemu, and only touch heap-budget semantics if
xemu shows a similar allocation pattern but simply has more room --
never raise the heap limit blind.

**The failure, read straight out of the existing (uninstrumented) log.**
`scda_runtime.log` already carries everything needed for step 1 without
new hooks: two identical `HEAP #9`/`#10` allocations of 20623360 bytes
each (`0x011CC000..0x02577000`, `0x02577000..0x03922000`), each
immediately preceded by an `NtReadFile` requesting an enormous `Length`
(17660472 and 17660840 bytes) that comes back short --
`got=3546` both times. Right after those two, a *third*, structurally
identical-looking read (`len=17665240`) succeeds in full
(`got=3616165`) and turns out to be the real `[General] MapName=Menu`
ini. The eventual failing allocation is a constant `10690560` bytes
against `used=43655168/50855936` -- and the heap-exhaustion histogram
confirms both 20MB blocks are still live at that point, never freed.

**Ruled out: session-cache bloat.** The two suspect files
(`recomp_saves\Cache\Default\{DynamicXbox,lipsyncxbox}.umd`) looked at
first like they might have grown unnaturally large across many earlier
debug/crash-restart cycles in this project's history. Checked the
disc-side originals under `Default\` instead: `dynamicxbox.umd`
7502261 bytes, `lipsyncxbox.umd` 17497530 bytes, `splintercell4xboxretail.umd`
21 bytes, all dated September 1st -- legitimate shipped data, not
session accumulation. Moved the cache copies out to
`.scratch_debug/cache_backup_20260910/` (backed up, not deleted) and
reran: **the failure was byte-for-byte identical** -- same 20623360
block size, same `used=43655168/50855936`, same `10690560` failure.
The `Length` values on the two short reads shifted by about 53 KB, but
the actual allocated block size did not move at all. That rules out
"years of dev-session cache growth" as the cause of the fixed 20623360
figure; the cache files were restored afterward (no lasting effect
either way).

**Caller chain, traced via two short-lived diagnostic hooks in
`kernel_bridge.c`** (both fully reverted afterward -- `git diff --stat`
on the file came back empty, confirming a clean revert, and the final
rebuild reproduced the same failure before either hook existed):

- `bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory`, gated on `size == 20623360`, logging
  `BRIDGE_MEM32(g_esp)` as a naive "caller retaddr" -- this first
  attempt was a dead end (kernel_thunk_dispatch already pops the real
  guest return address before dispatching to the bridge function, so by
  the time the bridge runs, `g_esp` points at arg0, not a return
  address). The *useful* signal turned out to be the existing
  `KERNEL_LOG_ON()` line already printed by `kernel_thunk_dispatch`
  itself one line earlier in the log (`ret=0x00371BDC`), which -- unlike
  the custom hook -- captures the address before the pop.
- That return address resolves to `sub_00371BC3`, a generic
  `VirtualAlloc`-style wrapper (call the kernel thunk at `MEM32(0x4F534C)`,
  raise an error via `sub_00052A85` on a negative NTSTATUS, otherwise
  return the base address). Its only two callers, `sub_00076849` and
  `sub_00076B70`, are both called exclusively from `sub_00077194`.
- `sub_00077194` turned out to be the *game's own custom heap
  allocator's arena-growth routine* -- a freelist allocator with fields
  at `esi+0x350` through `+0x374`, rounding the requested size up and
  pulling a fresh OS-backed block via `sub_00076B70(0, edi)` whenever
  its internal pool can't satisfy a request, then linking the new block
  into the freelist (`MEM32(edx) = chunk_size; MEM32(edx+4) = flags|2`).
  This is generic machinery any `malloc()`-shaped call in the title can
  trigger -- not cache/lipsync-specific code -- so the fact that both
  triggering requests land on exactly the same 20623360-byte figure
  points at two call sites asking for a similarly large amount, not a
  hardcoded constant baked into the allocator itself.
- `bridge_NtReadFile`, gated on `length > 10000000`, pointed at the
  read side: all three oversized reads share one call site,
  `source=0x0005174B` inside `sub_000516B7`. That function has 32
  distinct callers scattered across the title (matches the shape of an
  engine-wide `FArchive::Serialize`-style primitive), so it is not
  itself where `Length` gets decided -- the actual caller that computed
  17.6-odd million bytes for what turns out to be a 3546-byte read is
  still unidentified.

**Where this leaves it.** Two explanations remain open and were
deliberately not guessed at:
(a) this is normal first-boot behavior with a small/empty on-disk
    cache -- try a short read twice, come up short both times, fall
    back to reading the real disc data -- and real hardware hits the
    exact same pattern but has enough spare heap to shrug it off, or
(b) an actual bug computes `Length` as something like "the archive's
    total logical size" instead of "the size of the next chunk," which
    would make the two 20MB reservations pure recomp-side waste.
Picking between them needs the one-level-deeper caller of
`sub_000516B7` and, ideally, a live xemu check at that exact guest PC --
xemu was launched (`xemu.exe -s -S`, paused at boot) for this purpose
but closed again without a concrete correlation point to check, rather
than spend time on an undirected live comparison. Documented in
`PROJECT_STATUS.md` Update 92 with the concrete next step: log the
return address one level above `sub_000516B7` to name its actual
caller, then inspect that caller's own computation of `Length`.

## 2026-09-11: the oversized Length is a live heap pointer, not a miscomputed size -- traced through a three-hop icall chain, exact stack slip still unpinned

Continuation of the above, per the user's five-step plan (capture the
retaddr one level above `sub_000516B7`, name the caller, trace backward
where `Length` comes from, compare the three reads, only then check
xemu). All diagnostic hooks lived in the gitignored generated `.c` files
directly (`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_000{1,2,3}.c`) and
were fully removed after each finding, verified via `grep -rl "DIAG-\|_dbg_"`
coming back empty before every clean rebuild.

**The caller.** `sub_000516B7`'s one caller for these three reads is
`sub_0007188A` (return address `0x00040C85`) -- the same function that
sits at the top of the original, long-resolved Partition5 OOM chain from
much earlier sessions (`sub_0004721E -> sub_000464EC -> sub_0007188A ->
...`). Inside it, right before the problem calls: a vtable call
(`+0x50`) returns a small, correct string/name length (`edi` = 3526 or
170 across the three reads), then `sub_0010D5C1(&local, edi+2, 1)` is
called -- a generic, 30-plus-caller vector/string sizing helper that
itself calls `sub_001E460F`, the realloc/free primitive this project
already byte-verified against the real XBE in an earlier session's
"xemu bin[6] differential" work (not reopened here, just relied on as
known-good).

**The smoking gun.** The 3-DWORD local descriptor this call fills in
(`ebp-16` in `sub_0007188A`), read back live right after the call:
`[ebp-16] = 0x010D7A38` (a genuine heap pointer -- the buffer that was
just allocated), `[ebp-12] = 3528`, `[ebp-8] = 3528` (both correct,
`edi+2`). The very next instruction reads `ebx = [ebp-16]` -- the
pointer, not the count -- and that's confirmed byte-for-byte against
`compare/orig/default.xbe` (file offset `0x618C7`: bytes `8B 5D F0` =
`mov ebx, [ebp-0x10]`). So this specific read is not a translation gap;
the real compiled game code genuinely fetches the pointer here. Two
hops later, at the very entry of `sub_00040BB0` (the
`FArchiveFileReader::Serialize`-shaped vtable slot-4 method, hooked
fresh right after its `push ebp; mov ebp,esp` prologue so there's no
room for stack-offset ambiguity), the two parameters it actually
receives are: `Buffer(ebp+8) = 0x000718D3` -- which is `sub_00045738`'s
own return address, read back as if it were a destination pointer --
and `Length(ebp+0xC) = 0x010D7A38` -- the same heap pointer from three
paragraphs up, now standing in for a byte count. Both parameters are
demonstrably wrong for their role; a return address is not a valid
destination buffer, and no real UMD directory entry is 17 million bytes
long when the string length computed one call earlier says 3526.

One measurement round on the way to this produced a false "both pushed
values are identical" result from a hand-instrumented hook -- traced
back to a bug in the diagnostic itself (the hook re-evaluated the same
`MEM32(esp+0x10)` expression at the same `esp`, before the intervening
push it was supposed to be looking past, so it trivially matched what
had already been read). Recorded here as a caution for whoever
continues this: a fresh hook placed at the callee's own verified
prologue boundary, not reconstructed by hand from the caller's PUSH32
sequence, is what finally gave a trustworthy answer.

**Where the actual slip happens is still open.** `sub_0007188A` calls
`sub_00045738` (this session's own Update 91 fix -- a vtable thunk that
had literally never executed before this session's pipeline
regeneration) with the correct arguments (`edi=3526`, `ebx=0x010D7A38`,
in the right roles). `sub_00045738` in turn calls `sub_00040A88` (a
"Seek" method at vtable slot `+0x60`) and then `sub_00040BB0` (Serialize,
slot `+4`) via nested icalls. `sub_00040A88` was checked first as the
obvious suspect -- it already has a hand-written override in
`recomp_manual.c` from 2026-09-05 ("continued 45", the same
disassembly-fragmentation bug class as this session's Update 91 thunk
family), is correctly wired into `recomp_dispatch.c`'s normal jump
table, and its `ret 4` cleanly matches the one stack argument pushed
into it -- not the culprit. Somewhere across the three icall boundaries
inside `sub_00045738` itself, a stack slot ends up read one position off
from where the caller placed it, but pinning down exactly which push or
pop is missing needs disassembler-verified byte counts for every
instruction in `sub_00045738` (`0x45738-0x45775`), not more hand
arithmetic -- this session's own back-and-forth on that exact
calculation is why the false-positive diagnostic above happened in the
first place.

**No xemu comparison was needed to settle the decision rule.** A live
heap pointer is never a coincidentally-valid small read length on any
platform -- the qualitative shape of this bug (a pointer flowing where
an integer count belongs) proves the recomp-side origin on its own.
Real hardware/xemu would use the small, already-correctly-computed value
(3526/170) at this exact point; there is nothing to compare that a byte-
accurate disassembly check of `sub_00045738` won't answer more directly.

## 2026-09-11 (continued): found it -- a one-DWORD-off `ret 4` in a hand-written override, fixed, and the ~48.5MB heap OOM is gone

Followed through on the previous entry's own advice: stopped doing this
by hand and used `capstone` (Python) to disassemble `sub_00045738` and
the "Seek" method it calls through vtable slot `+0x60` (`sub_00040A88`)
directly against `compare/orig/default.xbe`, byte for byte, rather than
re-deriving push/pop counts from the generated C.

`sub_00045738`'s own push-and-call sequence for the Seek call matches
the real bytes exactly -- no bug there. `sub_00040A88` is a hand-written
override in `recomp_manual.c` from an earlier session (2026-09-05,
"continued 45" -- the disassembler had fragmented its real body across
six false function starts, so it got hand-translated from capstone
output directly). Its translation of the real `ret 4` instruction wrote
`esp += 4; return;`. That is one DWORD short: this runtime never
actually pushes/pops a native return address (calls are plain C
function calls, and "the return address" is a value the caller manually
writes to the emulated stack so the callee's own emulated `[ebp+4]`
reads something sane), but the accounting still has to charge 4 bytes
for that slot on every return, the same way it would for a real `ret`.
Every auto-generated function gets this right as a matter of course --
cross-checked against `sub_000518FE`'s own generated epilogue, a real
`ret 16` that correctly emits `esp += 20` -- so the convention itself
was never in doubt, just this one hand-written instance of it.

Confirmed live with a diagnostic hook printing the stack pointer right
after this Seek call returns, compared against the stack pointer
captured right before it was made: before the fix, they differed by
exactly 4 bytes on all three problem reads; after changing `esp += 4`
to `esp += 8`, they matched exactly, and the `edi` value `sub_00045738`
was about to forward as "Length" read back as the correct small numbers
(3526, 170) instead of the stray heap pointer. Swept the rest of
`recomp_manual.c` for the same mistake (`grep -n "esp +="`) -- every
other instance already follows the two-part "retaddr, then cleanup"
convention correctly; this was the only offender.

All diagnostic hooks (in the gitignored generated `.c` files and one
temporary one in `recomp_manual.c` itself) removed and verified absent
before the fix build. Rebuilt clean and reran: the `xbox_HeapAlloc: out
of memory (requested 10690560, ...)` failure from the past two sessions
is gone completely. Boot now runs past 10,000 kernel calls (versus a
couple hundred before) and successfully cycles through dozens of
different co-op map configs via `sub_001D5208`'s registration loop --
further than this project has ever recorded reaching.

**The next blocker, further out and structurally different**: a single
`NtAllocateVirtualMemory` call asking for 424,120,320 bytes
(`type=0x103000` -- MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE | MEM_TOP_DOWN, both commit
and reserve bits set, so the existing "pure reserve gets clamped"
special case in `kernel_bridge.c` doesn't apply) while the heap has used

`0x00044382` and `0x0004438C` -- and neither address is its own

(`0x4435A-0x443D0`, `detection_method: tail_jump_alias`), which is

## 2026-09-11 (continued): tracked the sub_000600AD crash down to a leaked global register, not a simple stack-offset bug -- eleven functions cleared, the actual culprit still open

Followed a tightly-gated diagnostic plan for this one: no broad hot
breakpoint, just precise hooks at the one suspected call site, removed
completely after each finding (verified via `grep -rl "DIAG-\|_dbg_"`
coming back empty before every rebuild).

The initial suspect, `source=0x00071D7F` inside `sub_00071B49` (an icall
passing two stack-local buffers as arguments to a virtual method), was
a dead end -- a hook gated on a null vtable target there never fired
across a full run. It turns out that call site is completely healthy;
it just happened to be nearby in the log, not causally related.

Fixed a real gap in the runtime's own diagnostics along the way:
`recomp_icall_not_code_log` (the function behind the `[ICALL] target
0x00000000 is not code` message) never printed which call site
triggered it, only the target address and a hit count. Added `source=`
(from `g_icall_source`) to its one log line -- a small, permanent,
zero-risk improvement, kept rather than reverted, since it would have
made straight for the answer instead of leading down the 0x71D7F dead
end.

With that in place, the actual null-vtable call turned out to be
`source=0x0005F701`, inside `sub_0005F6FF` -- a generic class-hierarchy
walk (16 callers across the project, looks like an `IsKindOf`/RTTI
check). Byte-verified against `compare/orig/default.xbe` including its
`ret 4` -> `esp += 8` cleanup: correct. A null vtable hit partway
through a type hierarchy walk is completely normal (this branch of the
hierarchy just doesn't implement that interface) -- not a bug. A hook
comparing `g_esi` immediately before and after this exact icall found
zero changes across the entire run, ruling it out directly as the esi
corruptor too.

The actual crash: `sub_000600AD` reads `ecx = MEM32(esi)` where `esi`
itself is fine (a small, deliberately stack-allocated "search object" at
`ebp-8` in an ancestor function, `sub_000661F1` -- a completely ordinary
C++ pattern, not a bug by itself) but its *content* is wrong:
`MEM32(esi)` held `0x00060B4C`, which is exactly the return-address
constant `sub_00060B2E` pushes for its own, more deeply nested call to
`sub_000600AD`. That constant can only land at this specific memory
address if `g_esp` had wandered all the way back up to `sub_000661F1`'s
own frame at the moment that inner push executed.

The bigger realization this produced: every register in this whole
runtime (`esi`, `eax`, `ecx`, ...) is a single shared global
(`g_esi` etc., via `#define esi g_esi`), not a per-function local. A
function that uses esi as scratch, saves it once at entry, and restores
it once before returning (exactly what `sub_000661F1` does) is trusting
that *nothing it calls*, however deeply nested, touches the shared
global without its own save/restore around it -- and something in this
call tree breaks that trust. This is a different bug shape than
Update 94's `ret 4` mistake (a fixed, local stack-offset error); this
one is a value leaking across several stack frames because some
function's translation clobbers a global register without the
corresponding push/pop the real assembly has.

Verified clean, one by one, against `compare/orig/default.xbe` (or by
reading the generated code and confirming a self-consistent, matching
push/pop pattern) and ruled out as the source: `sub_000600AD` itself,
`sub_00060B2E`, `sub_0005F354` (a lazy-singleton getter), `sub_0005F6FF`
(above), the three structurally-identical "call two helpers" wrappers
`sub_0005FFE1`/`sub_00060047`/`sub_00065DE0`, and their first
sub-helpers `sub_0005F486`/`sub_0005F59B`/`sub_0005F5E3`. Eleven
functions cleared in total.

Not yet checked, and the concrete next step: each wrapper's *second*
sub-helper (`sub_000758BF`, `sub_00074DD2`, `sub_00075BC8`,
`sub_000753EE`, `sub_00076115`, `sub_00075577`), `sub_0005F6FF`'s own
dynamically-resolved icall target (`MEM32(eax+0x54)`, class-dependent,
not statically known -- worth a hook on the resolved address itself to
name it), and the two singleton-init helpers `sub_0005F354` calls
(`sub_00073E73`, `sub_00073EE4`). Any of these is a candidate for
clobbering the shared `esi` global without the save/restore the real
binary has at that address.

## 2026-09-11 (continued): found it -- two Update-91 getters were missing their `esp += 4`, exact same bug shape as the ret-4 fix, and boot now reaches real multi-threading for the first time ever

Rather than keep walking the call graph function by function, planted
one precise canary: snapshot `g_esi` at `sub_000661F1`'s own entry, then
compare it against that snapshot right after each of its seven
sub-calls (`sub_0005FFE1` x2, `sub_00065DE0` x2, `sub_00060047` x2, the
direct `sub_000600AD` call). Six checkpoints showed no change at all.
Only the direct `sub_000600AD` call corrupted it -- narrowing the
search from "somewhere in a deep call tree" to "somewhere inside this
one call."

A second hook, right at `sub_000600AD`'s own vtable dispatch
(`loc_000600D3`), fired exactly once in the whole run -- the very first
time this particular object's cached-lookup field was still unset --
and named the resolved target: `0x00074792`. That's the getter this
session added via `recomp_manual.c` in Update 91 to fix the original
Partition5 OOM (`g_eax = MEM32(g_ecx + 0x2Cu);`).

The getter's real bytes end in a plain `ret` (0 args), but its
hand-written body does no `esp` adjustment at all. This runtime charges
4 bytes for the emulated return-address slot on every return -- the
same accounting this session already learned about fixing the
`sub_00040A88` `ret 4` mistake (Update 94) -- and since
`RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`'s resolved path just calls the target function
directly, the pushed continuation address (`0x000600DAu`) was never
popped. The next `POP32(esp,esi)` in `sub_000600AD`'s own epilogue then
read one slot too deep: a return-address constant belonging to a much
more distant nested call (`sub_00060B2E`'s own internal call to
`sub_000600AD`, `0x00060B4Cu`) that happened to be sitting there. That
value rode all the way back up to `sub_000661F1`'s own esi.

Worth noting explicitly why `esp += 4` is correct regardless of how the
getter is reached, not just for this ICALL_SAFE case: for `RECOMP_ITAIL`
(no continuation ever pushed), the exact same `esp += 4` instead pops
the *outer* caller's own return address -- precisely what a real
`jmp [reg]` followed by `ret` does on real hardware, since tail-call
optimization means the callee's `ret` is what actually returns control
past the whole chain. There's no invocation style for which omitting it
is correct.

Fixed both `scda_getter_00074792` and its sibling `scda_getter_00039E08`
(added the same session, same shape) by adding `g_esp += 4;`. Swept the
rest of `recomp_manual.c` for the same omission -- the `0x3EA10` thunk
family all end in `RECOMP_ITAIL(...)`, delegating the return
responsibility onward, so they need no `esp` handling of their own and
aren't affected.

Regenerated the pipeline output (no `function_seeds.json` change needed,
just the `recomp_manual.c` fix) and rebuilt clean. Verified: the
`sub_000600AD` crash is gone. Boot now runs to roughly **68,000 kernel
calls** (up from ~11,500) and, for the first time in this project's
recorded history, reaches genuine concurrent multi-threaded execution --
`PsCreateSystemThreadEx` spawns multiple workers whose kernel calls show
up visibly interleaved in the log. An earlier session's own note that
"only one host thread ever executes guest code in the observed boot"
was accurate when written; it no longer is.

**The next blocker lives in that brand-new territory.** Live-debugged
with `cdb.exe -g -G -c "g; !analyze -v; q" scda_recomp.exe` directly
(the crash handler's own minidumps come out empty/0-byte for this one --
plausibly because the handler itself is running in an already-broken
context on a non-main thread) and got a full stack: a worker thread
spawned via `PsCreateSystemThreadEx` crashes inside
`sub_00052A57` (`recomp_0002.c:50761`), which reads
`MEM32(ecx + eax*4)` where `ecx` comes from `xbox_fs_read32(4)` -- and
the call stack shows this happening inside what looks like CRT/SEH
error-reporting machinery (`sub_00052A85` -> `sub_00052A57`), meaning
something else faulted first and the handler itself crashes trying to
report it.

Reading `xbox_fs_read8/16/32` and `xbox_AllocThreadTib` side by side
turned up a likely explanation: **two disconnected TIB mechanisms**.
`xbox_fs_read/write*` (`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`) operate on a
dedicated `RECOMP_TLS uint8_t g_xbox_fs[0x10000]` array that lives
completely outside the flat guest memory map -- meaning it's fresh and
zeroed for every new host thread. Only `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit()`, called
once at process startup for the main thread, ever populates it via
`xbox_fs_write32`. `xbox_AllocThreadTib()`, called for every spawned
worker in `bridge_thread_main`, does something entirely different: it
allocates a TIB in real guest heap memory and points `g_fs_base` at it,
but never touches `g_xbox_fs` at all. Since `xbox_fs_read32` never
consults `g_fs_base`, a worker thread's `g_xbox_fs` stays all-zero
regardless of whether `xbox_AllocThreadTib` succeeded -- matching the
crash exactly (`xbox_fs_read32(4)` most likely returning 0 instead of a
real pointer, which then gets used as a table index into wild memory).

Not yet confirmed live, and deliberately left that way rather than
guessing at a fix: whether the correct repair is having worker threads
also populate their own `g_xbox_fs` (mirroring what
`xbox_MemoryLayoutInit` does for the main thread), or whether the
generated code at this address is supposed to go through
`g_fs_base`-relative guest memory instead of `xbox_fs_read32` in the
first place. Next session should hook `xbox_fs_read32(4)` on the worker
thread to confirm it really does return 0 before touching either
mechanism -- this is genuinely new territory (the project's own earlier
notes confirm multi-threaded guest execution had never been reached
before this session), so nothing about it should be assumed from the
single-threaded behavior alone.

## 2026-09-11 (continued): confirmed and fixed the worker-thread fs:[4] gap -- boot now survives its full run without crashing, and the next blocker is in the Bink video codec's own worker thread

Confirmed the previous entry's hypothesis directly: a diagnostic hook
in `xbox_fs_read32()` logging the OS thread ID showed the main thread
consistently reading a real pointer (`0x00770094`) at offset 4, while
two different `PsCreateSystemThreadEx`-spawned workers (each with a
correctly-allocated, distinct `g_fs_base` pointing at its own real
guest-heap TIB) both read exactly `0`.

Fixed at the source: `xbox_AllocThreadTib()` already computes the right
per-thread values (`0xFFFFFFFF` for the SEH chain head, `block+total`
for the TLS block pointer) and writes them into guest heap memory at
`tib+0` / `tib+4` -- but nothing mirrors them into `g_xbox_fs`, the
separate per-host-thread array that `xbox_fs_read32` actually reads.
Added two `xbox_fs_write32` calls right there to mirror exactly those
two already-computed values into the new thread's own `g_xbox_fs`.
Deliberately left the TIB's other main-thread-only fields (self
pointer, fake PRCB, fake TLS/RW-engine pointer) unmirrored -- no
observed failure has implicated them yet, and this project's own rule
for `function_seeds.json` entries ("only add with static or observed
evidence") applies just as well here.

Verified: removed the diagnostic hook, rebuilt clean, ran with a 90s
timeout. Every previous attempt died with a segfault at the same
kernel call number; this one runs the entire 90 seconds and gets killed
by the timeout itself (exit 124) instead of crashing -- the process is
alive and still making kernel calls (past #68,838) when the timeout
fires.

**The next blocker, identified but not yet fixed**, is in genuinely new
territory again: one of the worker threads is the Bink video codec
(thread routine `sub_004BBE90`; the failing call site,
`source=0x004BBDCF`, sits in `sub_004BBD90`, in the binary's own `BINK`
section -- matching the `menu_intro.bik`/`menu_loading.bik` files this
session's earlier logs already showed being opened). That thread is
stuck in a tight loop, 50+ identical repeats with `esp`/`eax`/`ecx`/
`esi`/`edi` all unchanged between them, each one failing the same
indirect call: target `0x00041D90`.

This is a different bug shape than every other icall failure this
session -- checked with capstone, and `0x00041D90` is not a function
boundary at all. It's the middle of `sub_00041B67`'s own body
(`push dword ptr [ebp+8]`, mid-way through an ordinary virtual-call
argument setup), so seeding it as a function start would be wrong. The
actual problem is upstream of the dispatch: whatever value the Bink
codec's own code is using as a function pointer here is itself
computed incorrectly. Immediately after, some thread ends up blocked
in `NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx(..., timeout=INFINITE)`, consistent with
this failed call being what was supposed to eventually signal whatever
it's waiting on.

Next step: trace `source=0x004BBDCF` live to find where this wrong
pointer value comes from, and whether it should have been
`0x00041B67` itself (the real function start -- maybe a vtable-slot
offset miscalculation) or points at a Bink codec object that wasn't
initialized correctly somewhere else. This is the first time this
project has ever reached Bink/multi-threaded code at all, so -- same
caution as the fs:[4] investigation -- nothing about it should be
assumed from single-threaded behavior; confirm everything live.

### 2026-09-11 (continued): the ebx corruption chain traced to its true source -- a missing 6th kernel-bridge argument, not a Bink bug at all

Picked up exactly where the previous entry left off: trace
`source=0x004BBDCF` live and find where the wrong `[esi+0x10]` value,
or the wrong `esi` itself, comes from. The chain turned out to run
five levels deep and land somewhere nobody would have guessed from the
symptom alone -- a stdcall argument-count mistake in the kernel bridge,
not anywhere in Bink's own code.

Working backward with the same five-question framework as before:

**1. Confirm the corruption live, tightly gated.** A canary hook inside
`sub_004BBD90` (the Bink list-traversal routine) proved that `ebx` --
which real x86 sets to zero exactly once at function entry via
`xor ebx,ebx` and never touches again anywhere in the whole function
body, confirmed by disassembling the complete function with capstone
-- changes from 0 to 1 during execution, even though our generated C
translation contains no write to `ebx` anywhere. Textbook leaked
shared-global-register corruption, same species as the sub_000600AD
bug from two updates ago, just reached through a much longer call
chain this time.

**2. Narrow down which callee is responsible.** Rather than hand-trace
every call, we turned on the project's own `-DRECOMP_ABI_CHECK`
instrumentation (already wired into the default SCDA build --
`projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt` turns it on unconditionally unless
`SCDA_AB_TRACE` is set) and let it name the offender directly:
`[ABI] sub_00052C5C: ebx esi edi`, called from `sub_00052D40`, itself
called from `sub_004BBD90`'s own line at `0x4BBE49`. This function
never reaches its own epilogue faithfully, even though its real x86
disassembly shows a completely ordinary, correctly-paired
`push ebx/esi/edi ... pop edi/esi/ebx` around a conditional early-exit
branch.

**3. Find exactly where inside that function it breaks.** A canary
placed immediately before the pop sequence (`loc_00052CD5`) showed the
saved `ebx` slot on the stack already held the wrong value (1, not the
original caller's 0) before any pop executed -- ruling out a bug in
the pops themselves and pointing at something upstream shifting what
memory they read from.

**4. Rule out a wild write.** The project's existing
`RECOMP_KERNEL_WATCH`/`g_kernel_watch_va`/`[KWATCH]` facility (built
for exactly this kind of question -- "which kernel bridge call
touched this exact guest address") was armed dynamically, from inside
the generated code, on the precise stack address holding the saved
`ebx`. Across a full run, no kernel bridge call ever touched it
directly. So this isn't a bridge scribbling into the wrong place --
it's a bookkeeping error in how much stack a bridge call gives back.

**5. Compare esp before and after the one indirect call in the
loop.** `sub_00052C5C` calls out through a global function-pointer
slot at guest VA `0x4F52F0` inside a small retry loop
(`loc_00052CA4`-`loc_00052CB9`). Capturing `esp` right before that
call's own six `PUSH32`s (`edi`, `[ebp+0x18]`, `1`, `ebx`, `eax`,
`esi` -- byte-verified against the real XBE with capstone, six pushes,
not five) and comparing it against `esp` at the eventual epilogue
showed the difference was exactly 4 bytes short of what six pushed
dwords require. One dword -- `edi`, the first one pushed and so the
deepest on the stack -- was never reclaimed. That is a stdcall stack
leak, and stdcall leaks are cumulative and silent: the next thing that
reads "the top of the stack" reads one slot lower than it should,
which is exactly what turned the saved `edi`/`esi`/`ebx` triple into
garbage by the time the epilogue popped them.

**Root cause.** `0x4F52F0` is, in the untouched original XBE image, a
classic Xbox kernel import-thunk marker: `0x800000EB`, where `0xEB` =
235 decimal = `NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx`. `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit`'s
thunk-patching pass correctly resolves it to the synthetic kernel VA
for that ordinal at boot, so the indirect call genuinely is a call to
our own `bridge_NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx`. That bridge, and its
`stdcall_args_for_ordinal(235)` entry, were both written against the
5-argument desktop-NT signature
(`Count, Handles, WaitType, Alertable, Timeout`) documented in
`docs/formats/kernel-exports.md`. But Xbox's kernel-mode version of
this call carries the same extra `PVOID WaitBlockArray` parameter that
the underlying `KeWaitForMultipleObjects` kernel routine takes -- six
arguments, 24 bytes -- which is exactly what the compiled game code
pushes. With only 20 bytes of cleanup declared, every single call
leaked 4 bytes of stack, and this loop (part of Bink's own read/wait
retry path, running on its own worker thread) called it often enough
for the leak to matter immediately, corrupting the caller's
callee-saved registers on the very first pass. Nothing about this was
a Bink bug, and nothing about it was specific to threads either -- it
would have misbehaved identically on the main thread the first time
any code exercised this exact retry pattern; Bink's worker thread was
just the first place in this game's boot that happened to call
`NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx` from inside a loop that also relied on
`ebx`/`esi`/`edi` surviving the call, which is what made a silent
4-byte leak visible as active corruption instead of a wasted stack
slot nobody reads.

**Fix**, `src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c`:
- `stdcall_args_for_ordinal`, case 235: `20` -> `24`.
- `bridge_NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx`: reads six stack args instead of
  five now; the new fifth argument (`WaitBlockArray`) is read (so the
  stack accounting stays honest) and otherwise ignored -- this runtime
  doesn't implement real kernel wait-block bookkeeping and doesn't
  need to for correctness here; `Timeout` moves to the sixth slot.
- `docs/formats/kernel-exports.md` ordinal 235 entry corrected to the
  6-argument signature, with a note pointing back at this
  investigation.

**Verification.** Removed every temporary diagnostic hook (the
canaries in `sub_004BBD90`/`sub_00052C5C`'s generated bodies, the
dynamic `g_kernel_watch_va` arming, the per-slot kernel-dispatch
prints) and ran a full `tools.recomp` pipeline regeneration to get a
clean generated tree, then rebuilt. A 90-second run:
- Does not crash (`exit 124`, a normal timeout kill of a still-running
  process, not a segfault).
- Kernel call throughput went from ~68,000 calls in 90 seconds
  (the previous update's number, where the Bink worker thread was
  stuck oscillating between corrupted `esi` values of 0 and 4) to
  **76+ million calls** in the same window. The stuck ping-pong loop
  is gone.
- A residual `[ABI] sub_00052C5C: ebx edi` finding remains in this
  run, but at a different call instance (its own `esp` delta is
  exactly correct this time -- no leak -- only the register contents
  differ, and `esi` this time is fine where `ebx`/`edi` are not). Its
  "recent icall targets" ring points at ordinals 301
  (`RtlNtStatusToDosError`) and 234 (`NtWaitForSingleObjectEx`)
  rather than 235, so it is very likely a second, distinct instance of
  the same argument-count bug class somewhere nearby, not a recurrence
  of the one just fixed. Not yet investigated.
- The `target=0x00041D90` icall failure from the previous entry still
  happens occasionally (capped at the existing 50-report limit, then
  silently skipped) but no longer hangs the process. With the much
  larger corruption gone, this is now cleanly isolated as its own,
  apparently much smaller, remaining issue -- worth a fresh look on
  its own terms rather than assuming it shares a cause with what was
  just fixed.

**For a future continuation:** the concrete next steps are (in rough
priority order) (1) chase the second `[ABI] sub_00052C5C` finding
(ordinals 301/234 in its icall ring) the same way this one was found,
(2) re-examine the `0x00041D90` failure in `sub_004BBD90` now that it
is isolated from the much larger corruption that was obscuring it, and
(3) simply keep booting -- 76 million kernel calls in 90 seconds is
far more activity than this project has ever seen, and none of it has
been characterized yet.

### 2026-09-11 (continued again): busy-wait hypothesis disproven; a new, rare crash surfaced; the second ebx/esi corruption chased through five thin thunks to a dead end -- and reopened by a live crash

Picked up the next assignment directly: prove or disprove that the
>76M-calls/90s throughput is a busy-wait from oversimplified wait
semantics, per the specific five-step procedure given (identify the
dominant wait call path, measure its API/objects/WaitAll-or-Any/
timeout/return value/repetition, check whether the kernel stub always
reports success, compare against real/xemu behavior if so, then fix
the semantics properly -- no artificial sleeps or throttling).

**Step 1-2: identify and measure the dominant call path.** Built a
proper measurement tool first, since the obvious one (parse existing
per-call logs) undercounts once the log budget caps out. Added an
O(1) per-ordinal call histogram to `kernel_thunk_dispatch` (direct
array index by ordinal, not a scan -- a linear-scan first draft
measurably throttled the very throughput it was measuring, cutting
90-second call counts by three orders of magnitude; the array-indexed
version costs one cached `getenv` check when disabled and one array
store when enabled). Env-gated as `RECOMP_KERNEL_HIST=1`, kept as a
permanent tool rather than a throwaway. Also added a tightly gated,
capped print directly inside `xbox_NtWaitForSingleObjectEx` showing
the actual computed millisecond timeout, the alertable flag, and the
raw 100ns interval alongside the Win32 result code (removed again once
the question was answered).

The histogram named the dominant calls immediately: `NtWaitForSingleObjectEx`
climbing into the millions, alongside `RtlNtStatusToDosError` and
`NtReleaseMutant` at similar volumes, all sourced from the same tight
neighborhood of addresses (`0x00052A89`-`0x00052D07`) already mapped in
Update 99 as Bink's read/wait retry-wrapper family.

**Step 3: check whether the wait always reports success.** It does not.
The live dump showed the wait being called with `alertable=0`,
`timeout_raw=0` (a genuine zero-timeout, non-alertable poll) on a fixed
event handle, and the result correctly alternating between
`WAIT_TIMEOUT` (`0x00000102`) and `WAIT_OBJECT_0` (`0x00000000`) --
not always signalled, not always timed out, but exactly the alternating
pattern a real non-blocking poll of a handle that's sometimes ready and
sometimes not should produce. The `STATUS_ALERTED` (`0x101`) retry path
inside `sub_00052C18` that the previous entry's disassembly flagged as
a possible spin source turned out not to be engaged at all here, since
it only fires when `Alertable` is set, and this call site passes zero.

**Step 4/5: conclusion, no fix needed.** The wait semantics are correct.
The huge call volume is simply what a 0ms-timeout poll loop does when
nothing yet paces this recompilation to a real clock -- no vsync, no
frame limiter, no Present call reached yet, so the host CPU runs the
poll as fast as it can issue calls, which is far faster than the same
loop would ever iterate against real Xbox hardware's frame-locked
pacing. This is not a wait/event/semaphore bug and was not "fixed" by
adding sleeps or throttling, per the explicit instruction not to paper
over it that way -- it is simply what unthrottled execution looks like
before real-time pacing exists. Per the standing decision rule, moved
straight to the fallback list: (1) `target=0x00041D90`, (2) the
residual `[ABI]` finding, (3) whatever else surfaced first live.

**A new blocker surfaced immediately, live, before either fallback item
could be pursued on purpose.** One run (with the histogram and wait
diagnostics both active, which apparently shifted thread timing enough
to expose it) crashed with a minidump, immediately preceded by:

```
[CONTIG] arena exhausted (3737600000 requested, 5857280 of 67108864 used)
```

3.7 GB requested against a 64 MB contiguous-memory window --
unambiguously a garbage size value reaching `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`.
That function itself fails safe (returns 0, no crash there), so the
crash has to be the caller dereferencing the NULL it got back --
the same NULL-check-missing shape as prior bugs in this project.
Added `source=`/`ecx=`/`esi=` to the exhaustion log line so the next
occurrence names its caller immediately. Eight further runs (25-60
seconds each, with and without the diagnostic overhead that seemed to
trigger it) failed to reproduce it even once, which points at a real
race condition -- `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s bump allocator
(`g_contig_next`) has no locking around it, so two threads racing on it

**Chased the second `[ABI] sub_00052C5C` finding from the previous
entry down a chain of five thin forwarding thunks, each individually

A canary placed at the vtable call site itself (logging `esi`

### 2026-09-11 (continued): the target=0x00041D90 divergence traced end to end, from the icall failure back to NtReadFile -- root mechanism still not found, but the second ebx/esi chain is now conclusively reopened

Picked up exactly where the previous entry left off, with a specific
mandate: treat `target=0x00041D90` as the primary lead (it's the
information-richest open item, correlating with the bimodal ~75K-vs-
39M+ call-count split), and specifically compare a succeeding run
against a failing run at the same semantic point rather than only
reading post-mortem failure logs.

**Built a transition-only tracker, because per-iteration logging
doesn't scale to this loop.** `sub_004BBD90`'s node-traversal can spin
the same handful of nodes for hundreds to thousands of iterations
before anything interesting happens, so a capped per-call log (as used
in earlier sessions) either misses the divergence entirely or drowns
in repetition before reaching it. Instead, a small per-"this"-object
state table (keyed by `ebp`, guarded by a simple spinlock since two
Bink stream instances run on separate threads) remembers the last
`esi`/`ebx`/`key` seen for each object and only logs when one of them
actually changes -- collapsing thousands of identical iterations into
the handful of moments that matter. A separate always-log "ALERT"
condition (`esi == 0` or `ebx != 0`, the two direct symptoms of the
bug) bypasses the sampling cap entirely, so the actual failure moment
is never the one thing that gets sampled away.

**Correction to the previous session's working assumption.** Before
chasing the divergence, several long "clean" runs were captured for
comparison -- including one reaching **105 million** kernel calls with
zero corruption. Cross-checking `sub_004BBD90`'s own iteration count in
that run showed it stayed in the low hundreds throughout, exactly like
the "short" ~75K-call runs. So the earlier hypothesis that bimodal
throughput and `sub_004BBD90`'s own iteration count were linked was
wrong -- they're independent. The 75K/39M split comes from something
else entirely (almost certainly the already-confirmed-normal 0ms poll
loop), and the `0x00041D90` divergence itself apparently happens (or
doesn't) within the first few hundred iterations of `sub_004BBD90`
regardless of how long the process has been running otherwise.

**Caught it live.** A run with the tracker active hit 24,759 ALERT
lines over 896,054 kernel calls. The log immediately preceding the
first bad transition reads:

```
[ABI] sub_004B8FC0: ebx esi
      ebx 00000000->00000094 esi 00000001->01199914 edi 00000000->00000000 esp 013F9F0C->013F9F28
[BD90-TRANS-ALERT] ... iter=18 ... ebx:0x00000000->0x00000094 key:0x00000000->0xFFFFFFF6 ...
[BD90-TRANS-ALERT] ... iter=19 ... esi:0x01199914->0x00000000 ebx:0x00000094->0x00000094 ...
```

This closes the loop completely. `sub_004B8FC0` -- the same function
flagged (but not root-caused) in the previous entry as part of the
"second ebx/esi chain" -- hands its own caller back a corrupted `ebx`
(`0x94` instead of `0`). `sub_004BBD90`'s own end-of-list check
(`cmp esi, ebx; jne <continue>`, meant to test "am I back at the
zero-sentinel, i.e. is the list exhausted") breaks the instant `ebx`
stops being a reliable zero: the very next iteration, the real last
node's `next` field legitimately evaluates to `0` via
`esi = MEM32(esi)`, but `esi(0)` no longer equals the now-corrupted
`ebx(0x94)`, so the loop wrongly treats `0` as a valid node pointer and
keeps going, computing `MEM32(0 + 0x10)` as the next call target --
`0x00041D90` in earlier runs, `0x00000000` in this one, both just
whatever garbage happens to sit at that guest address. **Per this
session's own reopening condition, this is exactly "0x41D90 leads
directly back to the second chain" -- it is formally reopened.**

**Traced the chain one more hop toward its actual source.**
`sub_004B8FC0`'s own icall ring named `sub_00035AA1` as its immediate
predecessor. That function's own `[ABI]` line showed `esi edi` flagged
but its `esp` delta exactly matching expectation (`+8`) -- ruling out
a stack-byte-leak of the kind fixed for ordinal 235 in Update 99; the
caller gets back the right *number* of bytes, just the wrong *content*.
Disassembled the whole function against capstone: three indirect
`call eax` sites (register-sourced rather than memory-sourced, but
translated identically via `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` -- checked and correct),
one push-esi/push-edi bracket at entry, one shared epilogue -- no
mismatch found there either. It calls onward through two direct calls,
one trivial (`sub_00051D2D`, bare `ret`, no args) and one
(`sub_000356F1`) that calls `sub_000516B7`, which itself calls
**ordinal 219, `NtReadFile`**, directly, at two separate call sites --
both pushing exactly 8 dwords (32 bytes), matching the declared byte
count exactly. No argument-count defect anywhere in this chain.

**Directly measured the streaming-read bookkeeping to test a buffer-
overflow theory**, since `NtReadFile` writing a 16KB chunk into an
undersized destination would produce exactly this kind of "everything
individually checks out, yet nearby memory ends up wrong" symptom.
Live values for the stream object's capacity/position/remaining-bytes/
write-pointer fields (offsets `+0x50`/`+0x5C`/`+0x78`/`+0x6C`) showed
textbook-correct streaming behavior: ~3MB total capacity, position and
write pointer both advancing by exactly `0x4000` per chunk, remaining
bytes counting down cleanly in `0x4000` steps toward the final partial
read. **No overflow. That hypothesis is disproven.** Also read
`xbox_NtReadFile`'s real Windows implementation directly
(`kernel_file.c:242` -- confirmed the only one actually compiled; an
identically-named function at line 870 is dead code behind
`#else`/`!_WIN32` and not a duplicate-symbol bug) and found nothing
obviously wrong in its `OVERLAPPED`/offset/status handling.

**Where this leaves things.** The complete causal path is now proven
end to end -- `sub_004BBD90` <- `sub_004B8FC0` <- `sub_004B89E0` <- a
vtable call <- `sub_00035AA1` <- `sub_000356F1` <- `sub_000516B7` <-
`NtReadFile` (ordinal 219) -- but the actual mechanism that turns a
correct `esi`/`ebx` into a wrong one, despite every individually
checked link having correct argument counts, correct stack balance,
and correct buffer bookkeeping, is still unknown. Three candidates for
whoever picks this up next: (1) a genuine **race condition** between
whatever thread performs the file read and the thread running
`sub_004BBD90`/`sub_004B8FC0`, both touching the same object's memory
without synchronization our model reproduces correctly; (2)
`bridge_complete_file_io`'s APC/event completion path, not yet
examined this session, which a `kernel_bridge.c` comment already notes
runs its APC "inline" rather than deferred -- a plausible place for
shared global register state to get disturbed unexpectedly; (3) a
smaller, non-argument-count bug at one of `sub_00035AA1`'s *other*
vtable call targets (only `0x004BD380` was directly observed live;
the loop has three separate vtable slots and this run may not have
exercised the same one previously traced through `sub_004B8F90`).

Removed all diagnostic hooks (transition tracker, the buffer-bookkeeping
probe) via a full `tools.recomp` pipeline regeneration, confirmed the
generated tree was clean, rebuilt, and verified a plain run still
completes without crashing.

**CONTIG crash:** per instruction, only watched passively this session
-- did not recur. The source/ecx/esi tag from the previous entry
remains in place for whenever it does.

### 2026-09-11 (continued again): heap-allocator race found and fixed -- meaningfully reduces but does NOT eliminate the sub_004B89E0/sub_004B8FC0 corruption; bug stays formally OPEN

Picked up the three candidates from the previous entry in order.

**Candidate 1 (an unchecked vtable slot) ruled out.** `sub_004B89E0`
walks an array of Bink stream objects (stride `0x17C`) and dispatches
through several function-pointer slots per element (offsets `+0`, `+4`,
`+8`, plus two completion callbacks inside `sub_00035AA1` at `+0xF0`/
`+0xF4`/`+0xF8`). A live canary at all four call sites in
`sub_004B89E0`, deduped by resolved target, showed the same callee
every time: `sub_004BD380`. Checked its argument count, `ret 4` stack
cleanup, and register behavior against the real XBE bytes via
capstone -- correct in every respect. Not the bug.

**New permanent diagnostic: `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE_STACK_CHECK`.** The
existing `RECOMP_ABI_CALL` check only flags esp coming back too LOW
(epilogue never ran). It cannot see an over-pop -- a callee that pops
more bytes than the call site actually pushed -- because it has no
notion of what "too high" would mean at that macro's scope. But
`RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` already threads a `saved_esp` (the esp value from
right before the call's own argument pushes) through to every indirect
call site, and `saved_esp` is a hard ceiling regardless of calling
convention: a stdcall-style callee that cleans its own arguments brings
esp back up to exactly `saved_esp`; a cdecl-style one that leaves them
for the caller comes back lower still. Esp can never legitimately end
up *above* `saved_esp`. Added `recomp_icall_stack_overpop_log` (mirrors
the existing `recomp_abi_violation_log`, same first-hit-per-VA dedup
pattern) and wired the check into `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` in
`templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`. Ran it hard across this whole
investigation -- it never fired once. No individual indirect call site
examined is over-popping its own frame. Kept anyway as a
general-purpose, always-worth-having diagnostic (free when
`RECOMP_ABI_CHECK` is off).

**The actual finding: fine-grained per-checkpoint tracing pins the
corruption to one exact 8-byte window.** Rather than only comparing
function entry/exit, added `esp`/`esi` printouts at every checkpoint
inside `sub_004B89E0` (entry, right after `sub_004BC190`, each loop
iteration, `loc_004B8C81`, `loc_004B8C8D`, exit). Caught the bug live
several times with an identical shape:

- All three loop iterations (calls into `sub_004BD380`) return with
  esp exactly where it should be -- clean.
- At `loc_004B8C81`, right before the call to `sub_004BC250`, the
  stack is still correct: the saved caller esi (always `1` in every
  observed case) sits at exactly the expected address.
- At `loc_004B8C8D`, right *after* `sub_004BC250` returns, esp in the
  failing case is exactly 8 bytes higher than expected, and the memory
  where the saved esi should be now holds `0x01199914` instead --
  which is not garbage, it is the other, concurrently-running Bink
  stream object's own pointer value.
- `sub_004BC250` itself (`ret 8`, both exit paths) and its conditional
  nested call `sub_00052BF8` -> `xbox_NtReleaseMutant` (ordinal 221,
  correct arg count) both check out byte-exact against capstone. The
  new overpop check on that exact indirect call never fires.

That rules out a mistranslated `ret N` as the source of the extra 8
bytes: the memory holding the saved `esi` is being overwritten from
*outside* this call, between two checkpoints only a few instructions
apart, by a value that belongs to a different, simultaneously-running
thread.

**Root cause: `xbox_HeapAlloc`/`xbox_HeapFree`/`xbox_ContiguousAlloc`
had no locking whatsoever**, despite SCDA running at least two Bink
decode worker threads for its entire lifetime, each doing its own
streaming-buffer heap traffic -- and `xbox_AllocThreadStack` (which
carves a spawned worker's own simulated stack) draws from this exact
same unsynchronized bump-pointer/block-table allocator. Two threads
racing `xbox_HeapAlloc` can both read the same stale `g_heap_next`,
both compute the same base address, and both believe they alone own
it -- one thread's "private" buffer or worker stack then physically
aliases memory another thread is actively using. This is the same
shape of bug as the already-known, rarer CONTIG-arena crash
(`g_contig_next`, also an unlocked bump allocator).

**Fix:** a single process-wide spinlock (`g_alloc_lock`, built on
`InterlockedCompareExchange`/`InterlockedExchange`, matching the
spinlock pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase) wrapping the
bookkeeping in all four functions (`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`).
The actual `memset` of freshly-reserved memory stays outside the lock
on purpose: the region is exclusively reserved the moment the
bump-pointer update happens, so holding the lock across a potentially
large zero-fill would only add contention with nothing to protect.

**Honest result after a proper regression pass -- do not read this as
a full fix:**

- Pre-fix reproduction rate across several batches: roughly 15-25% of
  runs.
- Post-fix, across multiple batches including a from-scratch rebuild
  with every temporary debug hook stripped: 35 runs total, 3 hits
  (~8.6%).
- That is a real, repeatedly measured ~2-3x reduction -- the heap race
  was a genuine, independent bug and the fix is correct and worth
  keeping. It is *not* the whole story: the corruption still recurs,
  with the identical signature (always exactly an 8-byte over-pop at
  the same spot, always the same foreign pointer value `0x01199914`
  landing at the same address).

**Side lead ruled out.** The rare conditional path in `sub_00052BF8`
(only taken when `NtReleaseMutant` fails) runs through `sub_00052A85`
into `sub_00052A57`, which does an `fs:[4]`-based TLS lookup and writes
through the resulting pointer. Live tracing showed this write lands
consistently and correctly on a fixed, thread-appropriate address
(e.g. `0x00770208`) -- never anywhere near the corrupted
`0x013F9Exx` stack region. Not the cause.

**Still open:** the second ebx/esi chain is NOT closed. The remaining
~8.6% points at least one more unidentified race on shared state that
does not go through `xbox_HeapAlloc`/`xbox_ContiguousAlloc`. Candidates
for continuation: (a) `bridge_complete_file_io`'s inline-APC path
(carried over from the previous entry, still not examined); (b) another
unlocked shared global in the same family as the heap allocator --
`g_icall_trace`/`g_icall_source` are themselves unsynchronized globals,
though as pure diagnostics they cannot affect program logic, their
cross-thread interleaving in these logs is itself evidence of how
tightly the two worker threads actually run concurrently; (c) an
over-pop on a *direct* call site (`RECOMP_ABI_CALL`, not
`RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE`) -- the new stack-overpop check only covers
indirect calls, so a mistranslated `ret N` on a direct callee would
currently be invisible to it.

Verified: full `tools.recomp` pipeline regeneration removed every
temporary `DBG-*` hook from generated code (`grep -rl "DBG-"` on the
gen tree comes back empty), the temporary probe-list additions to
`recomp_manual.c`/`recomp_types.h` from the vtable-slot investigation
were fully reverted (`git diff` on those two files is limited to the
two genuine fixes: the overpop check and the heap lock), rebuilt clean,
and confirmed several regression runs complete without a crash caused
by the fix itself. The one segfault observed this session belongs to
the already-known, separately and passively watched CONTIG-crash
class, not to this bug.

### 2026-09-11 (continued yet again): candidates (a)/(c) closed with zero findings; new candidate found and fixed (CPU affinity); 18/18 clean regression runs, bug still not declared fixed

Direct follow-up per explicit user instruction, prioritized over my own

before treating this as an open-ended race hunt, and never end a turn
asking the user to pick between technically self-decidable options
again (this was called out explicitly and is now written into
AGENTS.md's autonomous-continuation section).

**Candidate (c), direct/indirect call over-pop: re-checked, closed,
nothing found.** Went through every call in the immediate
`sub_004B8FC0` -> `sub_004B89E0` -> `sub_004BC190`/`sub_004BC250` ->
`sub_00052BF8` -> `xbox_NtReleaseMutant`/`sub_00052A85` ->
`sub_00052A57` chain (plus `sub_004B8FA0` and `sub_004BBD90`'s own
indirect call), this time exhaustively rather than spot-checking:
capstone-disassembled the real XBE bytes for each callee's `ret`/`ret
N` and diffed that against the exact `esp` adjustment the generated
`.c` emits at each call site. Every one matched exactly -- no
over-pop, no under-pop, on any direct or indirect call in this chain.
No manual stack arithmetic was used as evidence anywhere in this pass,
per the standing rule. `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE_STACK_CHECK` (added earlier
this session, kept as a permanent diagnostic) has not fired in any run
to date. This candidate is exhausted.

**Candidate (a), `bridge_complete_file_io`'s inline-APC path: tested
live, premise falsified.** Added a temporary trace inside
`bridge_complete_file_io()` recording `apc_routine`, `apc_context`,
thread id, `esp`, and `icall_source`, deduplicated per distinct
`apc_routine` value. Across every observed file-I/O completion in this
title, `apc_routine` was `0`. `deliver_one_apc` is never invoked on
this path at all for SCDA's Bink stream reads -- so the concern the
user raised (guest code running at a different point in time, or
reentrantly, through the APC delivery mechanism, versus xemu) doesn't
apply: there is no APC delivery here to be early, late, or reentrant.
This closes candidate (a) more strongly than "checked and safe" -- the
mechanism itself is unused in this bug's causal path. The trace was
fully reverted (`git checkout -- src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c`).

**New candidate, tried before the full race-tracker (Step 3): CPU
affinity.** With both documented candidates exhausted, rather than
immediately building the expensive, unscoped last-writer/race tracker
the user had specified as the fallback, I picked a cheaper, concrete
hypothesis first: real Xbox hardware has exactly one physical CPU
core. SCDA runs at least two persistent Bink decode worker threads for
its whole lifetime; code written against a single physical core can
implicitly rely on the fact that a preemptive scheduler on ONE core
still serializes every memory effect between two threads at
instruction granularity in a way true concurrent execution on separate
physical cores does not. That's a plausible, and cheap-to-test,
explanation for a corruption whose signature is "one Bink stream
object's own pointer value showing up inside a different, concurrently
running Bink stream's saved register" -- exactly what was observed
(the foreign value `0x01199914` recurring at the same corrupted
address every time).

Implemented as `SetProcessAffinityMask(GetCurrentProcess(), 1)` near
the top of `main()` in `projects/scda/src/main.c`, pinning the whole
process (and by inheritance its threads) to logical CPU 0. Failure is
ignored deliberately -- worst case, the process runs exactly as before
on whatever cores the OS scheduler happens to pick.

- Batch 1: 8 runs, 8/8 `exit=124` (survived the 30s timeout, i.e. ran

- A third batch (12 more runs) was requested to shore up the sample

**Where this leaves things:** both fixes from this session (the heap

### 2026-09-11 (continued once more): live cdb reachability chain for CreateDevice -- narrowed the divergence point to inside/after sub_0004934E; found and fixed a real cdb tooling bug

Per explicit user direction: cheapest falsifiable step first -- check
live reachability of `sub_0049D210` (CreateDevice) via a rebuild-free

**cdb tooling bug found and fixed (reusable for future sessions):** the
first three attempts to run `scda_recomp.exe` under `cdb.exe` with a
`-cf <script>` command file produced zero output -- not even a bare
`.echo`. Root cause, isolated via a controlled test: **`-g` combined
with `-G` prevents the `-cf` command file from being processed at
all** (the process apparently runs free before cdb reads the script).
Fix: drop `-g`, keep `-G` if wanted -- the process then stops briefly

**Category A (directly relevant):** several disasm/function-boundary

1. **`2bfb9e05a8` ("lifter: read the carry flag on branches after
   arithmetic") is missing, and the bug it fixes is independently
   confirmed present in our own `tools/recomp/lifter.py`.** Its
   `_make_condition` reconstructs `jb`/`jae` after `add`/`sub` as
   `lhs < rhs`/`lhs >= rhs` using post-write operand reads -- when
   `dst==src` (e.g. `add edx, edx`, a common MSVC bit-shift-into-carry
   idiom), this collapses to `X < X`, always false. For
   `shl`/`shr`/`sar`, there's no `jb`/`jae`/`jc`/`jnc` case at all --
   it falls through to `None`. This is exactly the bug class upstream
   documents (it silently faulted Half-Life 2's XCompress decompressor
   there). Not proven to be the cause of our current SCDA
   vtable/constructor-unreached symptom, but the bug *shape* --  a
   branch silently always evaluating the same way, no crash, no error
   -- matches structurally.
2. **Our own `NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx` fix (this session) likely
   has the wrong argument order**, even though the total byte count
   (24 bytes/6 args) matches. We placed the extra parameter
   (`wait_block_array`, unused) between `Alertable` and `Timeout`, by
   analogy with `KeWaitForMultipleObjects`. Upstream's `87fb4bcf8d`
   cites the real, documented ntoskrnl prototype: `Count, Handles,
   WaitType, WaitMode, Alertable, Timeout` -- the extra parameter
   (`WaitMode`) sits between `WaitType` and `Alertable`, not after
   `Alertable`. Both fixes resolve the stack-corruption bug (same total
   byte count either way), but ours would read `alertable` and the
   extra slot swapped relative to the real ABI -- a real, if probably
   secondary, correctness bug in our own session work.

## Update 113 (2026-09-11, continued): exhaustive static search for the vtable literal `0x5696D8` -- no third, unknown constructor site; both candidates from Update 110 fully confirmed

**Approach (cheaper than candidate (b) from Update 110):** instead of a
live trace of every vtable-pointer assignment in the `0x2E2xxx`-
`0x2E7xxx` range during a 30s boot window (which could miss an
instantiation outside that window), first an EXHAUSTIVE static grep
for the literal value `0x5696D8` (the renderer class's vtable base
address) across the ENTIRE generated C code
(`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/`, all 28,121 functions).

**Result:** exactly 2 hits in the whole binary
(`recomp_0015.c:106887`, `recomp_0015.c:108383`), both of the form
`MEM32(esi) = 0x5696D8;` -- and both are inside the already-known
functions `sub_002E7381` and `sub_002E7AC6` from Update 110. **There
is no third, previously undiscovered site that constructs this
object.**

**Significance:** since this is a complete search over the compiled
code (not a time-bounded sampling window like a live trace would be),
the result is stronger than a live trace could provide -- it
conclusively rules out ANY code path in the recompiled binary
literal-assigning this vtable pointer. Combined with the already
live-confirmed 0-hit result for both constructors (Update 110), this
establishes: **this renderer object is never instantiated through any
path present in the generated code, during the current stable boot.**

**Caveat:** this does not rule out an indirect/computed assignment
(e.g. a copy from a template object via `memcpy`, or a table-lookup
construction with no literal) -- such a pattern wouldn't show up in a
literal grep. That's a considerably rarer C++ idiom than a direct
`mov [this+0], vtable` constructor, and hasn't been observed anywhere
else in this codebase.

**This fully closes candidate (b) from Update 110 (vtable-pointer live
trace) via the cheaper static variant, with the same negative result
as the earlier live check.** The remaining productive path is
candidate (a) (allocation/construction-site correlation via object
size/RTTI) or candidate (c) from Update 110 (hand prioritization back
to the user) -- further blind deepening of the same vtable chain
without a new method would not be productive.
