## Update 193 (2026-09-20): Determined the exact extent of the zeroed region -- 0x8070 bytes, matching "header + one ring-buffer segment (0x4000)" precisely; off-by-8 pointer bug is now a concrete working hypothesis

**Methodology correction:** conditional CDB breakpoint actions with `.printf`/`kb` inside braces repeatedly hang silently in this sandbox (no error, no output, the target process simply stays stopped) -- reproduced with both a nested and a deliberately non-nested `.if` structure. This confirms the behavior already documented by the previous agent (CURRENT HANDOFF, earlier version) and will not be attempted further in this investigation. The only reliable method remains: minimally-invasive, repeated `cdb -pv` polling of several addresses in a single invocation (~1.3s per poll for 13 addresses).

**Precise core finding:** the boundary-tag header (`0x1135920`/`0x1135924`, the allocator's own size|flags field) and the vtable (`0x1135928`) are demonstrably zeroed within the same poll window (< 1.4 seconds apart) -- not in a separate sequence. Via binary search (multiple `cdb -pv` calls against the same, already-crashed process, so no further timing uncertainty), the exact upper boundary of the contiguously-zeroed region was determined: **between `+0x8068` (still zero) and `+0x8070` (already back to real, high-entropy data) relative to the object start `0x1135928`.**

**Total size of the zeroed region: approximately `0x8070` bytes**, starting at the allocator's boundary tag (`0x1135920`, i.e. 8 bytes before the user pointer). This matches **exactly** `0x4070` (header including the 8-byte allocator header) **+ `0x4000`** (a single ring-buffer segment -- exactly the double-buffer segment size already known from `sub_00040821`/`sub_00040766`, which switches an `edx` value between `0` and `0x4000` there). Confirmed by a SEPARATE, independent tight-timing measurement: at the exact poll transition where the header+boundary-tag were zeroed, the value at `this+0x8000` simultaneously flipped from real audio data to zero, while `this+0x10000`/`this+0x18000` (further into the ring buffer) stayed UNCHANGED with real data -- the zeroed region ends well before the end of the `0x24000`-byte ring buffer, not at its end.

**Disproven:** values before our object (`-0x494` (a legitimate free `0x120`-byte dlmalloc chunk), `-0x1000`, `-0x2020`) change in a SEPARATE, EARLIER poll round than our own object -- they are ordinary, independent heap noise, not part of the same event. This further narrows the "wide or multi-block bulk reset" idea discussed in Update 190/192: the actually-affected region is precise and narrow (`0x8070` bytes), not "the whole surrounding heap."

**New, concrete working hypothesis:** some function computes a target region as `(pointer, size)` with `size = header payload size + one buffer segment (0x4000)` and zeroes it (memset-style) -- but the PASSED-IN POINTER is **8 bytes too early** (at the allocator chunk start instead of the user pointer), causing the allocator's own boundary tag to be overwritten as collateral damage. This would be a classic off-by-8 pointer bug (possibly a mixup between "chunk size including header" and "user size," already observed elsewhere as `0x4070` vs `0x4068` -- see the boundary-tag analysis in Update 192).

**Next test:** search for a function that (a) produces a `memset`/`rep stosd`-style zero-fill block with a size close to `0x4068`/`0x4070` PLUS `0x4000` (additive, or as two separate calls with `0x4070` and `0x4000`), AND (b) whose target address is computed from a pointer that could plausibly start 8 bytes too early (e.g. `ptr - 8` instead of `ptr`, or a size calculation that accidentally includes the allocator header). Given the CDB breakpoint unreliability: prefer a targeted, narrow source search (text search for `stosd`/`memset` translation patterns WITH a size constant near `0x4070`/`0x4000`/`0x8070` nearby) over a live trace.

**Relevant new artifacts:** `tools/debug/poll_boundary_out.log` (boundary-tag+vtable poll, transition at poll #23->#24), `tools/debug/poll_extent_out.log` (13-address poll, transition at poll #13->#14, shows `this+0x8000` dropping simultaneously while `this+0x10000`/`+0x18000` stay unchanged).

## Update 194 (2026-09-20): Found a vtable family with a shared base class -- many inherited methods shared between our ring-buffer class and at least one sibling class

**Finding:** directly next to our subobject's vtable (`0x4F6940`) sits a SECOND, closely related vtable at `0x4F69C0` (exactly `0x80` bytes / 32 function pointers further). Slot 0 (destructor) and slot 1 (refill/"pump") differ (`sub_00040B00`/`sub_00040821` for our class vs. `sub_00040CCC`/`sub_00040BB0` for the sibling class), but MANY of the remaining slots are IDENTICAL between both vtables: `0x3ED16`, `0x3ED60`, `0x3E60E`, `0xEE9D1`, `0x39DA8`, `0x39DA3`, `0x370659`, `0x1AEFA1`, `0x3E7B6`, `0x4528E7` (and more) appear at the same relative slot positions in BOTH vtables.

**Interpretation:** this is the classic pattern of a C++ class hierarchy with a shared base class: several derived classes override only a handful of class-specific virtual methods (here: the destructor and the refill/pump method) while inheriting the bulk of the vtable from a common base. This refines the hypothesis from Update 192/193: an INHERITED, generic base-class method (e.g. a "cleanup"/"reset" path) could be correct for the "typical" sibling class with a smaller, differently-managed buffer, while making a wrong size assumption for OUR class (with its separately-allocated, much larger ring buffer), collaterally overwriting the allocator's boundary tag in the process.

**Checked every shared slot function individually -- this lead does NOT pan out:** `sub_0003ED16` (bit manipulation / free-list bitmap), `sub_0003ED60` (thin dispatch thunk), `sub_0003E60E`/`sub_000EE9D1`/`sub_001AEFA1`/`sub_00370659`/`sub_004528E7` (all trivial 1-5-byte no-op stubs, typical default implementations of a generic base-class interface), and `sub_00039DA3` (the one non-trivial shared function, 114 bytes -- turns out to be an iterator/value-comparison function, several small comparison routines packed into the same code block, no access to buffer-size fields). **None of these base-class methods contains a `rep stosd`/`memset` translation pattern.** The hypothesis "an inherited base-class cleanup method zeroes with the wrong size" is therefore disproven for THIS vtable family.

**Honest interim status:** the extent and character of the bug are now precisely known (Update 193: exactly `~0x8070` bytes starting at the allocator's boundary tag, matching `0x4070+0x4000`), but the CONCRETE function/call that triggers it has not yet been found. The obvious candidates (the class's own destructors, shared base-class methods) are disproven. Open candidates for the next round: (a) a function that does NOT dispatch through THIS vtable at all, but addresses the object/ring buffer via a raw, separately-stored pointer (e.g. a level/resource manager holding pointers in its own list); (b) a function in a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT, not-yet-investigated vtable family that happens to reference the same memory region; (c) an actual generic, non-virtual `memset`/`ZeroMemory` call with a size miscomputed at runtime, invoked from somewhere with nothing to do with C++ vtables at all (e.g. directly from `sub_00048B15`'s level-load flow).

**Model tier stays MAXIMUM** -- the obvious candidates are exhausted; the remaining search (candidate b/c above) needs either a much broader code search or a carefully re-engineered live-trace attempt that works around the CDB breakpoint unreliability seen repeatedly this session (e.g. finer-grained polling instead of conditional breakpoints).

## Update 195 (2026-09-20): Independent root-cause audit (MAXIMUM) -- allocator engine (Allocate/Realloc/Free/Slot 0xC) fully checked for zero-fill and ruled out; sub_00048B15 read and ruled out; new structural explanation for 0x8070

**This round's mandate:** instead of mechanically working through Update 194's candidate list, an independent audit was run: which mechanisms can even produce exactly `0x8070` bytes of zeroing, what do `0x8070`/`0x4070`/`0x4000` mean structurally, and which whole mechanism classes can be ruled out.

**1. Structural meaning of 0x8070/0x4070/0x4000 (refined):** the zeroed region starts exactly at the allocator chunk's own start (`this-8`, the boundary-tag/size field) and spans EXACTLY `our object's own chunk size (0x4070, including the 8-byte header) + one immediately-following ring-buffer segment (0x4000)`. Newly worked out: the end of the zeroing sits at `this+0x8068`, which arithmetically is EXACTLY `(this-8) + 0x4070 + 0x4000` -- the boundary is not a rounded estimate but a byte-exact sum of two concrete, known sizes. This implies the writer (a) operates on a CHUNK pointer (`this-8`/`this-4`), not the user pointer `this` itself, AND (b) uses a size composed of "this chunk's own size" plus "one buffer segment." This strongly constrains legitimate culprits: outside the allocator implementation itself, ordinary C++ code almost never holds a chunk pointer (only the user pointer); a caller would have to either (i) be allocator-internal code, or (ii) perform its own -4/-8 pointer arithmetic (e.g. its own bookkeeping field placed directly before a pointer it hands elsewhere).

**2. Allocator vtable Realloc engine (slot 4, `sub_00077B61` -> `sub_000778BC`) read in full -- ruled out:** `sub_000778BC` (521 bytes, 189 instructions) is a complete, correct dlmalloc-style `realloc()`: size-class computation, in-place growth into the top chunk, in-place growth by merging with a free neighboring chunk (including free-list unlink), fallback to fresh allocation (`sub_000774E6`) + `rep movsd`/`movsb` copy of the OLD payload + freeing the old chunk. **There is no zero-fill of the newly grown memory anywhere** -- a standard `realloc()` leaves that region as stale/undefined content, not zeroed. Additionally, this slot's actual call graph was traced (through the dispatcher `sub_0003EDCC`, which itself has zero direct callers anywhere in the generated code, and through two generic container-resize helpers in `recomp_0018.c`/`recomp_0023.c`, notably `sub_004518CC`, used at 30+ call sites scattered across the whole program) -- none of these call paths sit anywhere near our object (the `0x40xxx` address range) or near `sub_00048B15`. **The "our object gets reallocated" candidate is now ruled out both by code content and by call-graph evidence.**

**3. Free/coalescing path (`sub_0007708F`) read in full -- ruled out, with an important corollary:** the complete free-list insertion/coalescing logic (forward/backward coalescing, top-chunk extension, "trim back to the OS above an 0x8000 threshold") was read. **It contains no zero-fill of payload data anywhere** -- only the free list's own pointer/size fields are written. **Important new corollary:** since `Free()` never zeroes payload data at all, an erroneous or duplicate `Free()` call on our object -- even if such a bug exists somewhere -- CANNOT by itself explain the observed full zeroing of `0x8070` bytes. A pure Free() bug would leave stale garbage behind, not zeros. **The writer must therefore be an explicit, deliberate bulk-zero call (memset/ZeroMemory/a `rep stosd`-style loop), not a side effect of normal (or buggy) allocator bookkeeping.** This rules out a whole explanation class that had not been explicitly excluded before ("it's simply a double-free").

**4. Vtable slot 0xC (`sub_0007702F`) checked -- ruled out:** a small, conditional, one-time init/maintenance hook (checks a flag, conditionally calls `sub_00076F00` and enters/leaves the critical section `0x6B27A0`). No size or address parameters, no zero-fill. All five known allocator vtable slots (0=Allocate, 4=Realloc, 8=Free, 0xC=this hook, 0x10=the trivial 1-5-byte stub from Update 194) have now been individually read and ruled out.

**5. `sub_00048B15` (Update 194's candidate "c") read in full -- ruled out:** this function (1032 bytes/258 instructions) is the level/session bootstrap: at its very start it installs the fatal-handler pointer itself (`MEM32(0x5E6E0C) = 0x3FCA5`, i.e. `sub_0003FCA5` -- the callback where we observe the corruption) and then orchestrates roughly a dozen subsystem-init calls. It contains exactly one `rep stosd` zero-fill: `0x80` bytes at the FIXED global address `0x64D638` (near the allocator's own metadata block `0x64D29C`-`0x64D5EC`, but not itself an allocator field), immediately followed by populating that region with ~16 function pointers from various subsystems (a registration table, unrelated to our object). It also performs one independent `0x270`-byte allocation through the same allocator singleton (`0x5B57F8`) -- an unrelated size. One sub-call (`sub_001D47CF`, initially suspected as a possible audio-init call) was also read: it is a string/config-formatting helper, with no audio or buffer relevance. **Update 194's candidate (c) ("a generic memset call directly from sub_00048B15") is now disproven, not merely unexamined.**

**Honest interim status:** this MAXIMUM round definitively ruled out one large cause class (the allocator's own bookkeeping as the mechanism, including the corollary that "a pure Free bug" is insufficient) and disproved one concrete Update-194 candidate (sub_00048B15 directly). This sharpens the search: the writer is very likely an explicit zero-fill call outside the allocator's core routines, either (a) reached via a raw, separately-held pointer (still the most promising open candidate from Update 194) or (d, new/refined) via code that maintains its own chunk-like `ptr-4`/`ptr-8` bookkeeping (e.g. its own intrusive header field placed directly before a pointer it hands elsewhere) and miscomputes a combined size (its own record plus a following buffer). Candidate (b) (a completely different vtable family) remains open but lower priority, being expensive to check without a further lead.

**Model tier stays MAXIMUM** -- this round actively shrank the search space (ruled out a whole mechanism class, disproved a concrete candidate), meeting the progress bar; no reason to de-escalate.

## Update 199 (2026-09-20): Worker lifetime resolved; thread-local guest state rules out register-sharing race

**Fresh lifecycle evidence:** `tools/debug/cdb_worker_lifetime_at_fatal_out.log`

runtime declares every architectural guest register/state component as

## Update 204 (2026-09-20): Timer/APC mechanism and the virtual-memory release path fully ruled out; Lipsync's 4th call strongly (not absolutely) negative; search space now extremely narrow

**Test 1 -- timer-queue mechanism (KeSetTimer), completely new, never previously checked:** a simple, non-nested triple breakpoint (`xbox_KeSetTimerEx`, `xbox_timer_callback`, `sub_0003FCA5`) over a complete run to the fatal callback shows: **`KESETTIMER-CALL`=0, `TIMER-CALLBACK-FIRED`=0, `FATAL-HIT`=1.** The game does not use `KeSetTimer`/`CreateTimerQueueTimer` at all during this boot sequence. This entire, previously-unconsidered async mechanism candidate (a Windows-managed pool thread, independent of the already-investigated `PsCreateSystemThreadEx` worker-thread angle) is therefore **fully ruled out**.

**Test 2 -- Lipsync worker's last unresolved call (`sub_00039566+0x183`), strengthened negative finding:** the already-prepared breakpoint left by Update 202 was run for **8 minutes of wall-clock time** (substantially longer than the previous 30-second tool-limited attempts). A non-invasive interim check confirms: the main-thread object has long since been zeroed (fatal reached minutes ago), yet the breakpoint has not fired even once. This is a much stronger negative signal than Update 202's "inconclusive," though not an absolute proof (the call could theoretically still happen much later). Redundant orphaned processes from earlier attempts (PIDs `3660`/`15280`, `21136`/`29212`) were cleaned up; the explicitly protected pair `25164`/`27552` was left untouched.

**Test 3 -- full trace of the allocator's own OS memory grow/shrink chain (`sub_00076849`->`sub_00076CC6`->`sub_00371BC3`/`sub_00371BF1`), new this round:** this chain had never been read in this session before. It matches dlmalloc's classic `MORECORE`/`sysalloc` mechanism: `sub_00076849(size)` grows, for a positive `size`, through `sub_00371BC3` (resolved as a direct `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` call: `&addr, 0, &size, MEM_COMMIT=0x1000, PAGE_READWRITE=4`), and shrinks, for a negative `size`, in the `loc_00076A9D` branch through `sub_00371BF1` with flag `0x8000` = **MEM_RELEASE** (not decommit!) -- a potentially dangerous call that could cause real damage if the address computation were wrong.

**Decisive find:** reading the bridge code (`src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c`) turned up extensive PRE-EXISTING documentation of exactly these functions from an EARLIER, independent investigation (dated 2026-09-01/02, about a now-fixed "v0.6.0-merge regression hang"). That documentation explains: `bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory` treats a pure `MEM_COMMIT` on an already-reserved region as a no-op (our bump allocator commits everything immediately anyway); `bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory` synthesizes a simplified two-region memory picture specifically for this pool-growth loop.

**Empirically verified (in the already-captured log `tools/debug/threadroutine_stderr.log`):** `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` is called twice (early: an `MEM_RESERVE` of 1MB, and a `MEM_COMMIT` no-op at `0x00F80000` -- that address matches `[HEAP] #1` and the old, separate 2026-08-26 bug report about `sub_00056B22`/temp region `0x00F80000`). **`NtFreeVirtualMemory` is called ZERO times.** The dangerous `MEM_RELEASE` shrink path (`sub_00371BF1`) therefore never fires in a real run. **This entire mechanism is thus ruled out as an explanation for the `0x8070` zeroing.**

**Side finding (context, not a new lead):** the `[HEAP]` log lines show our object (`0x1135928`) sits inside a 1MB block reserved via `xbox_HeapAlloc` (`0x010CC000..0x011CC000`, `[HEAP] #8`). That specific block is never freed via `xbox_HeapFree` in the captured run (only two OTHER, smaller 512KB blocks are freed -- provably the two Bink worker thread stacks, since `xbox_AllocThreadStack`/`xbox_FreeThreadStack` operate directly on the same guest heap).

**Honest interim status:** the search space is now exceptionally narrow. Ruled out: the entire allocator engine, the entire visible main() call chain, the entire disk-read chain, both Bink workers (by timing), the timer/APC mechanism, and the virtual-memory release path. Strongly (but not absolutely) negative: the last open Lipsync call. What remains with meaningful plausibility: (1) an as-yet-unidentified mechanism inside the still-alive Lipsync worker, beyond the code already read; (2) the old, never-conclusively-followed connection to the 2026-08-26 bug report (`sub_00056B22`, free-list corruption, SPATIALLY in the same `xbox_HeapAlloc` region as our object); (3) a direct live catch of the transition itself (timing narrowing + `~*kb` exactly inside the transition window, never actually executed despite being recommended multiple times).

**Recommendation for the next round:** prioritize (3) -- directly catching the transition itself via timing narrowing (template: Update 193) followed by a single `~*kb` dump exactly inside the determined transition window, since this is the only remaining method that could directly reveal a still-unidentified mechanism (candidate 1 or 2) rather than continuing to eliminate candidates one at a time.

**Model tier stays MAXIMUM** -- this round definitively ruled out two more complete mechanism classes (real progress), even though the concrete writer remains unfound.

## Update 205 (2026-09-20): Four live-capture attempts for the GOOD->ZERO transition -- no GOOD state caught, but important timing and methodology corrections; a captured fatal-time stack yields three newly-checked, harmless functions

**Goal this round:** the prioritized test from Update 204 -- catch the GOOD->ZERO transition live via timing narrowing and run `~*kb` exactly inside the transition window. Result: NOT achieved (not a single fresh process showed a GOOD poll this round), but four independent attempts together produced several important, documentation-worthy corrections to the prior timing and methodology model.

**New core finding 1 -- total lifetime is much shorter than assumed:** a completely unobserved (zero cdb calls), freshly launched process reaches the fatal state (`sub_0003FCA5+0x17b0`, the known self-jmp loop) AND a stable memory plateau (`~173.7 MB`) within roughly 25-30 seconds of launch -- not after several minutes, as had been wrongly extrapolated from the old, already-long-running processes (Updates 190-204). The prior model ("GOOD state persists for a long time, >1 minute") rested on the fact that earlier sessions always examined ALREADY long-running processes, never brand-new ones. The actual GOOD window is likely only a few seconds long.

**New core finding 2 -- repeated `cdb -pv` polling has a cumulative side effect:** two independent processes (PID 3660: 13-address poll, ~400 iterations in a tight loop; PID 47872: 2-address poll, ~1.2s cadence, continuous) did not end in the expected GOOD/ZERO transition, but in a state where EVERY further `cdb -pv` attach fails with `Win32 error 0n156` ("Unable to examine process") -- permanently, reproducibly, independent of the target's actual state. A `~*kb` snapshot of one such thread additionally showed `Suspend: 40` on both threads -- an unusually high suspend count matching roughly the number of prior polls. Working hypothesis: non-invasive `-pv` attaches internally perform SuspendThread/ResumeThread cycles that do not fully balance out under very frequent repetition. **Methodology consequence:** polling must no longer be run as a continuous loop over minutes, only in short, targeted bursts.

**New core finding 3 -- a third, independent failure mode:** another fresh process (PID 31684, only lightly polled at a 3s cadence starting at second 0) got stuck at `56 KB` memory usage -- well BEFORE the 173 KB fatal plateau -- and showed zero progress for 120+ seconds, even though `attach_err=0` the whole time (the debugger could technically attach, but the target apparently stopped making progress). A subsequently launched process left completely undisturbed for 25 seconds (PID 21796), by contrast, reached the 173 KB plateau normally. This shows that even very early, light polling can block boot progress itself -- not just later attachability.

**Methodology correction (important for all future stack analyses):** the offset in a cdb stack frame such as `scda_recomp!sub_0007F412+0x32b7` refers to bytes within the COMPILED host x64 code of that C function, NOT bytes within the ORIGINAL guest x86 address range documented in the source comments (`Original: 0x0007F412 - 0x0007F8A6, 1172 bytes`). An offset that far exceeds the documented guest size (here 0x32b7 = 12983 vs. 1172 bytes) is therefore NOT evidence of a wrong symbol resolution -- the conversion "guest address + host offset = new guest address" (mistakenly attempted this session) is invalid, since guest-to-host C compilation has no fixed size ratio. All future stack interpretations must trust the reported function name and must not feed host offsets into guest-address arithmetic.

**One actual fatal-time stack was captured (process already in the fatal state, `~*kb`):** thread 0 shows exactly the chain already known from Update 197 (main -> xbe_entry_point -> ... -> sub_00048B15 -> sub_0004934E -> ... -> sub_00040821(refill) -> fatal), PLUS three frames not individually named before: `sub_0007DC43`, `sub_0007DE25`, `sub_001CA0A5`. All three have now been read fully and excluded:
- `sub_0007DC43` (11 bytes of guest code): a trivial vtable thunk (`ecx=[ecx+0x450]; eax=[ecx]; tail-jmp [eax+4]`), a sibling of the `sub_0007DC2D` thunk already identified in Update 203. No write access.
- `sub_0007DE25` (93 bytes of guest code): a small dispatch-relay function issuing several `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` calls (vtable slot 0x20) on various objects. No zero-fill.
- `sub_001CA0A5` (565 bytes of guest code, read in full): a constructor for a SMALL, UNRELATED object (fields up to at most offset `+0x1E8`, three `movsd` triples for vector copies, several scalar initializations) -- nowhere near the `0x8070`/`0x4070`/`0x4000` size class. No zero-fill of relevant magnitude.
Two further frames (`sub_0007F412+0x32b7`, `sub_00064B00+0x33ee`) have host offsets far exceeding their documented guest function size -- a reliable statement about them requires disassembling the host binary directly (not the source comments), which was deferred this round for time reasons. `sub_00064B00` had also already been read in an earlier round (657 lines, one harmless local `stosd+stosw` hit on a stack buffer).

**Progress criterion (per Update 204's own standard) -- assessment:** "transition window substantially smaller" is MET (from "unknown, presumed several minutes" to "verified < 30 seconds after process launch"). The GOOD state itself was not caught this round, but three new frames from a captured fatal-time stack are now checked and excluded -- the active candidate list keeps shrinking, even without a new writer being found.

**Do not repeat:** further identical "fresh process + immediate/continuous polling" attempts with the exact same setup -- four attempts with different poll cadences/timings all failed this round via different failure modes, none showing the GOOD state. Instead, for the next round: **a new measurement method (see CURRENT HANDOFF)** -- staggered sampling across multiple process instances instead of continuous polling of a single instance.

**Relevant new artifacts:** `tools/debug/poll_spatial_wide.sh`, `tools/debug/poll_boundary2.sh`, `tools/debug/poll_boundary3.sh` (this round's polling script variants); `tools/debug/poll_boundary2_out.log`, `tools/debug/poll_boundary3_out.log`, `tools/debug/poll_boundary4_out.log` (poll logs from the four attempts); `tools/debug/launch_timestamped.sh`, `tools/debug/wait_for_stall.sh` (discarded/partially-failed helper scripts, kept as a lesson learned).

**Method (as specified by CURRENT HANDOFF/Update 205):** each `scda_recomp.exe` process was attached with `cdb -pv` EXACTLY ONCE, then immediately killed. Object identity was not assumed as a fixed address; a `s -d` memory search for the vtable constant `0x4F6940` was additionally used as a cross-check.

**First round (8 timepoints, 10-32s):** ALL eight single samples (10s, 15s, 19s, 22s, 24s, 26s, 28s, 32s) showed the identical memory footprint (`~52-56 KB`, unchanged) AND an inaccessible target arena ("Memory access error"). This clearly contradicts Update 205's timing model (fatal by ~25-30s) -- **today's actual boot duration to the big memory jump is roughly 36 seconds**, not 25-30. Importantly, these eight single attaches did not additionally influence their respective process (each got exactly one attach, then was killed) -- the actual boot pace varies by day/system state, not (only) from debugger interference.

**Second method -- external, debugger-free jump detection:** since `tasklist` memory queries have repeatedly been shown to have NO side effect on the target process, a new script (`tools/debug/detect_jump_then_attach.sh`) was built: it polls memory usage via `tasklist` ONLY (no cdb) at a 0.15s cadence until a large jump (`>100000..168000 KB`, threshold varied across test rounds) is detected, and only THEN performs the single permitted cdb attach.

**Core finding -- GOOD/ZERO window bracketed:**
- At `kb=145,704-148,016` (during the memory jump), the main thread was demonstrably NOT YET in the fatal handler: the stack shows `ntdll!NtDelayExecution -> KERNELBASE!SleepEx -> scda_recomp!xbox_KeDelayExecutionThread` -- a real, deterministic Xbox kernel delay call, reproducible at exactly this memory mark (2 of 2 hits).
- At `kb=162,500-173,740` (shortly after), the process was ALWAYS already in the fatal handler (`sub_0003FCA5`), AND the target arena was already fully unmapped (not just zeroed!).

- **New finding about unmapping:** it does NOT happen slowly over minutes (as inferred in Update 204/205 from old, long-running processes), but PRACTICALLY IMMEDIATELY after reaching the fatal handler (within milliseconds to a few seconds).

**New finding -- four previously unknown functions in the fatal-handler cleanup path:** a `k 10` stack from an already-fatal sample showed that `sub_0003FCA5` (the fatal handler), BEFORE settling into its known self-jmp idle loop (`+0x17b0`), actively calls the following chain (`+0x1772`): `sub_0049CC50` -> `sub_0049CC10` -> `sub_004A13D0` -> `sub_004A12B0`/`sub_004A1360`. **Assessment:** these four functions are genuine, previously unmentioned parts of the fatal path, but after being read in full, they are EXCLUDED as the writer of our object (no bulk zero, no touch of the target address/size).

## Update 207 (2026-09-21): sub_0003FCA5 fully identified -- it is the localized "disc error" dialog, not a generic crash handler; explains downstream behavior but not the root cause

**Trigger:** a staggered single sample (Update 206 technique, finer `0.02s`
poll interval, `kb>150000` threshold) for the first time landed at a moment
where `sub_0003FCA5` itself was still actively executing code (not yet in
the final idle loop) -- a `k 10` stack showed `sub_0003FCA5+0xb80` calling
into a previously unknown chain (`sub_00072989` -> `sub_00052D5A` ->
`sub_00052CDC` -> `kernel_thunk_dispatch` -> `bridge_KeDelayExecutionThread`
-> `xbox_KeDelayExecutionThread` -> `SleepEx`/`NtDelayExecution`). This
showed for the first time that `sub_0003FCA5` itself does substantial work,
not just a `jmp $` body.

**Full read of `sub_0003FCA5` (459 bytes / 145 guest instructions, read in
full):** the function is a classic "show an error message and hang forever"
handler:
1. Lazy-init check (`MEM32(0x5E76AC)`), two interface-init icalls if needed.
2. Builds a 640x480 display surface (`sub_0049D320`, `sub_0049D210`,
   `MEM32(ebp-108)=0x280`, `MEM32(ebp-104)=0x1E0`).
3. Checks a global object (`MEM32(0x6500FC)`) and, if present, waits in a
   loop (`sub_000523F7`, then `sub_00072989` -- THIS is the source of the
   delay call found above) -- presumably an audio-system shutdown or
   message-pump wait.
4. Determines a language index (0-4) via `sub_000522B2` and uses it to pick
   one of FIVE message pairs from string constants.
5. Renders two lines of text at fixed screen coordinates (`sub_000587B0`,
   called twice, at (0x30,0x32) and (0x50,0x32)).
6. Flushes the result via an NV2A pushbuffer kick (`sub_0049CC50`, already
   read in Update 206).
7. `goto loc_0003FE6E;` -- the known infinite loop (self-`jmp`).

**The five string pairs were read directly from the XBE via Capstone/Python
(UTF-16LE, not ASCII):** all five are the SAME message in FIVE LANGUAGES
(code 0=German, 1=French, 2=Spanish, 3=Italian, 4=English): "There's a
problem with the disc you're using. It may be dirty or damaged." The
"error code" 0-4 is therefore NOT an error-type selector but a language
index -- **`sub_0003FCA5` is the standard, localized Xbox "disc error"
display, not a generic crash handler.**

**Significance for the root-cause search:** `sub_0003FCA5` is called by
`sub_00040821` (our refill function) precisely when its own disc read
fails. Since the object is already zeroed BEFORE that read (per Update
196), the "disc error" screen is a DOWNSTREAM SYMPTOM: the refill function
tries to perform a read using an already-broken/zeroed handle or pointer,
that read fails (looking, to the generic error-handling code, like a "disc
problem"), and the game reflexively shows the standard message -- **not
because there is an actual disc I/O problem (the disc image under emulation
is fine), but because an invalid handle value gets misclassified by the
generic error path as a disc problem.** This confirms and sharpens Update
196's finding, but still does not identify the concrete writer.

**Now fully excluded (no further investigation needed):** `sub_0003FCA5`
itself and its entire internal call chain (`sub_000677E4`, `sub_0049D320`,
`sub_0049D210`, `sub_000523F7`, `sub_00072989`, `sub_00052D5A`,
`sub_00052CDC`, `sub_00051673`, `sub_0003B7B3`, `sub_002536EB`,
`sub_00255615`, `sub_000587B0` x2, `sub_0049CC50`+subfunctions) -- all
generic, object-independent display/rendering/wait logic for the error
dialog, no bulk zero.

**Next test:** the actual root cause remains upstream of the refill call.
Recommendation: examine the EXACT return value/status code that
`sub_00040821` checks immediately before calling `sub_0003FCA5` (what
precise condition triggers the jump to the error dialog?) -- this could
sharpen the error type (invalid handle vs. wrong size vs. timeout) and
narrow the search further, without repeating the whole root-cause search.

**Model tier:** STRONG remains appropriate.

## Update 209 (2026-09-21): sub_00038A43 fully analyzed and byte-verified against the original XBE -- trigger mechanism understood, but several non-trivial causes remain open

**Goal this round:** fully understand `sub_00038A43` (the candidate named
in Update 208): which branch produces status `4` (triggering
`sub_0003FCA5`, the disc-error dialog), what condition leads there, and
where the value used for that condition comes from.

**Full trace of `sub_00038A43` (402 bytes / 134 instructions, read in
full):**
- `esi` = the decoder's "this" (category "game_video"); `eax =
  MEM32(esi+0xFC)` is a pointer to a smaller "reader" object (the parent/
  reader structure the user asked about).
- The DECISIVE comparison (address `0x00038AFB`/`0x00038B00`):
  `sub_00052A9C(...)` is called; if it returns `!=0`, execution continues
  normally (`loc_00038B0E`). If it returns `0`, `sub_00052A2F()` (a
  GetLastError equivalent, reading a thread-local error slot indexed via
  the FS segment/TEB) is called. If that result is NEITHER `0x26`
  (`ERROR_HANDLE_EOF`) NOR `0x3E5` (`ERROR_IO_PENDING`), status `4` is
  returned -- THIS is what triggers the disc-error dialog.

**`sub_00052A9C` read in full (the actual status source):** it treats the
reader object like an `IO_STATUS_BLOCK` (field `+0` = Status, field `+4`
= bytes transferred):
- If `Reader.Status == 0x103` (`STATUS_PENDING`): it may wait for
  completion via `sub_00052D2E` (a sync-primitive wrapper, already known);
  on a zero-size request or a failed wait, it explicitly calls
  `SetLastError(0x3E4)` (`ERROR_IO_INCOMPLETE`) and returns `0` (failure).
- If `Reader.Status != 0x103` (e.g. already completed OR zeroed): it
  copies `Reader.Information` (byte count) into the output parameter,
  re-reads `Reader.Status`, and: **if NON-NEGATIVE (sign bit clear,
  INCLUDING the value 0!): returns `1` (SUCCESS)** -- no GetLastError check
  follows in this case. Only if NEGATIVE (sign bit set, a real high-
  severity NTSTATUS error code) is that value relayed via `SetLastError`
  and `0` (failure) returned.

**Byte-exact verification against the original XBE (Capstone):** both the
comparison site in `sub_00038A43` (`0x38ae1`-`0x38b09`) and the complete
logic of `sub_00052A9C` (`0x52a9c`-`0x52afe`) were disassembled and MATCH
the generated C code EXACTLY -- **no recompiler bug in this chain.**

**Central, precise finding:** a simple, COMPLETE zeroing of the reader
object (`Status=0`, `Information=0`) would NOT trigger the observed error
path -- `Status=0` is NON-NEGATIVE and would be interpreted as "success
with 0 bytes" (`sub_00052A9C` returns `1`, GetLastError is never checked,
`sub_00038A43` proceeds normally instead of returning status `4`). The
simple explanation "the whole object got zeroed, therefore the read fails"
is therefore DISPROVEN for this specific mechanism -- the actual trigger
must be one of:
1. A REAL, NEGATIVE NTSTATUS error code in the reader's status field (not
   simply zero) at the time of the check, which additionally doesn't
   happen to equal exactly `0x26`/`0x3E5`.
2. The `sub_00052D2E` wait call fails, or the size check
   (`MEM32(esp+0x14)==0`) is true, leading to `ERROR_IO_INCOMPLETE`
   (`0x3E4`) -- independent of the reader object's own state.
3. The path actually taken in the real crash is one of the OTHER two call
   sites of `sub_0003FCA5` (`sub_000356F1` via `sub_000516B7`), not
   `sub_00038A43`/`sub_00038F96` -- not live-verified this round.

**Causal framing (as requested):** this round does not directly prove
"zeroing causes the read failure" OR "the read failure triggers zeroing"
-- it precisely shows that a simple bulk zero of THIS SPECIFIC reader
field is NOT sufficient to explain the observed error path. The most
plausible remaining picture is: both the `0x8070` zeroing AND the disc
error are consequences of an even earlier, shared fault state -- OR the
reader actually holds a genuine negative error code (not a simple zero),
which would point to a different kind of corruption than a plain zero-fill.

**Model tier:** several plausible causes remain despite complete,
byte-verified direct-evidence tracing, and the multi-hop indirection
(decoder -> reader pointer -> IO_STATUS_BLOCK-like status -> thread-local
error translation -> comparison against two constants) is conceptually
non-trivial.

MODEL STATUS: ESCALATION RECOMMENDED
Tier: MAXIMUM
Reason: despite a complete, byte-verified trace, several non-trivial,
mutually exclusive explanations remain open (a real negative status code
vs. a timeout path vs. a different call site), and the simplest hypothesis

## Update 213 (2026-09-21): ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND BYTE-VERIFIED -- the ring-buffer subobject's header fields are zeroed by an underflowing memcpy destination inside sub_00040821's own buffer-wraparound compaction logic; confirmed present verbatim in the original XBE, not a recompiler bug

**Correction to Update 212:** the "native kernel-bridge" hypothesis was wrong.
Update 212 concluded the corruption must be in native host code because two
back-to-back, same-thread entries into `sub_000516B7`'s own
`RECOMP_TRACE_PC` checkpoint appeared with no intervening return checkpoint
-- but this was an instrumentation gap, not evidence of reentrancy:
`sub_00040821` has **two separate call sites** to `sub_000516B7` (guest
`0x408E1` and guest `0x40983`), both textually near-identical, and Update
212's checkpoints only covered the second one. Once the first call site was
also instrumented (see below), the "two same-thread entries" resolved into
two perfectly ordinary, sequential calls within a single loop iteration --
no cross-thread activity, no APC, no native code involved at all.

**Method:** four more ring-buffer checkpoints (still the same Update
210-212 technique, still zero cdb polling), specifically chosen to bisect
the ~140-byte span between the two `sub_000516B7` call sites:
callsite 13 right after the FIRST call returns (`loc_000408E1`, previously
completely uninstrumented), callsite 14 at `loc_00040909` (start of the
"read two 4-byte record-header fields from the current cursor" block),
callsite 16 at `loc_00040942` (entry to the buffer-compaction block, right
before its two `memcpy`/`rep movsd`+`rep movsb` calls), and callsite 17
immediately after those same two copies complete. Ring buffer size raised
from 8 to 24 entries (`recomp_manual.c`) so one full cycle (up to 10+
checkpoint firings) stays visible without eviction. One more fresh,
undisturbed run, one single static read after the freeze.

**Result -- the transition is bracketed to two adjacent lines of code:**
in exact chronological order for the fatal cycle: callsite 17 (end of a
PRIOR iteration's compaction, valid) -> callsite 11 (`sub_000516B7` entry,
call site 1, valid) -> callsite 13 (call site 1 returns, valid) ->
callsite 14 (`loc_00040909`, valid) -> **callsite 16 (`loc_00040942`, right
before the two memcpy operations -- still fully valid: `this=0x1135928`,
`handle=0x48000005`, `buffer_size=0x24000`, `ring_ptr=0x1139998`) ->
callsite 17 (immediately after both memcpy operations complete --
`handle=0`, `buffer_size=0`, `ring_ptr=0`, all zeroed)**. Nothing else runs
between callsite 16 and 17 except the two copies themselves
(`recomp_0001.c:68725-68739`).

**The exact mechanism (byte-verified against `default.xbe` via Capstone,
`tools/debug/verify_40909_capstone.py`, guest `0x40909`-`0x40992` --
matches the generated C exactly, instruction for instruction, confirming
this is NOT a recompiler mistranslation):**
```
loc_0004087B: ecx = ring_buffer_size - cursor            ; "remaining contiguous space"
              edx = 0x4000                               ; fixed constant
              if (remaining >= record_length) goto loc_00040909  ; enough room, no wrap needed
              ... (only reached when remaining < record_length, i.e. a genuine
                   wraparound: the next record does not fit before the
                   buffer's physical end) ...
loc_00040942: esi = cursor_after_headers + ring_buffer_base       ; copy source
              edi = ring_buffer_base - remaining + 0x4000         ; copy DESTINATION
              memcpy(edi, esi, remaining);                        ; relocate the tail
```
`edi`'s destination formula, `ring_buffer_base - remaining + 0x4000`, is
only within the allocation when `remaining <= 0x4000`. If the record that
triggered the wraparound check declares a length greater than `0x4000`
while `remaining` (the actual leftover contiguous space) is *also* greater
than `0x4000`, `edi` computes to an address **before** the ring buffer's own
allocation -- directly underflowing into the ~0x4070-byte gap that
separates this buffer (`0x1139998`) from the owning subobject's own header
(`0x1135928`), exactly the region whose zeroing this entire investigation
(Updates 109-212) has been chasing since Update 190. The `memcpy` (a
`rep movsd`/`rep movsb` pair copying `remaining` bytes) then overwrites
that region with data read from the disc buffer -- appearing as "zeroed"
whenever the source bytes at that offset happen to be zero, which is common
for un-filled buffer tail space (consistent with `scda_disc_zero_short_read_tail`
elsewhere legitimately zeroing unread tail bytes, Update 186).

**This is present, byte-for-byte, in the original Xbox binary -- not a
scda_recomp bug.** Whether it is a genuine original-game edge case (only
triggered by a specific, rare combination of record length and buffer
cursor position that this recompiled environment's disc-image content
happens to reach, where real hardware or the retail disc's actual byte
stream may not) or a design assumption the original code makes that this
project's virtual disc/ISO content violates is the one remaining open
question -- but the corruption mechanism itself is now fully understood, to
the instruction.

**Model tier:** the technical mystery this whole arc was chasing is closed.
Remaining work is classification (game-data-dependent edge case vs. a
real ship bug vs. an XBE/ISO content difference from a retail disc), not
further reverse-engineering of unknown mechanisms.

MODEL STATUS: DE-ESCALATION RECOMMENDED
Tier: STRONG
Reason: the root cause is now fully identified and byte-verified against the
original binary; what remains is confirming the runtime values (the actual
record length and remaining-space numbers that trigger the underflow) and
deciding on a fix strategy, both more mechanical than the open-ended
reverse-engineering this investigation required through Update 212.

**Next test (for STRONG):**
1. Capture the actual runtime values of `ecx` (remaining space) and `esi`
   (record length) at the branch (`loc_00040940`, `jae 0x409a9`) for the
   fatal iteration, using the same ring-buffer technique, to confirm the
   exact numbers that trigger the underflow (expected: `esi > 0x4000` and
   `ecx` also `> 0x4000` but `< esi`).
2. Decide a fix: either (a) special-case the destination computation so it
   never underflows below `ring_buffer_base` regardless of `remaining`
   (defensive clamp -- changes recompiled behavior, needs a decision on
   whether that is in scope), or (b) determine why this project's disc
   content produces a record length that the original game apparently never
   encountered on real hardware/the retail disc (data-content root cause,
   fixed by correcting the served file content instead of the code).
3. Once resolved, revert ALL temporary `SCDA-DISC-ERR-INSTRUMENTATION`
   markers (seventeen callsites across `recomp_0001.c`/`recomp_0002.c`, the
   ring-buffer block in `recomp_manual.c`, and the three macro checks in
   `recomp_types.h`) per the standing instruction that this instrumentation
   must not remain as a permanent fix.

**Instrumentation status:** four more temporary checkpoints (13, 14, 16, 17)
added this round, ring buffer enlarged from 8 to 24 entries
(`SCDA_DISC_ERR_RING_SIZE`, `recomp_manual.c`). All still diagnostic only.

```
this=0x01135928 databuf=0x01139998 buffer_size=0x00024000
source=0x0113D999 destination=0x0111D999 copy_length=0x0001FFFF
remaining_space=0x0001FFFF record_length=0x7E000000 header_field_a=0x00000000
```

  and traced it to `common.lin`'s 15th chunk read live via cdb -- a short
  read of 89,969 bytes after 14 full 128 KiB (`0x20000`) chunks
  (`14 * 0x20000 = 0x1C0000`, exactly the offset found above independently

  recompiler bug** (independently re-confirmed by this session in Update
  213).
- Update 173 found the root mechanism: the write-cursor-advance formula at
  `loc_00040992` (`wpos = 0x4000 - remaining_space_before_read`) **never
  reads the actual transferred byte count** -- it always assumes the full
  requested chunk (`0x20000`) was delivered, regardless of what
  `IoStatusBlock->Information` actually reports. On a genuine short read,
  ~41 KiB of never-actually-written buffer space gets marked "valid"
  anyway, and the next record-header parse reads garbage from that
  region.
- Update 185 did the exact xemu ground-truth comparison this round's
  instruction asked for, already: `tools/debug/xemu_object_refill_wantgot.py`
  confirmed real hardware receives this **exact same short read**
  (`want=0x00020000 got=0x00015F71`, byte-identical to recomp) at the same
  object/position -- but afterward, real hardware issues **no further
  `sub_000516B7` calls for this stream at all**; it stops cleanly. No
  crash on real hardware.
- Update 186 fixed the dishonest byte-count reporting (`scda_disc_fill_overrun`,
  which used to pad a short read up to the full requested size) with
  `scda_disc_zero_short_read_tail` (`src/kernel/kernel_file.c`, still
  present, unchanged, and independently re-read by this session earlier in
  Update 212's now-superseded native-code detour): report the true byte
  count, defensively zero only the unwritten tail. This is confirmed
  active in the current build and produces the clean `0x00000000...` zero
  run this session found at the start of the captured `source` bytes today.
- Even with that fix, Update 186 found the SAME fatal callback still fires,
  via what looked at the time like a corrupted-handle `NtReadFile` call
  one step later, and left it explicitly open ("noch nicht auf Zeilenebene
  isoliert"). **Today's Update 213/214 is that missing isolation**: the
  zero-fill fix stops the corruption from writing plausible-looking garbage
  (like the `0xE1F9F6F3` handle Update 171 originally saw) into the
  object's header, but does not stop the underlying mechanism -- the code
  still tries to parse a record header from the (now cleanly zeroed, but
  still logically bogus) unconsumed tail, the `record_length` it reads is
  still nonsense (now shaped by adjacent stale ring-buffer content instead
  of by `scda_disc_fill_overrun`'s old padding), and the same underflowing
  `memcpy` still fires, still zeroing the object's own header fields
  (`+0x3C` handle, `+0x4058` size, `+0x405C` buffer pointer) -- which is
  exactly the "0x8070 zeroing" this entire Update-190-213 arc has been
  chasing under a different name.

**Directly answering this round's specific questions:**
- **Does `record_length` come directly from `common.lin`?** Yes and no --
  it is read from the exact buffer position that maps to `common.lin`
  byte offset `0x1C0000` and just past it, but that position is PAST the
  file's real 89,969-byte final chunk. What is actually parsed there is a
  handful of legitimately-zeroed defensive-padding bytes (Update 186's own
  fix) immediately followed by one stale, leftover byte (`0x7E`) from
  whatever a PREVIOUS, unrelated read cycle left in that same
  reused ring-buffer slot -- not real `common.lin` content at all. The
  `record_length` field is therefore a mis-parse of padding-plus-stale-data,
  not a genuine value ever present in `common.lin` on disk.
- **Does `remaining_space` come from ring-buffer bookkeeping?** Yes,
  confirmed exactly: `remaining_space = buffer_total_size(0x24000) -
  cursor_after_consuming_the_8-byte_header(0x4001) = 0x1FFFF`, both fields
  read directly from the subobject's own persistent bookkeeping fields
  (`+0x4058`, `+0x4060`), matching the code byte-for-byte.
- **Byte comparison against another SCDA copy:** not needed as a separate
  step -- Update 173 already did the equivalent comparison against a real
  retail ISO (`SC4_xbe_hack/output/scda_graphics_fixes_30fps.iso`, common.lin
  located at ISO offset `0x24F22000`, full 1,924,977-byte match confirmed).
  The bytes on the real disc immediately after common.lin's declared end
  are themselves real, deterministic XISO directory-table content (not
  padding) -- but that fact turned out not to be why real hardware
  survives (see below); Update 185 later established real hardware also
  sees a clean short read at this exact point, not a continuation into
  directory bytes.
- **Targeted xemu comparison (record length, remaining space, cursor, file
  offset, destination address):** already done, in Update 185, for the
  short read itself (want/got byte-identical). Real hardware does NOT
  reach the compaction memcpy at all for this stream afterward -- so there
  is no xemu "record_length"/"destination address" to compare at that
  deeper point; the divergence happens one level up, in whatever decides
  whether to call `sub_00040821`/`sub_000516B7` again after this short
  read completes.
- **Does the pre-object region belong to a larger parent/arena
  allocation?** This branch of the instruction was conditioned on "falls
  xemu dieselben Eingangswerte und dieselbe Zieladresse zeigt" -- it does
  not, per Update 185 (xemu never reaches this memcpy for this stream at
  all), so this question does not apply and was not pursued further this
  round.

**What is still genuinely unexplained (the real remaining question):** why
does the recompiled build issue another `sub_00040821`/`sub_000516B7` call
for this stream after the short read, when real hardware does not? Both
the short-read byte counts (Update 185) and `sub_00040821`'s own translated
code (Updates 171/213, byte-verified) are identical to the original XBE.
The write-cursor-advance formula at `loc_00040992` runs unconditionally
regardless of `sub_000516B7`'s return status (success or failure both reach
it), so a plain "return STATUS_END_OF_FILE instead of STATUS_SUCCESS for a
short-but-nonzero read" fix in `xbox_NtReadFile` would not, by itself,
prevent the bad cursor advance -- the divergence must be in whatever
higher-level code decides to loop back for more data at all, which has not
been located yet.

**No patch implemented this round, per explicit instruction** -- the
underflow's mechanism was already understood (Update 213) and is now fully

## Update 215 (2026-09-21): sub_000516B7 fully re-read end to end; the buggy cursor-advance formula is pinned to one exact line, proven structurally incapable of using the true byte count even with Update 186's honest-report kernel fix already active -- this is why the fix from four days earlier never fully closed the bug

**Goal this round:** finish tracing which of `sub_00040821`'s two
`sub_000516B7` call sites is the actual short read of `common.lin`'s last
chunk (Update 214 identified the file/offset but not which call), and
explain precisely why Update 186's already-active, already-verified
kernel-side fix (honest byte-count reporting) does not fully prevent the
corruption Update 213/214 traced.

**Full re-read of `sub_00040821`'s relevant span (`recomp_0001.c:68565-68790`,
guest `0x40821`-`0x40992`) in one pass, replacing several partial/wrong
assumptions from earlier updates this session:**
- `loc_0004087B` computes `remaining_to_buffer_end = buffer_size -
  cursor`. If `remaining_to_buffer_end >= 8` (room for a full record
  header), control goes straight to `loc_00040909` (no call yet). If it is
  `< 8`, control falls into `loc_0004089A`, which does a SEPARATE, smaller
  compaction (relocating the `<8` leftover bytes), then issues **call site
  1** (`sub_000516B7`, return address `0x000408E1`) to refill.
- **Call site 1 (`0x408E1`) is the one that actually performs `common.lin`'s
  final, short (89,969-byte) read** -- confirmed by the arithmetic: the
  buggy formula below produces exactly the `read_cursor=0x4001` this
  session captured in Updates 213/214 only if the pre-read
  `remaining_to_buffer_end` was `7`, and `0x4000 - 7 = 0x3FF9`, matching
  `0x4001 - 8` (the two 4-byte header fields consumed at `loc_00040909`
  land exactly on the captured cursor).
- At `loc_000408E1` (call site 1's return), `sub_00040821` does
  `test eax,eax; jne loc_000408F0` -- skipping the "chunk consumed"
  callback check/dispatch entirely whenever `eax != 0`. A full read of
  `sub_000516B7`'s own body (`recomp_0002.c:45924-46153`, all 100
  instructions, not just the fragment read in Updates 211/212) shows it has
  **two distinct return paths with different `eax` values**: an immediate,
  fully-synchronous completion returns `eax=1` via `loc_00051720`; a
  path that goes through the generic kernel-bridge wrapper
  `sub_00052A85` (used for anything that was `STATUS_PENDING` or is being
  relayed via `GetLastError`) returns `eax=0` via `loc_0005179B`. Since our
  host `ReadFile` is synchronous, a short-but-nonzero read completes
  immediately and returns `eax=1` -- which `sub_00040821` treats as
  "skip the callback", not as an error. This explains why no fatal
  dispatch happens right at call site 1: it is not reached, by design, for
  a plain synchronous completion (the callback exists to signal
  asynchronous completions specifically), not because anything is wrong
  with this particular check.
- **The actual bug, confirmed at the exact line, is unconditional and
  independent of the `eax` branch above:** both the `eax!=0` (skip) and
  `eax==0` (callback-checked) paths converge at `loc_000408F0`, which
  unconditionally executes:
  ```
  eax = MEM32(ebp-4);              // the TRUE number of bytes sub_000516B7 actually
                                    // wrote to the caller's out-param -- available right here
  MEM32(ebx+0x4064) += eax;        // correctly uses it for this running total
  eax = 0x4000 - MEM32(ebp-12);    // MEM32(ebp-12) is remaining_to_buffer_end computed
                                    // BEFORE the read, at loc_0004087B -- stale, and never
                                    // updated with the real transferred count
  MEM32(ebx+0x4060) = eax;         // ... but THIS -- the actual read/write cursor --
                                    // uses the stale pre-read value instead
  ```
  The real byte count is sitting in a register one line above and is
  simply never used for the cursor. This is line-for-line the same defect
  Update 173 already diagnosed on 2026-09-17 ("Diese Formel beruecksichtigt
  an KEINER Stelle die tatsaechlich gelesene Bytezahl"), now confirmed at
  the exact current source line with a concrete, real, captured instance.

**Why Update 186's already-active fix does not close this:** `scda_disc_zero_short_read_tail`
(`src/kernel/kernel_file.c`, unchanged, still active) makes `xbox_NtReadFile`
report the HONEST transferred byte count via `IoStatusBlock->Information`
-- and that honest count does reach the guest as `MEM32(ebp-4)` at
`loc_000408F0`. But the cursor-advance formula structurally never reads
`MEM32(ebp-4)` for the cursor -- only for the unrelated `+0x4064`
accumulator. No amount of honesty in the kernel's reported byte count can
fix a formula that does not consult it. This is a genuine defect in the
original, shipped game code (confirmed byte-identical to the retail XBE,
Updates 171/213) -- not something fixable by adjusting kernel-bridge
NTSTATUS/byte-count semantics, and not a recompiler bug.

**The one remaining open question, precisely scoped:** Update 185 already
proved real hardware receives the *identical* short read
(`want=0x20000 got=0x15F71`) at this exact point, via `xemu`. If real
hardware runs the same buggy formula (byte-identical code) and does not
crash, the only way to reconcile that is if the INPUT to the formula
(`MEM32(ebp-12)`, i.e. `remaining_to_buffer_end` computed one call earlier,
before call site 1 even fires) differs between real hardware and recomp at
the moment call site 1 is issued -- e.g. if real hardware's cursor happens
to sit exactly at a multiple of the chunk size when it reaches this stream
final read (`remaining_to_buffer_end == 0`), the buggy formula degenerates
to `cursor = 0x4000 - 0 = 0x4000` exactly, landing precisely on the
boundary where fresh (real, non-garbage) data begins -- avoiding the
mis-parsed record header entirely, by accident rather than by a real fix.
This has NOT been confirmed live and is the next concrete thing to check.

**No patch implemented, per explicit standing instruction for this round.**
The mechanism is now understood at the exact line level and reconciled
with the four-days-earlier Update 171-186 investigation; what remains is
confirming, via `xemu`, whether `remaining_to_buffer_end` differs from
recomp's `7` at the moment call site 1 fires for `common.lin`'s final
chunk, which would explain the real/recomp divergence without requiring
any code to be wrong beyond the (real, but hardware-invisible) cursor
formula defect.

**Next test (for STRONG):**
1. Extend `tools/debug/xemu_object_refill_wantgot.py` (Update 185, still
   present and directly reusable) to additionally read `MEM32(ebx+0x4058)`

2. Compare against recomp's own value (`7`, already known from this

3. Only after that: choose and implement the fix, verify, then revert all

fragments) plus a matching recomp-side capture (new callsite 18,

immediately before call site 2, mirroring exactly what the xemu script

This means the actual `common.lin`-exhausting short read on **recomp** most
likely happens via **call site 1**, while on **xemu** the byte-identical

stream while real hardware does not" remain live, and they call for three

## Update 217 (2026-09-21): Located the actual caller/loop that drives sub_00040821 -- no terminator tag anywhere, confirms explanation 2, but also finds the ring buffer is stack-allocated (alloca) and surfaces a concrete, testable unified hypothesis combining explanations 2 and 3

**Task followed:** continue Update 216's own next step (read `sub_0007DE25`,
`sub_0007F412`, `sub_00064B00` for terminator/tag logic). Read `sub_0007DE25`
in full immediately; before investing in the other two (714 and 656 lines),
pivoted to a more direct method -- grep the whole generated output for every
call site that targets `sub_00040821` and read its actual, real caller
first, since that is guaranteed to contain whatever governs the read loop,
rather than continuing to guess among Update 177's three candidates.

**`sub_0007DE25` ruled out:** full read (98 lines) shows a small, generic
vtable-dispatch object-teardown routine -- releases three sub-objects via
indirect calls through `MEM32(eax+0x20)`, conditionally calls `sub_00036582`,
and touches refcount-shaped fields at `+0x14/+0x18/+0x1C`. Not terminator
logic in any form.

**The real caller found: `sub_00042F00`/`sub_000430A5`.** Both of
`sub_00040821`'s call sites (`recomp_0001.c:80465` and `:80760`) return to
the same label `0x431C9`, and both live inside one logical function split
across two `void sub_...(void)` blocks at the C level (`sub_000430A5` is
marked `frameless: inherit caller's frame` -- it is a fallthrough/jump
target of `sub_00042F00`, not an independent call). This function is the
resource loader that opens the file, sets up the ring-buffer object, and
runs a loop that calls `sub_00040821` (refill) then `sub_000517A4`
(parse/consume) repeatedly.

**New, unexpected finding: the ring-buffer object is not a heap/arena
allocation at all -- it is `alloca`'d directly on this loader function's own
stack frame.** At the very top of `sub_00042F00`: `eax = 0x40B0; call
sub_00365C30;` -- `0x40B0` = 16560 decimal, and every later reference to the
ring-buffer object inside this function uses `ecx = ebp + -16560` as its
`this` pointer. `sub_00365C30` is called with the reservation size in `eax`
before any of the object's own field writes, matching the standard
MSVC `_alloca_probe`/`_chkstk` calling convention exactly. This means the
question this round's original instructions posed ("does the region before
the object belong to a larger parent/arena allocation") has a concrete
answer for this specific object: there is no heap arena involved here at
all -- "before the object" (in the underflow direction) means lower
addresses within this same loader function's own stack frame, i.e. its own
other locals and, past the alloca's base, its saved `ebx/esi/edi` and
eventually its own caller's frame.

**The actual read/parse loop, fully read (`recomp_0001.c:80746-80793`):**

```
loc_000431AE:
    ebx = min(MEM32(ebp-8), edi)      // edi = 0x1000 fixed chunk size
    MEM32(ebp-8) -= ebx
    call sub_00040821(this=ebp-16560, ..., ebx, MEM32(ebp+8))   // refill
loc_000431C9:
    call sub_000517A4(...)             // consume/parse
loc_000431DA:
    if (MEM32(ebp-8) != 0) goto loc_000431AE;   // loop while remaining != 0
```

This is a plain, unconditional byte-counted loop. There is no tag or
terminator comparison anywhere in it -- it runs until `MEM32(ebp-8)` reaches
zero, full stop. This directly confirms explanation 2 from Update 216 in
concrete form, one level higher than `sub_00040821` itself, and makes it
very unlikely that `sub_0007F412`/`sub_00064B00` (not yet fully read, but
already recognized to be a large constructor and a file-open/path-format
routine respectively based on partial reads) contain a terminator check
either -- they sit even further from this loop, not inside it.

**Where `MEM32(ebp-8)` (the loop's total) comes from -- fully traced:**
immediately before the loop, `sub_000430A5` does, in order: `SetFilePointer
(handle, -4, NULL, FILE_END)` (seek to 4 bytes before the file's true
physical end) -> `sub_000516B7(handle, &MEM32(ebp-8), length=4, &bytesRead)`
(a genuine disc read of exactly 4 bytes into `MEM32(ebp-8)`, checked
`bytesRead==4`) -> `SetFilePointer(handle, 0, NULL, FILE_BEGIN)` (seek back
to the start). **`MEM32(ebp-8)` is therefore the file's own embedded 4-byte
trailer value, read directly from `common.lin`'s last 4 bytes, and used
unconditionally as the total byte budget for the entire loop.**

**A second, independent size value exists alongside it.** Right after the
seek-back, the same function also calls `sub_00051B8B` -> `sub_00051B4D`,
which is a genuine `NtQueryInformationFile` wrapper: args match exactly
(`FileHandle`, `IoStatusBlock=ebp-8`, `FileInformation=ebp-64`,
`Length=0x38`, `FileInformationClass=0x22` = `FileNetworkOpenInformation`),
and the two dwords copied out (`MEM32(ebp-64+40)`/`+44`) land exactly at
that structure's `EndOfFile` field offset (0x28). This is a **live, genuine
query of the file's real physical size**, not a derived or cached value.
`(PhysicalSize - 4)` is then passed into `sub_00040766(this=ring_buffer_obj,
0, 0, PhysicalSize-4)` -- almost certainly telling the ring buffer object
how many bytes are actually available to it on disk, independent of what
the outer loop's trailer-derived counter says it should still ask for.

**Checked `kernel_file.c`'s own `NtQueryInformationFile` implementation for
a static bug -- found none.** Both the Windows path (`GetFileInformationByHandle`,
`recomp`'s `xbox_NtQueryInformationFile` around line 575/587) and the POSIX
path (`stat()`, around line 1164/1170) perform a genuine, live query against
the actually-open host file handle for `FileNetworkOpenInformation`'s
`EndOfFile`, with no hardcoded or derived value. This rules out a trivial
"wrong constant" bug in our own kernel bridge for this specific call.

**Checked the physical byte count of every `common.lin` copy on disk --
all match retail exactly.** All three build output trees
(`build/scda/bin/{Release,RelWithDebInfo}`, `build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo`)
report `Default/DataXb/LMaps/common.lin` at exactly 1,924,977 bytes, matching
the retail ISO extraction (`SC4_debug_compare/unpacked iso/Retail/...`)
byte-for-byte, consistent with Update 173's already-established full-content
match. (Aside: a completely unrelated, much larger `adv/System/common.lin`,
7,758,556 bytes, also exists in the disc tree -- different file, same
name/extension, not relevant here. A separate "proto" extraction under
`SC4_debug_compare` has a *different-sized* `LMaps/common.lin`, 1,922,128
bytes -- almost certainly an unrelated prototype/beta build artifact, not
used by any of our build outputs, noted only so it is not mistaken for a
live discrepancy later.) This rules out the naive "recomp is reading a
wrong-sized file" explanation -- our file is the correct, retail-matching
one on every build output checked.

**Refined, unified hypothesis (not yet confirmed empirically):** since the
file's own trailer value (`MEM32(ebp-8)`'s initial value) is read directly
from file bytes already proven byte-identical to retail, it must be
numerically identical on recomp and on real hardware -- both platforms start
this loop with the exact same total budget. Update 185/216 already showed
xemu experiences the *same* short read (`want=0x20000 got=0x15F71`) that
recomp does. The concrete difference established in Update 216 is only that
xemu issues *no further* `sub_000516B7` calls afterward while recomp does.
Combining this with what was found this round: **if real hardware's outer
loop counter (`MEM32(ebp-8)`) happens to reach exactly zero at the same
iteration where this short read occurs, the loop exits cleanly on its own
before ever asking `sub_00040821` for one more refill -- and the already-
confirmed cursor-formula defect (Update 215, explanation 3) never gets
exercised, because nothing calls into it again.** If recomp's own count of
"effective bytes consumed per iteration" differs even slightly (plausible,
given Update 216 already found recomp and xemu land the equivalent cycle on
different internal call sites of `sub_00040821`), recomp's counter would
still be nonzero after the same short read, causing the loop to call
`sub_00040821` one more time -- which is exactly the call that walks into
the already-corrupted/stale ring-buffer state and triggers the compaction
memcpy. This would mean explanations 2 and 3 are not competing alternatives
but two halves of one mechanism: no terminator check exists (2), and the
long-latent, byte-identical-since-the-original-XBE cursor defect (3) is
harmless as long as the outer trailer-driven loop never asks for a refill
after a short read -- which is a matter of exact byte-accounting parity
between the two platforms' loop iterations, not of either platform having
different code.

**Not yet done -- concrete next test:** capture, on a live recomp run, the
value of `MEM32(ebp_outer - 8)` (the outer loop's remaining-byte counter,
reachable from the existing corrupting-memcpy capture point as
`MEM32(ebx_object_this + 0x40B0 - 8)`, since `ebp_outer = this + 0x40B0`)
at the exact moment the ring-buffer object gets corrupted, to see whether it
is already zero (loop should have stopped -- points to a different bug) or
still nonzero (confirms the unified hypothesis above). This requires one
new, small, one-shot capture (not yet added) rather than reusing anything
already reverted.

**No fix implemented this round either** -- per the standing instruction,
still clarifying. **Model tier:** STRONG remains appropriate; the next step
is one bounded, well-specified memory read added to a single known location.

## Update 218 (2026-09-21): Live capture REFUTES Update 217's own unified hypothesis -- the outer loop's counter is already zero at the moment of corruption, meaning this is the loop's normal, expected final iteration, not an extra one; also discovered genuine run-to-run nondeterminism in which stream trips the pre-existing sub_0003FCA5 freeze first

**Task followed:** Update 217 proposed a specific, falsifiable hypothesis
(the outer loop in `sub_000430A5` calls `sub_00040821` one extra,
unnecessary time after a short read because its own byte counter has not
yet reached zero) and named the exact next test: capture
`MEM32(object_this + 0x40B0 - 8)` (the outer loop's own remaining-byte
counter, reachable from inside `sub_00040821` since `ebp_outer = this +
0x40B0`) at the moment of the known corrupting compaction. Implemented this
as a new, minimal, one-shot capture (`SCDA-DIAG-217` marker, gated on
`vtable==0x4F6940 && remaining_space>0x4000`, guarded to fire at most once)
directly in `recomp_0001.c` at `loc_00040942` (both textual occurrences,
`sub_00040821` and its duplicate `sub_0004086E`), rebuilt, ran.

**Result -- the hypothesis is REFUTED:**

```
SCDA-DIAG217 this=01135928 vtable=004F6940 bufsize=00024000 cursor=00004001
             remaining_space=0001FFFF outer_ebp=011399D8 outer_remaining=00000000
```

`outer_remaining=00000000`. The outer loop's own counter is *already zero*
at the exact moment the dangerous compaction fires. Given the loop
structure found in Update 217 (`ebx = min(remaining, 0x1000); remaining -=
ebx; call sub_00040821(...); call sub_000517A4(...); if (remaining != 0)
goto loop;`), a counter of exactly zero *entering* the call to
`sub_00040821` means this is not an extra, erroneous iteration -- it is the
loop's normal, final iteration, consuming the last (possibly partial)
`<=0x1000`-byte unit before the loop's own `!= 0` check would exit it. The
loop cannot skip this call; real hardware must make the exact same final
call, since the code is byte-identical. This rules out "the outer loop
asks for one call too many" as an explanation on its own.

**Refined mechanistic understanding.** `cursor=00004001` is itself highly
suspicious: it is exactly what the already-known buggy formula from Update
215 (`MEM32(ebx+0x4060) = 0x4000 - MEM32(ebp-12)`) would produce if the
"stale, pre-read remaining space" input were `0xFFFFFFFF` (-1), since
`0x4000 - (-1) = 0x4001` under 32-bit wraparound. This means the garbage
cursor value was almost certainly written by the *previous* invocation's
own execution of the exact defect Update 215 already found and byte-verified
against the original XBE -- and that garbage cursor is what then makes
`remaining_space = bufsize - cursor = 0x24000 - 0x4001 = 0x1FFFF` compute
as a huge, dangerous number on this, the very next visit to the compaction
path. Under this reading, **the cursor-formula defect (Update 215,
explanation 3) is independently sufficient to explain the corruption on
this exact, ordinary final loop iteration -- no terminator/tag question and
no outer-loop-iteration-count discrepancy (Update 217's own hypothesis) are
needed as additional mechanisms.** The remaining open question narrows
further, cleanly, to: why does the *previous* invocation's short read
produce a "stale" input of exactly -1 (or something that maps to a
dangerous cursor) on recomp, while the analogous moment on real hardware
apparently does not.

**Attempted a direct follow-up capture, could not complete it --
discovered a new, important environmental fact instead.** To verify the
"stale value = -1" arithmetic directly, added a second one-shot capture
(`SCDA-DIAG-218`) at `loc_00040992` (the line that writes the cursor),
logging every update for the specific object address `0x01135928` seen
above. Two things went wrong in sequence, and untangling them produced a
useful new finding:
1. First suspected the new capture itself caused a hang (two long,
   silent, 100%-CPU-pegged runs in a row with the new code present, after
   two earlier runs with only the first capture had returned quickly).
   Reverted the second capture and reran to isolate it.
2. The *same* silent, CPU-pegged behavviour then reappeared with only the
   already-proven first capture in place, ruling out the second capture as
   the cause. A live, non-invasive snapshot (`cdb -pv -p <pid> -c "r eip;
   kb 3; q"`, the exact safe method Update 210 already established) on a
   run that had been silently pegging one core for 64+ minutes showed the
   process was **not stuck or slow -- it had already reached the same
   pre-existing, long-documented terminal freeze from Update 210**
   (`jmp $` self-loop at `sub_0003FCA5+0x17b0`, reached this time via a
   *different* call into `sub_00040821+0x11cd`, i.e. a different streamed
   resource than the `common.lin` one this round's instrumentation is
   watching). Update 210 itself already saw the identical symptom once
   (36 minutes of silence before an equivalent snapshot found the same
   frozen state) and characterized it as normal variance, not a hang.

**New finding: which stream trips the pre-existing `sub_0003FCA5` freeze
first is not deterministic run-to-run**, even though the guest addresses
and computed values *within* a given stream's own processing are highly
reproducible (the exact same `this=0x01135928` recurred across multiple,
independently-launched runs this session). This is consistent with
`sub_000516B7`'s underlying disc I/O being asynchronous (`STATUS_PENDING`
/ callback-completion, per Update 213's own reading) -- real OS-level I/O
completion ordering can vary run to run even for single-threaded-looking
guest code, so whichever unrelated stream happens to reach the fatal
`MEM32(0x5E6E0C)` callback path first can differ between otherwise
identical launches. Two of four total runs this round reached the
`common.lin` diagnostic point productively; the other two happened to
freeze on a different stream first and never reached it. This is a useful,
durable environmental fact for future debugging of this whole area: a
single non-responsive run is not evidence of a regression by itself, and a
live `cdb -pv` snapshot (never a kill) is the correct, low-cost way to
distinguish "still progressing" from "already at the known terminal
freeze" before deciding whether to wait longer or restart.

**Housekeeping:** both one-shot captures (`SCDA-DIAG-217`, the never-
completed `SCDA-DIAG-218`, and the `#include <stdio.h>` they needed) have
been fully removed from `recomp_0001.c` again, verified via grep (zero

**No fix implemented.** The root cause is now understood one level more
precisely than Update 217 left it: the cursor-formula defect from Update
215 is very likely sufficient by itself to explain the corruption on this
stream's own final loop iteration, without needing an additional
outer-loop-iteration-count mismatch. What remains open is *why* the
previous invocation's short read produces a dangerous stale input on
recomp specifically -- this has not yet been captured directly (the

**Next test:** retry the `SCDA-DIAG-218`-style capture (full sequence of
cursor-formula updates for the specific object, not just the final one),
accepting that it may take 2-4 attempts due to the newly-understood

**Model tier:** STRONG remains appropriate -- this is a bounded, well-
specified capture task with an understood, characterized source of run
