## Update 220 (2026-09-21): Chain directly confirmed with exact numbers -- CORRECTS the stale==-1 guess to stale==7 (a legitimate value); true defect isolated to a hardcoded 0x4000 assumption instead of the already-available real transfer count; minimal register-liveness-safe fix implemented and verified to change runtime behavior (process now progresses past the old freeze into new territory)

**Task followed:** per explicit instruction, confirm the chain
`stale_value -> cursor formula -> remaining_space -> memcpy underflow`
directly, using minimal one-shot instrumentation with a host-side success
marker, fresh processes per attempt, max ~3 minute bounded waits, a single
`cdb` snapshot instead of long silent waits, and immediate restart if a run
is found already stuck in the known unrelated `sub_0003FCA5` freeze on a
different stream. Once confirmed, trace `stale_value`'s origin or determine
the correct fix; no clamp on cursor/remaining_space until this is understood.

**Orchestration built and used exactly as specified**
(`tools/debug/diag219_orchestrate.sh`, kept as a reusable tool): launches a
fresh `scda_recomp.exe`, polls for a marker file every few seconds, takes
one `cdb -pv -p <pid> -c "r eip; kb 3; q"` snapshot after 180s if the marker
hasn't appeared, kills and retries immediately if that snapshot shows the
known `sub_0003FCA5` freeze, otherwise gives it one more slice. This
directly avoids repeating the long, blind waits from Update 218.

**First two gate attempts missed the target (both cheaply diagnosed, not
symptoms of a real problem):**
1. A first one-shot capture gated on the same condition already proven at
   the *corrupting* call site (`remaining_space>0x4000`) but placed at the
   cursor-formula site itself fired in 34s -- but on the *first, completely
   ordinary* cycle for this object, since `remaining_space>0x4000` turns out
   to be true on almost every normal cycle for this buffer shape
   (`bufsize=0x24000`, formula output always in `[0,0x4000]`), not a sign of
   anything wrong.
2. Tightening the gate to `stale>0x4000` (expecting a wrapped/negative-
   looking sentinel) never fired across 8 fresh attempts in a row -- all 8
   independently landed in the pre-existing, already-documented
   `sub_0003FCA5` freeze on a *different* stream before ever reaching this
   one. Diagnosed via the orchestration's own `cdb` snapshots (each showed
   `sub_0003FCA5+0x17b0`'s `jmp $`, reached through a *different*
   `sub_00040821` call site than the one this instrumentation was watching)
   -- confirms Update 218's own finding about freeze-order nondeterminism,
   not a flaw in the new instrumentation.

**Final, successful design: reuse the already-proven trigger, not a new
guess.** Rather than gate a *new* condition at the cursor-formula site,
added a small, cheap, unconditional ring buffer (4 entries) recording every
cursor-formula update for this object (no I/O on the hot path), and dumped
its contents only when `sub_00040821`'s already-validated dangerous-
compaction condition (the exact one Updates 217/218 relied on) fires. This
reliably reproduced in 36 seconds on the very first attempt -- twice.

**First successful capture (ring recorded only one of the formula's two
textual sites) showed a gap:** the ring's most recent entry
(`cursor_after=0x21DE`) did not match the corrupting call's own reading
(`cursor=0x4001`) -- a missing link. Root cause: Update 215 already noted
the formula exists at **two** separate textual locations
(`loc_000408F0`, following call site 1, and `loc_00040992`, following call
site 2); the first capture only instrumented the second. Added the same
cheap recorder to `loc_000408F0` too, reran -- **gapless result:**

```
SCDA-DIAG220 CORRUPTING-CALL this=01135928 bufsize=00024000 cursor=00004001 remaining_space=0001FFFF ring_count=4
SCDA-DIAG220 ring[3] this=01135928 stale=00000007 cursor_before=00023FF9 cursor_after=00003FF9
```

`cursor_after=0x3FF9` plus the two 4-byte record-header field reads at
`loc_00040909` (each advancing the cursor by 4, +8 total) lands exactly on
`0x3FF9 + 8 = 0x4001` -- matching the corrupting call's own reading
bit-for-bit. **The chain is now fully, numerically confirmed with no gaps:**
`stale=7 -> cursor=0x4000-7=0x3FF9 -> +8 (header parse) -> cursor=0x4001 ->
remaining_space=bufsize-cursor=0x1FFFF -> underflowing memcpy destination.`

**This corrects the standing `stale==-1` hypothesis from Update 217/218.**
`stale=7` is not a wrapped/garbage sentinel -- it is a small, entirely
plausible "bytes remaining before the ring buffer's physical end" value.
The actual defect is not in `stale` itself, but in how the formula uses it:
`new_cursor = 0x4000 - stale` is only correct if the read that just
completed transferred *exactly* 0x4000 bytes (the formula's implicit,
hardcoded assumption -- matching Update 215's own description, "never uses
the actual transferred count"). Critically, **the real transferred byte
count is already loaded into `eax` two lines earlier in the exact same
block** (`eax = MEM32(ebp+-4); MEM32(ebx+0x4064) += eax;`, used to update an
accumulator) -- the very next lines then needlessly discard it
(`eax = 0x4000;` at `loc_00040992`, or `edx = 0x4000; eax = edx;` at
`loc_000408F0`) before computing the new cursor from the wrong, fixed
constant instead.

**Fix implemented (not a clamp -- a correction using data already at
hand):** removed exactly the one instruction at each site that discards the
already-correct transferred count, so `eax` (already holding
`MEM32(ebp+-4)`) flows directly into `eax = eax - MEM32(ebp+-12)`.
One subtlety required care: at `loc_000408F0`, `edx = 0x4000` is *also*
needed, unchanged, further down by the compaction's own destination formula
(`edi = edi + edx` inside `loc_00040942`) -- that assignment was
deliberately left untouched; only the subsequent `eax = edx` copy (which
served no purpose other than discarding the transferred count) was removed.
At `loc_00040992` there is no such second use, so the corresponding
`eax = 0x4000` line was simply removed outright. Applied identically to
both textual occurrences of each site (the `sub_00040821`/`sub_0004086E`
duplication already established this session).

**Verified the fix changes runtime behavior, not just the formula in
isolation.** Rebuilt clean, ran a fresh instance with the same bounded-wait
discipline: after ~4 minutes the process was found (via `cdb` snapshot, not
a kill) executing in `sub_004A12B0`/`sub_004A1600`/`sub_004A1740` -- three
addresses never seen anywhere in this session's entire investigation --
with CPU usage around 16% (a real, low-overhead poll/wait loop, not the
~100%-pegged hard `jmp $` spin the old freeze always showed) and a stable,
unchanging call stack across a further 2-minute recheck. **The process no
longer reaches the old corruption/freeze point at all** -- it has genuinely
progressed further than any run has in this entire investigation arc, and
is now blocked on a new, later, previously-unreachable synchronization
point. This is the next blocker referred to in the standing instruction
sequence ("...weiter bis zum naechsten Blocker"), not yet investigated.

**Critical caveat, not yet resolved: this fix currently has no permanent
home.** `recomp_0001.c` is gitignored, generated output; a full pipeline
regenerate from the original XBE (the "vollstaendige Recomp-Pipeline" step
in the standing instruction sequence) would silently reproduce the
original, byte-identical-to-the-XBE buggy instructions and erase this fix
with no warning, since the lifter has no per-function override/patch

**Housekeeping:** all `SCDA-DIAG-219`/`SCDA-DIAG-220` diagnostic code has

loop as a separate next blocker.

**Native I/O audit, via a one-shot capture directly in `xbox_NtReadFile`

```
SCDA-DIAG221 #3 handle=0x290 requested=131072 transferred=0     offset=... filesize=1924977 ...
```

specified method (compare against xemu):** Updates 185/216 already
established, via live xemu ground truth on a **fresh boot, not a reused
log**, that real hardware experiences the *exact same* short read for this
exact stream: `want=0x20000 got=0x15F71` (0x15F71 = 89969, the identical
number). **xemu does not deliver 0x4000 while recomp delivers less -- both
platforms deliver the identical, much-larger-than-0x4000 short transfer.**
The round's own explicit fallback condition ("wenn xemu 0x4000 liefert und
Recomp weniger, behebe die I/O-Semantik") therefore does not apply: there
is no I/O-semantics discrepancy between the platforms to fix. Our kernel
bridge, the host filesystem, and commit e1b6823's honest-reporting change
are all confirmed correct and are not the cause. **The defect is
exclusively in the guest-side cursor formula's own hardcoded 0x4000
assumption** (Updates 215/220), which silently assumes every wrap-
triggering refill transfers exactly 0x4000 bytes when transfers routinely
run up to 0x20000 -- it happens to surface here specifically because this
particular wrap coincides with the stream's genuine, honestly-reported end
of data. This resolves the dimensional-soundness doubt raised above too:
using the real transferred count (however large) is not an arbitrary
substitution, it is restoring the one piece of already-available, always-
correct information (`eax`, loaded from `MEM32(ebp-4)` two lines earlier
for the accumulator update) that the original formula discarded in favor
of a constant that was never actually representative of the true transfer
size for this call.

## Update 222 (2026-09-21): New blocker diagnosed -- sub_004A12B0's poll loop spins forever waiting on a PFIFO/PGRAPH-style hardware completion bit through a D3D/NV2A device pointer that was never properly created, confirming and sharpening the pre-existing "no video backend wired in" gap

**Task followed:** per this round's own final instruction, investigate the
new `sub_004A12B0`/`sub_004A1600`/`sub_004A1740` poll loop as a separate
next blocker, checking first whether `recomp_manual.c`'s existing
`sub_00040A88` comment (an earlier, 2026-09-05/11 UMOD-reader investigation
that already mentions this same address) already covers it.

**Read `sub_004A12B0` (`recomp_0026.c:133445`, category `game_render`,
original 0x004A12B0-0x004A1360, 176 bytes/47 insns).** The live `cdb`
snapshots from Updates 220/221 (alternating `+0x1e8`/`+0x1d0`, a tight,
2-instruction self-loop in the compiled x64 output) match this exact
source location:

```
loc_004A12C9: ;
    eax = MEM32(0x4AB668);        // the known D3D/NV2A device pointer
    eax = MEM32(eax + 0x1C28);    // -> PFIFO/PGRAPH-style register block
    ecx = MEM32(eax + 0x100410);
    ecx = ecx | 0x10000;
    MEM32(eax + 0x100410) = ecx;  // set a "kick" bit

loc_004A12F0: ;
    if (TEST_NZ(MEM32(eax + 0x100410), 0x10000)) goto loc_004A12F0; // spin
```

This is a classic hardware register poll: set a control bit to kick off
some GPU operation (offset `0x100410` strongly resembles an NV2A
PFIFO/cache-control register by its shape), then spin waiting for the
hardware to clear it on completion.

**Confirmed live that the device pointer is not valid.** Read
`MEM32(0x4AB668)` on a fresh, live instance stuck in this exact loop (via
`cdb`, translating through `g_xbox_mem_offset`): **`0x7400087D`** -- an
address far outside this recompiler's 64MB guest RAM range
(`XBOX_TOTAL_RAM = 0x04000000`), meaning this is not a legitimate,
initialized guest heap pointer to a real device structure. Dereferencing it
(`+0x1C28`, then `+0x100410`) lands on whatever the guest-memory access
implementation resolves an out-of-range guest address to (not a crash --
the process is observed only spinning, at a stable ~16% CPU, never
faulting) -- almost certainly wrapped/masked into some unrelated region of
the 64MB guest RAM that has no reason to ever have its `0x10000` bit
cleared, since nothing in this recompiler emulates real NV2A/GPU hardware
completion for it.

**This is the concrete confirmation of an already-known gap, not a new,
unrelated bug.** Memory (this session's own standing notes, "SCDA no video
pipeline") already recorded: "D3D device (0x4AB668) never created and
scda_recomp has zero video backend wired in, so nothing can render yet;
next step is a cheap cdb reachability check, not more soak or an input
framework." This update *is* that reachability check, and the answer is
now definitive: after the Update 220/221 cursor-formula fix cleared the
earlier, unrelated `sub_00040821`/`sub_0003FCA5` corruption, the boot
sequence now progresses far enough to actually *try* to use the graphics
device for the first time -- and immediately hangs here, because there is
still no real device behind `0x4AB668` for it to talk to.

**`sub_00040A88`'s own comment does not cover this instance.** That
2026-09-05/11 investigation's mention of `sub_004A12B0` ("...why the whole
chain ... looks like it spins forever in sub_004A12B0...") was about a
completely different symptom -- an UMOD archive reader stuck re-parsing a
wildly wrong file-count due to a bad `Seek` position, which that fix
(the `sub_00040A88` override already in `recomp_manual.c`) already
resolved. This is a structurally different hang in the *same* function
(a real hardware-register poll with no backing device, not a software
parsing loop with a wrong iteration count) -- the earlier fix's presence
confirms the address is a recurring point of interest in this codebase,
not that it is already solved for this cause.

**Scope assessment, not started:** resolving this properly means wiring up
an actual NV2A/D3D device (creation of the `0x4AB668` structure, and at
minimum a stub PFIFO/PGRAPH register model that acknowledges kicks) --  a
substantial new subsystem, not a bounded bug fix, and squarely the
"no video backend wired in" milestone already flagged in memory rather
than a quick patch. No fix attempted this round; this is a diagnosis and
scope call, matching the "cheap reachability check" the standing memory
note asked for.

**Model tier:** the diagnosis itself was STRONG-appropriate (bounded,
confirmed via one live read). Actually implementing a video backend is a
different, much larger class of work and should get its own scoping
discussion before starting.

## Update 223 (2026-09-21): CORRECTION to Update 222 -- this is NOT a missing video backend, it is a real memory-corruption bug; live breakpoints prove device creation succeeds and the existing NV2A_ACK machinery is already sufficient, but MEM32(0x4AB668) gets overwritten with garbage between two good uses and a bad one

**Trigger:** user asked to start building a "minimal video backend stub" based on
Update 222's framing ("no video backend wired in"). Before writing any stub
code, checked `projects/scda/CMakeLists.txt`'s own extensive prior-session
history (2026-09-04 through 2026-09-11) on this exact `sub_004A12B0` address,
which Update 222 had not cross-referenced. That history flatly contradicts
the "missing backend" framing and explicitly warns against the exact kind of
fix a stub would be.

### What the prior sessions already established (missed by Update 222)

1. `src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c` already implements a working, generic
   NV2A acknowledgement mechanism: `NV2A_ACK[]` (a table of
   `{register_offset, busy_mask}` pairs serviced by a background
   `nv2a_ack_thread`) already contains `{0x100410, 0x00010000u}` -- comment:
   "PFB flush kick, Halo 0x001EF930" -- i.e. **the exact register
   `sub_004A12B0` polls is already handled**, added for a different title
   that hit the same hardware behavior.
2. A dedicated xemu ground-truth script
   (`tools/debug/xemu_004a12b0_devptr_check.py`, still present, reusable)
   already answered the "is this missing hardware emulation?" question for
   this exact spin: on real hardware, `MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x004AB670` (a valid
   device struct) and `struct+0x1C28 = 0xFD000000` (the real NV2A aperture
   base) **every single time**, ~500/500 hits. Real hardware's own PFB
   register is answered by real silicon; our `NV2A_ACK` table already
   reproduces that correctly once the pointer chain is valid.
3. That same investigation (docs, pre-"Update N" numbering, the "continued
   52" entry) found `scda_recomp` reaching the same spin with
   `MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x0C47C708` -- not zero, not the valid device pointer,
   a stray value aliasing into `.text` -- and concluded explicitly:
   **"forcing the device-pointer chain to a fake value here would be exactly
   the kind of workaround this project rules out."** The recommended next
   step, never completed, was to trace what writes garbage into `0x4AB668`
   on this specific call path.

This means Update 222's "no video backend wired in" framing, while true of
the *original* 2026-09-11 finding (`MEM32(0x4AB668)` read as `0` for an
entire 10-minute soak, before the cursor-formula fix), does not describe the
*current* situation at all: substantial NV2A bring-up work already exists
and was already found sufficient for this exact register in this exact
function, by a session that got further than Update 222 did.

### Live re-verification this round

Built a real (non-`-pv`, breakpoint-based) `cdb` session launching a fresh
`scda_recomp.exe` directly under the debugger (`cdb -cf <script>
scda_recomp.exe`, not `-pv -p <pid>` -- genuine breakpoints require owning
the debug session), with breakpoints at `scda_recomp!sub_0049D210` (device
creation) and `scda_recomp!sub_004A12B0` (the poll loop), each printing
`MEM32(0x4AB668)` (via guest-VA-to-host translation using this build's own
`0x0000700000000000` guest memory offset) and a short stack, then
auto-continuing (`g`).

Result, three hits in order:

1. `sub_0049D210` entry, called via `sub_002E2BB1 -> sub_002E75CE ->
   sub_0004934E` (the exact chain earlier "continued 38" xemu work
   identified as the real hardware device-creation trigger) -- device
   creation runs.
2. `sub_004A12B0`, called via `sub_004A13D0 -> sub_004A2220 ->
   sub_0049D210` (immediately following device creation):
   `MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x004AB670` -- **the correct, valid device pointer**,
   matching real hardware exactly and matching the literal constant
   `sub_0049D210` itself writes on success.
3. `sub_004A12B0` again, called via `sub_0049B0C0 -> sub_004A1740 ->
   sub_004A1600` (a different call path, further downstream):
   `MEM32(0x4AB668) = 0x7400087D` -- **the same garbage value Update 222**
   **captured**, now confirmed to appear *after* two confirmed-good reads,
   not from the start.

**Device creation is not the problem, and the existing NV2A acknowledgement
machinery is not the problem. Something overwrites a previously-valid
`0x4AB668` with garbage between hit #2 and hit #3.** This is a corruption
bug, structurally the same class as every other bug fixed this entire
session (the ring-buffer cursor formula, the disc-error trap, etc.) -- not
a new subsystem.

### First attempt to catch the write: inconclusive, not a dead end

Re-launched fresh under `cdb` with a hardware write breakpoint
(`ba w4 <host address of 0x4AB668>`) armed from process start. It correctly
fired once, on the same legitimate `sub_0049D210` write observed above
(value `0x004AB670`), proving the breakpoint and the address translation are
both correct. It did not fire a second time in two separate ~2-3 minute
observation windows, even though a follow-up non-invasive `cdb -pv` snapshot
on the same running process confirmed it had, by then, already reached the
corrupted spin (`sub_004A12B0+0x1e8`, stack showing `0x7400087D`). So the
corrupting change to that memory happened without tripping a 4-byte-aligned
write watchpoint on it -- consistent with this project's own prior
experience on this exact question (`continued 53`'s cdb hardware-watchpoint
attempts were also "defeated by tooling/environment issues rather than a
clean negative result"). Not yet resolved; candidate explanations to try
next: a wider/differently-aligned store that still overlaps those 4 bytes
but was set up before the breakpoint synced to a later-created thread, a
non-CPU-store write path (unlikely but not excluded), or simply needing a
longer observation window / multiple attempts given this project's
well-documented run-to-run non-determinism in thread scheduling.

### Explicit correction and recommendation

**Withdrawing Update 222's "needs a new video backend subsystem, scope with
user first" framing.** The right next step is the same kind of root-cause
hunt this whole session has already done successfully six times over: find
what writes into `0x4AB668` between the two confirmed calls above (most
likely another guest write through a miscomputed/stale pointer, given
`sub_0049D210`'s own three static writers were already ruled out by the
prior session's static grep). **Explicitly not recommended:** writing a
"video backend stub" that forces `0x4AB668` to a fake valid value -- this
was already tried in spirit and rejected by name in this exact codebase's
own history for this exact address, for good reason (it would hide the real
bug rather than fix it, and the existing `NV2A_ACK`/`nv2a_ack_thread`
machinery already proves no new hardware-emulation code is needed once the
pointer is valid).

### Process hygiene

Two temporary `cdb` command scripts used from the scratchpad directory only
(`cdb_devcreate_check.txt`, `cdb_write_watch_4ab668.txt`); no source files
touched this entry. Logs kept for reference:
`tools/debug/devcreate_check_out.log`,
`tools/debug/write_watch_4ab668_out.log`. `git diff --stat` confirms no
source changes. All `scda_recomp.exe`/`cdb.exe` instances killed at the end
of this entry.

## Update 224 (2026-09-21): Minimally-invasive GOOD->BAD bisection along the actually-executed path narrows the 0x4AB668 corruption to a specific row-copy loop inside sub_004AED5D; the loop's own destination range does not overlap 0x4AB668, no other thread is active at the moment of corruption, and a precisely-gated hardware write watchpoint still does not fire -- pointing at a host memory-aliasing gap rather than an ordinary guest store

**Method, per explicit instruction this round:** hierarchical, one-shot
checkpoint bisection along the real call path between the last confirmed
GOOD device-pointer read (right after `sub_0049D210` returns) and the
first confirmed BAD read (inside `sub_004A12B0`), reading only
`MEM32(0x4AB668)` (plus a few registers) at each checkpoint via live `cdb`
breakpoints -- no source-code instrumentation, no hot-path output, fresh
process per launch. Narrowed hierarchically:

```
sub_0004934E (icall +0x3263f, GOOD) -> sub_002E75CE -> sub_002E2BB1 ->
sub_0049D210 [[device creation succeeds, writes 0x004AB670]]
    ... (sub_0004934E's own body, ~60 generated-C lines, one candidate
         store at recomp_0002.c:8023-ish ruled out directly) ...
sub_0004934E (icall +0x34b3e, still GOOD right before) -> sub_00037274 ->
sub_002E5F95 -> sub_0049B0C0 [[BAD already at entry]]
```

Re-bisecting inside `sub_002E5F95` (714 generated-C lines) pinned the
transition to a 150-line window, then to one call: `sub_004AE0A7`
(GOOD before, BAD after). Re-bisecting inside `sub_004AE0A7` pinned it to
one call: `sub_004ADE9D` (GOOD before, BAD after). Re-bisecting inside
`sub_004ADE9D` (its own ~260 lines, no direct non-local stores by static
grep) pinned it to one call: `sub_004B0F92` (GOOD before line 14747, BAD
by its own exit at line 14967). Re-bisecting `sub_004B0F92`'s nine
chained state-setter calls found only one (`sub_004AED5D`) is even
reached this run -- the other eight are skipped via an early-success
branch. **Final localization: the corruption happens somewhere inside
`sub_004AED5D` (`recomp_0027.c:7881-8080`), specifically after its
per-row copy loop begins (`recomp_0027.c:8016-8041`, live-confirmed still
GOOD at line 8023) and before its own exit (BAD by line 14967's
outer-caller checkpoint).**

### A genuine, independent defect found along the way: the row-copy loop never advances

Sweeping every iteration of the loop at `recomp_0027.c:8023` (480
iterations captured in one run) shows `esi`/`edi` **frozen at the exact
same values (`0x00000394`/`0x00000398`) on every single iteration** --
the per-row pitch added at the end of each iteration
(`recomp_0027.c:8034-8035`, `MEM32(ecx+0x1048)`/`MEM32(ebx+0x1048)`) must
be reading as zero. This is a real, reproducible defect (a "copy every
row to the same place forever" bug) independent of the 0x4AB668 question,
not yet root-caused or fixed -- flagged for follow-up, not chased further
this entry per the user's bisection-first instruction.

### The addresses this loop copies to/from do not overlap 0x4AB668 at all

`esi=0x394, edi=0x398, ecx(dwords)=0x3a4` (destination range
`[0x398, 0x1228]`) is nowhere near `0x4AB668`. Live-confirmed the device
pointer flips from GOOD to BAD exactly between loop iteration 115 and 116
in one run (`dd 0x7000004ab668` checked every iteration) -- but the
copy's own addresses never change across any of those iterations. **This
specific memcpy cannot be the direct writer of 0x4AB668 by its own stated
source/destination range.**

### Cross-thread race ruled out directly

At the exact moment of the GOOD->BAD transition, dumped all 5 live
threads (`~*kb 3`): thread 0 (ours) sitting at the checkpoint inside
`sub_004AED5D`/`sub_004B0F92`/`sub_004ADE9D`; threads 1-3 are idle
thread-pool workers in `NtWaitForWorkViaWorkerFactory`; thread 4 is this
project's own `nv2a_ack_thread`, sitting in `SleepEx` (mid-sleep, not
touching guest memory). **No other thread is active or could be writing
guest memory at this instant** -- the corruption is single-threaded on
thread 0, ruling out the race-condition hypothesis this update initially
suspected.

### Plan B (hardware write watchpoint), precisely gated this time: still does not fire

Per instruction ("Hardware-Watchpoint nur als Plan B"), armed
`ba w4 <host address of 0x4AB668>` but held it *disabled* until the loop
counter at `recomp_0027.c:8023` reached 100 (comfortably before the
115-116 transition observed above), then enabled it
(`bd`/`be` on the breakpoint id, avoiding the nested-quote nesting a
dynamic `ba` inside another breakpoint's action would need) and let the
process run free from there. Confirmed via a `cdb -pv` snapshot afterward
that the process had already reached the terminal `sub_004A12B0` spin
(i.e., the corruption already happened) -- **the watchpoint never fired**,
even armed for only the ~15-iteration window in which the transition is
known to occur. This is a much tighter, more conclusive negative result
than the wide, noisy attempt in Update 223 (there, the watchpoint had to
survive minutes of unrelated execution; here it only had to survive a
few dozen loop iterations of already-isolated code, and still missed it).

### Requested check: does 0x7400087D appear elsewhere in guest memory?

Searched the entire 64MB guest RAM (`s -d` over
`0x7000000000000` L?`0x4000000`) for the dword pattern `0x7400087D` on
the already-corrupted, still-running process: **zero matches anywhere
else** (a small-range sanity search around `0x4AB668` itself confirmed
the search command works correctly). Inconclusive on its own -- the
source data, if any, could have been overwritten by further execution in
the time since the corrupting write -- but does not support a simple
"stray copy from a live, still-intact buffer" explanation either.

### Working hypothesis, not yet confirmed: host-side memory aliasing

The combination of (a) the identified copy's own addresses never
overlapping `0x4AB668`, (b) no other thread active, and (c) a precisely
gated hardware watchpoint still not firing, most plausibly points at
something already flagged as an open architectural gap much earlier in
this project's history (docs, "continued 53", 2026-09-06): guest memory
may be reachable through more than one host virtual address (e.g. a
separate mapping/view used by a bulk-copy fast path), so a watchpoint
armed on the "canonical" `g_xbox_mem_offset`-translated address would
never see a write that goes through a different host VA backing the same
guest page. This was never confirmed for THIS corruption specifically --
it is the most consistent explanation of the evidence gathered this
entry, not a proven root cause.

### Explicitly not done, per instruction

No clamp, no fake/stub device pointer, no other workaround. No source
files modified this entry -- `git status`/`git diff` confirm doc-only
(plus new debug scripts in `tools/debug/`). All `scda_recomp.exe`/`cdb.exe`
instances terminated at the end.

### Next step recommendation

Root-causing this fully now needs a different kind of investigation than
the bisection done so far: auditing this project's guest-memory
allocation/mapping code (`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`,
`kernel_bridge.c`'s `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` path already flagged once
before) for any case where the address range containing `0x4AB668` (or
the loop's own destination range) is reachable through more than one host
VA. If no such aliasing exists, the alternative is a page-guard-based
(not debug-register-based) memory trap, which catches any access
regardless of host-address aliasing at the cost of being far slower and
more invasive -- a materially different technique from anything tried so
far this session.

## Update 225 (2026-09-21): CONCRETE WRITER FOUND -- the 0x4AB668 corruption is a tiled-aperture surface/row copy inside sub_004AED5D whose destination range overlaps the D3D device pointer's physical location; a cdb `.frame N` methodology pitfall (retracted) and one round of real, minimal, one-shot source instrumentation confirm it precisely

**Two false leads investigated and explicitly retracted this entry, in the
interest of an honest record:**

1. **Host memory-aliasing via RAM mirrors was checked and does not directly
   apply to this loop.** `XBOX_PTR(addr) = (uintptr_t)(uint32_t)(addr) +
   g_xbox_mem_offset` (`templates/runtime/recomp_types.h:460`) does no
   wraparound/masking, so a small guest address like the `0x394` observed
   earlier in a *different* (unrelated, harmless) call to this same shared
   copy routine cannot itself reach a 64MB RAM mirror. The RAM-mirror
   mechanism in `xbox_memory_layout.c` (documented there in detail) is real
   but was not the mechanism at play here.
2. **A suspected stack-pointer corruption (`ebp` reading as `0x3C0` in three
   different `cdb` stack frames via `.frame N; ? ebp`) was investigated and
   is a debugging-methodology artifact, not a real finding.** Re-checking
   with the frame-aware `dv` command (rather than `? name`, which can
   silently fall back to a pseudo-register/wrong scope when `.frame` context
   switching doesn't fully apply to a same-named local) shows completely
   normal, distinct, correctly-nested stack addresses per frame
   (`ebp=0xf7b0cc` in `sub_004AED5D`, `ebp=0xf7b188` in `sub_004ADE9D`, two
   frames up) -- the stack is healthy. Lesson for future `cdb` work in this
   project: never trust `? name` across a `.frame` switch for a variable
   name that also exists in outer frames; use `dv` (frame-scoped locals
   listing) instead.

### The real mechanism, caught directly via one round of source instrumentation

Per the user's own explicit fallback authorization ("instrumentiere
ausschließlich die Stores dieses kleinen Pfads, die die konkrete
Device-Pointer-Adresse überlappen"), added a minimal, one-shot, static-flag-
gated diagnostic directly to the generated `sub_004AED5D` in
`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_0027.c` (gitignored, temporary,
fully reverted at the end of this entry): a small static helper comparing
`MEM32(0x4AB668)` against the known-good `0x004AB670` at five checkpoints
bracketing the row-copy loop's dword copy, byte-tail copy, per-row pointer
recompute, outer-loop test, and function exit -- firing (writing a marker
file and one `fprintf`) only the first time the value is ever seen to
change after having first been observed correct. One fresh launch (build
required recompiling only the one changed translation unit) produced,
via the game's own `scda_runtime.log` (its `stderr` is `_dup2`'d there by
`main.c` -- an external `cdb`/redirect capture never sees it, which is why
the very first launch attempt showed nothing in the console-redirected log
until this was found and `scda_runtime.log` was checked instead):

```
SCDA-DIAG224 cp=after-dwordcopy bad=7400087D esi=F0253E00 edi=F04ABE00
    ecx=00000000 ebx=00000A00 edx=F0253400 eax=F04AB400 ebp=00F7B0CC
```

This checkpoint fires immediately after the loop's dword `memcpy`
(`recomp_0027.c` -- the `if (!g_df) { memcpy(...); esi += ecx*4; edi +=
ecx*4; }` branch at what was line ~8047 before instrumentation). At this
point `esi`/`edi` already reflect the post-copy (advanced) pointers, and
`ebx` still holds the pre-shift byte count (`0xA00` = 2560 bytes) computed
two lines earlier -- so the copy that just executed moved 2560 bytes from
source `[esi_before, esi_before+0xA00) = [0xF0253400, 0xF0253E00)` to
destination `[edi_before, edi_before+0xA00) = [0xF04AB400, 0xF04ABE00)`.

**Both addresses are in the tiled aperture** (`XBOX_TILED_BASE =
0xF0000000`, documented in `xbox_memory_layout.c` as "The NV2A exposes
physical RAM a second time here and titles render through it" -- a `view`
of the *same* file-mapping section as base RAM, at a `+0xF0000000` guest
offset). Subtracting the tiled base gives the physical range this copy's
destination actually touches: `[0x004AB400, 0x004ABE00)`.

**`0x004AB668` (the device pointer's own address) falls squarely inside
that range** (`0x004AB400 <= 0x004AB668 < 0x004ABE00`, at offset `0x268`
into the 2560-byte destination span). **This one `memcpy` call is the
direct writer.** It overwrites the device-pointer global with whatever
happened to be at the corresponding offset in the *source* surface data
(`[0xF0253400, 0xF0253E00)`, i.e. physical `[0x00253400, 0x00253E00)`) --
which is why the corrupted value (`0x7400087D`) looked like arbitrary
data rather than a null or an obviously-invalid sentinel: it is real
pixel/surface bytes from an unrelated buffer, not garbage in the usual
sense.

### Why the earlier hardware watchpoint (Update 224) never fired -- fully explained now

The watchpoint was armed on `g_xbox_mem_offset + 0x004AB668` -- the
**base-RAM view's** host address for that guest byte. The corrupting
write instead goes through `XBOX_PTR(edi)` with `edi` in the **tiled
aperture**, i.e. `g_xbox_mem_offset + 0x004AB668 + 0xF0000000` translated
through `g_tiled_view`'s *separate* `MapViewOfFileEx` mapping (a different
host virtual address, aliasing the same physical bytes via the shared
file-mapping section documented in `xbox_memory_layout.c`). A CPU
data breakpoint matches *linear address*, not physical page identity, so
a watchpoint on the base view's address can never fire for a write that
goes through the tiled view's address, no matter how tightly the
observation window is gated. This is exactly the "host memory aliasing"
working hypothesis from Update 224, now identified precisely (the tiled
aperture specifically, not a 64MB RAM mirror) and confirmed against a live
capture rather than inferred from a process of elimination.

### Also explains the earlier "loop never advances" observation as a separate, correct call

Update 224's finding that this same loop's `esi`/`edi` were frozen at tiny
values (`0x394`/`0x398`) across 480 iterations in an earlier run is not
contradicted by this entry -- `sub_004AED5D` is evidently a **generic,
shared row-copy routine called for many different surfaces** throughout
this phase of boot (both the tiny-address run and this tiled-aperture run
share the exact same call chain skeleton down to
`sub_0004934E`/`sub_00037274`/`sub_002E5F95`/`sub_004AE0A7`/
`sub_004ADE9D`/`sub_004B0F92`, confirmed identical across multiple
captures). Different runs' non-deterministic timing evidently reach
*different individual calls* to this same shared function first --
sometimes a harmless one with degenerate near-zero addresses (a separate,
real defect: that call's own pitch/size fields read as zero, worth a
follow-up but not the cause of this corruption), sometimes -- as in this
entry -- the specific call whose destination overlaps the device pointer.
This also means the "loop that never advances" defect found in Update 224
is confirmed to be independent of this one; both are real, both live in
copies made by this same shared function, for different callers/surfaces.

### Not yet done: tracing the destination address back to its ultimate source, and comparing against the original x86

Per the user's own next-step instruction, the remaining work is to trace
where `edi`'s tiled destination address (and the byte count in `ebx`)
actually come from -- i.e. which surface/texture descriptor feeds
`sub_004AED5D` this particular call's parameters, whether that
descriptor's base address or pitch is itself computed correctly relative
to the original x86, and whether the true bug is (a) the destination
surface's base address/size being computed wrong (an overrun that would
also occur, in some form, on real hardware, just not necessarily hitting
this exact global), or (b) a discrepancy specific to this recompilation's
placement of the device-pointer global relative to where the original
XBE's linker actually placed the colliding surface buffer. This has not
been started this entry -- flagged as the clear next step, matching the
user's own explicit instruction, and squarely a faithful-translation
question this project's established methodology (Capstone byte-level
comparison against `default.xbe`) is well suited to answer.

```
row=2   esi=F020D400 edi=F0465400
row=3   esi=F020DE00 edi=F0465E00
...
row=114 esi=F0253400 edi=F04AB400
row=115 esi=F0253E00 edi=F04ABE00   <- cur=7400087D (Update 225's transition)
```

**The destination address advances by exactly `0xA00` (2560 bytes) every

This is a completely healthy, correctly-bounded copy -- 2560 bytes/row
matches a 640-pixel-wide, 4-bytes-per-pixel (32bpp) surface exactly, and

0x004AB668 < 0x00590000`), not at some edge reached only by an
out-of-bounds write. There is no copy-loop bug here at all: given this

The bug is not in `sub_004AED5D`'s copy loop, and not in a "zero pitch"

## Update 228 (2026-09-21/22): ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED, no fix yet -- the 0x4AB668 corruption is a genuine architectural gap in this recompiler's memory-aperture model: the contiguous-memory window (0x80000000+) is deliberately NOT backed by the same physical storage as base RAM, but the tiled aperture (0xF0000000+) IS only an alias of base RAM, so a contig-allocated surface accessed through its tiled alias silently lands on unrelated base-RAM bytes instead of its own storage

**Per explicit user instruction, this entry is audit-only: no patch
applied.** Directed to audit `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`/the tiled-memory
model directly (free-region tracking, whether `0xF0464000` should be
allocatable at all under this project's own memory layout, boundaries/
reservations/exclusions vs. the real NV2A/MMIO/framebuffer apertures,
and explicitly 32-bit overflow/wraparound, inclusive/exclusive end
addresses, alignment, and size arithmetic) rather than continuing the
mechanical backward call-chain trace from Updates 223-227.

### The three apertures and how each is actually backed in this recompiler

Read `src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`'s own setup and comments for all
three relevant guest-address windows:

1. **Base RAM** (`XBOX_MAP_START = 0x00000000`, `XBOX_TOTAL_RAM` = 64MB):
   backed by `g_memory_base`, a `CreateFileMappingA` + `MapViewOfFileEx`
   section -- deliberately a *file mapping* (not plain `VirtualAlloc`)
   specifically so other apertures can share the same physical bytes via
   additional views of the same section (the file's own comment: "Using
   file mapping instead of VirtualAlloc allows us to map the same
   physical pages at multiple virtual addresses via MapViewOfFileEx").
2. **Tiled aperture** (`XBOX_TILED_BASE = 0xF0000000`): `g_tiled_view =
   MapViewOfFileEx(g_mapping_handle, ..., tiled_native, ...)` -- a
   genuine *view of the same file-mapping section* as base RAM. Its own
   comment confirms the intent precisely: "A view of the same section
   rather than fresh storage: the title writes a surface through the
   tiled address and reads it back through the normal one, so the two
   have to be the same bytes." **This aperture only, and correctly,
   aliases base RAM.**
3. **Contiguous window** (`XBOX_CONTIG_BASE = 0x80000000`,
   `XBOX_CONTIG_SIZE` = 64MB, both from `src/kernel/kernel.h`): backed by
   `g_contig_memory`, a **separate, plain `VirtualAlloc`** -- explicitly
   and deliberately *not* a view of the same file-mapping section. The
   code's own comment states the reasoning outright: "Deliberately NOT a
   view of the 64 MB RAM mapping. On hardware this window aliases
   physical RAM, but we load the XBE image into the low addresses of
   that same region, so aliasing would put a title's pinned pools on top
   of its own code. Separate storage costs an extra mapping and behaves
   correctly; nothing here depends on the aliasing."

### Where the assumption breaks

That last comment's premise -- "nothing here depends on the aliasing" --
is the crux, and this investigation has now found a concrete case where
it does not hold. This project's own further comments document the
*intended* real-hardware round trip precisely: "`MmAllocateContiguousMemory`
hands back physical memory, and on Xbox physical page P is visible at
`0x80000000 + P`" (`xbox_memory_layout.c`, above `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`),
and separately "Xbox D3D writes its pushbuffer position to the NV2A as
`VA & 0x0FFFFFFF` and reads the GPU's position back as `GET |
0x80000000`" -- i.e. **the exact same physical-page number `P` is meant
to be reachable through *three* apertures on real hardware: base RAM
(`0x00000000 + P`), the contiguous window (`0x80000000 + P`), and the
tiled aperture (`0xF0000000 + P`), all as views of one single, unified
physical address space.**

In this recompiler, `P` is tracked by **two independent counters that
both start at zero and know nothing about each other**: base RAM's own
occupied range (executable image, static data -- including the device
pointer global at guest VA `0x004AB668`, which is a *physical* address
in the `0x00000000+` sense) and `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s bump allocator
`g_contig_next` (starting at `XBOX_CONTIG_BASE`, counting up from its own
zero). **A contig allocation that lands `0x464000` bytes into the 64MB
contig window gets `P = 0x464000`.** When the game's own (faithfully
translated, byte-verified) D3D8/driver code converts that surface's
address into its tiled-aperture form via the exact documented formula
(`0xF0000000 | (VA & 0x0FFFFFFF)`), it computes `0xF0464000` -- and this
recompiler's tiled aperture, being wired *only* to base RAM's file
mapping, resolves that address to **base RAM's own physical offset
`0x464000`**, not to `g_contig_memory`'s storage at all. Since
`0x004AB668` (the device pointer) is a *base-RAM* address whose own
physical offset (`0x4AB668`) happens to fall inside the row-copy's
2560-byte-per-row, 480-row destination span starting at physical offset
`0x464000` (span `[0x464000, 0x590000)`, per Update 226), the copy
silently overwrites it -- **not a bounds violation by the copy's own
logic, and not an overflow/off-by-one in `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s own
arithmetic (its exhaustion check already correctly uses `uint64_t` to
avoid 32-bit wraparound, and its alignment/size handling is
unremarkable), but a structural consequence of two independently-numbered
"physical" spaces being funneled through one shared-only-with-one-of-them
aliasing aperture.**

### Answering the audit's specific questions

- **Free-region tracking:** `xbox_ContiguousAlloc` is a pure bump
  allocator (`g_contig_next`, never freed -- "contiguous blocks are
  framebuffers and pushbuffers, which a title allocates once", per its
  own comment) bounded only by `XBOX_CONTIG_BASE + XBOX_CONTIG_SIZE -
  XBOX_GPU_INSTANCE_DEFAULT`. It has no concept of, and no interaction
  with, base RAM's own occupied ranges at all -- by design, since the two
  are meant to be (and, for every access path except the tiled aperture,
  successfully are) independent storage.
- **Is `0xF0464000` "allowed" under this project's own memory layout?**
  Yes, unconditionally -- `xbox_ContiguousAlloc` has no exclusion logic
  referencing the tiled aperture, the NV2A MMIO aperture, or base RAM's
  own layout at all, and none of the three is even aware of the other
  two's occupied ranges.
- **Comparison against actual NV2A/MMIO/framebuffer mappings:** the NV2A
  register aperture (`XBOX_NV2A_BASE = 0xFD000000`, 16MB, backed by its
  own separate `g_nv2a_memory` `VirtualAlloc`) and the MCPX aperture are
  both independent of this question -- they do not overlap `0xF0000000
  -0xF4000000` (the tiled aperture's own span, `xbox_TiledApertureSize()`
  bounded) or `0x80000000-0x84000000` (contig window). The collision is
  specifically between the tiled *alias of base RAM* and *contig-window*
  addresses, not with either hardware MMIO aperture.
- **32-bit overflow/wraparound, inclusive/exclusive bounds, alignment,
  size arithmetic:** all individually checked and clean.
  `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s exhaustion check casts to `uint64_t` before
  comparing, so it cannot wrap. Alignment is forced to a 4096-byte
  minimum before the bump-pointer arithmetic, which cannot overflow for
  any realistic size. The RAM-mirror code elsewhere in this same file
  (Update 224/225's earlier reading) already handles 64MB-multiple
  wraparound deliberately and correctly for a *different* reason (the
  documented address-bus wrap). **None of these is the bug here** -- the
  bug is the aliasing gap described above, which exists regardless of
  how carefully any individual allocator's arithmetic is written.

### Why this was not caught by the earlier (Update 223) hardware-watchpoint or the RAM-mirror hypothesis

This is the same underlying category of explanation floated as a
"working hypothesis" in Update 224 (host memory aliasing) and refined in
Update 225 to "the tiled aperture, specifically" -- this entry completes
that thread by identifying *which* two guest address ranges are
incorrectly treated as aliasing (base RAM and the contig window, via the
tiled aperture) and *why* (a deliberate, documented, but -- for this one
access pattern -- incorrect simplification), rather than a mirror-wrap
or a copy-loop bug.

### Not yet done

No fix implemented, per instruction. This is now a genuine design
decision, not a one-line correction: possible directions include (a)
making the tiled aperture correctly reachable from *both* base RAM and
the contig window at their respective physical offsets (requires knowing
which aperture a given physical offset "belongs to," which the current
flat-file-mapping design does not track), or (b) giving the contig
allocator its own dedicated, non-overlapping slice of tiled-aperture
address space so its offsets never coincide with base RAM's own layout,
or (c) something else -- not decided or scoped further this entry. No
clamp, no fake pointer, no workaround. This entry made no source changes
of any kind (pure reading/analysis of already-committed, tracked code);
`git status`/`git diff` are clean.


## Update 229 (2026-09-22): FIX IMPLEMENTED for the 0x4AB668 corruption -- a genuine physical-memory alias for dynamically bump-allocated contiguous memory, verified by a startup self-test and a clean extended run with zero recurrence of the old corruption/crash signature

Per explicit user instruction, rejected a pure workaround (e.g. clamping or
relocating the one colliding allocation) in favour of fixing the underlying
architectural gap Update 228 identified: the contiguous-memory window
(0x80000000+) was backed by storage with no physical identity with base RAM,
so a contig surface's tiled-aperture alias silently read/wrote base RAM's
own bytes at the same physical offset instead of the surface's own.

### The fix: a second, genuinely-aliased view for dynamic contig allocations

`src/kernel/xbox_memory_layout.c`:

- **New globals** (declared near `g_contig_memory`, before `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`
  needs them): `g_contig_alias_view` (the new mapping), `g_contig_alias_base`
  (its guest VA), `g_contig_alias_need` (how far the tiled aperture must
  reach to cover it), and `g_contig_next`/`g_contig_top` moved up from their
  old spot next to `xbox_ContiguousAlloc` so `xbox_MemoryLayoutInit` can set
  them before that function is ever called.
- **Physical-offset choice**: `contig_alias_phys_off = max(g_memory_size,
  XBOX_CONTIG_SIZE)` -- the first physical offset guaranteed to be past
  *both* base RAM's own fully-claimed layout (image + stack + heap, which
  reaches exactly `g_memory_size` via `XBOX_HEAP_TOP`) *and* the legacy
  contig window's own `VirtualAlloc` span, so the new region can never
  overlap either. Computed and stored (`g_contig_alias_base`,
  `g_contig_alias_need`) immediately after `g_memory_size` itself, before
  `CreateFileMappingA` is even called.
- **File mapping grown**: the same `g_mapping_handle` section used for base
  RAM, its mirrors, and the tiled aperture is now sized
  `g_contig_alias_need` bytes (`g_memory_size` plus one `XBOX_CONTIG_SIZE`
  tail) instead of exactly `g_memory_size`. The base view and every RAM
  mirror are unchanged -- they only ever map file offset `[0, g_memory_size)`
  -- so this costs nothing for anything already working and cannot shift
  where the 64 MB address-bus-wrap mirrors land (a real, load-bearing
  behaviour for other titles; see the mirror-setup comment).
- **New view mapped right after the legacy contig window, *before* the
  RAM-mirror loop**: `g_contig_alias_view = MapViewOfFileEx(g_mapping_handle,
  ..., contig_alias_phys_off, XBOX_CONTIG_SIZE, XBOX_CONTIG_BASE +
  contig_alias_phys_off)`. Ordering caught a real bug during this session's
  own testing (see below) -- it has to commit before the mirror loop runs,
  not after, or a generic wraparound mirror silently claims the same address
  first.
- **`xbox_TiledApertureSize()` extended** to also cover
  `g_contig_alias_need` (still bounded by the same two hard ceilings --
  0xFD000000 and the 4 GB wrap -- it already encoded), so the tiled
  aperture's own `MapViewOfFileEx` reaches the new region's physical offset
  too.
- **`xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s bump pointer redirected**: on success,
  `g_contig_next`/`g_contig_top` move to the alias region (no
  `XBOX_GPU_INSTANCE_DEFAULT` carve-out needed there --
  `bridge_MmClaimGpuInstanceMemory` always computes its own address from the
  legacy `XBOX_CONTIG_BASE` window directly and never consults this bump
  pointer, so the two mechanisms stay independent exactly as before). Falls
  back to the legacy, unaliased window (today's old behaviour, known gap) on
  any failure -- mapping failure, tiled aperture not reaching far enough, or
  the self-test itself failing -- rather than refusing to start, matching
  every other aperture's failure policy in this function.
- **`fence_readable()` extended** to also recognise the alias region as
  backed, so the NV2A-fence-polling thread still follows a chain into a
  GPU-written semaphore living in a dynamically-allocated contig buffer.
- **The legacy window (`g_contig_memory`, 0x80000000-0x84000000 by default)
  is completely untouched**: still its own independent `VirtualAlloc`,
  still what Halo's fixed low-address pins and the fake kernel page at
  0x80010000 use. Nothing here is reachable through the tiled aperture on
  its own, so the missing three-way alias that fix targets was never
  observable for it -- see the long comment on that block for the full
  reasoning.

### Startup self-test

Runs once the tiled aperture is mapped (the alias-view mapping itself
happens earlier -- see the mirror-collision note below -- but proving the
round trip needs the tiled window to already exist): writes a marker
through the contig alias, reads it back through the tiled aperture at the
matching physical offset, then writes a different marker through tiled and
reads it back through contig. Both directions have to match or the fix
falls back to the legacy window and prints a WARNING rather than silently
trusting an unproven mapping. Confirmed passing in this session's test runs
(`Contig alias verified (both directions, contig<->tiled)`).

**Not a three-way test.** Base RAM itself deliberately does not reach this
region (see the long comment on `g_contig_alias_view` in the source) --
extending base RAM's own reach there was rejected because it would either
shift the mirror wraparound boundary (breaking the RenderWare memory
walker's documented 64 MB wrap behaviour for other titles) or require
shrinking the heap's own ceiling to free genuinely spare room in the same
64 MB (a real reduction in what a title can allocate). The two-way
contig<->tiled alias this fix provides is sufficient: a dynamic contig
allocation's bytes can no longer physically coincide with any base-RAM
global, because the two no longer share a physical offset at all -- there
is nothing left for a three-way test to prove that the two-way one does not
already cover.

### A real bug caught during this session's own verification: mirror/alias address collision

The first build of this fix mapped `g_contig_alias_view` *after* the tiled
aperture (so the self-test could run immediately), which put it after the
RAM-mirror loop too. The mirror loop tiles the entire 4 GB range above
`g_memory_base` in 64 MB steps with no awareness of what any particular
slice conceptually means, and mirror index 32 (0-based) covers exactly
guest `[0x84000000, 0x88000000)` -- this fix's chosen alias address. That
mirror mapped successfully first (nothing occupied the address yet), and
`g_contig_alias_view`'s own `MapViewOfFileEx` then failed with
`ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS` (error 487) against an address that looked free but
was not:

```
WARNING: contig alias view at 0x84000000 failed (error 487); dynamic
contiguous allocations will use the legacy window and remain subject to
the tiled-aperture aliasing gap (Update 228)
```

Fixed by moving the alias-view mapping to right after the legacy contig
window, *before* the mirror loop -- the same position the legacy window and
the kernel page already occupy. The mirror loop's own `VirtualQuery`-based
occupied-range fallback (already there for exactly this situation -- see
its own comment about the legacy contig window, NV2A, MCPX, and flash
apertures) then correctly detects the now-already-committed alias region
and fails over/skips it:

```
Mirror 32: FAILED at 0000700080000000 (error 487)   <- legacy contig window (unchanged, pre-existing)
Mirror 33: FAILED at 0000700084000000 (error 487)   <- new alias region (expected, now correctly detected)
```

The self-test itself stays where it was (after the tiled aperture is
mapped) since it only needs the view to already exist, not to be mapped at
that exact point in the function.

### Verification

Full pipeline rebuild (`cmake --build build/scda_upgrade --config
RelWithDebInfo --target scda_recomp`), clean except pre-existing warnings
unrelated to this change (implicit `getenv`/`strtoul`/`atoi`/`_exit`
declarations, an `old_protect` shadow warning, both present before this
session).

Two independent test runs (`scda_recomp.exe`, `build/scda_upgrade/bin/
RelWithDebInfo`), ~20 s and ~100 s respectively, both reaching roughly
180,000+ kernel calls and 5,000+ runtime-log lines:

- `Contig alias verified (both directions, contig<->tiled)` printed in both.
- Zero occurrences, in either full log, of the old corruption value
  (`7400087D`), the old crash site (`004A12B0`), a `[CONTIG] arena
  exhausted` message, or any access-violation/exception text.
- Both runs settle into the same steady-state loop (repeating `[KERNEL]
  summary` lines, ordinals 277/246/294 -- `RtlEnterCriticalSection`/
  `RtlLeaveCriticalSection`/`ObReferenceObjectByHandle`, consistent with a
  Bink worker thread's own critical-section polling, not a new fault or
  hang introduced by this change) regardless of run length, so this is a
  plateau rather than a truncated run. Whether this steady state is itself
  the next real blocker, or an artifact of this test environment lacking
  real disc data, is **not yet determined** -- flagged for the next entry
  rather than assumed either way.

Not done this entry: locating and single-stepping the exact former
corruption site (`sub_004AED5D`'s row-copy / `sub_004B1377`'s construction
path) live under `cdb` to watch it *not* corrupt 0x004AB668 -- the self-test
proves the underlying aliasing mechanism directly and the extended run shows
no recurrence, which is the evidence this entry relies on; a live
re-confirmation at the exact original site would be strictly more thorough
but was not required to reach this conclusion.

## Update 230 (2026-09-22): the post-Update-229 "steady state" identified and CONFIRMED as a genuine new divergence (not a test-environment artifact, not related to the contig-alias fix) -- a menu-tree node pointer that should be a dynamic heap allocation is instead a hardcoded, unaligned address inside the executable image itself, verified against live xemu ground truth

Per the user's explicit instruction, this entry answers one narrow question:
is the steady-state loop observed at the end of Update 228/229's test runs
(originally mischaracterized there as "Bink-worker critical-section
polling") a real new blocker, or an artifact of the test environment? The
governing constraint stood throughout: the Update 229 contig-alias fix
itself is considered closed and was not reopened, since nothing found here
implicates it.

### Step 1-2: what the loop actually is (not what Update 229 guessed)

Update 229's characterization was wrong. The repeating `[KERNEL] summary`
lines with ordinals 277/246/294 are generic RTL critical-section/object-
reference noise that happens to coincide with the real symptom, not the
symptom itself. The actual repeating event, visible in the same log as
`[ICALL] target 0x00000000 is not code -- skipped N time(s) ... source=
0x0005F701` (N climbing past 1000 within the test window), is on the
**main thread**, not a worker thread at all.

One-shot source instrumentation (temporary, in the gitignored
`recomp_0002.c`, fully reverted afterward -- `git status`/`git diff` clean)
at `sub_0005F6FF` (the generic `this=ecx; call [[ecx]+0x54]` vtable-slot
dispatcher that source address belongs to) captured, on every one of 8
consecutive hits: `ecx(this)=0x81660000`, all of `[ecx+0]`, `[ecx+4]`,
`[ecx+8]`, `[ecx+0xC]` reading zero, and (by reading the emulated guest
stack at the exact point of the call, the same trick used throughout this
session to identify a caller without a native backtrace) a full, unbroken
call chain:

```
[caller at 0x622DA, inside sub_00062237's recursive tree-walk]
  -> sub_00060B2E(manager=ebx, cursor=stack-local)
       cursor.bucket = manager             ; = 0x00390037
       cursor.element = MEM32(manager+0x38) ; = 0x81660000
  -> sub_000600AD(cursor)                   ; walks cursor as a linked list
       ecx = cursor.element                 ; = 0x81660000
       -> sub_0005F6FF(ecx)                 ; this=0x81660000, all-zero object
            eax = MEM32(ecx)      = 0        ; vtable pointer itself is 0
            target = MEM32(eax+0x54) = 0     ; -> null indirect call, skipped
```

`sub_00062237` is a **recursive menu/scene-node tree walker** (`ebx` =
current node, tested via `MEM8(ebx+0x90)&4`; child list head at `ebx+0x24`;
recurses into itself for children whose flag bit is set). It is reached,
in this run, via the same deep call chain into the main initializer
already established in earlier updates
(`... -> sub_0003B78F -> sub_001D79F6 -> sub_00065F31 -> sub_00062237 ->
...`), immediately after `Menu.lin.dlf` (the main menu's level file) is
read successfully.

### Step 3-4: the constant is baked into the XBE image itself -- not a runtime computation, not missing disc/streaming data

`ebx = 0x00390037` is used as an object: `MEM8(ebx+0x90)` (a flag byte) and
`MEM32(ebx+0x38)` (the "first registered listener/child" field) are both
read directly. Parsing `default.xbe`'s own section table and reading the
**static, on-disk image bytes** at file offset for guest VA
`0x00390037+0x38` (`0x0039006F`) gives `00 00 66 81 ...` -- i.e. the exact
value `0x81660000` observed at runtime is **hardcoded in the executable
image itself**, section 0 (`vaddr=0x11000`, `vsize=0x454aa8`, the merged
code+data section, `flags=0x36`), not computed, not corrupted by any
allocator, and not dependent on any external disc/streaming file. Both
`lipsyncxbox.umd` and `splintercell4xboxretail.umd` are present in the test
environment and open/read successfully in the same log (`[SCDA-UMD-OPEN]`,
`[SCDA-UMD-READ]` both succeed) -- **the test environment is not missing
data relevant to this symptom.** This also, independently, rules out any
connection to Update 229's contig-alias fix: `0x00390037` is a base-RAM
image address, not a contig-window address, and `0x81660000`'s bytes come
from the static image, not from `xbox_ContiguousAlloc`'s bump pointer.

`0x00390037` is itself suspicious on its own terms: it is not 4-byte
aligned, unusual for a genuine C++ object address. That observation is
exactly what motivated the xemu ground-truth check below, rather than
accepting "the image just contains this constant" as the final answer --
the open question was whether `ebx` legitimately becomes `0x00390037` here
on real hardware too (in which case the constant is an intentional,
harmless "nothing registered yet" sentinel design), or whether `ebx`
itself is wrong in this recompilation.

### Step 5-6: xemu ground truth -- decisive, no ambiguity

A live GDB-remote session against the user's xemu build (real MCPX/BIOS/
disc image, `-s -S`, the established protocol from this project's existing
`tools/debug/xemu_*.py` scripts) set a software breakpoint at guest EIP
`0x000622D1` -- the exact `push ebx` immediately before the call to
`sub_00060B2E`, address-identical on both platforms since it is the same
XBE. No source or binary changes on either side; pure observation.

**92 hits collected** (helped along by the user manually advancing the
game past the passive main menu into a level, which produced far more
menu/HUD tree activity than sitting idle):

- `ebx` took on 40+ distinct values, **all in the `0x0080xxxx`-`0x00Dxxxxx`
  range** -- ordinary dynamically-allocated heap addresses on the real
  console's own allocator, changing hit to hit as objects are
  created/destroyed (e.g. `0x0081FD60`, `0x0082B420`, `0x00A27470`,
  `0x00D6BEF0`, ...).
- `[ebx+0x38]` was **either legitimately `0x00000000`** (empty, no
  children/listeners yet -- the harmless case, which never even reaches
  `sub_000600AD`'s loop body) **or another live heap pointer**
  (`0x0082F1C0`, `0x00822900`, `0x00A99300`, ...), consistent hit-to-hit
  for the same `ebx` as objects persist across frames, changing as the
  real allocator reuses/moves memory (e.g. `0x0083DD70`'s `+0x38` value
  moves from `0x0082D1A0` to `0x00A99300` to `0x00A99550` across
  successive hits -- exactly what a live, dynamically-updated list looks
  like).
- **`ebx == 0x00390037` never occurred, not once, in any of the 92 hits.**
- No hit ever showed a static-image-range value (`0x0000xxxx`-`0x00400000`
  or thereabouts) at either `ebx` or `[ebx+0x38]`.

**Conclusion: this is a genuine, confirmed divergence, not a benign
sentinel design and not a test-environment artifact.** On real hardware,
whatever computation feeds `sub_00062237`'s node pointers always produces
either a valid dynamically-allocated heap object or a clean empty (`0`)
state. In this recompilation, at least one call path instead produces a
raw, unaligned address that resolves to a fixed byte sequence baked into
the executable's own code/data section -- almost certainly a wrong pointer
computed (or a wrong branch taken) somewhere upstream of `sub_00062237`,
not a bug in `sub_00062237`/`sub_000600AD`/`sub_0005F6FF` themselves, which
faithfully do what any correctly-fed call chain would do with whatever
pointer they are handed.

### Not yet done

The producer of the bad `0x00390037` value -- i.e. which caller of
`sub_00062237` (or which upstream write to a node's own `+0x24` child-
pointer field) supplies this address instead of a real heap pointer -- has
not been traced. This is the concrete next step: find that producer,
compare its original x86 against the generated C at that exact point, and
identify the first wrong value, per the user's standing instruction.

No stub, no fake signal, no clamp, and no Bink-specific workaround were
introduced. The one temporary diagnostic added to `sub_0005F6FF`
(gitignored `recomp_0002.c`) was fully reverted and the clean baseline
rebuilt before the xemu comparison; `git status`/`git diff` show no tracked
changes from this entry. The xemu side made no changes at all (read-only
GDB-remote memory/register inspection).

## Update 231 (2026-09-22): traced the bad 0x00390037 value one call level further back -- it is a pass-through of an inherited `ebx`, not something sub_00062237's own caller computes fresh; the producer is narrowed to inside sub_00048B15's own body but not yet pinpointed

Direct continuation of Update 230, per the same standing instruction (find
the first wrong value, no shortcuts). This entry does not change the
conclusion of Update 230 (still a genuine, confirmed divergence, still
unrelated to the Update 229 contig-alias fix) -- it narrows where the bad
value comes from.

### The external caller of sub_00062237, and its own triple-push

One-shot instrumentation (temporary, gitignored `recomp_0002.c`, reverted
and rebuilt clean afterward -- confirmed via `git status`) at
`sub_00062237`'s own entry, reading the raw stack before its prologue
executes, caught all 5 hits with `incoming_ebx_param == 0x00390037` at the
**identical caller return address `0x0004A31D`**, every time. That call
site, inside `sub_0004934E` (`recomp_0002.c:19467-19472`), is:

```c
ecx = MEM32(0x6012D4);
ecx = MEM32(ecx + eax * 4);   /* ecx (the new "this"/edi) = a real array lookup */
PUSH32(esp, ebx);
PUSH32(esp, ebx);
PUSH32(esp, ebx);              /* all three arguments are the SAME ebx */
call sub_00062237
```

This is byte-faithful to the original x86 (`push ebx` three times is
exactly what the disassembly says) -- not a translation bug at this call
site. `ecx` (the tree's root/"this") is a legitimate array-indexed lookup,
unrelated to the bad value. The bad value is purely `ebx`, inherited
unchanged from whatever `sub_0004934E` itself was called with.

### ebx is a pass-through all the way up through two more functions

Static check: neither `sub_0004934E` nor `sub_00048F1D` (searched their
full bodies for any `ebx = ...` assignment) ever write to `ebx` -- exactly
matching real x86 cdecl callee-saved semantics for a function that simply
doesn't use that register. If the original x86 for these two functions
also never touches `ebx` (consistent with clean recompilation, and no
other bug pattern seen in either function during this check), `ebx`
reaching `sub_0004934E` must be **whatever their common caller passed
in/left there**.

Followed the chain up: `sub_0004934E` is reached from `sub_00048B15` via a
**tail call** (`recomp_0002.c:15529`, `sub_0004934E(); return; /* tail jmp
0x0004934E */`) -- not a normal `RECOMP_ABI_CALL`, which is why an earlier
grep for direct callers came up empty and had to be corrected. Static
search of `sub_00048B15`'s entire ~550-line body finds exactly **one**
`ebx` assignment: `ebx = 0` right after its stack-probe prologue
(`recomp_0002.c:15014`), and nothing else reassigns it before the tail
call at line 15529.

### The open contradiction

Taken at face value, this says `ebx` should be `0` by the time
`sub_0004934E` (and therefore `sub_00062237`) is reached -- not
`0x00390037`. Since the live diagnostic proves it is in fact
`0x00390037`, one of the following is true, and has not yet been
distinguished:

1. **A register-preservation bug in one of `sub_00048B15`'s ~25 direct
   callees** (listed this entry: `sub_00035F65`, `sub_00036116`,
   `sub_000370F1`, `sub_000371A6`, `sub_0003E9D9`, `sub_0003EAE3`,
   `sub_00042082`, `sub_00043455`, `sub_00044C15`, `sub_00045584`,
   `sub_00045647`, `sub_00048856`, `sub_00067886`, `sub_000679C1`,
   `sub_00070854`, `sub_00070B06`, `sub_00070BDA`, `sub_00070CC6`,
   `sub_000715C7`, `sub_00071B49`, `sub_001CAD08`, `sub_001CB603`,
   `sub_001D47CF`, `sub_001D589D`, `sub_0026AF03`) -- if the original x86
   treats `ebx` as callee-saved there and this recompilation's translation
   of one of them fails to restore it correctly, `ebx` would silently pick
   up whatever unrelated value that callee left behind.
2. **A different code path is actually taken** than the simple linear
   read of `sub_00048B15` suggests -- e.g. a branch this static read
   didn't account for that skips the `ebx = 0` line entirely, leaving
   `ebx` as whatever `sub_00048B15`'s own caller passed, pushing the
   search one level higher still.

### Not yet done

Distinguishing between these two requires either bisecting live (checking
`ebx`'s value at successive points inside `sub_00048B15`, narrowing to
the exact callee or branch responsible -- the same one-shot-instrumentation
technique used throughout this investigation) or a byte-exact register-
preservation audit of the listed callees against the original x86. Neither
done this entry; flagged as the next concrete step. Update 230's
conclusion stands unchanged: this is confirmed via xemu ground truth to be
a genuine bug, not a test-environment artifact, and is unrelated to the
Update 229 fix (which remains closed).

No stubs, no fake signals, no clamps. All instrumentation this entry was
temporary, in the gitignored `recomp_0002.c`, fully reverted, and the
clean baseline rebuilt before this entry was written; `git status`/`git
diff` show no tracked changes.

## Update 232 (2026-09-22): ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED for the menu tree node pointer bug (Updates 230-231) -- a code-generator bug in `_fixup_icall_esp_save`'s FPO-prologue detection, not a data/pointer problem at all

Direct continuation of Update 231's live bisection plan, per the same
standing instruction (narrow the exact call boundary where ebx flips from
0 to the observed 0x00390037, live-checkpoint by live-checkpoint, no
static-only guessing once a live bisection is possible).

### Bisection: from sub_00048B15 down into sub_0026940F

One-shot instrumentation (temporary, in the gitignored generated `.c`
files, fully reverted by a full pipeline regeneration afterward) placed
sequential checkpoints along the exact call chain identified in Update
231, narrowing in each round:

1. `sub_00048B15`'s own body (CP0-CP6): `ebx` stays `0` at every point
   checked, including the tail-call boundary into `sub_0004934E` --
   confirmed clean, consistent with Update 231's static reading.
2. Realized `sub_0004934E` has **two independent entry paths** into the
   array-loop call site that reaches `sub_00062237`: the tail-call from
   `sub_00048B15` (rare -- observed exactly once per process run, a
   one-time init path), and a `fallthrough`/tail-call chain through
   `sub_00048F1D` -> `sub_000491BA` -> `sub_000492FA` -> `sub_00049336`
   that is in fact the game's own per-frame update path (this function
   family has no real call/return boundary in the original binary --
   `sub_00048B15` through `sub_0004934E` are one contiguous procedure,
   split into separate C functions purely for translation-unit size).
   `ebx` was `0` at the entry of every one of these, confirmed live.
3. Bisected `sub_0004934E`'s own ~3000-line body (quarter/half/three-
   quarter checkpoints, then progressively finer) and isolated the flip
   to between two adjacent checkpoints at addresses `0x00049FC7` (still
   `0`) and `0x0004A0E9` (already `0x00390037`) -- a ~190-line window.
4. Within that window, per-callee checkpoints isolated the flip further:
   `ebx` is still `0` after `sub_004528E7` returns, and already
   `0x00390037` after `sub_001D8842` returns. `sub_001D8842` is the
   direct culprit call.

### Inside sub_001D8842: a genuine 8-byte stack imbalance, empirically measured

Instrumented `sub_001D8842`'s own prologue and epilogue to record `esp`
and the raw stack contents at its saved-register slots. Prologue:
`esp=0x00F7B710`, slot values `edi=0, esi=0x00F7B798, ebx=0` (correct).
Epilogue: `esp=0x00F7B718` -- **8 bytes higher than the prologue's esp**,
a directly measured, unambiguous stack imbalance, not a guess. Bisecting
with quarter-point and then finer esp-delta checkpoints (all reading
`esp - <prologue esp>`, expected `0` throughout a balanced function)
narrowed the introduction of this `+8` to a single call: `sub_0026940F`.
Checkpoints immediately before and after that specific call (in
`sub_001D8842`) confirmed the entire `+8` appears inside `sub_0026940F`
itself -- not before or after it.

### Inside sub_0026940F: byte-exact disassembly comparison, then a second empirical bisection

Disassembled `sub_0026940F` (301 bytes, `capstone`, byte-exact against
`default.xbe`) end to end and compared every instruction against the
generated C -- structurally identical, including the closing `pop ecx;
pop edi; mov [...],eax; pop esi; ret` (matching `POP32(ecx); POP32(edi);
...; POP32(esi); esp+=4; return;` exactly). The function issues 10
identical-shaped indirect calls (`ecx = MEM32(g); eax = MEM32(ecx); ...;
call [eax+0x14]`) against the same object, 9 of them followed by
`push eax; mov ecx,<const>; call sub_000D28EC` and the 10th by
`push eax; call sub_000678A4` instead. A first pass suspected
`sub_000678A4` (which tail-jumps twice, through `sub_00368B0E` into
`sub_00368AAF`, a small integer-parsing routine) or `sub_000D28EC`
(called 9x) -- both were instrumented directly (entry/exit `esp`,
per-call counters) and both proved **perfectly balanced on every single
call**, including all 9 real invocations of `sub_000D28EC` from this
exact loop (matched by their distinctive `ecx` constants, isolated out of
11154 total calls to that shared, widely-reused helper across the whole
run). That left only the 10 indirect calls themselves; printing each
one's resolved target confirmed **all 10 read the identical vtable slot,
same object, same value (`0x000460C5`)** -- ruling out "different callee
behaves differently" and pointing at the resolution mechanism itself.

### The actual root cause: an unregistered indirect-call target correctly triggers RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE's fallback, but the fallback's saved rewind-point was captured too early -- by the code GENERATOR, not by any hand-written code

`0x000460C5` is not a registered function entry in this recompilation --
it falls in the middle of `sub_000460BB`'s own address range (a
different, separately named function starting a few bytes earlier), so
`recomp_lookup()` cannot find it. Directly probing this from generated
code (`recomp_lookup_manual` / `recomp_lookup` / `recomp_lookup_kernel`,
all returning null) confirmed it: `RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE` takes its designed
safety fallback for an unresolved-but-code-range target -- `g_esp =
saved_esp; eax = 0;` -- for every one of the 10 calls, every run. This
fallback is correct in general; `saved_esp` is exactly the `_icall_esp`
value the code generator inserts via `_fixup_icall_esp_save()` in
`tools/recomp/translator.py`, meant to be captured immediately before
the call's own argument pushes so a failed lookup can cleanly unwind
*only* those arguments.

For 9 of the 10 calls in this function, that is exactly what happens.
For the *first* call specifically, `_fixup_icall_esp_save()` places the
save one step too early -- before the function's own one-time
`PUSH32(esp, esi); PUSH32(esp, edi);` register-preservation pair, not
after it. Root-caused in `_fixup_icall_esp_save()` itself (verified by
reading, not guessing): the function locates a leading FPO-style
register-save run by scanning forward from the very first line after the
entry label's `RECOMP_TRACE_PC()`, requiring a `PUSH32(esp, ebx|esi|edi)`
line *immediately* there. `sub_0026940F`'s body has two ordinary setup
lines first (`ecx = MEM32(g); eax = MEM32(ecx);`, the vtable fetch shared
by all 10 calls) before the two saves -- so the scan sees a non-push line
first and stops immediately, leaving `prologue_end_idx` at 0 and the
icall-save backward-scan free to walk past the saves. The function's
*other* safeguard -- treating a push as a "save" whenever it is pushed no
more than it is popped -- also misses this specific case, because both
`esi` and `edi` are separately reused as a repeated constant argument
value across the other 9 calls in the same function: each is pushed 11
times total and popped only once (the real epilogue restore), so by
count alone they look exactly like arguments, not saves. Confirmed via
the disassembly that these two conditions (leading non-push setup lines,
plus a callee-saved register reused many times over as a literal
argument later in the same function) can and do occur together in real,
unremarkable game code -- this is not a hypothetical edge case.

With `_icall_esp` captured before the `esi`/`edi` saves instead of after
them, the fallback's `g_esp = saved_esp` on the very first call's
resolution failure permanently discards those two pushes -- 8 bytes --
from `sub_0026940F`'s idea of its own stack depth for the rest of its
execution. Every subsequent push/pop in the function (all 9 remaining
calls, all individually correct in isolation) now runs 8 bytes off from
where the function's own epilogue expects, and the epilogue's `pop edi;
pop esi;` at the very end reads two stack slots that are no longer the
ones it saved -- garbage is loaded into what should be the restored
`edi`/`esi`, propagated back into the caller `sub_001D8842`, whose own
epilogue's `pop ebx` (at an offset now also permanently displaced by the
same 8 bytes) is where `ebx = 0x00390037` was actually manufactured, many
calls before it ever reaches `sub_00062237`.

### The fix

`tools/recomp/translator.py`, `_fixup_icall_esp_save()`: added a skip
loop before the existing FPO-save-detection loop, advancing past leading
lines that are pure register/memory-load setup with no stack or
control-flow effect (no `esp`, `PUSH32`, `POP32`, `RECOMP_`, `goto`,
`return`, `if (`, or a label), stopping the moment it finds either a
`PUSH32(esp, ebx|esi|edi)` (hands off to the existing detection loop
unchanged) or anything else (falls back to today's behavior, unchanged).
This is strictly additive: it only widens what counts as "the start of
the FPO prologue," it does not change how that prologue is validated
once found (the existing push/pop-count matching still applies).

Added a fourth regression test to `tools/recomp/test_icall_esp_save.py`,
`test_fpo_save_after_vtable_fetch_setup`, modeled directly on
`sub_0026940F`'s real structure (two setup lines, two FPO saves, ten
calls with two of the pushed registers reused as repeated arguments) --
verifies the `_icall_esp` save lands after both the setup lines and both
FPO saves, not before either. All four tests in the file pass
(`py -3 tools/recomp/test_icall_esp_save.py`).

### Verified: full pipeline regeneration, clean rebuild, and a live retest

Regenerated the entire SCDA output via the canonical recomp-only command
(existing `scda_v060` disassembly, `--exclude-manual
projects/scda/src/recomp_manual.c`) -- 28159/28162 functions, 0 failed,
identical scale to the pre-fix generation. Confirmed in the fresh
