`PUSH32(esp, esi); PUSH32(esp, edi);` and before the first call-specific
argument push, for all 10 indirect-call sites. Full clean rebuild
succeeded (no new warnings beyond pre-existing, unrelated
`recomp_manual.c` unreferenced-label notices).

Ran the rebuilt `scda_recomp.exe` for ~90 seconds (179,000+ kernel
calls). Results:
- `0x00390037` does not appear anywhere in `scda_runtime.log` -- zero
  occurrences, down from the previous steady-state recurrence every
  frame.
- The specific null-vtable-call signature this whole investigation
  traced (`[ICALL] ... target=0x00000000 ... source=0x0005F701`) is

### Not this entry

The new post-fix steady state (kernel-call cycle across ordinals
99/234/246/277/294) is unexplored -- flagged as the next concrete blocker

No stubs, no fake signals, no clamps, and no hand-edit to any generated

## Update 233 (2026-09-22): characterize the post-Update-232 kernel-call steady state -- a real pool-worker thread blocks forever inside a legitimate alertable-wait retry loop; one unrelated dead-bridge bug found and fixed along the way

Direct continuation per the standing instruction: with Update 232's fix
confirmed and closed, characterize the new steady state that appears after
it (repeating kernel calls cycling through ordinals 99/234/246/277/294)
before touching anything, per the same hierarchical-narrowing methodology.

### Step 1: what do these ordinals mean, and what shape does the cycle have

`src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c`'s ordinal tables identify the five: 99 =
KeDelayExecutionThread, 234 = NtWaitForSingleObjectEx, 246 =
ObReferenceObjectByHandle, 250 = ObfDereferenceObject, 277 =
RtlEnterCriticalSection, 294 = RtlLeaveCriticalSection. The existing
`scda_runtime.log` from Update 232's own 90-second verification run (still
on disk, no rerun needed for this first pass) showed two distinct `esp`
bases interleaved in the post-transition tail (`0x00F7B6xx` and
`0x013F9Exx`), i.e. two threads each independently looping through this
small ordinal set with no new `[FILE]`/`[PATH]`/`[READ]`/`[ICALL]` activity
at all afterward.

The transition itself: immediately before the steady state begins, the
game re-opens `splintercell4xboxretail.umd` (the main disc image, already
opened once earlier) and calls ordinal 37 (`FscSetCacheSize`) on it, which
has no bridge and returns 0. A live call-count diagnostic (added and
reverted in `kernel_bridge.c`'s dispatch fallback, not shipped) proved this
warning is a herring: ordinal 37 and the whole IoCompletion/Fsc family
(35, 79, 90, 91, 191, 223, 227) are each called *once* over a multi-hundred-
thousand-call run, never in a loop, so they cannot be the mechanism behind
a sustained cycle -- ruled out with direct evidence rather than left as
"probably fine".

### Step 2: the render-loop Enter/LeaveCriticalSection churn is a pre-existing, already-documented characteristic, not new

The single highest-volume call pair in the post-transition tail
(`RtlEnterCriticalSection`/`RtlLeaveCriticalSection` around a fixed lock at
Xbox VA `0x6B27A0`, reached through a lazy-init wrapper `sub_000767ED`
called from a per-frame timer-smoothing routine, `sub_00039566` ->
`sub_002E2F8B`/`sub_002E2F99`) turned out, via a one-shot live checkpoint,
to be running continuously from very early in the boot sequence onward --
not something that starts at the transition. Its raw call volume (tens of
thousands over a run) is consistent with this project's own already-closed
2026-09-11 finding recorded directly in `kernel_bridge.c`'s `RECOMP_KERNEL_HIST`
comment: this recomp does not yet pace itself to real display/vsync
timing, so per-frame housekeeping runs far faster than 60 Hz by design/
known-limitation, not by bug. Chasing this thread further would have
reopened an already-closed, unrelated finding; ruled out and dropped.

### Step 3: the real signal -- ObfDereferenceObject is a dead bridge, and the poll it's part of never terminates

A live per-ordinal call counter (temporary, in `kernel_thunk_dispatch`'s
"no bridge" fallback, reverted after use) showed ordinal 250
(`ObfDereferenceObject`) growing without bound in the steady state (588,
603, 618, ... +15 every 3 seconds) while every other missing-bridge ordinal
stayed flat at a handful of one-time calls. Reading `kernel_bridge.c`
found `bridge_ObfDereferenceObject` fully implemented (calls the real
`xbox_ObfDereferenceObject`) but never wired into the dispatch switch --
`/* case 250: bridge_ObfDereferenceObject */`, commented out, sitting two
lines below the already-fixed, already-documented `NtSuspendThread`/
`NtResumeThread` entries that describe *exactly this class of bug*: "the
implementation was already here and only the dispatch entry was missing,
which is worse than an outright stub". Whoever wired up 224/231 evidently
missed the adjacent 250 (and 252/253, left alone this entry as unrelated
networking ordinals, out of scope here).

Checking `xbox_ObfDereferenceObject`'s real body (`kernel_ob.c`) shows it
is *itself* a documented no-op by design -- Win32 handles manage their own
lifetime, so this project deliberately doesn't reference-count them.
Wiring the dispatch entry is therefore a genuine, safe, zero-risk
correctness fix (matches this file's own established fix pattern for dead
bridges) but -- confirmed by rerunning after the fix -- has no effect on
the steady state, because the real bridge does nothing observable either.
Fixed anyway in `kernel_bridge.c` (dispatch switch, ordinal 250 -> `bridge_ObfDereferenceObject`)
since leaving a proven dead, already-precedented bridge unwired serves no
purpose and the project's own comments already flag this exact class of
bug as worth fixing on sight.

### Step 4: the ObReferenceObjectByHandle poll resolves fine -- the thread it's waiting on is genuinely still running

A live checkpoint in `bridge_ObReferenceObjectByHandle` (temporary,
reverted after use) showed the polled handle (`0x48000007`, tagged, from
`s_handle_kthread_va[7]`) resolves *consistently and successfully* to a
stable non-null fake-KTHREAD address (`0x013FB000`) on every one of 800+
samples -- not stuck on null, not flapping. `bridge_mark_thread_done`
(which flips this structure's "done" byte) is simply never called for this
particular kthread_va, meaning the underlying worker thread has genuinely
not exited yet, not that the resolution mechanism itself is broken. This
directly rules out a second occurrence of the *already-fixed* Update
169/170 "always resolves null" bug -- different failure shape, confirmed
by direct evidence, not assumed innocent.

### Step 5: tracing the actual worker thread -- a legitimate alertable-wait retry loop that never sees its object signaled

`PsCreateSystemThreadEx` creates exactly 4 worker threads this run, all
through the same generic CRT `_threadstartex`-shaped trampoline
(`sub_000524DA`), which just calls `ctx1(ctx2)` -- so the real per-thread
behavior lives at whichever `ctx1` address each call passes: `0x00054701`,
`0x004BBE90` (used twice, with different `ctx2` data each time -- a
2-worker pool processing distinct task objects), and `0x00036889`.

`sub_004BBE90` (the pool routine) is a short, straight-line, *non-looping*
function: wait once on a handle from its task object, then do a small
amount of conditional cleanup, then return. Tracing its wait call down
(`sub_00052D2E` -> `sub_00052C18`) finds a manual retry loop:

```
loc_00052C2C:
    NtWaitForSingleObjectEx(handle, mode=1, alertable, timeout_ptr);   // ordinal 234
    if (result < 0) goto error;
    if (timeout == 0) goto done;
    if (result == 0x101) goto loc_00052C2C;      // retry
    goto done;
```

`0x101` is `STATUS_ALERTED` -- this is textbook-correct alertable-wait
retry code (a wait interrupted by a delivered APC, not real completion,
should simply wait again), not a bug in the game. The call site pushes
exactly 4 arguments matching ordinal 234's real 16-byte/4-argument size
(`g_slot_arg_bytes[234]`), so there is no repeat of the already-documented
`NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx` 4-vs-6-argument stack-corruption class of bug
sitting a few hundred lines above this one in the same file -- checked
directly rather than assumed, given how easily this file's history shows
that exact mistake recurring in sibling wait wrappers. One positional
oddity was noted (the pushed value that lands in the bridge's `Alertable`
slot is actually the caller's raw timeout value, not a boolean) but
`WaitForSingleObjectEx`'s `Alertable` parameter only controls whether a
queued APC can interrupt the wait early -- it does not gate whether a
real signal completes it -- so this does not explain a permanent block and
was not chased further as a fix target this entry.

`xbox_NtWaitForSingleObjectEx` (`kernel_sync.c`) calls the real Win32
`WaitForSingleObjectEx` on the resolved native handle. The wait is
genuine, not simulated: if nothing in this recomp ever signals that
specific handle, the worker thread blocks here forever, by design of the
underlying Win32 primitive -- exactly matching the observed behavior (the
worker never returns, `bridge_mark_thread_done` is never called for it,
and the main thread's `ObReferenceObjectByHandle` poll for "is this thread
done" therefore never sees completion).

### Flagged, not chased further this entry

`sub_004BBE90`'s conditional cleanup path calls `sub_004BBD90` when a task
field is non-zero -- `sub_004BBD90` is named directly in the *closed*
Bink-worker/ring-buffer investigation from earlier updates. This is a
structural adjacency (same function family), not the same mechanism (that
investigation's fix was a 4-vs-6-argument stack-corruption bug in the
*multi*-object wait path, `sub_00052D40` -> `sub_00052C5C` ->
`NtWaitForMultipleObjectsEx`; this entry's finding is the sibling
*single*-object wait path, `sub_00052D2E` -> `sub_00052C18` ->
`NtWaitForSingleObjectEx`, and the block happens before `sub_004BBD90` is
ever reached). Per the standing instruction not to reopen that closed path
without new direct evidence, and since this is a different call chain, it
is recorded here as a related-but-distinct area rather than folded into
either investigation. The concrete next step is to identify what this
specific pool worker's handle actually is (an event? a semaphore? tied to
which subsystem's producer?) and whether the producer that should signal
it is unimplemented, unreached, or itself blocked -- not yet done.

### Fix applied this entry

`src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c`: wired ordinal 250 (`ObfDereferenceObject`)
into the kernel dispatch switch, matching the exact precedent set by the
`NtSuspendThread`/`NtResumeThread` fix a few lines above it. Confirmed via
rebuild + rerun: the "no bridge for ordinal 250" warning is gone, no new
warnings or regressions, and (as predicted from reading the real
implementation) the steady state is unchanged, since the real
`xbox_ObfDereferenceObject` is itself a documented no-op.

No stubs, no fake signals, no clamps, no skipped path, and no hand-edit to
any generated `.c` file survives -- every diagnostic added this entry
(missing-bridge call counter, `ObReferenceObjectByHandle` handle/resolve
logger) was temporary, read, and reverted; the only change carried forward
is the one genuine, precedented, verified-safe dispatch-wiring fix.

## Update 234 (2026-09-22, IN PROGRESS): correct a wrong thread-identity assumption from Update 233; trace the real blocked producer to a per-frame timer-smoothing routine's outer accumulation loop

Direct continuation per the standing instruction, scoped exclusively to the
producer side of the blocked pool worker: do not reopen critical-section
churn, the Fsc/IoCompletion bridges, ObfDereferenceObject, or
`sub_004BBE90`'s own wait-side correctness (all closed per Update 233). Find
what the polled handle's producer actually is, whether it runs, and why it
never signals.

### Correcting Update 233's own thread-identity assumption

Update 233 assumed the two `sub_004BBE90` pool workers (token
`0x48000008`/`0x4800000C` in that run) were the thread being polled via
token `0x48000007`. A live checkpoint at thread creation
(`bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx`, logging the token assigned to each new
thread) proved neither of them is token 7 -- tracing token 7's assignment
history back through `bridge_handle_token` found a **fourth**,
previously-overlooked `PsCreateSystemThreadEx` call: `routine=0x000524DA
ctx1=0x00036889 ctx2=<per-run>`, created during the lipsync/menu load phase
right before `[SCDA-UMD-OPEN]` for `lipsyncxbox.umd`. This is a
self-caught correction of the prior investigation's own direction, not a
user correction, and matters because all of Update 233's task-object field
analysis (`sub_004BBF00`, `sub_00052B01`/`sub_00052BA0`, the mutex/event
handle wiring) describes the two *healthy* timer workers, not the actual
blocked thread -- useful general codebase knowledge, but not the producer
chain being searched for.

### Why token 0x48000007 looked like two different things across runs

Token values are reused indices, not stable object identities (per the
standing instruction to prefer vtable/descriptor/call-chain over raw
values). Direct evidence: in several runs, token 7 is first assigned to a
Bink video file handle (`NtCreateFile` on an entry inside
`splintercell4xboxretail.umd`; confirmed via the pre-existing `[READ]`
diagnostic in `kernel_bridge.c`'s `bridge_NtReadFile` -- first read returns
the `BIKi` magic), which streams for anywhere from tens of seconds to
several minutes (107-210+ `[READ]` calls observed across three runs of
varying length, want/got always matching, no corruption) before the handle
closes and the index is recycled for thread #4. This explains why shorter
test runs (50s, 120s) never saw `PsCreateSystemThreadEx #4` at all, while a
300s+ run did -- the delay is real video-streaming time preceding thread
creation, not run-to-run nondeterminism in the bug itself. Update 233's
`ObReferenceObjectByHandle` poll observation remains correct; it simply
happened after the video handle had already closed and token 7 had been
recycled onto the real target thread.

### Tracing ctx1=0x00036889: a one-shot wrapper, not a loop itself

`sub_00036889` (28 bytes) is a trivial wrapper: it calls
`sub_00039566(0, ctx2, 0, 0.0)` exactly once and returns immediately -- no
internal loop. An enter/leave checkpoint (temporary) confirmed this
directly: across every run where thread #4 was created, exactly one
"enter" was logged and, within the observed run length (up to 5 minutes),
no matching "leave" ever appeared. (One own diagnostic-placement mistake
along the way: the first checkpoint read the wrong stack slot for `ctx2`
-- `MEM32(esp+8)` instead of `MEM32(esp+4)` -- verified by recomputing the
caller's `PUSH32` sequence at `sub_000524DA`'s `loc_00052546`, which pushes
`MEM32(ebp+0xC)` (i.e. `ctx2`) immediately before the indirect call; fixed
and reconfirmed against the same run's own `PsCreateSystemThreadEx #4` log
line.)

### sub_00039566's outer loop: iterates a bounded number of times, then the whole call chain stalls

`sub_00039566` (884 bytes, frame-delta smoothing) contains an outer
accumulation loop (`loc_000396B6` .. `loc_000398AC`) that: enters a
critical section via a singleton's vtable slot `+0x118`
(`MEM32(0x5E3E2C)`), walks a 3-element list at `ctx2+0x14`
(`count = MEM32(ctx2+0x18)`, observed constant at 3 across all runs),
calls seven further subroutines (`sub_002E65A4`, `sub_00038F96` twice,
`sub_004BB930`, `sub_000368A5`, `sub_0049CC50`), leaves the critical
section via slot `+0x11C`, calls `sub_00052D5A`, then checks
`MEM32(0x5A6F20) > accumulator` to decide whether to loop again.

A live iteration counter (temporary) shows this loop running a bounded,
small number of times (observed stopping at iteration 20 in one run, at
iteration 7 in another, both times still well inside a live, non-crashed
process) and then producing **no further iteration-counter output at all**
for the remainder of the run (up to several more minutes observed) --
i.e. the outer loop is not spinning forever on its own termination check;
execution stalls somewhere *inside* one particular iteration's call chain
(the critical section, or one of the seven subroutine calls). Finer-grained
checkpoints after each of these calls (`SCDA-DIAG234J`, gated to only log
during iterations 15-30 to avoid flooding the log) have been added and a
run is in progress to pin down exactly which call is the last one reached
before the stall.

### Not yet concluded

The exact subroutine (or the critical-section enter/leave itself) where
execution stalls inside the loop body is still being isolated live; this
entry will be extended once that result lands. No fake signaling, no
manual `SetEvent`, and no skipped wait loop has been used at any point --
consistent with the standing constraint.

## Update 239 (2026-09-22, Claude session takeover): the active transform program's oPos degenerates to a single point because R12 is never written

Picked up mid-session after a context reset; a stale chat history still
carried an already-superseded Bink/thread-4 hypothesis from an early
Update-234 draft. Per instruction, the repository was treated as ground
truth: HEAD unchanged at `23a82e6`, and Codex's own Updates 235-236 had
already reproduced three clean runs disproving that hypothesis and closing
both the video-read and post-thread-4 stall questions. The real state was
already at Update 238 (programmable NV2A vertex path, DRAW_ARRAYS decoded,
first attribute confirmed non-screen-space). This entry continues exactly
from there.

### Register semantics verified directly against the local xemu source

`SC4_xbe_hack/third_party/xemu_0_8_66_source/hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/pgraph.c`
(`DEF_METHOD_INC(NV097, SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM/CONSTANT)`,
`DEF_METHOD(NV097, SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM_LOAD/START)`,
`DEF_METHOD(NV097, SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT_LOAD)`) confirms: `0x1E9C`/`0x1EA4`
set the row/constant load pointer directly from `param`, `0x1EA0` sets the
start PC, and each 32-word upload window (`0x0B00`/`0x0B80`) advances its
pointer only after a complete four-word row (`slot % 4 == 3`). Execution
mode (`0x1E94`, low 2 bits) is 2 for "vertex program", 0 for "fixed
function" per `pgraph/shaders.c:pgraph_get_shader_state`.

### Capture-only implementation, then evaluation

`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c` now captures `program_data[136][4]`,
`program_load`/`program_load_high`, `program_start`, `transform_mode`,
`vsh_constants[192][4]` and `const_written[]`, with new cases for
`0x1E94/0x1E9C/0x1EA0/0x1EA4` and both 32-word upload windows using the
verified pointer logic above. A canonical build and a controlled run
(`RECOMP_PB_EXEC=1 RECOMP_PB_EXEC_VERBOSE=1`) captured, at the first real
draw: `mode=2 start=0 rows_loaded=14` -- a complete, self-contained
14-instruction program, not the false "one-instruction" impression an
earlier, differently-labelled scan log had left (that log predates the
already-fixed `SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM`/`SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT`/
`INLINE_ARRAY` label swap).

### Decoding against xemu's own field table, not guessed

A one-off analysis script (`decode_vsh.py`, scratchpad, not committed)
mirrors `hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/glsl/vsh-prog.c`'s `field_mapping[]`,
`convert_c_register()`, and `mac_opcode_params[]` bit-for-bit and decodes
all 14 rows. Only five opcodes appear: MAC `MUL`/`ADD`/`MAD`, ILU `MOV`/
`RCC`. The program is a plausible vertex transform: `R0`/`R9`/`R10`/`R11`
accumulate `c[163..170] * v0` row by row (a standard split matrix-vector
multiply across four MAC pairs), `oT0..oT3` receive `R11/R10/R0/R9 +
c[166]` (texcoord passthrough), `oD0` is set constant via ILU `MOV` from
`c[96].zzzz`, and `oPos` is written three times: fully at row 4 (`R0 +
c[165]`), then `.xyz` only at row 7 (`R12.xyz * c[58].xyz`), then `.xyz`
again at the final row 13 (`R12.xyz * R1.xxxx + c[59].xyz`, where `R1.x`
comes from a MAC-paired ILU `RCC(R12.w)` at row 6 -- the pairing/R1-forcing
itself checked directly against xemu's `decode_opcode()` routing, not
assumed).

`R12` is read at rows 6, 7, and 13 but written by none of the 14 rows.

### Interpreter built and run; the degenerate-position hypothesis is proven, not just suspected

A minimal capture-only evaluator (`vsh_evaluate_capture_only`,
`nv2a_pb_exec.c`) implementing exactly the five observed opcodes was built
and exercised at draws #1/#10/#50/#200 with three distinct synthetic `v0`
probes, cross-checked row by row against an independent hand calculation
via a temporary trace (`vshtrace`, left in the code gated to one probe).

One self-caught false alarm along the way: the first probe `v0=(0,0,0,1)`
legitimately evaluates to an all-zero row-1 input under the real `xyzz`
swizzle (which never selects `w`), which briefly looked like a broken
interpreter before the trace was pointed at the non-trivial probe
`v0=(1,2,3,1)` instead. With that probe, rows 0-4 compute `oPos` correctly
and vertex-dependently (`R0` after row 2 = `(1.0,-2.25,0,1)`; `oPos` after
row 4 = `(0.9984,-2.2479,0,1)`, a plausible, `v0`-dependent screen
position). Rows 7 and 13 then both overwrite `oPos.xyz` back to `(0,0,0)`,
because `R12` is `(0,0,0,0)` at both points -- confirmed identically at
draw #1, #10, #50, and #200, including after `c[163..168]` had since been
populated by the title, so this is not a warm-up-window artifact.

Cross-checked against `update237_pbscan_runtime.log`: `SET_TRANSFORM_
PROGRAM_LOAD`/`_START` (`0x1E9C`/`0x1EA0`) appear a flat "x2" for the
entire run (no growing counter), while `SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT_LOAD`
(`0x1EA4`) grows continuously (155 to 514+). The program is loaded exactly
once and never replaced or extended by a second load later in the run, so
`R12` is not merely "not yet written" -- it is structurally never written
for the program's entire active lifetime.

### What this proves and what remains open

Proven: for this program, every vertex's final `oPos.xyz` is `(0,0,0)`
regardless of its actual position -- degenerate geometry collapsing onto a
single clip-space point. This is a direct, mechanistic explanation for the
black framebuffer despite a proven-clean command-submission and pixel-write
path (Update 237). Open: why the title never writes `R12` -- whether this
recomp is missing or mis-decoding an earlier opcode/register path that
should populate it (checked against xemu's PGRAPH model, which
zero-initialises all R-registers per vertex unconditionally, same as this
evaluator), or whether real hardware also leaves it zero here and some
other mechanism this bridge does not yet model compensates for it.

Exact next test: trace `R12`'s expected producer statically -- which guest
code path(s) precede this 14-row program's `SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM`/`_LOAD`
sequence, and whether there is a second register write (e.g. an implicit
skinning/normal-transform stage) that a correct model would need to
reproduce before this vertex program runs.

No stub, no fake signal, no skipped step, and no hand-edit to generated
code survives this entry; the only carried-forward change is
`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`'s capture-only transform-program state and
evaluator, plus the diagnostic-labelling and DMA-resolution work already
committed to Codex's prior updates.

## Update 239 continuation: five candidate explanations for the missing R12 producer ruled out by static analysis alone

Before committing to a live xemu comparison, five increasingly specific
candidate explanations for "why does the game never write R12" were checked
directly against the code and the raw XBE, not assumed:

1. A second, later `SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM_LOAD` reloads or extends the
   program -- ruled out: both `0x1E9C` and `0x1EA0` appear a flat "x2" for
   the entire `update237_pbscan_runtime.log` run, versus `0x1EA4`
   (constant load) growing continuously (155 to 514+).
2. A DMA_PUT ring-buffer wraparound silently drops an earlier segment that
   would have written R12 -- a real, previously undocumented bug was found
   in `xbox_memory_layout.c`'s scan loop (it only processes `put > last_put`
   but unconditionally updates `last_put`, so a wrapped segment is lost with
   no retry), but the archived run shows zero wraps across all 505 logged
   `DMA_PUT` samples, so it does not apply here. Left in place as an
   independent, separately worth-fixing finding.
3. An implicit fixed-function skinning stage pre-populates R12 before the
   vertex program runs -- ruled out: xemu's skinning codegen
   (`vsh-ff.c::append_skinning_code`) only exists for `state->fixed_function`
   (mode 0); this program runs in mode 2, where xemu's own model has no such
   preprocessing.
4. A neighbouring shader block, stored as raw data in the XBE right next to
   this program, actually writes R12 but is never loaded by this recomp --
   the exact 14 rows were located byte-for-byte in
   `build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/default.xbe` at file offset
   `0x5C6680` (found via a literal little-endian dword search, not
   assumed). The on-disk layout does not match the runtime `program_load`
   order: an unrelated shader block with additional texture-coordinate
   writes sits between rows of this program, including one structurally
   similar instruction (`MUL R12.xyzz * c[58].xyzz` paired with
   `RCC(R12.w)`, writing `oPos.xyz`) that also only reads R12. A systematic,
   16-byte-aligned scan of a 64 KB window (4096 candidate rows) around this
   cluster for any instruction whose effective write target (accounting for
   the MAC/ILU R1-forcing pairing rule) is R12 found zero matches.
5. A register-index remap (analogous to `convert_c_register` for constants)
   shifts the real target index -- ruled out: `vsh-prog.c` has no equivalent
   correction for `FLD_A_R`/`FLD_B_R`/`FLD_C_R_HIGH+LOW`/`FLD_OUT_R`;
   register indices are used as extracted.

With all five ruled out, no remaining explanation is reachable through
static analysis of the code, the raw XBE data, or xemu's source alone. The
next test needs a live xemu run: not a pushbuffer byte comparison (both
recomp and xemu load identical bytes from the same XBE, per point 4 above),
but checking with `-s -S`/gdbstub whether xemu's guest code takes the exact
same `SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM_START` path for this object, or whether a
control-flow divergence somewhere upstream in this recomp skips a setup
call that real hardware/xemu reaches. Context from an earlier session
(memory note `xemu-smoke-aa-render-bug`, user-confirmed): SCDA already
renders visibly and correctly under xemu well into actual gameplay, so the
open question is specifically where that correct run's R12-equivalent value
comes from, not whether xemu renders at all.

logic `nv2a_pb_exec.c` uses. This is a from-scratch Python re-implementation
of that capture logic against xemu's live guest memory, not a reuse of our
own (known-buggy-on-wrap) C scanner.

Result, in under 2 seconds and 88 watchpoint hits from cold reset: xemu
loads the **exact same 14-row program**, word for word, at draws #9-12
(`mode=2 start=0 rows_loaded=14`) that our recomp's canonical run captured
at draw #1/#10/#50/#200. A genuine DMA_PUT ring-buffer wrap did occur once
during the run (hit #74) and was correctly detected and skipped by the new
script -- an independent live confirmation of the wraparound bug Update 239
already found by static analysis, with no effect on this result since the
match was already established either side of it. xemu was killed cleanly
(`taskkill`) from its already-halted state -- no `continue`, no input, no
save.

This directly answers the comparison's first two questions with yes: xemu
takes the same `SET_TRANSFORM_PROGRAM_START=0` path and loads the same 14
instructions. There is no semantic difference between xemu and this recomp
in the pushbuffer/program itself.

**The decisive finding, on the third question ("is R12 genuinely
unwritten/uninitialized there"): the premise was wrong, not just unproven.**
R12 is not a 13th general-purpose temp register on NV2A hardware at all --
it is a direct hardware alias for `oPos`. Two independent sources agree,
not one:

1. xemu's own GLSL codegen
   (`SC4_xbe_hack/third_party/xemu_0_8_66_source/hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/glsl/
   vsh-prog.c:605`): `#define R12 oPos  /* R12 is a mirror of oPos */` --
   every read or write of "R12" in the compiled shader is literally the
   same storage as `oPos`, which starts each vertex at `(0,0,0,1)`
   (`vsh.c:57`), not `(0,0,0,0)`.
2. **Our own, already-shipping** `src/d3d/d3d8_vsh.c` (lines 522, 602,
   955-957) already implements the identical alias correctly (`/* R12 is
   aliased to oPos on NV2A */`, `#define R12 oPos`). This was already
   known and correctly modeled elsewhere in this project -- just not in the
   brand-new `vsh_evaluate_capture_only` diagnostic interpreter this
   session built.

This refutes Update 239's central claim ("the game never fills R12, so
oPos collapses to a constant point every vertex, explaining the black
framebuffer"). The interpreter had a modeling bug (treating R12 as an
independent, never-written register instead of a live mirror of oPos), not
evidence of a real hardware/recomp divergence. Rows 6/7/13 read back
whatever `oPos` currently holds (already vertex-dependent from row 4
onward) -- a valid, intentional "read position, refine, write back"
pattern, not degenerate geometry.

**Fix applied (corrects the diagnostic interpreter's own bug; not a shader
patch, not a fake value):** `vsh_read_slot()` in `src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`
now takes the current `opos` value as a parameter and returns it for
register index 12 instead of `r[12]`; the R-register write-back path
(`mac_mask`/`ilu_mask` branch) symmetrically writes to `opos` instead of
`r[12]` when the target register is 12. Rebuilt canonically
(`build/scda_upgrade`, clean) and re-ran with `RECOMP_PB_EXEC_VERBOSE=1`:
the trace now correctly shows row 7 reading the real oPos value written by
row 4 for its `a` operand (`a=(0.9984,3.0021,0.0000,0.0000)` at draw #1,
exactly `opos.xyzz` after row 4) instead of the previous `(0,0,0,0)`.

**Noticed in passing, not chased further:** the final `oPos` after rows
7/13 still lands near zero in this trace, because the interpreter's paired
MAC/ILU forced-R1 routing (row 6 -> R1, per Update 239's decode) is gated
on `ilu_mask != 0`, which may not match xemu's `decode_opcode()` if that
forced assignment is unconditional there. Left open: irrelevant to this
round's actual question (is R12 a hardware alias, yes/no) and moot for now
since this interpreter is not in the real rendering path anyway (next
point).

**The more important finding, which supersedes the original question:**
`raster_batch()`/`draw_primitive()` in `nv2a_pb_exec.c` **deliberately and
documentedly** skip any batch that needs a vertex program executed (own
file header, lines 10-17): `batch_is_screen_space()` returns false ->
`s_gpu.batches_untransformed++`, nothing rasterized. Only already
screen-space, flat-shaded 2D geometry (UI/HUD) is actually drawn. The
comment explicitly points to an "upgrade path" in
`src/nv2a/nv2a_pgraph_d3d11.c` for real vertex-program/texture/depth
execution. That file exists (652 lines) but, on inspection, currently
handles only 2D menu rendering (`INLINE_ARRAY`, textured quads, 640x480
screen space, comment says "Menu rendering profile") -- **no reference to
R12, oPos, or vertex programs anywhere in it**. So no code path currently
executes NV2A vertex programs for visible rendering at all; the new
`vsh_evaluate_capture_only` interpreter is pure diagnostics, never called
from `raster_batch()`/`draw_primitive()`.

**Reassessed overall picture:** the R12/degenerate-geometry explanation
chain built up across Updates 237-239 was a diagnostic artifact, not a real
rendering cause. The actual, simpler, already-documented reason SCDA's 3D
gameplay geometry does not render yet is: **no code path exists yet that
actually executes NV2A vertex programs and rasterizes their result** --
neither in `nv2a_pb_exec.c` (documented as skipped) nor in the intended
D3D11 upgrade path (2D menus only so far). This is a missing capability /
open scope item, not a bug to patch.

**Proven (Update 240):** (1) xemu and this recomp reach the identical
start point and the identical 14-row program for this object, byte for
byte. (2) R12 is a documented hardware alias for oPos, not an independent
"unwritten" register -- confirmed by both xemu's source and this project's
own pre-existing `d3d8_vsh.c` translator. (3) The diagnostic interpreter's
modeling bug is fixed and re-verified. (4) `raster_batch()` skips
vertex-program batches deliberately and by design; the D3D11 upgrade path
currently covers only 2D menu rendering.

**Refuted:** Update 239's central claim that the game never fills R12, so
oPos collapses to a constant point and that explains the black framebuffer.
R12/oPos semantics are fine; that is not the cause.

**Open (restated more precisely):** no code path currently executes NV2A
vertex programs for 3D geometry. The next useful work is not another
diagnostic pass but an architecture/scope decision: (a) extend the existing
CPU interpreter (`vsh_evaluate_capture_only`, now with the correct R12
alias) from capture-only into real execution feeding `raster_batch()`/
`fetch_attr()` (remaining loose end: resolve the paired-routing detail
noted above, add clip/screen-space conversion), or (b) extend
`nv2a_pgraph_d3d11.c` with real vertex-program translation (could reuse/
adapt the already-correct, hardware-accurate translator in
`src/d3d/d3d8_vsh.c`, which already gets the R12 alias right for the D3D8
code path). This choice should be made before the next implementation
round, since it sets that session's scope.

**Artifacts:** the gdbstub comparison script was run from the scratchpad
(not committed; full result captured above);
`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`'s R12-alias fix (tracked); a fresh canonical
build and verification run in `scda_runtime.log`
(`build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/`). No processes left running.
**Model tier:** STRONG remained sufficient -- the decisive finding came
from two independently agreeing primary sources (xemu source, this
project's own `d3d8_vsh.c`), no persistent contradiction.

## Update 241: the CPU vertex-program interpreter is now a real render path
## (built, tested, wired in) -- the new, precisely diagnosed blocker is a
## pushbuffer-capture gap, not the interpreter

This round's assignment, given Update 240's finding that R12 is a documented
oPos alias and that no code path executes vertex programs for real
rendering yet: extend the existing CPU interpreter into an actual render
path, correctness before performance, general NV2A model (no SCDA special
cases), with early regression tests.

**Interpreter extracted into its own testable module.** `src/kernel/
vsh_interp.h`/`.c` (new, tracked) now holds the complete NV2A vertex-program
semantics, decoupled from `s_gpu`/pushbuffer state: all 13 MAC opcodes
(MOV/MUL/ADD/MAD/DP3/DPH/DP4/DST/MIN/MAX/SLT/SGE/ARL) and all 7 ILU opcodes
(MOV/RCP/RCC/RSQ/EXP/LOG/LIT), each formula ported directly from xemu's
actual GLSL function bodies (`vsh-prog.c`'s `_MOV/_MUL/.../_LIT`), not a
paraphrase of them. Also added A0-register / FLD_A0X-relative constant
addressing for completeness, even though SCDA's captured program does not
use it.

**A real correction to Update 239's write-back model, checked directly
against `decode_opcode()`'s actual branch structure, not just re-described:**
the earlier assumption ("ILU is forced to R1 when ILU owns the shared
O-output") was wrong. In fact: ILU's R-register write is ALWAYS forced to R1
whenever a non-NOP MAC is paired with it, regardless of which of the two
owns the shared muxed O-output. MAC's own R-write is dropped entirely only
when paired AND its own target register is also R1 (not on every pairing).
This correction is covered by its own regression test
(`test_paired_mac_ilu_routing`).

**Regression tests (`tests/vsh_interp/test_main.c`, new, tracked; build
instructions in the file header).** A bit-exact row encoder (`enc_row`, the
exact field-by-field inverse of `vsh_interp.c`'s own `vshf()` reads, not a
second guess at the bit layout) builds synthetic instructions for seven
groups: (1) the R12/oPos alias, including a round trip through R1 and the
shared O-write path, (2) temp registers, including mask persistence across
rows, (3) constants (the bank/offset encoding maps onto a flat 0..191 index;
`vsh_convert_c_register` turned out to be algebraically an identity function
on 8-bit input -- checked, not assumed), (4) vector/scalar ops (DP3/DP4/
MIN/MAX/SLT/MAD, plus ILU RCP/RSQ including the RSQ(0)=+Inf special case),
(5) output registers (the shared muxed write only fires when FLD_OUT_MUX
actually names an active slot), (6) the corrected paired MAC/ILU routing,
(7) clean stop when FLD_FINAL is never reached. All 33 checks pass (built
with `cl.exe` via vcvars64; hit and worked around a Git-Bash/MSYS quirk
along the way -- a leading `/c` gets path-rewritten by MSYS, so `cmd.exe`
invocations need `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1`). The first run found two real bugs in
the *test*, not the interpreter: FLD_V and FLD_CONST are each a single field
shared across every operand slot on real hardware -- two different
v-attributes cannot be read by one instruction, which is a hardware
constraint the encoder now mirrors, not a bug to fix.

**Wired into `raster_batch()` (`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`).** Batches that
fail `batch_is_screen_space()` are no longer unconditionally skipped. When
`transform_mode==2` and a program is loaded, `raster_batch_vertex_program()`
-> `transform_vertex()` runs: real attribute fetch for v0..v15
(`fetch_vattr`), program execution via `vsh_run_program`, perspective divide
(`oPos.xy / oPos.w`), the standard D3D viewport transform onto the tracked
clip rect, colour from `oD0` (hardware default (0,0,0,1) if the program
never writes it -- not an SCDA special case). A vertex that cannot be placed
(unimplemented opcode, `|w|<1e-8`) drops only its triangle, not the whole
batch. New counter `s_gpu.batches_vertex_program`; the report line is
updated. The existing 2D screen-space path (`raster_batch_screen_space()`)
is untouched.

**Canonical build:** `build/scda_upgrade` clean (`cmake --build`
regenerated the VS projects automatically once `vsh_interp.c` was added to
`src/kernel/CMakeLists.txt`).

**Runtime test -- milestone not yet reached, but the cause is now precisely
located, not guessed.** Controlled run with `RECOMP_PB_EXEC_VERBOSE=1
RECOMP_FB_DUMP=fbtest`. After roughly 200 draws: **292 batches now actually
run through the vertex-program interpreter** (previously: unconditionally
skipped) -- the structural part of this round's assignment is done. But
still **0 triangles drawn**. Hand-decoded the raw instruction words
completely (not guessed) to see exactly what each field reads: row 7
multiplies `oPos.xyz *= c[58].xyz` (not `R1`, as Update 239 assumed), row 13
(final) computes `oPos.xyz = oPos.xyz(after row 7) * R1.xxxx + c[59].xyz`.
`c[58]` and `c[59]` appear in NONE of the four program/constant dumps (draws
#1/#10/#50/#200) among the constants actually seen written (only
0,1,60-62,96,97 have ever been observed) -- they sit at the hardware default
of 0 for the entire observed run, so row 7 multiplies the position to zero
and row 13 cannot recover it. **This is a direct, mechanical confirmation
that the interpreter computes correctly** -- it produces exactly the result
its actual known inputs force, not a miscalculation.

**Most likely cause (well-reasoned, not yet conclusively proven) -- a gap
in pushbuffer capture, not the interpreter:** `src/kernel/
xbox_memory_layout.c`'s DMA_PUT diff-polling (a separate `nv2a_ack_thread`,
not touched this round) only scans
`if (last_put && put > last_put)` -- `last_put` starts at 0 as a sentinel,
so the very first segment up to the first actually-observed `put` value is
NEVER scanned. The canonical run confirms this directly: the very first
logged `DMA_PUT` value is `0x00000000`, the next already `0x0400A000` -- a
large jump that could plausibly have swallowed early, one-time constant
uploads (e.g. exactly `c[58]`/`c[59]`, immediately before the `c[60..62]`
block that WAS captured) before our polling thread ever got scheduled.
Polling itself also depends on OS scheduling of that thread (no fixed
cadence), which would explain ongoing gaps beyond just the first one.

**Proven:** (1) The interpreter now correctly implements the full MAC/ILU
opcode set (regression tests plus manual recomputation of the real 14-row
program agree exactly). (2) The R12/oPos alias and the corrected paired
write-back routing are implemented and verified correctly. (3)
`raster_batch()` now actually executes vertex programs instead of skipping
them (292 batches this round). (4) The current "0 triangles" result for
THIS early object is a correct consequence of the actually-captured
(incomplete) constants, not a malfunction in the new code.

**Refuted:** That the interpreter itself is the reason geometry is still
missing -- it has been verified twice (synthetic regression tests, manual
field-by-field recomputation of the real program) and demonstrably produces
the mathematically correct result for the inputs it actually receives.

**Open / exact next test:** confirm whether the pushbuffer-capture gap
actually swallows `c[58]`/`c[59]`. Concretely: instrument a write-triggered
capture instead of time-based polling for `NV097_SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT`/
`DMA_PUT` (or, as a quick experiment, also scan the very first segment from
an assumed ring-buffer base) and check whether `c[58]`/`c[59]` then show a
nonzero value. If yes: cause confirmed, the real fix is replacing/
augmenting the periodic diff-poll with a mechanism that does not lose the
first burst. If no (still zero even with full capture): open again, since
this early object might then genuinely be invisible at this point on real
hardware/xemu too (Update 240's xemu confirmation only covered the
program/row content, not this specific constant's value) -- the "first
visible geometry" milestone would then need to target a later/different
object whose required constants are demonstrably fully captured.
`xbox_memory_layout.c` deliberately NOT touched this round -- it already
carries other, not-mine changes, and a fix to the core capture mechanism
deserves its own carefully verified round rather than a quick patch tacked
onto the end of this one.

**Relevant artifacts:** `src/kernel/vsh_interp.h`/`.c` (new, tracked);
`tests/vsh_interp/test_main.c`, `build_and_run.bat` (new, tracked);
`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c` (render-path integration, tracked); the
canonical test run in `build/scda_upgrade/bin/RelWithDebInfo/
scda_runtime.log` (`run2_stdout.log` alongside it). The manual field
decoding of all 14 rows was done with a one-off Python snippet, not saved

the periodic DMA_PUT diff-poll in `xbox_memory_layout.c`, which only
decides WHEN a segment gets scanned, never what happens once it is): for
every `SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT` write with `const_load` in [55,62], the

pushbuffer address (`va` -- `nv2a_pb_exec_method`/`nv2a_pb_scan.c` gained a
`va` parameter for this, the one call site updated), current DMA_GET/

dwords) get written, immediately followed by `PROGRAM_START`. Every `DRAW`

`c[58].written=0 c[59].written=0`. This is the direct, write-triggered
evidence for case B, not just an absence inferred from incomplete polling:

and would have seen a write to 58/59 anywhere in the scanned stream.

**Independent xemu cross-check (same method as Update 240, new script
`xemu_c58c59_trace.py` in the scratchpad, not committed).** Launched xemu

[55,62]. Ran gap-free (a hardware watchpoint, no polling, no sampling gap

## Update 247: first title-owned visible geometry; texture/pixel evaluation is
## now the blocker

The xemu source audit exposed three general NV2A gaps in the small PB executor.
`SET_VIEWPORT_SCALE` (`0x0AF0..0x0AFC`) writes vertex constant c[58] and
`SET_VIEWPORT_OFFSET` (`0x0A20..0x0A2C`) writes c[59]; these values do not have
to arrive through `SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT`. NV2A vertex programs also leave
oPos.xy in screen space: xemu's `vsh-prog.c` converts that result back to host
clip space and multiplies by w only to cancel the host GPU's later divide. A
CPU rasterizer must consume oPos.xy directly. Finally, the title's actual
attribute-0 type is UB_D3D, a normalized BGRA byte format that xemu binds as
`GL_BGRA`; type 0 was previously rejected by `fetch_attr()`. Programmable mode
must also take precedence over the screen-space heuristic, because normalized
0..1 shader inputs otherwise look like valid pixel coordinates.

The write-triggered Update-245 run captured, immediately before draw #1,
c[58]=(320,-240,16777215,0) and c[59]=(320.53125,240.53125,0,0). With UB_D3D
decoded, the four inputs become (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1). The final
controlled 24-second run (PID 47708, deliberately stopped, no crash) produced
a 640x480 screen-space spread from the real program, ran 283 batches through
the vertex-program interpreter, and rasterized 566 triangles without any
unmapped/refusal error. `update247_vshpath_000.bmp` is the first title-owned
visible geometry: a white full-screen region with a black triangular shape;
`_001.bmp` is black. This is not yet a correct game frame because texturing,
interpolation, and pixel combiners are still unimplemented. All 33 standalone
vertex-interpreter regression checks pass. Canonical EXE timestamp 2026-09-22
23:07:48, SHA-256
`5B33EA1031C45A71C198B9E81BC2695A8A3A7BAF07F80D1E95C0CAC1D9625C14`.

Proven: vertex program, viewport constants, UB_D3D input, and CPU raster path
now produce title geometry. Refuted: Update 242's inference that c[58]/c[59]
were effectively unwritten/zero; only the generic constant method did not
write them, while the dedicated viewport methods did. Also refuted: a Bink or
vertex-program stall as the current blocker. Open: which texture stage and
pixel-combiner configuration the first full-screen quad uses, and whether its
source is linear or swizzled. The exact next test captures all four stages'
texture offset/format/address/control/image-rect state plus oT0..oT3 for the
first draw, resolves and bounds-checks the texture DMA range, and dumps a few
source texels before implementing the smallest observed sampler/combiner path.
Artifacts: `update245_viewport_000.bmp` through `_003.bmp`,
`update247_vshpath_000.bmp`/`_001.bmp`, and current `scda_runtime.log`. No
relevant process remains. Model tier remains STRONG.

least draw #1400. The old diagnostic simply keeps reporting the last state of

This directly refutes a missing final 1,784-byte read as the current blocker
and restores the three-run Update-235 interpretation: the unchanged values are

The actual open problem remains the renderer. In particular, observing no

## Update 257: source-texture writer found live -- wrong alias watched, not a
## missing thread; writer is very likely the original game's own MMX YUV-to-
## RGB Bink color-conversion routine

Picked this up after syncing against a large amount of work done since this
agent's last turn (Updates 245-256c, not previously in this context): the
Update 244 Bink-stall conclusion was refuted (Update 245) -- the game keeps
progressing after that log snapshot, reaching first visible title geometry
(Update 247), first real textures (Update 250), a fixed primitive-decode
off-by-one that revealed the complete Ubisoft logo (Updates 253-254), and
finally isolated the remaining olive/green tint and blocky artifacts to the
*source* surface itself (Update 255e, physical `0x04464000`), not the
sampler/combiner. Updates 256a-c built a CDB hardware watch on that source
address's "high"/contiguous alias (`0x84464000`) and got no hit, concluding
(256c) that the writer must run on a thread that didn't exist yet when the
watch was armed.

**Two real methodology bugs found and fixed before the actual breakthrough.**
Reproducing 256c's own recommended next test (`~*e` on all existing threads
plus a `KERNEL32!BaseThreadInitThunk` hook for new ones) appeared to hang for
several minutes (CPU time kept climbing, but `nv2a_pb_exec_report` was never
hit). Rather than concluding "too much watchpoint overhead," the actual cause
was found: `RECOMP_PB_EXEC=1` was missing from the CDB launch environment --
the exact same mistake Update 255d already documented for its own early
runs. Without it, `nv2a_pb_scan_report()`/`nv2a_pb_exec_report()` are never
called at all, so that breakpoint can never fire no matter how long the wait.
With the variable set correctly, the same all-threads approach completed in
under a minute -- there was no overhead problem.

**A plain, watch-free `~*kb` snapshot at the first report** (no live
watchpoints at all) showed the full thread landscape: the main thread deep
in `sub_004A12B0` (the already-known, now-working NV2A pushbuffer kick,
category `game_render`), three idle generic `ntdll!TppWorkerThread` pool
workers, this project's own `nv2a_ack_thread` (naturally on the report
breakpoint itself), and two Bink pool workers via
`bridge_run_thread_inline`/`sub_004BBE90`, both idle in
`NtWaitForSingleObjectEx` at that instant. None was caught writing a pixel
at that specific moment, but this gave the complete thread inventory needed
for the next, more targeted tests.

**Media Foundation hypothesis raised and definitively refuted.** Since
`MFPlat.DLL`/`MFReadWrite.dll` load early in every run, a plausible theory
was that a hardware-accelerated Media Foundation decoder writes raw,
unconverted YUV bytes directly into a D3D11 texture via GPU/DMA (invisible
to CPU hardware watches, and matching the olive tint one would expect from
misread YUV bytes). Reading `src/video/video_pump.c`/`video_player.c`
disproves this outright: that module opens a **completely separate window**
("XboxRecompVideo") with its **own** D3D8 device and present cycle. Its own
file header says so explicitly: *"Nothing here reads or writes guest memory
and nothing runs on the guest's thread."* It is a purely cosmetic,
guest-independent FMV convenience feature (likely for intro videos played
via `xbox_VideoPlayFile()`), unrelated to the guest texture surface under
investigation.

**Breakthrough -- the tiled-aperture alias test.** `src/kernel/
xbox_memory_layout.c`'s own architecture (already the root cause of a
*different* corruption once before, Updates 224/225) maps contiguous
physical memory through at least two separate host views of the same file-
mapping section: the standard window (`XBOX_CONTIG_BASE=0x80000000`, the
only one watched so far) and the "tiled aperture"
(`XBOX_TILED_BASE=0xF0000000`, the same physical page under a *different*
host virtual address). x86 hardware watchpoints watch virtual addresses, not
physical ones -- a writer going through the tiled-aperture address can never
be caught by a watch armed only on the contiguous-window address, even
though both views show the same content once written.

A new script (`tools/debug/cdb_update257_tiled_alias_watch.txt`) computed
`0xF4464000 + g_xbox_mem_offset` (the same physical page `0x04464000`
through the tiled aperture) alongside the existing high/contig watch, on
every thread. With `RECOMP_PB_EXEC=1` correctly set: **74 hits on the tiled
alias versus only 2 on the contig alias**, all with the identical value
`0x7F7F7F12`, all at PC `0x00007ff7eb6a3190` (XBE address
`sub_004C6140+0x950`), all on the same thread. At the final report both
aliases agree (`high_bg=tiled_bg=0x7F7F7F12`) -- the two views do
synchronize correctly; the earlier watch was simply on the wrong one.

**The writing function, read in full**
(`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_0027.c:69970-70030`,
XBE address around `0x004C5xxx-0x004C6140`): an **MMX SIMD block**
(`PADDW`/`PADDSW`/`PUNPCKLWD`/`PUNPCKHWD`/`PSLLD`/`POR`) that reads two
lookup tables (`MEM32(eax*4+0x6C0698)`, `MEM32(eax*4+0x6C0E98)`), combines
them with packed-word adds, shifts results into the G/B byte lanes of a
packed 32-bit pixel (`PSLLD 8`/`PSLLD 16`), ORs them together, and stores
the finished pixel with `MMX_STORE`. This is a textbook, table-driven
**YUV/YCbCr-to-RGB conversion** pattern, exactly what era-appropriate Bink
decoder reference implementations use. The call chain
(`sub_004C6140 <- sub_004C2180 <- sub_004C6090 <- sub_004B9F20 <-
sub_004BB170 <- sub_00038F96 <- sub_000398DA <- sub_00039A05`) is a
faithful 1:1 recompilation of the original game's own code, not a
translation bug (no TODO gaps on this write path besides the already-known-
harmless `psubusw` placeholders elsewhere in the same block).

**Reading `0x7F7F7F12`:** as packed ARGB, A=0x7F (~50% alpha), R=0x7F,
G=0x7F, B=0x12 -- high red/green, very low blue, half-transparent alpha.
Qualitatively this matches the observed olive/green tint with bright
patches (a 50%-alpha blend of a dark olive value over a brighter background
looks exactly like that). That **74 writes produced the identical value**
points more toward a **constant/degenerate Y/U/V input** than a bug in this
specific conversion routine -- real, varying frame content run through a
correct conversion would not yield the same output 74 times in a row.

**Proven:** (1) the source texture is written through the tiled-aperture
address, not (primarily) the contiguous address -- explaining why every
Update 256 watch found nothing. (2) Media Foundation is not the writer;
`video_pump.c` is a fully separate, guest-memory-independent feature. (3)
the actual writer is the original game's own MMX-optimized YUV-to-RGB
conversion function (`sub_004C6140`), correctly recompiled 1:1. (4) both
memory aliases do synchronize correctly (no aliasing bug in our own memory
management here).

**Refuted:** (a) Update 256c's theory that the writer runs on a thread that
did not exist yet at boot -- it ran the whole time on an already-watched
thread, just under the wrong address. (b) this round's own Media Foundation
hypothesis. (c) that the all-threads watch strategy itself is too slow to be
practical -- the real bug was the missing environment variable.

**Open / exact next test:** do not patch the conversion function itself (it
is original code and looks correct). Go one level up instead: read
`sub_004C2180`/`sub_004C6090`/`sub_004B9F20` to find the actual Y/U/V source
feeding `sub_004C6140` -- is the input buffer real, UMD/Bink-stream-
decompressed frame data, or is the chain at this point reading a not-yet-
filled (zeroed or placeholder-preset) intermediate buffer? Since
`sub_004BB170`/`sub_004B9F20` sit in the call stack near the already-known
Bink I/O chain from Updates 234-236 (`sub_004B8F10`/`sub_004B9000`/
`sub_004BBD90`), first check whether this is that same or an adjacent Bink
decode path, and whether the associated Bink frame has actually produced a
real decompressed frame yet at this very early point (first report, very
early draw). Concrete next step: set a hardware read watch (`ba r4`) on
whatever source address `sub_004C6140` reads its Y/U/V input from (read via
`kb`/`dv` at its entry to get the exact register/stack argument), and check
whether the source itself already holds constant `0x7F7F7F12`-like bytes
(pointing further upstream, into Bink decode/UMD read) or genuine varying
image data (pointing at this conversion's own address/table-lookup math
instead).

**Relevant artifacts:** `tools/debug/cdb_update257_allthreads_snapshot.txt`,
`cdb_update257_targeted_watch.txt`, `cdb_update257_tiled_alias_watch.txt`

## Update 258: at least one of the three source streams feeding sub_004C6140
## is a constant placeholder chroma plane (0x80 repeated), not real decoded
## image data -- a direct, mechanical explanation for the color deviation

Building on Update 257 (writer function `sub_004C6140` identified, three
source pointers held in global variables `0x6BF278`/`0x6BF280`/`0x6BF284`,
each a normal guest virtual address needing the usual `+g_xbox_mem_offset`
translation): read all three source pointers directly at the entry of the
first call to `sub_004C6140` (before any conversion work happens):
`srcA=0x01222440`, `srcB=0x0126a240`, `srcC=0x0125bc40`.

**Methodology note worth keeping for future CDB scripts in this project.**
Several intermediate attempts failed with `Bad register error`. The cause
was mundane but easy to miss: **user-defined CDB pseudo-registers (`$t0`...)
are limited to a small range** -- numbers from roughly `$t20` upward are
already invalid. Nested `poi()` expressions were repeatedly (and wrongly)
suspected as the problem; the actual issue was simply picking register
numbers too high. The exact same approach worked cleanly the moment it used
`$t1`-`$t7` instead.

Inspecting `srcA`/`srcB` via `db` still hit an unresolved address-
computation quirk in the script itself (the high 32 bits `db` displayed did
not match the expected `g_xbox_mem_offset` value, likely a register-
assignment edge case not tracked down in the remaining time available).
**`srcC`, however, was read cleanly with a correctly-formatted address**
(`00007000\`0125bc40`) and shows **nothing but the byte value `0x80`,
consistently across at least 32 bytes read.**

**Reading this:** `0x80` (128) is the canonical "neutral/colorless"
placeholder value for a chrominance component in YUV-style encoding (U=V=128
means "no color shift"). Per the disassembly already read in Update 257,
`srcC` is read byte-by-byte through `ebx` with a stride of 2 (a classic
interleaved-chroma access pattern) and feeds one of the four lookup tables
(`0x6C0698`/`0x6C0E98`/`0x6C0298`/`0x6C0A98`) that `sub_004C6140`'s MMX
block folds into the final pixel value. A fully constant `0x80` plane as ONE
of the inputs plainly explains why the output value (`0x7F7F7F12`, Update
257) stayed identical across all 74 observed writes: at least one channel of
the computation is literally constant across the whole observed surface,
regardless of whether the other two sources (`srcA`/`srcB`, presumably
luma/index data) vary or not.

**Proven:** at least one of the three source streams feeding the pixel
conversion function is a constant `0x80` plane at the time of the first
call, not real, varying decoded image data. This is a direct, mechanical
(partial) explanation for the color deviation observed since Update 254.

**Refuted:** that the color deviation necessarily requires a math bug in
`sub_004C6140`'s MMX conversion itself -- a correct conversion function fed
degenerate input produces an equally wrong but internally consistent
result.

**Open / exact next test:** (1) fix the address-computation issue for
`srcA`/`srcB` in the next attempt (e.g. verify each `r $tN = ...` assignment
immediately with its own `.printf` before building the next one) and check
whether those two streams are also constant/degenerate or contain real,
varying data -- this decides whether only the chroma source is missing
(e.g. a Bink chroma plane that stays empty for this early frame/object,
either intentionally or due to its own bug) or the entire frame source is
degenerate. (2) go one level up
(`sub_004C2180`/`sub_004C6090`/`sub_004B9F20`/`sub_004BB170`) and find where
`0x6BF284` (the `srcC` pointer) gets its value from -- does it permanently
point at a static, intentionally-neutral default buffer (in which case
`0x80` would actually be CORRECT behavior for an object with no chrominance
of its own, e.g. a plain grayscale/alpha overlay, and the color deviation
would have a different cause), or at a Bink ring buffer that simply has not
been filled yet at this early point (in which case it is a genuine timing/
ordering bug in the decode path)?

**Relevant artifacts:** `tools/debug/cdb_update258e_source_probe.txt` (the
last failing intermediate attempt, documents the `$t20+` register bug),
`cdb_update258f_source_probe.txt` (the working version, trackable but
currently untracked like other tools/debug diagnostics); matching
`update258e_source_probe_out.log`/`update258f_source_probe_out.log`
(`...f...` holds the decisive `0x80` finding). No processes left running.
No code changed this round (diagnosis only). **Model tier:** STRONG
remained sufficient.

## Update 259: root cause of the color deviation found and fixed -- missing
## psubusw/paddusw MMX opcodes in the translator, not Update 258's constant
## chroma source

While tracing `sub_004C2180`/`sub_004C6090` (the callers of `sub_004C6140`)
to find where the `srcC` pointer from Update 258 gets its value, a much
more direct culprit turned up in `sub_004C6140` itself: not one but **four
`psubusw` instructions** were left as untranslated `/* TODO: ... */`
comments, exactly where the luma/chroma intermediates get corrected by a
bias vector (`mm7`) after the color-matrix multiply, before being packed
into R/G/B/A. The pattern `PADDSW(mm, mm7)` followed by `PSUBUSW(mm, mm7)`
is the standard fixed-point YUV->RGB trick: add with signed saturation,
then subtract back with unsigned saturation (which also floors the result
at zero). A grep across the whole generated codebase found **56 such gaps
in two files** -- a systematic translator gap, not a one-off.

**Root cause:** `tools/recomp/lifter.py`'s `_MMX_BINARY` table had
`paddusb`/`psubusb` (byte-sized saturating add/sub) but was missing the
**word-sized variants `paddusw`/`psubusw`** entirely -- both in the
translation table and as a runtime macro in `templates/runtime/recomp_types.h`.
Without the second half of the clamp trick, the added bias stayed baked
into every color channel: a per-channel-different additive error, which
shows up as a color cast rather than a uniform brightness shift -- an exact
match for the observed olive/green tint.

**Fix:** added a `recomp_sat_u16()` helper plus `MMX_PADDUSW`/`MMX_PSUBUSW`
macros to `recomp_types.h` (mirroring the existing byte-sized variants),
and added `"paddusw": "MMX_PADDUSW", "psubusw": "MMX_PSUBUSW"` to
`lifter.py`'s `_MMX_BINARY` table. Ran a full pipeline regen
(`py -3 -m tools.recomp ... --all --split 1000 ...`, 28159/28162 functions,
0 failed) -- all 56 TODO gaps disappeared; `sub_004C6140` now contains real
`MMX_PSUBUSW(...)` calls instead of comments.

**Two build obstacles found along the way, both pre-existing and unrelated
to the fix itself:**
1. `tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_types.h` is deliberately
   copied from the template **only once** by the tool (`translator.py`,
   comment: "Never overwritten... Delete it to get the current one back"),
   so a project's hand edits to that copy survive a regen. The regen run
   therefore did not refresh it, and the first rebuild failed with
   `C2440: "int" cannot be converted to "RecompMmx"`. Fixed by manually
   overwriting that copy with the current template (no generated .c file
   touched, no `git clean`).
2. `src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c` already carried unfinished, never-committed
   diagnostic instrumentation from an earlier, undocumented investigation
   (`g_diag235d_*`, `g_diag236_*`) -- declared `extern` and read by a
   periodic debug print, but defined NOWHERE in the repository (confirmed
   via grep and `git diff HEAD`: every line is a pure addition in the
   working tree with no matching definition anywhere). This broke every
   full build/link regardless of the psubusw fix. Removed the dead
   declarations and their two `fprintf` blocks, since they never linked
   and had no writer anywhere. **Unrelated to the color-deviation
   investigation.**

After both fixes: a clean build, `scda_recomp.exe` rebuilt (0 errors).

**Live verification (CDB, freshly built exe):** a lightweight conditional
breakpoint on `scda_recomp!sub_004C6140` (`dwo(0x6BF270+offset) ==
0xF4464000`, the same target surface as Update 257), followed by `gu`
(run until the function returns) and a read of the target address.
**21 out of 21 consecutive hits now read exactly `0x00000000`** (pure
black) -- versus **74 out of 74 reading exactly `0x7F7F7F12`** (olive) in
Update 257 before the fix. A clear, reproducible behavioral change that
matches the mathematical role of the missing `psubusw` precisely: values
that should have floored to black were previously pushed up to a mid-tone
olive by the uncompensated bias.

**Methodology notes (three, worth keeping for future CDB scripts in this
project):**
1. **`poi()` in this x64 host process defaults to an 8-byte read.** Guest
   pointer variables in memory are only 4-byte DWORDs, so
   `r $tN = poi(<guest_addr>+offset)` reads 4 bytes of real data plus 4
   bytes of (usually wrong) neighboring memory as the upper half --
   **this retroactively explains Update 258's still-open srcA/srcB
   anomaly.** Fix: use `dwo(<guest_addr>+offset)` instead of `poi(...)`
   for 4-byte guest values; `poi()` remains correct for genuine 8-byte
   host globals such as `g_xbox_mem_offset` itself.
2. **Line-based breakpoints (`` bp `file.c:line` ``) are unreliable in
   RelWithDebInfo-optimized code** -- the address actually hit did not
   correspond to the expected source line (a store was expected; a load
   from an unrelated line was hit instead). More robust for "has this
   function finished": use `gu` (go-until-return) right after the
   function-entry breakpoint instead of guessing an internal line number.
3. **Hardware watchpoints across every thread (`~*e ba w4 ...` re-armed
   via `bp KERNEL32!BaseThreadInitThunk`) can carry substantial overhead**
   -- one attempt with this method ran for over an hour without a single
   hit, even though the target process was demonstrably still computing
   (~100% CPU per `wmic ... PercentProcessorTime`, not deadlocked).
   Markedly faster: an ordinary conditional breakpoint on the producing
   function that checks the target address in software
   (`dwo(...) == <expected address>`) and `gc`s immediately on a miss --
   this found the same hit in seconds instead of never. Log line growth
   is NOT a reliable liveness signal for a quietly running watch (no new
   threads means no new console lines even while the process is actively
   computing) -- the target process's CPU usage is the right signal.

**Proven:** the missing `psubusw`/`paddusw` MMX opcodes in the translator
are a genuine, codebase-wide translation gap (56 sites) and fixing them
demonstrably and reproducibly changes the runtime behavior of the affected
pixel conversion (21/21 black instead of 74/74 olive at the identical
address).

**Refuted:** that Update 258's constant `0x80` chroma plane was itself the
(sole or primary) cause of the color deviation -- a mathematically correct
conversion with `U=V=128` (neutral) should only ever produce grayscale
under correct bias compensation, never an olive/green cast. The actual
mechanism was the missing `psubusw` clamp, independent of the values in
`srcA`/`srcB`/`srcC`.

**Open / exact next test:** (1) remove or raise the hit cap in
`cdb_update259f_verify_psubusw.txt` and watch more frames to see whether
the value actually transitions from black into real, varying colors
(confirms a fade-in-from-black reading rather than a stuck-at-black bug).
(2) cross-check against xemu as ground truth for whether the very first
logo frames are black there too. (3) run `scda_recomp.exe` with a visible
window through the logo sequence and confirm the olive/green tint is
visually gone -- so far only verified via memory dump, not visually.
(4) Update 258's still-open srcA/srcB question (real vs. degenerate data)
is now secondary given this finding, but remains easy to check with the
corrected `dwo()` method whenever convenient.

**Relevant artifacts:** `templates/runtime/recomp_types.h` and
`tools/recomp/lifter.py` (the actual fix, uncommitted);
`tools/recomp/output/scda_v060/gen/recomp_types.h` (manually resynced);
`src/kernel/kernel_bridge.c` (dead diagnostic code removed);
`tools/debug/recomp_regen_update259_psubusw.log` (regen log, 0 failed);
`tools/debug/build_update259c_psubusw.log` (successful build);
`tools/debug/cdb_update259f_verify_psubusw.txt` +
`update259f_verify_psubusw_out.log` (the decisive 21-hit measurement);
further intermediate attempts `cdb_update259b`-`cdb_update259e_verify_psubusw.txt`
(document the methodology notes above, in particular the `poi()` vs
`dwo()` bug and the `gu`-vs-line-breakpoint finding). No processes left

## Update 260b: xemu ground truth confirms clean rendering; found the first
## semantic difference -- missing NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_* handling, already
## documented in the code itself as a known gap

Task: render the same early frame (Ubisoft logo) in xemu as ground truth;
if xemu is clean, find the FIRST semantic difference, prioritizing the
unhandled pushbuffer methods and the `nonzero_draws=0` discrepancy.

**1. xemu screenshot methodology (new, never needed before):** this xemu
build does **not** support `screendump` over the QEMU monitor protocol
(`-monitor tcp:...`) -- `unknown command: 'screendump'`, likely because
xemu's own SDL-based `-display xemu` backend doesn't hook into the
standard QEMU display surface that `screendump` reads from. Working
substitute: a PowerShell script that finds the xemu window's client area
via `user32.dll` (`GetClientRect`/`ClientToScreen`) and saves it as a PNG
via `System.Drawing.Graphics.CopyFromScreen`
(`tools/debug/...capture_xemu_window.ps1`, `...burst_capture_xemu.ps1`
for a burst). **Timing trap worth keeping:** xemu boots real hardware
emulation extremely fast -- Xbox BIOS logo at ~1s, Ubisoft logo sequence
at ~2.5-3.5s, already at the "Press Start" screen by ~8s. Separate,
sequential PowerShell invocations (~1s assembly-load overhead each) are
too slow for this and miss the Ubisoft logo entirely; a single PowerShell
process with an internal capture loop (100ms cadence) was needed to catch
the right moment.

**2. Result -- xemu renders the Ubisoft logo completely cleanly:**
screenshot `tools/debug/xemu_burst_update260/burst035.png` (~3.5s after
the window appears) shows the complete logo: swirl icon smooth with no
noise whatsoever, wordmark **"UBISOFT™" complete and sharply legible, all
seven letters plus the trademark symbol, no cutoff, no vertical glitch
bar**. This proves beyond doubt that Update 260's documented noise
artifacts and text truncation are a recomp-specific bug, not a property
of the original data.

**3. First semantic difference -- found directly from recomp's own
diagnostics, no xemu-side tracing needed:** `nv2a_pb_exec.c` already
maintains a frequency-ranked table of unhandled pushbuffer methods
(`s_unhandled[]`, comment: "which things dominate, because that is the
order to implement them in"). Read directly via CDB
(`dt`/`dd scda_recomp!s_unhandled`, `s_unhandled_count=204` distinct
method values, `unhandled_total=2419` hits total): by far the most
frequent are **method 0x100 (307 hits)**, **0x310 (220)**, **0x1d70
(218)**, **0x110 (154)**, plus a cluster at **0x180-0x1a8** (1-3 hits
each: 0x180, 0x184, 0x188, 0x18c, 0x190, 0x194, 0x198, 0x19c, 0x1a0,
0x1a4, 0x1a8) and three exactly-equal hit counts at **0x181c/0x1820/
0x1824 (110 each)** -- suspiciously close to `NV097_INLINE_ARRAY`
(0x1818) and nearly identical to the draw count (111).

**The 0x180-0x1a8 cluster matches the well-known
`NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_*` method family exactly** (NOTIFIES/A/B/STATE/
COLOR/ZETA/VERTEX_A/VERTEX_B/SEMAPHORE/REPORT, each set once up front --
consistent with the low per-method hit counts). **This is not a new
discovery; it is an already-documented, deliberately unimplemented gap in
the code itself:** the comment at `NV097_SET_SURFACE_COLOR_OFFSET`
(`nv2a_pb_exec.c` around line 47-60) reads: *"NV097_SET_SURFACE_COLOR_OFFSET
is an offset within the colour DMA object, not a guest virtual address,
and this executor has always used it as one. [...] Getting the address
right needs the DMA object base this ignores
(NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_COLOR); until that exists, writing nothing is
strictly better than writing over the guest."* This mechanically explains
why textures/vertex data could be misaddressed: every subsequent "offset"
method value (surface, texture, vertex-array offset) gets treated as a
raw guest VA instead of being correctly resolved relative to the base of
whichever DMA object is actually bound -- exactly the kind of mismatch
that produces texture/geometry noise and misaddressed vertex data (such
as the truncated "T").

**Proven:** (a) xemu renders the identical Ubisoft logo completely
correctly -- the recomp artifacts are a bug, not a property of the
original data. (b) `NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_*` is demonstrably never
handled by this executor (zero handler cases in the code, 1-3 hits per
method in `s_unhandled[]`, exactly where expected in the pushbuffer).
(c) this gap is already documented in the code itself as the cause of
misresolved offset methods, not merely suspected.

**Refuted:** nothing new refuted this round -- this round confirms and
sharpens Update 260's characterization.

**Open / exact next test:** (1) implement `NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_*`:
track the bound DMA object handle per context slot (NOTIFIES/A/B/COLOR/
ZETA/VERTEX_A/VERTEX_B/SEMAPHORE/REPORT) in `s_gpu`; then change the
`dma_resolve()` call sites for `SET_SURFACE_COLOR_OFFSET`,
`SET_TEXTURE_OFFSET`, and the vertex-array offsets to resolve relative to
the base of whichever object is actually bound, instead of assuming the
raw guest VA -- exactly what the existing code comment names as missing.
(2) after implementing, take the Ubisoft-logo screenshot again via
`RECOMP_FB_DUMP` and compare against `xemu_burst_update260/burst035.png`
-- do the noise and text truncation disappear? (3) if not fully fixed:
separately identify the second frequency spike (method 0x100 with 307
hits and 0x110 with 154, well above a once-per-frame binding --
potentially a frequently-called-per-draw-or-per-vertex, still-unknown
Kelvin method pair). (4) Update 259b's `nonzero_draws=0`/sentinel anomaly
remains open but is now secondary to this finding.

## Update 261: reconstructed SCDA's real DMA handle bindings live from xemu
## -- base=0 is empirically CONFIRMED correct for color/texture, not
## refuted. The SET_CONTEXT_DMA_* hypothesis does not explain the noise.

Task: observe SCDA's real DMA binding during the Ubisoft logo sequence via
xemu/GDB (which SET_CONTEXT_DMA_* methods, which handles, which
objects/bases, which offsets), reconstruct at least one concrete draw
numerically, and only then implement a minimal, observation-based
resolver -- no blanket "base is always 0" assumption.

**1. New methodology -- decoding xemu's live pushbuffer via GDB:** xemu
launched with `-s -S`, connected over the GDB remote protocol (Python,
raw `socket`, RSP packets), run for ~3.3s (the Ubisoft logo window), then
halted via break-in (`0x03` + a `?` query). `DMA_PUT`/`DMA_GET` (the
physical pushbuffer cursor registers) read at guest VA
`0xFD800040`/`0xFD800044` (`XBOX_NV2A_BASE + NV2A_USER_DMA_PUT/GET`, the
same constants `xbox_memory_layout.c` already uses), then a 32KB window
before `PUT` read as guest VA `0x80000000 | physical` and decoded with the
exact same algorithm as `nv2a_pb_scan.c` (subchannel/method/count header,
non-increment bit). **Result: recomp's own scanner decode logic is
correct** -- the real pushbuffer layout matches the expected encoding
exactly.

**2. Real DMA bindings found for the drawing channel (subch=0):**
`NOTIFIES=0x2, DMA_A=0x3, DMA_B=0x3, STATE=0x4, COLOR=0x9, ZETA=0xA,
VERTEX_A=0x3, VERTEX_B=0x3, SEMAPHORE=0x8, REPORT=0xC`. **Notable side
finding:** SCDA also binds the same Kelvin 3D class on subchannels 1, 2,
and 3 with their own (partly different) handles -- the existing "3D class
only lives on subchannel 0" assumption (`nv2a_pb_exec.c` around line 1955)
does not hold for the BINDINGS, even though the actually-executed draws/
textures/vertex data in this window all ran through subchannel 0.
Subchannel 5 repeatedly carries method 0x310 with timestamp-like
increasing values (0x7277AC3C, 0x7277B644, ...) -- likely a sync/vblank
channel, not render-relevant, not pursued further.

**3. DMA object handles resolved via RAMHT/PRAMIN (empirically, not
assumed):** `PRAMIN` sits at MMIO offset `0x00700000` within the 16MB
register aperture (guest VA `0xFD700000`), matching the classic NV04/
nouveau layout -- confirmed by blindly searching for the handle values as
raw dwords in that window (a clean, regular 8-byte stride starting at
`PRAMIN+0x10010`). Each hash entry: `[handle][context]`,
`context=0x8000IIII` with `instance = IIII*16`. For handle 0x9 (COLOR):
`instance=0x11150` -> object `{class/flags=0x0000B03D, limit=0x07FFAFFF}`.
Handles 0x2/0x3/0x4/0x9/0xA/0xB/0xC all show the same pattern: class
`0x3D` (the classic linear NV DMA class) with a very large limit (~127MB)
-- **structurally a flat object spanning essentially all of physical
memory, with no separate nonzero base visible in the format read.**

**4. Empirical cross-check -- base=0 is already correct:** direct memory
reads in xemu (during the same halted session) at guest VA
`0x80000000 | offset` for both the color surface (`0x036DC000`/
`0x03808000`, handle 0x9) and the stage-0 texture (`0x035B0000`, handle
0x3): **the center of each shows plausible, consistently purple-toned
pixel values** (e.g. `91 40 57 00`), matching the visible swirl color. An
initial check at the image corner (row 0) wrongly showed nothing but
zeros -- that is simply the legitimately black background there, not
evidence of a wrong address (a methodology mistake, corrected here). A
broad scan for bright pixel blocks between physical `0x00000000` and
`0x08000000` found the expected bright regions exactly where the color
surfaces were already identified (`0x03300000`-`0x03580000`), nowhere
else.

**5. The highest-frequency unhandled methods (0x100 x307, 0x110 x154)
carry `param=0` throughout:** extracted directly from the capture -- a
recurring `0x100, 0x100, 0x110` pattern (always zero payload) before
essentially every draw, likely a cache-flush/sync pair with no data that
could be wrong. Not a plausible candidate for the visible defects.

**Proven:** (a) the DMA handle->object->base resolution for the tested
handles (color, texture) is unambiguous and empirically confirmed:
base=0, exactly what the existing (naive) recomp implementation already
assumes. (b) the highest-frequency unhandled methods (0x100/0x110) carry
no payload and are unlikely causes.

**Refuted:** Update 260b's leading candidate -- that missing
`NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_*` resolution explains the noise/text-truncation
artifacts. For the specific resources actually checked (color surface,
stage-0 texture), the already-existing naive resolution (offset = base 0
+ parameter) demonstrably produces correct, plausible image data. **This
code-documented gap is real (handles bind across multiple subchannels,
the generic handling is missing), but it is not the cause of THIS visible
defect.**

**Open / exact next test:** the actual semantic difference is still not

that are genuinely translated-but-unimplemented with real payloads right

`SET_BEGIN_END`) -- names not yet identified; check whether one of these

modulation that would explain visible noise if missing. (2) read the
